title: Step 1 · Biochemistry, Molecular Biology, Genetics & Immunology
meta: Exam: Step 1 · Molecular & cell biology, metabolism, nutrition, inborn errors, medical genetics, lab techniques, immunology · Approx study time: 5–6 days (notes) + 1 day (questions)

sections.heading: Overview
sections.html:
From NEET PG to USMLE

  • Mechanism over memory. NEET PG asks "enzyme deficient in X?" USMLE asks the 2nd/3rd step: "Which substance is increased in the urine?", "Which dietary change helps?", "Why does giving glucose worsen this patient?" Learn every disorder as block → what piles up upstream → what is missing downstream → how the body compensates.
  • Vignette decoding. US stems rarely name the disease. Ethnicity (Ashkenazi Jewish, Northern European), age at onset, odor of urine, response to fasting, and lab clues (low BUN, orotic acid, hypoketotic hypoglycemia) are the giveaways.
  • Units. US labs use mg/dL for glucose (70–100 fasting; 18 mg/dL ≈ 1 mmol/L), cholesterol (mg/dL; 38.7 mg/dL ≈ 1 mmol/L) and BUN (7–20 mg/dL), not mmol/L.
  • US drug names. Enzyme replacement therapies and biologics are tested by generic name (imiglucerase, agalsidase beta, alglucosidase alfa, eculizumab, abatacept, belatacept, tacrolimus). Learn the suffix logic (-mab, -cept, -kinra).
  • Vaccines differ. The US does not give BCG routinely and uses only inactivated polio vaccine (IPV). A BCG-vaccinated adult from India may have a false-positive tuberculin skin test — US practice prefers an interferon-γ release assay (IGRA). This is a personal issue for you too (US residency onboarding).
  • Ethics of genetics. Newborn screening is state-mandated in the US; carrier screening for CF and SMA (and hemoglobinopathies when indicated) is offered to all pregnant patients (ACOG). GINA (Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act) protects against discrimination in health insurance and employment — not life/long-term care insurance.

sections.heading: 1. Nucleotides & DNA replication
sections.html:
Purines (A, G) have two rings; pyrimidines (C, T, U) have one. G–C pairs share 3 hydrogen bonds (higher melting temperature) vs 2 for A–T. Deamination of cytosine yields uracil (repaired by base excision repair); thymine is 5-methyluracil (methyl donor: N5,N10-methylene-THF via thymidylate synthase). Nucleoside = base + sugar; nucleotide = base + sugar + phosphate. DNA is antiparallel and synthesized only 5'→3'; the 3'-OH attacks the incoming nucleotide's α-phosphate.

Replication componentFunctionClinical / drug link
HelicaseUnwinds at replication fork (ATP)Bloom (BLM) and Werner (WRN) helicase defects → genomic instability
Single-stranded binding proteinsPrevent re-annealing—
Topoisomerase INicks one strand to relieve supercoilsIrinotecan, topotecan
Topoisomerase II (DNA gyrase/topo IV in bacteria)Cuts both strands, relieves supercoilsEtoposide, doxorubicin (human); fluoroquinolones (bacterial)

Mutation types: silent (same amino acid; often 3rd-position wobble), missense (sickle cell: Glu6Val in β-globin), nonsense (premature stop → truncated, often degraded by nonsense-mediated decay), frameshift (insertion/deletion not multiple of 3; Duchenne), in-frame deletion (Becker — milder), splice-site (some β-thalassemias), and trinucleotide repeat expansion.

DNA repair

PathwayDamage repairedKey enzymesDisease when defective
Nucleotide excision repair (NER)Bulky helix-distorting lesions, UV pyrimidine (thymine) dimersEndonucleases excise oligonucleotide; pol δ/ε; ligase (G1 phase)Xeroderma pigmentosum (AR): extreme photosensitivity, freckling in childhood, early BCC/SCC/melanoma
Base excision repair (BER)Single altered base (deamination, oxidation, depurination)Glycosylase removes base → AP endonuclease → lyase → pol β → ligase (all cell cycle)MUTYH-associated polyposis (AR)
Mismatch repair (MMR)Mispaired bases on newly synthesized strand (G2)MSH2, MSH6, MLH1, PMS2Lynch syndrome (HNPCC, AD): microsatellite instability; right-sided colon, endometrial, ovarian, gastric, urothelial cancers
Nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ)Double-strand breaks, no template (error-prone)Ku, DNA-PKcs, Artemis, ligase IVSome SCID (Artemis, DNA-PKcs) — also needed for V(D)J recombination; ataxia-telangiectasia (ATM is the DSB sensor)

High-yield: Two sun-induced vignettes — a child with freckles and SCC on the face (XP, NER defect) vs. a young adult with colon cancer and microsatellite instability (Lynch, MMR defect). Ataxia-telangiectasia: cerebellar ataxia + spider angiomas + IgA deficiency + ↑AFP + radiosensitivity (avoid unnecessary X-rays/CT) + lymphoma.

sections.heading: 2. Transcription, RNA processing & translation
sections.html:
Promoter (TATA box ~25 bp and CAAT box ~75 bp upstream) binds RNA polymerase and general transcription factors; mutation → ↓ transcription. Enhancers/silencers act at a distance through DNA looping. Eukaryotic genes are monocistronic; prokaryotic operons are polycistronic (lac operon: repressor released by allolactose; CAP-cAMP enhances when glucose is low).

RNA polymeraseMakesLocationInhibitor
RNA pol IrRNA (28S, 18S, 5.8S)Nucleolus—
RNA pol IImRNA (hnRNA), most snRNA, miRNANucleusα-amanitin (Amanita phalloides → severe hepatotoxicity)
RNA pol IIItRNA, 5S rRNANucleusHigh-dose α-amanitin
Prokaryotic RNA pol (single, σ factor)All RNACytoplasmRifampin; actinomycin D intercalates in both

Processing of pre-mRNA (nucleus): 5' 7-methylguanosine cap; 3' poly-A tail (signal AAUAAA; no template needed); splicing by spliceosome (snRNPs + pre-mRNA; lariat intermediate). Autoantibodies: anti-Smith (snRNP core; highly specific for SLE) and anti-U1 RNP (mixed connective tissue disease). Alternative splicing produces protein variety. miRNA base-pairs with 3'-UTR to silence translation or degrade mRNA. siRNA-based drugs (inclisiran targets PCSK9 mRNA; patisiran targets transthyretin mRNA).

tRNA: 3' CCA end binds amino acid; anticodon reads mRNA (wobble at 3rd codon position). Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase uses ATP and is the fidelity checkpoint ("charging").

StepEukaryote (80S = 40S + 60S)Prokaryote (70S = 30S + 50S)Toxins / drugs
InitiationMet-tRNA at AUG; eIFs; GTPfMet (N-formylmethionine — a neutrophil chemoattractant); Shine-DalgarnoLinezolid (50S, blocks initiation complex); aminoglycosides (30S, misreading)
ElongationA site (aminoacyl) → P site (peptidyl) → E site (exit); peptidyl transferase is rRNA (ribozyme); EF-2 translocation (GTP)Same; EF-GDiphtheria toxin & Pseudomonas exotoxin A ADP-ribosylate EF-2; Shiga toxin & ricin cleave 28S rRNA of 60S; tetracyclines (A site), chloramphenicol (peptidyl transferase), macrolides/clindamycin (translocation)
TerminationStop codon (UAA, UAG, UGA) → release factorSame—

Energy: ATP for tRNA charging; GTP for initiation, tRNA binding (EF-1/EF-Tu) and translocation. Post-translational: trimming of signal peptides/propeptides; phosphorylation, glycosylation, hydroxylation, methylation, acetylation, ubiquitination (proteasomal degradation; UBE3A in Angelman; ubiquitin-proteasome defects in Parkinson disease). Chaperones (heat shock proteins) assist folding; misfolded CFTR (F508del) is retained in the ER and degraded.

Cell cycle

G1 → S (DNA synthesis) → G2 → M. G1/S checkpoint: Rb (hypophosphorylated Rb binds E2F; CDK4/6–cyclin D phosphorylates Rb → releases E2F) and p53 (induces p21 → inhibits CDKs; arrests cells with DNA damage; triggers apoptosis via BAX). HPV E7 binds Rb, E6 degrades p53. CDK4/6 inhibitors (palbociclib) in HR+ breast cancer. Permanent cells (neurons, cardiomyocytes, skeletal muscle, RBCs) stay in G0; stable (hepatocytes, PCT cells) re-enter G1 when stimulated; labile (marrow, gut crypts, skin basal layer, hair follicles) cycle continually — hence chemotherapy toxicity sites.

Collagen synthesis — six steps, six diseases

Step (location)RequirementDefect
1. Translation of α chains (Gly-X-Y repeats) — RERGlycine every 3rd residue (smallest amino acid fits inside helix)Osteogenesis imperfecta: glycine substitutions are severe (dominant-negative)
2. Hydroxylation of proline & lysine — RERVitamin C, Fe²⁺, O₂, α-ketoglutarate (prolyl/lysyl hydroxylase)Scurvy: swollen bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhage, corkscrew hairs, poor wound healing; kyphoscoliotic EDS (lysyl hydroxylase)
3. Glycosylation of hydroxylysine; triple helix (procollagen) — RERDisulfide bonds at C-terminal propeptidesOI type I (↓ amount of normal type I collagen; COL1A1/COL1A2)
4. Exocytosis of procollagen——
5. Cleavage of N- and C-terminal propeptides → tropocollagen — extracellularProcollagen peptidasesSome EDS (dermatosparaxis type)
6. Covalent cross-linking of lysine–hydroxylysine — extracellularLysyl oxidase (copper)Menkes disease (ATP7A, XLR): brittle "kinky" hair, hypotonia, seizures, growth failure, ↓ serum copper & ceruloplasmin; vascular EDS (type III collagen, COL3A1)

Collagen types: I bone, skin, tendon, dentin, cornea, late wound repair (OI); II cartilage, vitreous, nucleus pulposus; III skin, vessels, uterus, granulation tissue (vascular EDS — arterial/uterine/bowel rupture); IV basement membrane (Alport — α3/α4/α5, hearing loss + hematuria + lens problems; Goodpasture — antibodies to α3 NC1 domain). OI (usually AD): multiple fractures with minimal trauma, blue sclerae (thin collagen shows choroid), conductive hearing loss, dentinogenesis imperfecta — distinguish from child abuse. Elastin: rich in Gly/Pro/Lys; cross-linked by lysyl oxidase; degraded by elastase (α1-antitrypsin inhibits). Marfan (FBN1, chromosome 15, AD): tall, arachnodactyly, upward/temporal lens dislocation, aortic root dilation/dissection, mitral valve prolapse. Williams syndrome: elastin deletion (supravalvular aortic stenosis).

Exam trap: Lens dislocation upward/temporal with normal intelligence = Marfan (fibrillin); downward/nasal with intellectual disability and thromboses = homocystinuria (cystathionine β-synthase). Both are "marfanoid."

sections.heading: 5. Medical genetics
sections.html:
Core terms (USMLE loves these as answer choices)

TermMeaningExample
CodominanceBoth alleles expressedABO blood group AB; α1-antitrypsin alleles
Variable expressivitySame genotype, different severityNF1 (café-au-lait spots only vs. plexiform neurofibromas)
Incomplete penetranceNot all with mutant genotype show the phenotypeBRCA1 carriers who never develop cancer
PleiotropyOne gene → many unrelated phenotypic effectsPKU (ID, fair skin, musty odor); Marfan
AnticipationEarlier onset/greater severity in successive generationsTrinucleotide repeat disorders
Loss of heterozygositySecond allele lost in tumor suppressor ("two-hit")Retinoblastoma (RB1), Li-Fraumeni (TP53)
Dominant negativeMutant protein blocks the normal oneOI glycine substitutions; p53 mutants
Linkage disequilibriumAlleles at two loci occur together more than expected by chance (population-specific)HLA haplotypes
MosaicismGenetically distinct cell lines in one person. Somatic: McCune-Albright (GNAS; café-au-lait with ragged "coast of Maine" border, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, precocious puberty). Germline (gonadal): affected siblings born to unaffected parents with an "AD" disease—
Locus heterogeneityMutations at different loci → same phenotypeAlbinism, retinitis pigmentosa
Allelic heterogeneityDifferent mutations at the same locus → same phenotypeβ-thalassemia, CF
HeteroplasmyMixture of normal and mutant mtDNA in a cell → variable expression of mitochondrial diseaseMELAS, LHON
Uniparental disomy (UPD)Both homologs from one parent (heterodisomy = meiosis I error; isodisomy = meiosis II error/duplication); euploidPrader-Willi (maternal UPD 15)

Hardy-Weinberg

For alleles p (normal) and q (mutant): p + q = 1 and p² + 2pq + q² = 1. Disease prevalence (AR) = q²; carrier frequency = 2pq ≈ 2q when q is small. For X-linked recessive: male prevalence = q; female prevalence = q². Assumptions: large population, random mating, no mutation, no selection, no migration.

Scenario (AR disease, prevalence 1/2500)WorkingAnswer
Carrier frequency in populationq = 1/50; 2pq ≈ 2 × 1/501/25
Unaffected sibling of an affected person is a carrierOf the 3 unaffected genotypes (AA, Aa, aA), 2 are carriers2/3
That sibling + a random partner have an affected child2/3 × 1/25 × 1/41/150
Two known carriers: child is affected / carrier / unaffected non-carrierPunnett square1/4 / 1/2 / 1/4

Modes of inheritance

[[figure:ch01-fig01]]
ModePedigree cluesHigh-yield diseases
Autosomal dominantEvery generation; male-to-male transmission; 50% risk to offspring of heterozygote. Often structural proteins/receptors; late onsetADPKD (PKD1 chr16, PKD2), FAP (APC, 5q), familial hypercholesterolemia (LDLR), hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, hereditary spherocytosis, Huntington (4p), Li-Fraumeni (TP53), Marfan (FBN1), MEN1/MEN2 (RET), myotonic dystrophy, NF1 (17q), NF2 (22q), tuberous sclerosis (TSC1/2), von Hippel-Lindau (3p), achondroplasia (FGFR3 gain-of-function; ↑ paternal age; most cases de novo), BRCA1/2, Lynch, acute intermittent porphyria, von Willebrand (most types)
Autosomal recessiveSkips generations; both sexes; consanguinity; 25% risk for carrier couples. Usually enzyme deficiencies; earlier onsetAlbinism, ARPKD, CF (CFTR chr7), Friedreich ataxia, glycogen storage diseases, hemochromatosis (HFE C282Y), Kartagener, most lysosomal storage diseases, PKU, sickle cell, thalassemias, Wilson (ATP7B, chr13), mucopolysaccharidoses (except Hunter), 21-hydroxylase deficiency, SMA (SMN1)
X-linked recessiveMostly males; no male-to-male transmission; carrier mother → 50% sons affected; affected father → all daughters carriers. Females affected by skewed lyonization or TurnerBruton agammaglobulinemia, Wiskott-Aldrich, Fabry, G6PD deficiency, ocular albinism, Lesch-Nyhan, Duchenne/Becker, Hunter, hemophilia A/B, OTC deficiency, X-linked SCID (IL2RG), CGD (CYBB form, ~2/3 of cases), Menkes
X-linked dominantAffected father → all daughters, no sons; affected mother → 50% of all childrenHypophosphatemic rickets (PHEX; ↑ FGF23 → phosphate wasting; burosumab treats), fragile X (complex), Rett (MECP2; nearly all girls; regression at 1–4 y, hand-wringing), Alport (most common form)
MitochondrialMaternal transmission only — affected mother → all children may be affected (variable severity: heteroplasmy); affected father → noneMELAS (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, stroke-like episodes), MERRF (myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fibers), LHON (Leber hereditary optic neuropathy; acute bilateral vision loss in young men). Muscle biopsy: ragged-red fibers (Gomori trichrome)
High-yield: Duchenne = frameshift deletion of dystrophin (Xp21; largest human gene) → Gowers sign by age 3–5, calf pseudohypertrophy (fibrofatty replacement), ↑ CK, dilated cardiomyopathy (leading cause of death with respiratory failure); diagnose with genetic testing (deletion/duplication analysis). Becker = in-frame deletion, later onset. Treatment: glucocorticoids (prednisone/deflazacort); exon-skipping antisense oligonucleotides for selected deletions.

Cystic fibrosis

CFTR (chr 7) is an ATP-gated Cl⁻ channel. In lungs/GI it secretes Cl⁻ (defect → thick secretions, ↑ Na⁺/water reabsorption via ENaC); in sweat ducts it reabsorbs Cl⁻ (defect → ↑ sweat Cl⁻ ≥60 mmol/L). Most common mutation F508del (Phe508del) = misfolding → ER retention → proteasome degradation. Presents with meconium ileus, failure to thrive, steatorrhea and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, recurrent S. aureus (early) then Pseudomonas (later) pneumonia, bronchiectasis, nasal polyps, digital clubbing, male infertility (congenital bilateral absence of vas deferens; azoospermia), CF-related diabetes. Newborn screen: ↑ immunoreactive trypsinogen → confirm with sweat chloride. Modulators: ivacaftor (potentiator; gating mutations like G551D); elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (correctors + potentiator; ≥1 F508del allele); a once-daily vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor combination was FDA-approved in Dec 2024.

Trinucleotide repeat disorders

DiseaseRepeat / geneInheritance; anticipation viaFeatures
HuntingtonCAG — HTT (chr 4)AD; expansion in spermatogenesis (paternal)Chorea, depression, dementia, caudate atrophy (↑ dopamine, ↓ GABA & ACh); onset 30s–50s
Myotonic dystrophy type 1CTG — DMPK (chr 19)AD; maternal (congenital form)Myotonia (can't release grip), distal weakness, frontal balding, cataracts, testicular atrophy, arrhythmias (conduction block), insulin resistance
Fragile XCGG — FMR1 (Xq27.3); hypermethylation silences geneX-linked; expansion in oogenesis (premutation 55–200 → full >200)Most common inherited cause of ID; long face, large jaw, large everted ears, macroorchidism (post-pubertal), MVP, autism, hypermobility. Premutation carriers: primary ovarian insufficiency (women), FXTAS (tremor/ataxia in older men)
Friedreich ataxiaGAA — frataxin (FXN, chr 9; intronic)ARMitochondrial iron overload; onset in adolescence: gait ataxia, loss of DTRs, vibration/proprioception loss, Babinski, kyphoscoliosis, pes cavus, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (leading cause of death), diabetes. Omaveloxolone (Nrf2 activator) approved 2023

Repeat pairing to memorize: fragile X = CGG, Huntington = CAG, myotonic = CTG, Friedreich = GAA. Spinocerebellar ataxias are also CAG (polyglutamine) disorders. Coding-region CAG repeats cause toxic gain of function; non-coding repeats (CGG, GAA, CTG) act by silencing or RNA toxicity.

Genomic imprinting

One allele is silenced by methylation depending on the parent of origin. On 15q11–q13: paternal copy of SNRPN and related genes is normally active; maternal UBE3A is the only active copy in neurons.

SyndromeMissing expressionMechanisms (frequency)Features
Prader-WilliPaternal 15q11–13 genesPaternal deletion (~70%), maternal UPD (~25%), imprinting center defectNeonatal hypotonia & poor feeding → later hyperphagia & obesity, ID, hypogonadism (hypogonadotropic), short stature, small hands/feet, behavioral problems. Methylation testing is the first-line test (detects all mechanisms)
AngelmanMaternal UBE3AMaternal deletion (~70%), paternal UPD (~5%), UBE3A mutation, imprinting defectSevere ID, seizures, ataxia, absent speech, inappropriate laughter ("happy puppet")
Beckwith-WiedemannOverexpression of IGF2 (chr 11p15)Paternal UPD, imprinting errorsMacrosomia, macroglossia, hemihypertrophy, omphalocele, neonatal hypoglycemia; ↑ Wilms tumor & hepatoblastoma (screen with abdominal US and AFP)

Chromosomal disorders

DisorderCauseKey findingsPrenatal screen
Down (trisomy 21)~95% meiotic nondisjunction (maternal meiosis I; ↑ maternal age); ~4% Robertsonian translocation (e.g., t(14;21) — recurrence risk higher, test parents); ~1% mosaicFlat facies, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, single palmar crease, sandal gap, hypotonia, ID; endocardial cushion defects (AV septal defect), duodenal atresia ("double bubble"), Hirschsprung; ALL & AML (acute megakaryoblastic <5 y); early Alzheimer (APP on chr 21); hypothyroidism; atlantoaxial instability; celiac disease1st trimester: ↓ PAPP-A, ↑ free β-hCG, ↑ nuchal translucency. Quad: ↓ AFP, ↑ hCG, ↓ estriol, ↑ inhibin A. Cell-free DNA = most sensitive screen; confirm with CVS/amniocentesis

Turner (45,X)Usually paternal sex-chromosome loss; not related to maternal age; mosaics commonShort stature (SHOX), webbed neck, lymphedema of hands/feet at birth, shield chest, bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation, horseshoe kidney, streak ovaries → primary amenorrhea, ↑ FSH/LH, ↓ estrogen; normal intelligence; cystic hygroma in utero. Y material present → gonadectomy (gonadoblastoma risk)—
Klinefelter (47,XXY)Nondisjunction (either parent)Tall, eunuchoid proportions, gynecomastia, small firm testes, azoospermia/infertility, ↓ testosterone, ↑ FSH & LH, ↓ inhibin B; Barr body present; ↑ breast cancer risk—
47,XYYPaternal meiosis II nondisjunctionTall, severe acne, normal fertility; ↑ ADHD/autism risk—
22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge / velocardiofacial)Microdeletion (usually de novo; AD if inherited) → aberrant 3rd & 4th pharyngeal pouch developmentCATCH-22: Cardiac (truncus arteriosus, tetralogy, interrupted aortic arch), Abnormal facies, Thymic hypoplasia (T-cell deficiency), Cleft palate, Hypocalcemia (parathyroid aplasia); later psychiatric illness (schizophrenia)FISH or chromosomal microarray
Williams7q11.23 microdeletion (includes elastin)"Elfin" facies, extreme friendliness, ID with good verbal skills, hypercalcemia, supravalvular aortic stenosis—
Cri-du-chat5p deletionHigh-pitched cat-like cry, microcephaly, ID, VSD—

Robertsonian translocation: fusion of long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes (13, 14, 15, 21, 22). Balanced carriers are phenotypically normal but have recurrent miscarriage and unbalanced offspring; a 45,XX,t(14;21) mother has a much higher recurrence risk for Down syndrome than the age-related baseline; a t(21;21) carrier has ~100% risk of trisomy 21 offspring.

Exam trap: "No deletion on FISH" does not exclude Prader-Willi — maternal UPD shows two chromosome 15s (both maternal). The methylation study catches deletion, UPD and imprinting-center defects.

Causes: alcoholism, pregnancy, methotrexate, trimethoprim, phenytoin. Neural tube defect prevention: 0.4 mg/day for all women capable of pregnancy (USPSTF); 4 mg/day if prior NTDCan mask B12 deficiency hematologically
B12 cobalaminMethionine synthase (homocysteine → methionine) and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA)Megaloblastic anemia + subacute combined degeneration (dorsal columns, lateral corticospinal tracts, peripheral nerves); ↑ homocysteine and ↑ MMA. Causes: pernicious anemia (anti-IF/anti-parietal cell), vegan diet, ileal resection/Crohn, Diphyllobothrium latum, metformin, PPIs, nitrous oxideStores last years
C ascorbateProlyl/lysyl hydroxylation; dopamine β-hydroxylase; keeps iron Fe²⁺ (↑ absorption)ScurvyOxalate stones; iron overload in hemochromatosis

Malnutrition: kwashiorkor = protein deficiency with adequate calories → edema (↓ oncotic pressure), fatty liver (↓ apolipoprotein synthesis), skin lesions, flaky-paint dermatosis; marasmus = total calorie deficiency → muscle and fat wasting, no edema. Ethanol metabolism: alcohol dehydrogenase (zero-order kinetics) and aldehyde dehydrogenase both generate NADH → ↑ NADH/NAD⁺ ratio → pyruvate → lactate, OAA → malate (↓ gluconeogenesis → fasting hypoglycemia), DHAP → glycerol-3-P (↑ TG synthesis → steatosis), ↓ β-oxidation, ↑ ketogenesis (β-hydroxybutyrate predominates). Fomepizole inhibits ADH (methanol, ethylene glycol); disulfiram inhibits aldehyde DH (metronidazole, some cephalosporins cause disulfiram-like reactions).

sections.heading: 7. Metabolism — the integrated map
sections.html:
[[figure:ch01-fig02]]

TCA cycleIsocitrate dehydrogenaseADPATP, NADHMitochondria

HMP shuntG6PDNADP⁺NADPHCytosol

De novo purine synthesisGlutamine-PRPP amidotransferase—AMP, IMP, GMPCytosol

Fatty acid synthesisAcetyl-CoA carboxylase (biotin)Insulin, citrateGlucagon, palmitoyl-CoACytosol
Fatty acid oxidationCarnitine palmitoyltransferase I—Malonyl-CoAMitochondria
KetogenesisHMG-CoA synthase——Liver mitochondria
Cholesterol synthesisHMG-CoA reductaseInsulin, thyroxine, estrogenGlucagon, cholesterol, oxysterols (statins)Cytosol/ER
Heme synthesisALA synthase (B6)—Heme, glucoseMitochondria + cytosol

ATP yield: aerobic oxidation of glucose ≈ 32 ATP (malate-aspartate shuttle — heart, liver) or 30 ATP (glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle — skeletal muscle, brain); anaerobic glycolysis = 2 ATP. RBCs have no mitochondria → glycolysis only. Activated carriers: ATP (phosphoryl), NADH/NADPH/FADH₂ (electrons), CoA & lipoamide (acyl), biotin (CO₂), THF (1-carbon), SAM (methyl — needs ATP + methionine), TPP (aldehydes). NAD⁺ is used in catabolism; NADPH in anabolism, respiratory burst, glutathione reduction and cytochrome P450.

Glycolysis & its regulation

Hexokinase (most tissues): low Km (high affinity), low Vmax, inhibited by G6P. Glucokinase (liver, pancreatic β cells): high Km, high Vmax, induced by insulin, regulated by glucokinase regulatory protein (sequestered in nucleus by F6P); heterozygous loss → MODY2 (mild stable fasting hyperglycemia). Irreversible steps: hexokinase/glucokinase, PFK-1, pyruvate kinase (activated by F1,6-BP — feed-forward; inhibited by ATP, alanine and, in liver, glucagon-mediated phosphorylation).

Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate is the hormonal switch. PFK-2 and FBPase-2 are one bifunctional enzyme. Fed: insulin → ↓ cAMP → dephosphorylated enzyme → PFK-2 active → ↑ F2,6-BP → ↑ PFK-1 (glycolysis) and ↓ FBPase-1. Fasting: glucagon → ↑ cAMP → PKA phosphorylates → FBPase-2 active → ↓ F2,6-BP → gluconeogenesis. (Muscle isoform is not regulated by PKA in the same way.)

RBC enzyme deficiencyMechanismSmear / labTrigger
G6PD deficiency (XLR; common in South Asia, Africa, Mediterranean)↓ NADPH → ↓ reduced glutathione → oxidant damage → Hb precipitatesHeinz bodies (supravital stain), bite cells; episodic intravascular + extravascular hemolysis. Enzyme level may be falsely normal during acute hemolysis (young RBCs) → retest at 2–3 monthsFava beans, infection (most common), sulfonamides, dapsone, primaquine/tafenoquine, nitrofurantoin, rasburicase, methylene blue
Pyruvate kinase deficiency (AR)↓ ATP → rigid RBCs; upstream ↑ 2,3-BPG → right-shifted O₂ curve (better tolerated anemia)Echinocytes (burr cells); chronic extravascular hemolysis, splenomegaly, no Heinz bodiesChronic; mitapivat (PK activator) approved
High-yield (bridge): Before giving primaquine or tafenoquine for P. vivax/ovale radical cure — common in Indian practice — US guidelines require documented normal G6PD activity (tafenoquine requires quantitative testing).

Pyruvate, TCA cycle & electron transport

Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (mitochondrial; irreversible): needs B1 (TPP), B2 (FAD), B3 (NAD⁺), B5 (CoA), lipoic acid. Activated by ↑ NAD⁺/NADH, ADP, Ca²⁺ (exercise) and insulin; inhibited by its products (acetyl-CoA, NADH) and by PDH kinase. α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase uses the same cofactors. Arsenic inhibits lipoic acid (garlic breath, rice-water diarrhea, vomiting). PDH deficiency (most often X-linked PDHA1): neurologic defects, lactic acidosis, ↑ serum alanine starting in infancy. Treatment: ↑ intake of ketogenic nutrients — high-fat diet or ↑ lysine and leucine (the only purely ketogenic amino acids); some patients respond to thiamine.

Four fates of pyruvate: alanine (ALT, B6; carries amino groups to liver), oxaloacetate (pyruvate carboxylase, biotin; replenishes TCA intermediates/gluconeogenesis), acetyl-CoA (PDH), lactate (LDH, B3; RBCs, exercising muscle, Cori cycle).

TCA order: citrate → isocitrate → α-KG → succinyl-CoA → succinate → fumarate → malate → OAA. Per acetyl-CoA: 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP, 2 CO₂ (≈10 ATP). Succinyl-CoA also feeds heme synthesis and receives propionyl-CoA (odd-chain FAs, Val, Ile, Met, Thr) via methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (B12).

ETC siteInhibitorsEffect
Complex I (NADH DH)Rotenone, metformin (weak)Electron transport inhibitors: ↓ proton gradient, ↓ O₂ consumption, ↓ ATP
Complex III (cytochrome bc₁)Antimycin A—
Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase)Cyanide, CO, azide, H₂SCyanide: bitter almond odor, lactic acidosis, ↑ venous O₂ (bright red venous blood); Rx hydroxocobalamin
Complex V (ATP synthase)OligomycinATP synthase inhibitor: ↑ gradient, ↓ O₂ consumption, ↓ ATP
Uncouplers2,4-dinitrophenol (weight-loss supplements), aspirin overdose, thermogenin (UCP1) in brown fat↑ membrane permeability → ↓ gradient, ↑ O₂ consumption, ↓ ATP, ↑ heat (hyperthermia)

Gluconeogenesis

Irreversible bypass enzymes: pyruvate carboxylase (mitochondria; biotin; activated by acetyl-CoA), PEPCK (cytosol/mitochondria; GTP; induced by glucagon, cortisol), fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, glucose-6-phosphatase (ER; liver, kidney, intestinal epithelium — absent in muscle, so muscle glycogen cannot raise blood glucose). Substrates: lactate (Cori cycle), alanine, glycerol, odd-chain fatty acids (via propionyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA). Even-chain fatty acids cannot make net glucose (acetyl-CoA → 2 CO₂ in TCA). Deficiency of any key enzyme → fasting hypoglycemia.

HMP shunt (pentose phosphate pathway)

Oxidative phase (irreversible): G6PD makes NADPH (+ CO₂) — essential in RBCs, liver, adrenal cortex, lactating mammary glands, phagocytes. Non-oxidative phase (reversible): transketolase (TPP) interconverts sugars and makes ribose-5-P for nucleotides. NADPH uses: fatty acid/cholesterol/steroid synthesis, glutathione reductase, respiratory burst (NADPH oxidase), cytochrome P450, nitric oxide synthase.

Fructose, galactose & sorbitol

DisorderEnzymeFindingsTreatment
Essential fructosuria (AR)FructokinaseBenign; fructose in urine (reducing sugar; glucose oxidase dipstick negative)None
Hereditary fructose intolerance (AR)Aldolase BSymptoms when fruit, juice, honey or sucrose introduced (weaning): vomiting, hypoglycemia, jaundice, hepatomegaly, cirrhosis, Fanconi-like proximal tubulopathy. Mechanism: fructose-1-P accumulates and traps phosphate → ↓ ATP and ↓ Pi → inhibits glycogenolysis (phosphorylase) and gluconeogenesis; ↑ uric acidRemove fructose, sucrose, sorbitol
Galactokinase deficiency (AR)GalactokinaseGalactitol in lens → infantile cataracts; otherwise mild (no liver or brain toxicity)Remove galactose/lactose
Classic galactosemia (AR)Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT)Begins with milk feeding: vomiting, failure to thrive, jaundice, hepatomegaly, cataracts, ID, E. coli sepsis; ovarian insufficiency later. Toxic galactose-1-P and galactitolExclude galactose and lactose (soy formula) — newborn screening

Sorbitol (polyol) pathway: glucose → sorbitol (aldose reductase) → fructose (sorbitol dehydrogenase). Tissues with little or no sorbitol dehydrogenase (Schwann cells, retina, lens, kidney papillae) accumulate sorbitol in chronic hyperglycemia → osmotic damage (cataracts, retinopathy, neuropathy). Liver, ovaries, seminal vesicles have both enzymes. Lactase deficiency: ↓ brush-border lactase (age-related; common in Asian/African ancestry); osmotic diarrhea, ↑ breath hydrogen, ↓ stool pH; normal villi in primary form.

Glycogen metabolism & storage diseases

Glycogen: α-1,4 chains with α-1,6 branches. Synthesis: UDP-glucose + glycogenin; glycogen synthase (α-1,4) and branching enzyme (α-1,6). Breakdown: glycogen phosphorylase releases glucose-1-P (B6-dependent) until 4 residues from a branch → debranching enzyme (4-α-D-glucanotransferase moves 3 residues; α-1,6-glucosidase releases free glucose). Lysosomes degrade a small amount via acid α-glucosidase. Liver glucose-6-phosphatase releases glucose to blood.

TypeEnzymeHallmarks
I — von GierkeGlucose-6-phosphatase (Ia; Ib = G6P translocase with neutropenia)Severe fasting hypoglycemia (seizures 3–4 h after feeds), ↑↑ hepatic glycogen (hepatomegaly, enlarged kidneys), lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia (gout), hypertriglyceridemia, doll-like face, thin extremities; glucagon/epinephrine do not raise glucose. Rx: frequent feeds, uncooked cornstarch overnight, avoid fructose/galactose
II — PompeLysosomal acid α-1,4-glucosidase (acid maltase)Infantile: cardiomegaly/hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, hypotonia, macroglossia, exercise intolerance, early death; normal glucose. Rx: alglucosidase alfa / avalglucosidase alfa.
III — CoriDebranching enzyme (α-1,6-glucosidase)Milder von Gierke picture (hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly) but normal lactate (gluconeogenesis intact); abnormal short-branched glycogen ("limit dextrin"); myopathy in IIIa
IV — AndersenBranching enzymeAbnormal amylopectin-like glycogen → infantile cirrhosis, liver failure
V — McArdleMuscle glycogen phosphorylase (myophosphorylase)Painful cramps and myoglobinuria with intense exercise; "second wind" (↑ blood flow delivers glucose/FFAs); flat venous lactate with normal ammonia rise on forearm exercise test; ↑ CK; normal blood glucose
VI — HersHepatic glycogen phosphorylaseMild hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, ketosis

Lysosomal storage diseases

DiseaseEnzymeSubstrateInh.Distinguishing features

Niemann-Pick A/BSphingomyelinaseSphingomyelinARAshkenazi; neurodegeneration + hepatosplenomegaly + cherry-red spot + foam cells (lipid-laden macrophages). Type C = NPC1/2 cholesterol trafficking defect
Gaucher (most common)Glucocerebrosidase (β-glucosidase)GlucocerebrosideARType 1 (Ashkenazi, adult, non-neuronopathic): hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, bone crises, avascular necrosis of femoral head, Erlenmeyer-flask distal femurs; "crumpled tissue paper" macrophages; GBA variants ↑ Parkinson risk. Rx: imiglucerase/velaglucerase (ERT), eliglustat (substrate reduction)
Fabryα-Galactosidase ACeramide trihexoside (globotriaosylceramide, Gb3)XLRChildhood episodic burning pain in hands/feet, angiokeratomas (bathing-trunk area), hypohidrosis, cornea verticillata; later proteinuria/CKD, LVH, stroke. Rx: agalsidase beta/alfa; migalastat (oral chaperone for amenable variants)
KrabbeGalactocerebrosidaseGalactocerebroside, psychosineARPeripheral neuropathy, developmental regression, optic atrophy, globoid cells
Metachromatic leukodystrophyArylsulfatase ACerebroside sulfate (sulfatides)ARCentral & peripheral demyelination: ataxia, dementia; metachromatic granules; gene therapy (atidarsagene autotemcel) available
Hurler (MPS I)α-L-iduronidaseHeparan & dermatan sulfateARDevelopmental delay, gargoylism, airway obstruction, corneal clouding, hepatosplenomegaly, valve disease. Rx: laronidase, HSCT
Hunter (MPS II)Iduronate-2-sulfataseHeparan & dermatan sulfateXLRMilder Hurler + aggressive behavior, no corneal clouding. Rx: idursulfase.
Exam trap: Cherry-red spot appears in Tay-Sachs and Niemann-Pick (and central retinal artery occlusion in adults). Hepatosplenomegaly is the discriminator. Fabry and Hunter are the only X-linked ones — expect a boy.

Fatty acid metabolism & ketones

Synthesis (liver, adipose, lactating breast; cytosol): mitochondrial acetyl-CoA exits as citrate (citrate shuttle; ATP-citrate lyase — target of bempedoic acid) → acetyl-CoA carboxylase (biotin) → malonyl-CoA → fatty acid synthase (NADPH) → palmitate. Degradation (mitochondria): fatty acyl-CoA crosses inner membrane via carnitine shuttle (CPT I inhibited by malonyl-CoA — prevents futile cycling) → β-oxidation → acetyl-CoA (+ propionyl-CoA from odd chains).

DisorderDefectPresentation
Systemic primary carnitine deficiencyOCTN2 plasma-membrane carnitine transporter↓↓ free carnitine, hypoketotic hypoglycemia, dilated cardiomyopathy, weakness; Rx oral L-carnitine
MCAD deficiency (most common FAO disorder; newborn screen)Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenaseInfant/toddler with fasting or illness → vomiting, lethargy, seizures, hypoketotic hypoglycemia, hyperammonemia, liver dysfunction; ↑ C8 (octanoyl)carnitine, dicarboxylic aciduria; can mimic SIDS/Reye. Rx: avoid fasting, IV dextrose during illness
VLCAD / LCHADLong-chain β-oxidationCardiomyopathy, rhabdomyolysis; LCHAD fetus → maternal acute fatty liver of pregnancy/HELLP
CPT II deficiency (adult form)Carnitine palmitoyltransferase IIMyalgia/rhabdomyolysis after prolonged exercise, fasting or cold; normal lactate rise; no second wind

Ketone bodies: liver mitochondria make acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate from acetyl-CoA via HMG-CoA synthase/lyase when OAA is diverted to gluconeogenesis (fasting, DKA, alcoholism). Exported to brain, heart, muscle, which convert acetoacetate to acetoacetyl-CoA using succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase (thiophorase) — the liver lacks this enzyme, so it cannot use its own ketones; RBCs lack mitochondria. Urine nitroprusside test detects acetoacetate, not β-hydroxybutyrate (may underestimate ketosis in DKA/alcoholic ketoacidosis). Breath smells fruity (acetone).

StateMain glucose sourceKey changes
Fed (0–4 h)DietaryInsulin ↑: glycolysis, glycogen synthesis, lipogenesis, protein synthesis
Fasting (4–24 h)Hepatic glycogenolysis (glycogen depleted after ~24 h) then gluconeogenesisGlucagon/epinephrine ↑; lipolysis → FFAs for muscle/liver; adipose releases glycerol
Starvation days 1–3Gluconeogenesis (alanine, lactate, glycerol, propionyl-CoA)Rising ketones; muscle protein used
Starvation >3 daysKetones become brain's main fuelProtein spared until adipose depleted; then vital-organ protein loss → death (cardiac)

Lipoproteins & familial dyslipidemias

Key apolipoproteins: A-I (HDL; activates LCAT), B-48 (chylomicrons; made by intestine via RNA editing), B-100 (VLDL, IDL, LDL; binds LDL receptor), C-II (cofactor for lipoprotein lipase), E (remnant uptake by liver). Lipoprotein lipase (capillary endothelium of adipose/muscle) hydrolyzes TG in chylomicrons and VLDL; hepatic TG lipase acts on IDL; hormone-sensitive lipase mobilizes adipocyte TG (activated by epinephrine, inhibited by insulin). CETP transfers cholesteryl esters HDL → VLDL/LDL. PCSK9 promotes LDL-receptor degradation.

TypeDefect↑ LipoproteinClinical
I — Familial chylomicronemia (AR)LPL or apo C-II deficiencyChylomicrons (TG ↑↑)Acute pancreatitis, eruptive xanthomas, lipemia retinalis, hepatosplenomegaly; no ↑ atherosclerosis; Rx very low-fat diet, MCT oil
II — Familial hypercholesterolemia (AD)LDL receptor (most), apo B-100, gain-of-function PCSK9LDL (IIa); LDL + VLDL (IIb)Heterozygotes LDL ~190–400 mg/dL, homozygotes >500; tendon (Achilles) xanthomas, xanthelasma, corneal arcus before 45; premature MI (homozygotes in childhood). Rx high-intensity statin ± ezetimibe ± PCSK9 inhibitor (evolocumab, alirocumab, inclisiran)
III — DysbetalipoproteinemiaApo E2/E2 homozygosity (+ second hit)Chylomicron & VLDL remnants (IDL)Palmar crease xanthomas, tuberoeruptive xanthomas, premature CAD/PAD
IV — Familial hypertriglyceridemia (AD)Hepatic VLDL overproductionVLDLPancreatitis if TG >1000 mg/dL; associated with insulin resistance

Abetalipoproteinemia (AR; microsomal triglyceride transfer protein, MTTP): no chylomicrons/VLDL/LDL → fat malabsorption, steatorrhea, failure to thrive, acanthocytes, spinocerebellar degeneration and retinitis pigmentosa (vitamin E deficiency); enterocytes filled with lipid on biopsy. Rx: high-dose vitamin E and other fat-soluble vitamins.

sections.heading: 8. Amino acids, urea cycle & inborn errors
sections.html:
Essential amino acids: phenylalanine, valine, threonine, tryptophan, isoleucine, methionine, histidine, leucine, lysine (arginine is conditionally essential in growth). Purely ketogenic: leucine and lysine. Glucogenic and ketogenic: Ile, Phe, Thr, Trp, Tyr. Basic: Arg (most basic), Lys, His (no charge at physiologic pH) — histones are rich in Arg and Lys (positive charge binds DNA). Acidic: Asp, Glu.

Ammonia transport: muscle amino groups → alanine (glucose-alanine cycle) and glutamine; in liver, ALT/AST (B6) transfer amino groups to α-ketoglutarate → glutamate → NH₃ (glutamate dehydrogenase) → urea cycle. Hyperammonemia depletes α-ketoglutarate (inhibits TCA) and raises glutamine in astrocytes (cerebral edema): tremor/asterixis, vomiting, slurred speech, somnolence, blurred vision. Treatment: restrict protein; lactulose (acidifies colon → NH₄⁺ trapping), rifaximin (hepatic encephalopathy); sodium benzoate / phenylacetate / phenylbutyrate (conjugate glycine/glutamine for renal excretion), arginine (except arginase deficiency), carglumic acid (activates CPS I in NAGS deficiency), hemodialysis for severe neonatal crisis.

[[figure:ch01-fig03]]

High-yield: Approach to a sick neonate with metabolic crisis — check glucose, ammonia, blood gas/anion gap, lactate, ketones. ↑ NH₃ + normal anion gap (respiratory alkalosis) = urea cycle defect. ↑ NH₃ + anion-gap acidosis + ketosis = organic acidemia. Hypoketotic hypoglycemia = fatty-acid-oxidation defect (or hyperinsulinism). Lactic acidosis + hypoglycemia + hepatomegaly = von Gierke.

sections.heading: 9. Purine & pyrimidine metabolism
sections.html:
[[figure:ch01-fig04]]

De novo pyrimidines build the ring first then add ribose-5-P (from PRPP): glutamine + CO₂ + 2 ATP → carbamoyl phosphate (CPS II, cytosolic — differs from mitochondrial CPS I of the urea cycle) → + aspartate → dihydroorotate → orotate (dihydroorotate dehydrogenase — leflunomide/teriflunomide) → + PRPP → UMP (UMP synthase: orotate phosphoribosyltransferase + OMP decarboxylase) → UDP → CDP/dUDP (ribonucleotide reductase — hydroxyurea) → dUMP → dTMP (thymidylate synthase — 5-FU; needs N⁵,N¹⁰-methylene-THF regenerated by DHFR — methotrexate, trimethoprim, pyrimethamine).

De novo purines are built on ribose-5-P: PRPP → IMP (glutamine-PRPP amidotransferase rate-limiting; needs glycine, aspartate, glutamine, THF, CO₂) → AMP and GMP (IMP dehydrogenase — mycophenolate, ribavirin). 6-mercaptopurine/azathioprine inhibit de novo purine synthesis (6-MP metabolized by xanthine oxidase and TPMT). Salvage: HGPRT converts hypoxanthine → IMP and guanine → GMP; APRT converts adenine → AMP. Degradation: adenosine → inosine (adenosine deaminase) → hypoxanthine → xanthine → uric acid (xanthine oxidase — allopurinol, febuxostat).

DisorderDefectBiochemistryPresentation / treatment
Lesch-Nyhan (XLR)HGPRTPurines cannot be salvaged → degraded to uric acid; ↑ PRPP → ↑ de novo purine synthesis → more uric acidBoys: hyperuricemia, gout, orange "sand" (urate crystals) in diaper, self-mutilation (lips, fingers), dystonia, ID. Allopurinol/febuxostat treats hyperuricemia but not neurologic disease
Adenosine deaminase deficiency (AR)ADA↑ dATP → inhibits ribonucleotide reductase → ↓ dNTPs → lymphocyte deathSCID (T, B and NK deficiency); PEG-ADA enzyme replacement (elapegademase), HSCT, gene therapy

Two-signal rule: naive T cells need (1) TCR recognition of peptide–MHC and (2) costimulation — B7 (CD80/CD86) on the APC binding CD28. Signal 1 without signal 2 → anergy. Activation → calcineurin dephosphorylates NFAT → IL-2 transcription; IL-2 acts on CD25 (IL-2Rα) → mTOR → proliferation. CTLA-4 (on activated T cells/Tregs) binds B7 with higher affinity to shut the response off; PD-1 on exhausted T cells binds PD-L1. Checkpoint inhibitors (ipilimumab — CTLA-4; nivolumab, pembrolizumab — PD-1; atezolizumab — PD-L1) unleash T cells → immune-related adverse events (colitis, hepatitis, thyroiditis, hypophysitis, pneumonitis, T1DM). Conversely, CTLA-4-Ig fusion proteins (abatacept — RA; belatacept — kidney transplant) block costimulation. B-cell activation/class switching: Tfh (CD4) cell CD40L (CD154) binds CD40 on B cell + cytokines (IL-4 → IgE/IgG; IL-5 → IgA; IFN-γ → opsonizing IgG) → activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID). Superantigens (TSST-1, staphylococcal enterotoxins, streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin A) cross-link the Vβ region of TCRs to MHC II outside the groove → polyclonal activation → cytokine storm (toxic shock).

sections.heading: 12. Antibodies, complement & cytokines
sections.html:
Structure: 2 heavy + 2 light chains. Fab (variable regions; hypervariable CDRs; idiotype) binds antigen. Fc (constant region; isotype; carbohydrate side chains) fixes complement (IgG, IgM) and binds Fc receptors. Diversity: V(D)J recombination (RAG1/2), junctional imprecision (TdT adds nucleotides), random pairing of heavy/light chains, somatic hypermutation and class switching (AID).

IsotypeStructureKey facts
IgMMonomer on B cells; pentamer (J chain) secretedFirst antibody of primary response; best complement activator; doesn't cross placenta (fetal IgM = congenital infection)
IgGMonomer; 4 subclassesMost abundant in serum; secondary response; opsonizes, fixes complement, neutralizes, crosses placenta (FcRn) → passive immunity for ~6 months
IgADimer (J chain) + secretory component (from poly-Ig receptor during transcytosis)Most produced antibody overall; mucosa, breast milk, tears; does not fix classic complement

title: Step 1 · Microbiology
meta: Exam: Step 1 (with Step 2 CK management hooks) · Bacteriology, virology, mycology, parasitology, systems-based infectious disease, antimicrobial pharmacology · Approx study time: 5–6 days (plus 1 day of questions)

sections.heading: Overview
sections.html:
From NEET PG to USMLE

  • Mechanism over lists. NEET PG asks "which organism causes X". USMLE gives a vignette, makes you identify the organism from a lab clue (catalase, oxidase, lactose, hemolysis), then asks the toxin mechanism, drug mechanism, the resistance mechanism, or the toxicity of the treatment. Always learn the chain: clue → organism → virulence factor → drug → adverse effect.
  • Geography flips. In India you think typhoid, TB, leptospirosis, scrub typhus, malaria, dengue, kala-azar, JE. On USMLE the "local" organisms are Lyme (Northeast/upper Midwest), RMSF (South-central/Southeast), Ehrlichia, Babesia, Histoplasma (Ohio/Mississippi valleys), Blastomyces, Coccidioides (Southwest). India-endemic diseases appear as the immigrant/traveler vignette: "a 28-year-old man who recently emigrated from India..." — think TB, typhoid, malaria (P. vivax relapse), neurocysticercosis, Strongyloides, HEV, leprosy.
  • US guidelines and drug names. US gonorrhea dose is ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose (CDC 2021); chlamydia first-line is doxycycline 7 days; C. difficile first-line is oral fidaxomicin or oral vancomycin (metronidazole is no longer first-line, IDSA 2021); latent TB uses short rifamycin-based regimens (3HP, 4R, 3HR) rather than 6–9 months of isoniazid alone; HIV initial therapy is an integrase inhibitor + 2 NRTIs.
  • BCG matters. She is BCG-vaccinated. For US screening, an IGRA (QuantiFERON/T-SPOT) is preferred over the tuberculin skin test (TST/PPD) in BCG recipients. This will also matter for her own residency onboarding.
  • Vocabulary. "Enteric fever" = typhoid fever; "PUO" = FUO; "ATT" = RIPE therapy; "PPD/Mantoux" = TST; "DOTS" = directly observed therapy (DOT). US exams say "acid-fast bacilli", "gram-negative rods", "lactose nonfermenter".

sections.heading: 1. Bacterial structure, stains and culture
sections.html:
Gram-positive organisms have a thick peptidoglycan layer with lipoteichoic acid (triggers TNF-α/IL-1 via TLR2). Gram-negative organisms have a thin peptidoglycan layer in the periplasm and an outer membrane containing LPS (lipid A = endotoxin, recognized by CD14/TLR4/MD-2). The outer membrane is why many gram-negatives are intrinsically resistant to vancomycin and penicillin G, and why porins (OmpF) govern entry of β-lactams. Mycobacteria have a waxy envelope rich in mycolic acids (acid-fast). Mycoplasma has no wall at all — it has sterols (cholesterol) in its membrane and is resistant to every cell-wall drug.

Other virulence factors

  • Protein A (S. aureus): binds Fc of IgG → blocks opsonization and complement. Coagulase: fibrin coat.
  • M protein (GAS): antiphagocytic, inhibits complement (binds factor H); molecular mimicry with cardiac myosin → rheumatic fever (type II hypersensitivity).
  • IgA protease: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae type b, Neisseria — colonize mucosa.
  • Lipooligosaccharide (LOS) of N. meningitidis: very potent endotoxin → Waterhouse–Friderichsen (adrenal hemorrhage).
  • Cord factor (trehalose dimycolate, M. tuberculosis): activates macrophages and granuloma formation, inhibits neutrophils; sulfatides inhibit phagolysosome fusion.
  • Type III secretion system ("injectisome"): Pseudomonas, Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, EPEC/EHEC.
  • Siderophores and iron: iron overload (hemochromatosis, deferoxamine therapy) predisposes to Yersinia, Vibrio vulnificus, Listeria and mucormycosis.

Bacterial genetics

ProcessDescriptionExample
TransformationUptake of naked DNA from the environment (competence); DNase-sensitiveS. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, Neisseria (Griffith experiment)
ConjugationF+ × F−: plasmid transferred via sex pilus; Hfr × F−: chromosomal genes transferredSpread of resistance plasmids among gram-negatives (ESBL, carbapenemases)
Generalized transductionLytic phage accidentally packages random bacterial DNAAny gene
Specialized transduction / lysogenic conversionTemperate phage integrates (prophage) and carries adjacent bacterial genes, or phage-encoded genes are expressedToxins encoded by phage: ShigA-like, Botulinum (some), Cholera, Diphtheria, Erythrogenic (scarlet fever) toxin ("ABCDE")
TranspositionTransposon "jumps" between chromosome and plasmid; can carry multiple resistance genesvanA in Enterococcus (Tn1546)
High-yield: Phage-encoded toxins arise by lysogenic conversion. Conjugation spreads resistance between different gram-negative species; transposons move genes within a cell (including onto plasmids that then conjugate).

sections.html:

Staphylococci

OrganismKey featuresDiseasesTreatment
S. aureusCatalase +, coagulase +, β-hemolytic, golden colonies, ferments mannitol; protein AInflammatory: skin abscess, impetigo (bullous), cellulitis, septic arthritis, acute osteomyelitis (most common overall), post-influenza pneumonia, acute endocarditis (tricuspid in IV drug users). Exam trap: MRSA resistance is due to mecA → PBP2a (altered target with low β-lactam affinity), not β-lactamase — so adding a β-lactamase inhibitor does nothing. Ceftaroline and ceftobiprole (5th-generation cephalosporins) are the only β-lactams that bind PBP2a.

OrganismIDDiseasesNotes
S. pneumoniaeα-hemolytic, lancet-shaped diplococci, optochin S, bile soluble, Quellung +, capsuleMOPS: Meningitis, Otitis media, Pneumonia (lobar, rusty sputum), Sinusitis; SBP in children with nephrotic syndromeMost common cause of CAP, adult meningitis, otitis media. Toxigenic: scarlet fever, strep TSS. In India rheumatic heart disease is still common; in the US it is rare — on USMLE expect it in an immigrant with mitral stenosis.

Respiratory and "fastidious" gram-negatives

OrganismKey points
Haemophilus influenzaeCoccobacillus; needs X + V. Type b capsule (polyribosylribitol phosphate, PRP) → epiglottitis ("cherry-red", tripod, drooling), meningitis, septic arthritis in unvaccinated children. Nontypeable strains → otitis media, sinusitis, conjunctivitis, COPD exacerbations. Treat meningitis with ceftriaxone; mucosal infections with amoxicillin-clavulanate (β-lactamase producers). Rifampin prophylaxis for contacts. Conjugate Hib vaccine (PRP conjugated to diphtheria or tetanus toxoid) at 2, 4, (6), 12–15 months
Bordetella pertussisCatarrhal → paroxysmal ("whoop", post-tussive emesis) → convalescent ("100-day cough"). Lymphocytosis (pertussis toxin blocks lymphocyte homing). Infants: apnea. Treat azithromycin (also for close contacts). Tdap in every pregnancy at 27–36 weeks
Legionella pneumophilaAerosol from water (cooling towers, hot tubs, hotels, cruise ships), no person-to-person spread. Atypical pneumonia with high fever, hyponatremia, GI symptoms (diarrhea), confusion, ↑LFTs. Gram stain shows neutrophils but few organisms. Dx urinary antigen; culture on BCYE (cysteine + iron). Treat azithromycin or levofloxacin. Pontiac fever = mild flu-like illness

Burns (blue-green pus), CF pneumonia (mucoid alginate), ventilator-associated pneumonia, otitis externa (swimmer's) and malignant otitis externa in elderly diabetics, hot-tub folliculitis, osteomyelitis after puncture through sneaker, IV drug users, ecthyma gangrenosum in neutropenia. Treat with antipseudomonal agents: piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime/ceftazidime, carbapenems (not ertapenem), aztreonam, fluoroquinolones (cipro/levo), aminoglycosides, colistin; newer: ceftolozane-tazobactam, ceftazidime-avibactam

sections.heading: 7. Spirochetes
sections.html:
OrganismTransmissionClinicalDiagnosis / treatment
Treponema pallidumSexual, vertical (any trimester)Primary: painless indurated chancre, nontender inguinal nodes. Secondary (weeks–months): diffuse maculopapular rash incl. palms/soles, condyloma lata, patchy alopecia, mucous patches, hepatitis, nephrotic. Latent. Tertiary: gummas, aortitis (vasa vasorum endarteritis → ascending aortic aneurysm, "tree-bark"), tabes dorsalis (dorsal columns: ataxia, + Romberg, lightning pains), Argyll Robertson pupil (accommodates but does not react), general paresis. Neurosyphilis can occur at any stage (ocular/otic syphilis)Screening: nontreponemal (RPR/VDRL; titers follow disease activity; false + in SLE/antiphospholipid, pregnancy, EBV, leprosy) and treponemal (FTA-ABS, TP-PA, EIA/CIA; stay positive for life). US labs often use the reverse sequence (treponemal EIA first). Darkfield microscopy of chancre. Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM once (primary, secondary, early latent); weekly × 3 for late latent/unknown; neurosyphilis: aqueous IV penicillin G 10–14 days. Pregnant and penicillin-allergic → desensitize
Congenital syphilisTransplacentalStillbirth, hydrops; early: snuffles, rash, hepatosplenomegaly, periostitis; late: Hutchinson teeth, mulberry molars, saddle nose, saber shins, CN VIII deafness, interstitial keratitisScreen every pregnant woman at the first visit; repeat at ~28 weeks and at delivery (ACOG 2024 advises this for all patients; CDC for those at risk or in high-prevalence areas)
Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme)Ixodes scapularis (deer tick); white-footed mouse reservoir, deer host for adults; transmission usually requires ≥36 h attachment. US Northeast, mid-Atlantic, upper MidwestEarly localized (3–30 days): erythema migrans (expanding, ≥5 cm, often central clearing), flu-like. Early disseminated: multiple EM, facial nerve palsy (often bilateral), meningitis, radiculopathy, carditis (AV block). Late: monoarticular arthritis (knee), encephalopathyEM is a clinical diagnosis — treat without serology. Two-tier serology (EIA then immunoblot or second EIA) for later stages. Doxycycline (all ages for short courses); amoxicillin or cefuroxime in pregnancy. IV ceftriaxone for hospitalized carditis (e.g., PR >300 ms) or refractory arthritis; oral doxycycline acceptable for Lyme meningitis and facial palsy (IDSA 2020). Prophylaxis: single dose doxycycline within 72 h of an engorged Ixodes bite in endemic area
Borrelia recurrentis / B. hermsiiLice (epidemic) / soft ticks (endemic, western US cabins)Relapsing fever (antigenic variation)Giemsa/Wright stain of blood; doxycycline. Jarisch–Herxheimer common
Leptospira interrogansWater contaminated by rat urine (monsoon flooding in India, surfers in Hawaii, Puerto Rico)Fever, myalgia (calves), conjunctival suffusion; severe Weil disease: jaundice, AKI, pulmonary hemorrhageDoxycycline (mild); penicillin G or ceftriaxone (severe)
High-yield: Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction — fever, rigors, myalgia, hypotension within 24 h of treating a spirochetal infection (classically syphilis) — is caused by cytokine release (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-8) as lysed spirochetes release lipoproteins. It is not penicillin allergy; treat with antipyretics and continue therapy.

sections.heading: 8. Mycobacteria
sections.html:
Tuberculosis

Primary TB: inhaled bacilli → lower/middle lobe subpleural granuloma (Ghon focus) + hilar node (Ghon complex; calcified = Ranke complex). Macrophages present antigen via IL-12 → TH1 → IFN-γ → macrophage activation, caseating granuloma. Usually contained (latent infection). Secondary (reactivation): apical cavitary lesions (high O2), fever, night sweats, weight loss, hemoptysis. Extrapulmonary: Pott disease (vertebral), scrofula (cervical lymphadenitis), TB meningitis (basal exudates, cranial neuropathies, very low glucose), adrenal insufficiency, constrictive pericarditis, genitourinary (sterile pyuria), miliary TB.

TestInterpretation (US)
TST (Mantoux, PPD) — read induration at 48–72 h≥5 mm: HIV, recent contact, fibrotic CXR, organ transplant, immunosuppressed (≥15 mg/day prednisone for ≥1 month, TNF-α inhibitors). ≥10 mm: recent immigrants from high-burden countries (e.g., India), IV drug users, residents/employees of high-risk settings (health care workers, prisons, shelters), children <4 y, mycobacteriology lab staff, silicosis/diabetes/CKD. ≥15 mm: no risk factors. False + with BCG and nontuberculous mycobacteria
IGRA (QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus, T-SPOT.TB)Measures T-cell IFN-γ release to ESAT-6/CFP-10 (absent from BCG and most NTM) → preferred in BCG-vaccinated persons and those unlikely to return for reading. One visit
Positive TST/IGRA→ Chest radiograph. Normal CXR + no symptoms = latent TB infection (LTBI). Abnormal CXR or symptoms → 3 sputa for AFB smear, culture and NAAT
RegimenDetails
LTBI (CDC 2020, preferred)3HP: isoniazid + rifapentine weekly × 12 doses; 4R: daily rifampin × 4 months; 3HR: daily isoniazid + rifampin × 3 months. Alternative: isoniazid 6–9 months (with pyridoxine). Check drug interactions (rifamycins induce CYP3A4: OCPs, warfarin, many antiretrovirals)
Active drug-susceptible pulmonary TBRIPE (rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) × 2 months, then rifampin + isoniazid × 4 months (total 6). 4-month rifapentine–moxifloxacin regimen is an alternative in eligible patients ≥12 y. Directly observed therapy; report to health department
MDR-TB (resistant to INH + rifampin)All-oral regimens built around bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid ± moxifloxacin (BPaL/BPaLM, 6 months). India has a large MDR burden — Xpert MTB/RIF detects rpoB mutations
DrugMechanismKey toxicity
Isoniazid (INH)Prodrug activated by bacterial catalase-peroxidase (KatG) → inhibits mycolic acid synthesis (InhA). Resistance: KatG or inhA mutationsHepatitis (age-related), peripheral neuropathy and sideroblastic anemia (vitamin B6 depletion — give pyridoxine), drug-induced lupus, seizures in overdose (treat with pyridoxine), CYP inhibition. Slow acetylators (NAT2) → higher levels
RifampinInhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (rpoB). Monotherapy → rapid resistanceOrange-red body fluids (stains contact lenses), hepatotoxicity, potent CYP3A4/2C9 inducer (OCP failure, ↓warfarin, ↓azoles, ↓protease inhibitors), flu-like syndrome with intermittent dosing. Rifabutin is preferred with many PIs (less induction)
PyrazinamideConverted to pyrazinoic acid; active in acidic phagolysosomesHepatotoxicity (most hepatotoxic), hyperuricemia → gout
EthambutolInhibits arabinosyl transferase (arabinogalactan)Optic neuritis: ↓acuity, red-green color blindness (monitor vision)
Streptomycin / amikacin30SOtotoxicity, nephrotoxicity
BedaquilineInhibits mycobacterial ATP synthaseQT prolongation

Other mycobacteria

  • Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC): disseminated disease in AIDS with CD4 <50 (fever, night sweats, diarrhea, ↑ALP, hepatosplenomegaly). Treat clarithromycin/azithromycin + ethambutol (± rifabutin). Primary prophylaxis (azithromycin) is no longer recommended if ART is started immediately (DHHS). Pulmonary MAC: elderly thin women with bronchiectasis ("Lady Windermere").
  • M. marinum: fish-tank granuloma; nodules spreading along lymphatics (sporotrichoid).
  • M. abscessus / fortuitum: post-procedural skin infections (cosmetic surgery, tattoos, pedicures), CF lungs.
  • M. leprae (Hansen disease): prefers cool areas (skin, peripheral nerves, nose, testes); cannot be cultured in vitro — grows in armadillo footpads. Tuberculoid (TH1, few lesions, hypoesthetic plaques, thickened nerves, lepromin +) vs lepromatous (TH2, diffuse, leonine facies, lepromin −). India accounts for the largest share of global new cases; US cases are rare (Gulf states, armadillo exposure; immigrants). Treat: rifampin + dapsone ± clofazimine (multibacillary). Erythema nodosum leprosum → thalidomide or steroids. Dapsone → hemolysis in G6PD deficiency, methemoglobinemia.

sections.heading: 11. Virology: structure and general principles
sections.html:
[[figure:ch02-fig05]]
  • Genome sense: (+) ssRNA works as mRNA → purified genome is infectious (picorna, flavi, toga, corona, calici). (−) ssRNA and dsRNA viruses must carry their own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (not infectious as naked RNA). Retroviruses are (+) but need reverse transcriptase.
  • Envelope source: plasma membrane (most), nuclear membrane (herpesviruses — the exception), ER/Golgi (flavi, corona).
  • Genetic interactions: reassortment of segmented genomes (influenza antigenic shift → pandemics); recombination (crossover between two viruses); complementation (one virus supplies a functional protein to a mutant — e.g., HDV uses HBsAg); phenotypic mixing (genome of one virus coated by surface proteins of another; progeny revert).
  • Live attenuated vaccines (contraindicated in pregnancy and severe immunodeficiency): MMR, varicella, yellow fever, oral typhoid (Ty21a), intranasal influenza, rotavirus, BCG, oral polio (OPV — still used in India, not in US), dengue (Dengvaxia — only in seropositive children 9–16 in endemic US territories; being discontinued). MMR may be given to HIV patients with CD4 ≥200. Inactivated: IPV, HAV, rabies, injectable influenza. Subunit/recombinant: HBV, HPV, recombinant zoster (Shingrix), acellular pertussis, meningococcal. mRNA: COVID-19, RSV (mRESVIA, adults ≥60).

DNA viruses

HerpesviridaeHSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, EBV, CMV, HHV-6, HHV-7, HHV-8See herpes table below. Latency; Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells (HSV, VZV), Cowdry A inclusions

Molluscum: umbilicated flesh-colored papules with molluscum (Henderson–Patterson) bodies; widespread in HIV. Mpox: 2022 outbreak mainly MSM; vesiculopustular lesions, lymphadenopathy; tecovirimat; JYNNEOS vaccine

Avoid NSAIDs. Zika: microcephaly, sexual transmission. West Nile (Culex, birds): most common US arboviral encephalitis; flaccid paralysis. Yellow fever (Aedes; Africa/S. America): hepatitis with jaundice, Councilman bodies; live vaccine. JE: India/Asia, Culex, pigs/birds

US: bats (most human cases), raccoons, skunks, foxes. India: dogs (~1/3 of global deaths). PEP: wound washing + human rabies immune globulin (into wound) + vaccine days 0, 3, 7, 14 (4 doses if immunocompetent)

ArenaviridaeLCMV, LassaLCMV: rodent (house mouse, pet hamsters) — aseptic meningitis, congenital chorioretinitis/hydrocephalus
Bunyavirales (Hantaviridae etc.)Hantavirus (Sin Nombre), CCHF, Rift ValleyHantavirus pulmonary syndrome: deer-mouse droppings in Four Corners/rural West → noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, thrombocytopenia, hemoconcentration

sections.heading: 12. HIV
sections.html:
[[figure:ch02-fig06]]

Structure: diploid (+) ssRNA, enveloped. Genes: env (gp160 → gp120 attachment + gp41 fusion), gag (p24 capsid, p17 matrix), pol (reverse transcriptase, integrase, protease). Coreceptors: CCR5 early (macrophage-tropic; homozygous CCR5Δ32 confers resistance), CXCR4 later (T-cell tropic). Diagnosis: 4th-generation HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody immunoassay (p24 antigen + antibodies; positive ~2–3 weeks after infection) → HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay → if indeterminate/negative, HIV-1 RNA NAAT (acute infection). Western blot is obsolete. Infants of HIV+ mothers: HIV RNA/DNA NAAT (maternal IgG crosses placenta). USPSTF: screen everyone 15–65 at least once and every pregnancy.

Acute HIV: mononucleosis-like illness (fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, rash, mucocutaneous ulcers) 2–4 weeks after exposure with very high viral load. Treatment: start ART in everyone, ideally same day/rapidly. Preferred initial regimens (DHHS): bictegravir/tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine, dolutegravir + (TAF or TDF) + (FTC or 3TC), or dolutegravir/lamivudine (not if HBV coinfection, VL >500,000, or no genotype). Prevention: PrEP with TDF/FTC or TAF/FTC daily, injectable cabotegravir every 2 months, or lenacapavir twice yearly (FDA-approved 2025); PEP = 3-drug ART within 72 h for 28 days. Undetectable = untransmittable (U=U).

ClassDrugsMechanism / toxicity
NRTIsTenofovir (TDF, TAF), emtricitabine, lamivudine, abacavir, zidovudineNucleoside analogs; need intracellular phosphorylation (tenofovir is a nucleotide — needs fewer steps); lack 3′-OH → chain termination. Class: lactic acidosis/hepatic steatosis (mitochondrial toxicity, older drugs). TDF: nephrotoxicity (Fanconi), ↓bone density (TAF less). Abacavir: HLA-B*57:01 hypersensitivity (test before use), ↑MI risk. Zidovudine: macrocytic anemia/bone marrow suppression, myopathy. FTC/3TC/TDF also treat HBV (flare when stopped)
NNRTIsEfavirenz, rilpivirine, doravirine, nevirapineBind allosteric site of RT (no phosphorylation needed). Efavirenz: vivid dreams, CNS effects, false + cannabinoid screen. Rilpivirine: needs food and acid (no PPIs). Nevirapine: hepatotoxicity, SJS
INSTIsBictegravir, dolutegravir, raltegravir, cabotegravir, elvitegravirBlock integrase strand transfer. Weight gain, insomnia, ↑creatine kinase (raltegravir). Chelated by polyvalent cations (antacids, iron, calcium) — separate dosing. Dolutegravir and bictegravir inhibit tubular creatinine secretion (↑serum creatinine without true GFR loss)
Protease inhibitorsDarunavir, atazanavir, lopinavir (boosted with ritonavir or cobicistat)Block cleavage of gag-pol polyprotein → immature virions. Hyperglycemia, lipodystrophy, dyslipidemia; atazanavir: indirect hyperbilirubinemia (UGT1A1 inhibition), nephrolithiasis; ritonavir: potent CYP3A4 inhibitor (used as booster)
Entry inhibitorsMaraviroc (CCR5), enfuvirtide (gp41), ibalizumab (anti-CD4 mAb), fostemsavir (gp120)Maraviroc needs tropism test (R5 virus only). Enfuvirtide: injection site reactions
Capsid inhibitorLenacapavirHeavily treatment-experienced HIV and twice-yearly PrEP
CD4 countOpportunistic infectionPrimary prophylaxis
Any (often <500)Oral candidiasis/hairy leukoplakia (EBV), TB, zoster, Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8), bacterial pneumoniaTreat LTBI if TST/IGRA +
<200Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, esophageal candidiasis, HIV dementia, PML, cryptococcal antigenemia (screen if <100)TMP-SMX (alternatives: dapsone [check G6PD], atovaquone, aerosolized pentamidine)
<100Toxoplasma encephalitis (multiple ring-enhancing lesions), cryptococcal meningitis, histoplasmosis (disseminated, endemic areas), cryptosporidiosis, primary CNS lymphoma (EBV; solitary periventricular lesion)Toxoplasma IgG + → TMP-SMX (covers PCP too)
<50Disseminated MAC, CMV retinitis/colitis/esophagitis, Bartonella, invasive aspergillosisMAC prophylaxis only if not starting ART immediately; no routine CMV prophylaxis
High-yield: PCP with PaO2 <70 mm Hg or A–a gradient ≥35 mm Hg → add prednisone to TMP-SMX (reduces mortality from inflammatory worsening as organisms die). IRIS (immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome) = paradoxical worsening of an OI after starting ART as CD4 recovers; continue ART (exceptions: defer ART ~4–6 weeks after starting antifungals in cryptococcal meningitis; in TB meningitis start ART after ~2 weeks of TB therapy rather than immediately).

sections.heading: 15. Mycology
sections.html:
Endemic (dimorphic) mycoses — "mold in the cold (25 °C, environment), yeast in the heat (37 °C, tissue)"

Coccidioides is the exception: in tissue it forms spherules filled with endospores, not yeast. All are acquired by inhalation of spores (not person-to-person), cause a self-limited pneumonia in most people, and disseminate in immunocompromised hosts. Granulomatous inflammation; mimic TB and sarcoid.

FungusUS region / exposureTissue morphologyClinical cluesTreatment
Histoplasma capsulatumOhio and Mississippi River valleys; bird and bat droppings (caves, chicken coops, demolition). sections.html:
Meningitis

AgeMost common bacteriaViralEmpiric therapy (IDSA)
0–1 monthGBS, E. coli (K1), ListeriaEnteroviruses, HSV-2Ampicillin + cefotaxime (or ceftazidime/cefepime) or ampicillin + gentamicin; add acyclovir if HSV possible. Avoid ceftriaxone in neonates (biliary sludging, displaces bilirubin, precipitates with IV calcium)

Sequence: blood cultures → dexamethasone (10–15 min before or with first antibiotic; benefit proven for pneumococcal meningitis in adults and Hib in children) + antibiotics immediately → CT before LP only if immunocompromised, history of CNS disease, new seizure, papilledema, altered consciousness, or focal deficit — never delay antibiotics for imaging.

Pneumonia

Setting / clueLikely organisms
Typical CAP (lobar, productive)S. pneumoniae (#1), H. influenzae, Moraxella (COPD), S. aureus (post-influenza, cavitary)
Atypical CAPMycoplasma, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, Legionella, respiratory viruses

CFS. aureus (young), Pseudomonas (adults), B. cepacia, M. abscessus
ExposuresBirds: psittacosis, Cryptococcus, Histoplasma; farm animals' birthing: Coxiella; rabbits: tularemia; deer mice: hantavirus; air conditioning/water: Legionella; caves: Histoplasma

CAP treatment (ATS/IDSA 2019): Outpatient, healthy: amoxicillin 1 g TID, or doxycycline, or a macrolide only if local pneumococcal macrolide resistance <25%. Outpatient with comorbidities: amoxicillin-clavulanate or cefpodoxime/cefuroxime + macrolide or doxycycline, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) alone. Inpatient non-severe: β-lactam (ceftriaxone, ampicillin-sulbactam) + macrolide, or respiratory FQ alone. Severe/ICU: β-lactam + macrolide or β-lactam + respiratory FQ; add MRSA/Pseudomonas coverage only with prior isolation or recent hospitalization with IV antibiotics plus local risk.

Urinary tract infection

  • Organisms: E. coli (~75–90%, P fimbriae), S. saprophyticus (young women), Klebsiella, Proteus (alkaline urine, struvite), Enterococcus, Pseudomonas and Serratia (catheter/hospital).
  • Urinalysis: leukocyte esterase (WBCs) and nitrite (gram-negative enterics reduce nitrate; Enterococcus and S. saprophyticus are nitrite −); WBC casts = pyelonephritis.
  • Uncomplicated cystitis (IDSA): nitrofurantoin × 5 days, TMP-SMX × 3 days (if resistance <20%), fosfomycin single dose. Fluoroquinolones reserved (adverse effects). Pyelonephritis: ciprofloxacin/levofloxacin or TMP-SMX (if susceptible); ceftriaxone if inpatient.
  • Asymptomatic bacteriuria: treat only in pregnancy (screen at 12–16 weeks or first visit; USPSTF) and before urologic procedures with mucosal bleeding. Do not treat in elderly, catheterized or diabetic patients.
  • Nitrofurantoin: avoid near term (≥38 weeks: neonatal hemolysis) and if CrCl <30 (ineffective, toxic); pulmonary fibrosis with chronic use.

DiseaseOrganismClinicalTreatment

TrichomoniasisT. vaginalisSee protozoaMetronidazole
High-yield: Doxy-PEP — a single 200 mg dose of doxycycline within 72 h after condomless sex — is now recommended by CDC (2024) for MSM and transgender women with a bacterial STI in the past year, to reduce syphilis and chlamydia (less effect on gonorrhea).

TORCH and congenital infections

AgentMaternal acquisitionCharacteristic neonatal findings
ToxoplasmaCat feces, undercooked meatClassic triad: chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, diffuse intracranial calcifications; ring-enhancing lesions absent in neonates
SyphilisSexualEarly: rhinitis ("snuffles"), desquamating rash of palms/soles, hepatosplenomegaly, periostitis; late: Hutchinson incisors, saddle nose, saber shins, interstitial keratitis, CN VIII deafness
VaricellaRespiratoryLimb hypoplasia, cicatricial skin scarring, cortical atrophy, eye defects (exposure 8–20 weeks). Maternal rash 5 days before to 2 days after delivery → severe neonatal varicella (give VariZIG)

ZikaAedes mosquito, sexualSevere microcephaly, ocular anomalies, arthrogryposis

CMVSexual, saliva, urine (daycare workers)Most are asymptomatic at birth; sensorineural hearing loss (most common), periventricular calcifications, microcephaly, chorioretinitis, petechiae; valganciclovir for symptomatic infants
HIVSexual, parenteralRecurrent infections, failure to thrive; transmission <1% with maternal ART and suppressed viral load; infant zidovudine (± more drugs if high risk). In the US, breastfeeding is discouraged but supported with suppressed viral load after counseling (updated DHHS 2023)
HSVBirth canal (primary infection highest risk)Skin/eye/mouth vesicles, encephalitis, or disseminated sepsis at 1–3 weeks → IV acyclovir
Listeria, GBS, E. coliFood / colonizationNeonatal sepsis, meningitis, granulomatosis infantiseptica (Listeria)

Other organ-system pearls

SyndromeOrganisms to remember
OsteomyelitisS. aureus (most); sickle cell → Salmonella (and S. aureus); IV drug users → Pseudomonas, Candida, S. aureus (vertebral); puncture through sneaker → Pseudomonas; cat/dog bite → Pasteurella; diabetic foot → polymicrobial; prosthesis → S. epidermidis; TB → Pott disease. MRI is most sensitive imaging
Infective endocarditisAcute: S. aureus (IV drug users, tricuspid). Subacute: viridans strep. Prosthetic valve early: S. epidermidis. After GI/GU procedure: Enterococcus. Colon cancer: S. gallolyticus. Culture-negative: Coxiella, Bartonella, HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella). Dental prophylaxis (amoxicillin) only for prosthetic valves, prior IE, certain congenital heart disease, cardiac transplant with valvulopathy (AHA)
Septic arthritisS. aureus (most common overall); N. gonorrhoeae in sexually active young adults; Kingella in toddlers; Lyme (knee, less inflammatory)
Skin and soft tissueImpetigo (S. aureus, GAS), erysipelas (GAS, raised sharp border), cellulitis (GAS, S. aureus), necrotizing fasciitis (GAS, polymicrobial, C. perfringens, V. vulnificus; pain out of proportion → surgical debridement), hot tub (Pseudomonas), fish tank (M. marinum), rose thorn (Sporothrix), human bite (Eikenella)
Infections by immune defectNeutropenia: Pseudomonas, S. aureus, Candida, Aspergillus. T-cell defect: viruses, fungi (Candida, PCP), intracellular bacteria. B-cell/antibody defect: encapsulated bacteria, enteroviruses, Giardia. Terminal complement: Neisseria. Asplenia: encapsulated organisms, Babesia, Capnocytophaga
Fever in returned traveler (India)Malaria first (always smear/rapid test), dengue, typhoid, chikungunya, rickettsia (scrub typhus), leptospirosis, hepatitis A/E, TB, amebic liver abscess

Protein synthesis inhibitors ("buy AT 30, CCEL at 50")
