High-yield prophylaxis list: Meningococcal contacts → rifampin, ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone. Gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum → erythromycin ointment. Recurrent cellulitis → penicillin. Endocarditis (high-risk cardiac lesion + dental work) → amoxicillin. Pregnant GBS carrier → IV penicillin intrapartum. Splenectomy → vaccines (and amoxicillin for children). HIV with CD4 <200 → TMP-SMX. Malaria travel → atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine. Surgical site → cefazolin within 60 min before incision.
Exam trap — drugs to avoid in pregnancy ("SAFe Children Take Really Good Care"): Sulfonamides (kernicterus near term), Aminoglycosides (ototoxicity), Fluoroquinolones (cartilage), Clarithromycin (embryotoxic), Tetracyclines (teeth/bone), Ribavirin (teratogen), Griseofulvin, Chloramphenicol (gray baby). Safe: penicillins, cephalosporins, azithromycin, nitrofurantoin (not at term), metronidazole (after 1st trimester commonly used).

title: Step 1 · General Pharmacology, Biostatistics, Epidemiology, Ethics & Communication
meta: Exam: Step 1 (heavily re-tested on Step 2 CK) · General principles: pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, autonomic pharmacology, toxicology; biostatistics & epidemiology; medical ethics, US law, communication, patient safety & quality improvement · Approx study time: 4–5 days (do every calculation question by hand)

sections.heading: Overview
sections.html:
From NEET PG to USMLE

  • Biostatistics and ethics together are roughly 15–20% of Step 1 and more of Step 2 CK. In NEET PG these are a few PSM questions. On USMLE they are "free points" only if you can calculate fast: build a 2×2 table for every question, even when it looks easy.
  • US drug names: acetaminophen (= paracetamol), albuterol (= salbutamol), epinephrine/norepinephrine (= adrenaline/noradrenaline), meperidine (= pethidine), glyburide (= glibenclamide), isoproterenol (= isoprenaline), cyclosporine (= ciclosporin). Brand names are rarely used in stems.
  • Units: US stems use mg/dL (glucose, creatinine, BUN), °F as well as °C, and lb as well as kg. PK questions are usually given in mg, L, and hours. Write the units at every step.
  • Ethics follows US law and norms, not Indian practice. Patient autonomy outranks family wishes. A competent adult decides who hears their diagnosis. Professional interpreters are mandatory; family members should not interpret. Disclosure of errors is expected. A minor can consent on their own to contraception, STI care, prenatal care and substance-use treatment. In India, telling the family first is common; on USMLE it is almost always wrong.
  • The USMLE answer style for ethics: choose the option that is patient-centered, non-judgmental and least drastic, and that keeps the conversation open. Typical good openings: "explore the patient's concerns" or "ask what they understand." Avoid answers that refer the patient away, lie, threaten, or skip a step (for example, going straight to a court order or an ethics committee).
  • Screening follows USPSTF, not ICMR or WHO. Learn the grade A/B recommendations; Step 2 CK asks "most appropriate next screening step."

sections.heading: 1. Pharmacokinetics (what the body does to the drug)
sections.html:
ParameterFormulaKey points
Bioavailability (F)F = AUCoral / AUCIVIV F = 1 (100%). Reduced by incomplete absorption and first-pass hepatic metabolism. Drugs with high first-pass metabolism: nitroglycerin (given SL/transdermal), lidocaine (IV), propranolol, morphine.
Volume of distribution (Vd)Vd = amount of drug in body / plasma concentrationAn apparent volume. Low Vd (~3–5 L, plasma): large, charged or highly protein-bound drugs (heparin, warfarin). ECF (~14 L): small hydrophilic drugs (aminoglycosides, mannitol). Total body water (~40 L): small lipophilic drugs (ethanol). Vd greater than total body water means the drug binds tissue (amiodarone, chloroquine, digoxin, TCAs); these drugs are poorly dialyzable. Hypoalbuminemia raises the free fraction of protein-bound drugs (phenytoin).
Clearance (CL)CL = rate of elimination / Cp = Vd × ke = 0.693 × Vd / t½The volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time. Reduced by renal failure (renally cleared drugs), liver disease, and heart failure (low hepatic flow).
Half-life (t½)t½ = 0.693 × Vd / CLFirst-order only. After a constant infusion, steady state is 50% reached at 1 t½, 75% at 2, 87.5% at 3, 93.75% at 4, and 96.9% at 5. The time to steady state depends only on t½, never on dose or rate; dose sets the level. Elimination after stopping follows the same percentages.
Loading dose (LD)LD = Cp,target × Vd / FGets to the target concentration immediately. Usually unchanged in renal or hepatic impairment, because Vd is unchanged.
Maintenance dose (MD)MD = Cp,ss × CL × τ / Fτ = dosing interval. Matches the rate of elimination. Reduce it in renal or hepatic impairment (CL falls).
Infusion rateRate = Cp,ss × CLDoubling the infusion rate doubles Css, but steady state is still reached in about 4–5 t½.
FeatureFirst-order eliminationZero-order elimination
Amount eliminated per unit timeA constant fraction (proportional to concentration)A constant amount (enzymes saturated)
Half-lifeConstantNot constant (increases as the dose increases)
Concentration–time plotExponential decay (straight line on a semilog plot)Straight line on a linear plot
ExamplesMost drugs"PEA": Phenytoin, Ethanol, Aspirin (at high or toxic doses). Phenytoin follows Michaelis–Menten kinetics: it is first-order at low doses and becomes zero-order near the therapeutic range, so a small dose increase can cause a large jump in level (nystagmus, ataxia).
[[figure:ch03-fig01]]

Absorption, distribution and excretion: ion trapping

Only the non-ionized (lipid-soluble) form crosses membranes and is reabsorbed in the tubule. For a weak acid, alkalinizing the urine increases the ionized fraction and traps the drug in the urine, so more is excreted. Weak acids: aspirin and other salicylates, phenobarbital, methotrexate. Treatment is sodium bicarbonate. Weak bases (amphetamine, TCAs) are classically trapped by acidic urine (ammonium chloride). Urine acidification is not used clinically today, but it is still tested as a mechanism. Henderson–Hasselbalch: for a weak acid, pH − pKa = log([A−]/[HA]). When pH = pKa, the drug is 50% ionized.

Metabolism and pharmacogenomics

PhaseReactionsClinical point
Phase IOxidation, reduction, hydrolysis (CYP450); produces slightly polar metabolites, which may be activeDeclines in the elderly. Prefer drugs eliminated by phase II in older adults (for benzodiazepines: lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam).
Phase IIConjugation: glucuronidation, acetylation, sulfation, glutathione; produces very polar, renally excreted metabolitesSlow acetylators (NAT2) taking isoniazid, hydralazine or procainamide have more toxicity, including drug-induced lupus and INH neuropathy.
Gene / variantDrugConsequence

CYP2C19 poor metabolizerClopidogrel (prodrug)Less platelet inhibition and a risk of stent thrombosis. Use prasugrel or ticagrelor.
CYP2C9 / VKORC1 variantsWarfarinNeed lower doses; higher bleeding risk.

HLA-B*15:02 (SE Asian and some South Asian ancestry)Carbamazepine, phenytoinSJS/TEN.
HLA-B*58:01AllopurinolSJS/TEN and DRESS.

Pseudocholinesterase (BCHE) deficiencySuccinylcholine, mivacuriumProlonged apnea after anesthesia.

sections.heading: 2. Pharmacodynamics (what the drug does to the body)
sections.html:
Enzyme kinetics

Michaelis–Menten: V = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S]). Km is the [S] at ½Vmax and is inversely related to affinity. Lineweaver–Burk (double reciprocal): 1/V = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax. The y-intercept is 1/Vmax, the x-intercept is −1/Km, and the slope is Km/Vmax. "The further right the x-intercept (closer to zero), the larger the Km and the lower the affinity. The higher the y-intercept, the lower the Vmax."

Competitive inhibitor (reversible)Noncompetitive inhibitorUncompetitive (rare)
BindsActive site (resembles substrate)Allosteric site (enzyme or ES complex)ES complex only
Overcome by ↑[S]?YesNoNo
VmaxUnchanged↓↓
Km↑Unchanged↓
Lineweaver–BurkSame y-intercept; steeper slope; lines cross on the y-axisSame x-intercept; higher y-intercept; lines cross on the x-axisParallel lines
Potency / efficacy analog↓ potency↓ efficacy—
[[figure:ch03-fig02]]

Drug–receptor concepts

TermMeaningExamples / exam angle
PotencyThe amount of drug needed for a given effect (EC50). A left-shifted curve means more potent.Potency is about affinity, not maximal benefit.
EfficacyThe maximal effect (Emax), whatever the doseEfficacy matters more clinically than potency.
Full agonistGives the maximal responseMorphine, isoproterenol
Partial agonistLower Emax even at full receptor occupancy. With a full agonist present, it acts as an antagonist. Potency can be higher or lower than the full agonist's.Buprenorphine (μ; precipitates withdrawal in a patient on heroin or methadone), varenicline (α4β2 nicotinic), aripiprazole (D2), pindolol and acebutolol (β; "ISA"), buspirone (5-HT1A)
Inverse agonistLowers constitutive receptor activity (an effect opposite to the agonist's)H1 antihistamines and many "antagonists" at constitutively active receptors
Competitive antagonistReversibly binds the same site; shifts the curve right (↑EC50); Emax unchanged; surmountableAtropine, naloxone, flumazenil, propranolol, prazosin, cetirizine
Noncompetitive antagonistIrreversible or allosteric; ↓Emax; not surmountablePhenoxybenzamine (covalent α), ketamine (NMDA channel block)
Physiologic antagonistOpposes the effect through a different receptor or pathwayEpinephrine reverses histamine-induced bronchoconstriction and hypotension in anaphylaxis; glucagon vs insulin
Chemical antagonistBinds the drug itselfProtamine–heparin, digoxin immune Fab, idarucizumab–dabigatran, chelators
Spare receptorsMaximal response at less than 100% occupancy; EC50 < KdLow concentrations of an irreversible antagonist first shift the curve right before lowering Emax.
Therapeutic index (TI)TI = TD50 / ED50 (LD50/ED50 in animals). A higher TI means a safer drug. The therapeutic window runs from the minimum effective concentration to the minimum toxic concentration.Narrow-TI drugs that need level monitoring: warfarin (INR), digoxin, lithium, theophylline, phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproate, aminoglycosides, vancomycin, cyclosporine/tacrolimus.
Tachyphylaxis / toleranceA rapid or gradual loss of responseNitrates (needs a nitrate-free interval), ephedrine/amphetamine (depletes stores), opioids

Cholinergic drugs

ClassDrugUse / key fact

Toxicity: "hot as a hare, dry as a bone, red as a beet, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter, full as a flask" (hyperthermia, anhidrosis, flushing, mydriasis/cycloplegia, delirium, urinary retention). Can precipitate acute angle-closure glaucoma.

High-yield (organophosphate or carbamate poisoning, e.g., a farmer, malathion/parathion, or sarin): muscarinic signs are DUMBBELSS (diarrhea, urination, miosis, bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, bradycardia, emesis, lacrimation, salivation, sweating). Nicotinic signs are fasciculations, then weakness and paralysis (including respiratory muscles), plus tachycardia and hypertension from ganglionic stimulation. CNS signs are confusion and seizures. Treatment: decontaminate (remove clothing; protect staff), give atropine titrated to drying of bronchial secretions (muscarinic only), give pralidoxime early, before "aging" of the phosphorylated enzyme (it regenerates AChE, so it helps nicotinic weakness), and give benzodiazepines for seizures. Avoid succinylcholine for intubation, because it is metabolized by the inhibited plasma cholinesterase and paralysis is prolonged.

Nonselective βPropranolol, nadolol, timolol, pindolol (ISA), sotalol (also class III)Essential tremor, thyroid storm, migraine prophylaxis, variceal bleeding prophylaxis (propranolol, nadolol), glaucoma (timolol ↓ aqueous humor). Bronchospasm in asthma.

High-yield (β-blocker adverse effects): bradycardia and AV block, bronchospasm (nonselective agents), masking of hypoglycemic tremor and tachycardia (sweating, which is cholinergic, persists), fatigue and erectile dysfunction, and a possible rise in triglycerides. Overdose: give glucagon (raises cAMP independently of the β receptor), atropine, IV calcium, and high-dose insulin with dextrose.
Exam trap: "epinephrine reversal." After an α-blocker (phentolamine or phenoxybenzamine), epinephrine lowers BP, because unopposed β2 vasodilation remains. Norepinephrine (little β2) gives a smaller pressor response and does not reverse, and phenylephrine's pressor effect is abolished. After a β-blocker, epinephrine raises BP more (unopposed α1) and isoproterenol has no effect. Expect "a drug is given, then an agonist; what happens to BP and HR?" questions.

sections.heading: 7. Biostatistics: evaluating diagnostic tests
sections.html:
Method for every question: draw the 2×2 table with disease in the columns and the test result in the rows, fill it in from the stem (if you are given prevalence, start from a round number such as 1000 or 10,000 people), then compute. Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test (they read down the columns). PPV and NPV depend on prevalence (they read across the rows).

[[figure:ch03-fig05]]
MeasureDefinitionClinical use / mnemonic
SensitivityTP / all diseased: the proportion of diseased people who test positive. 1 − Sn = false-negative rate.SN-N-OUT: a highly sensitive test, if Negative, rules OUT. Use for screening (HIV ELISA/4th-generation Ag/Ab, D-dimer).
SpecificityTN / all non-diseased. 1 − Sp = false-positive rate.SP-P-IN: a highly specific test, if Positive, rules IN. Use for confirmation (HIV-1/2 differentiation assay, biopsy).
PPVTP / all test-positiveRises with prevalence (and with pretest probability)
NPVTN / all test-negativeFalls as prevalence rises
LR+Sn / (1 − Sp)>10 is a strong rule-in. Independent of prevalence.
LR−(1 − Sn) / Sp<0.1 is a strong rule-out
Post-test oddsPretest odds × LROdds = p/(1 − p); probability = odds/(1 + odds)
Accuracy(TP + TN) / total—
Worked example: prevalence 10%, Sn 90%, Sp 80%, population 1000. Diseased = 100: TP 90, FN 10. Non-diseased = 900: TN 720, FP 180. PPV = 90/270 = 33%. NPV = 720/730 = 98.6%. LR+ = 0.9/0.2 = 4.5. The same test at 50% prevalence gives a PPV of 450/550 = 82%. Prevalence changes PPV/NPV, never Sn/Sp.
[[figure:ch03-fig06]]

sections.heading: 8. Measures of disease frequency and risk
sections.html:
MeasureFormulaNotes
IncidenceNew cases during the period / population at risk during the periodExclude people who already have the disease (or are immune) from the denominator
Prevalence (point)Existing cases / total population at that timePrevalence ≈ incidence × average duration (steady state)
Changing prevalence↑ with longer survival without cure (new drugs such as insulin or ART), ↑incidence, immigration of cases. ↓ with cure, rapid death, or ↓incidence (vaccination). A new treatment that prolongs life raises prevalence and leaves incidence unchanged.
Relative risk (RR)Riskexposed / RiskunexposedCohort studies and RCTs. RR = 1 means no association.
Odds ratio (OR)ad / bcCase–control studies; approximates RR when the disease is rare (<10%)
Attributable risk (AR)Riskexp − RiskunexpAttributable risk percent (ARP) = (RR − 1)/RR × 100
Absolute risk reduction (ARR)Control event rate (CER) − experimental event rate (EER)—
Relative risk reduction (RRR)ARR / CER = 1 − RRDrug ads quote RRR because it sounds bigger
Number needed to treat (NNT)1 / ARR (round up)Rates must be decimals: an ARR of 5% = 0.05 gives an NNT of 20
Number needed to harm (NNH)1 / attributable risk (increase in adverse events)Round down (conservative). A larger NNH is safer.
Hazard ratio (HR)Ratio of instantaneous event ratesSurvival analysis (Cox regression)
Case fatality rateDeaths from the disease / people with the disease—
Mortality rateDeaths / total populationInfant mortality: deaths <1 year / live births
Attack rateCases / people exposed (in an outbreak)A form of incidence (for example, food poisoning)
Worked example (RCT): stroke occurs in 8% on placebo and 6% on the drug. ARR = 0.08 − 0.06 = 0.02, so NNT = 1/0.02 = 50. RR = 0.06/0.08 = 0.75, so RRR = 25%. If GI bleeding occurs in 3% on the drug vs 1% on placebo: the absolute risk increase is 0.02, so NNH = 50.

sections.heading: 9. Study designs
sections.html:
[[figure:ch03-fig07]]
DesignStrengthsWeaknesses / bias
Case–controlFast and cheap; good for rare diseases and several exposuresRecall bias, selection of controls; cannot measure incidence
CohortTemporal sequence; incidence and RR; several outcomes; good for rare exposuresExpensive and slow (if prospective); loss to follow-up (attrition bias)
Cross-sectionalPrevalence; surveysCannot establish temporality (chicken-or-egg)
EcologicalUses existing population dataEcological fallacy (group associations may not apply to individuals)
RCTRandomization controls known and unknown confounders; blinding reduces observer biasExpensive; ethical limits; generalizability (strict inclusion criteria)
Crossover trialEach subject is their own control (needs a washout period)Carryover effects
Meta-analysisPools studies, ↑powerLimited by the quality of the included studies; publication bias (funnel plot) and heterogeneity
Clinical trial phaseSubjectsQuestion
Phase 0Very few, micro-dosesPharmacokinetics (exploratory)
Phase ISmall number of healthy volunteers (or patients, in oncology)Is it safe? PK/PD, maximum tolerated dose
Phase IISmall number of patients with the diseaseDoes it work? Efficacy, optimal dose, short-term adverse effects
Phase IIILarge number of patients, randomized against standard of care or placeboIs it better or as good? Needed for FDA approval
Phase IVPost-marketing surveillanceRare or long-term adverse effects (FDA MedWatch/FAERS)

Analysis types: intention-to-treat analyzes patients in the group they were randomized to, regardless of adherence or crossover. It preserves randomization and is preferred for superiority trials. Per-protocol analysis includes only adherent patients and can inflate the effect. A noninferiority trial asks whether the new drug is not worse by more than a prespecified margin. Validity: internal validity means the results are correct for the study population (little bias). External validity (generalizability) means they apply to other populations.

sections.heading: 10. Bias and confounding
sections.html:
BiasDescription / clue in the stemHow to reduce it
Selection bias (sampling)The study population is not representative. Berkson: hospital-based controls. Healthy worker effect: workers are healthier than the general population. Non-response: volunteers differ from people who decline.Random sampling; community controls
Attrition biasLoss to follow-up differs between groups (cohorts, RCTs)Intention-to-treat analysis; aggressive follow-up
Recall biasCases remember exposures better than controls do (for example, mothers of children with birth defects)Use medical records; confirm exposures
Measurement / information biasSystematic error in data collection; misclassificationStandardized, validated instruments
Observer-expectancy (Pygmalion)The researcher's belief influences how outcomes are recordedBlinding (double-blind)
Hawthorne effectSubjects change behavior because they know they are being studiedHard to eliminate; use a control group that is also observed
Lead-time biasScreening detects disease earlier, so survival from diagnosis looks longer although the time of death is unchangedCompare mortality rates, not survival from diagnosis
Length-time biasScreening preferentially detects slowly progressing (indolent) disease, which has a better prognosisRCT randomizing people to screening vs no screening
OverdiagnosisDetection of disease that would never have caused symptoms (for example, some prostate cancers)—
Procedure biasSubjects in different groups are treated differently (more attention)Blinding; placebo
Confounding by indicationSicker patients are more likely to get the treatment, which makes the treatment look harmfulRandomization
Publication biasNegative studies go unpublishedTrial registration (ClinicalTrials.gov); funnel plots in meta-analysis
ConceptDefinitionHow to recognize / control
ConfoundingA third variable linked to both exposure and outcome distorts the association (for example, coffee → lung cancer, confounded by smoking). After stratification, the stratum-specific RRs are similar to each other and differ from the crude RR.Design stage: randomization, restriction, matching. Analysis stage: stratification, multivariable regression. Crossover trials control for patient-level factors.
Effect modification (interaction)The effect of the exposure truly differs between strata of a third variable (for example, OCPs raise VTE risk much more in smokers). This is a real biologic phenomenon, not a bias.The stratum-specific RRs differ from each other. Report them separately; do not "control" it away.

sections.heading: 11. Hypothesis testing, error, and confidence intervals
sections.html:
H0 actually true (no difference)H0 actually false (real difference)
Reject H0 (significant result)Type I error (α): false positive. "Seeing a difference that is not there."Correct: power = 1 − β
Fail to reject H0CorrectType II error (β): false negative. "Missing a real difference."
  • p-value: the probability of obtaining results at least as extreme as those observed if H0 were true. A p-value below α (usually 0.05) is statistically significant. It is not the probability that H0 is true, and it says nothing about clinical importance.
  • Power ↑ with a larger sample size (the factor investigators control most easily), a larger effect size, a larger α, and less variability (smaller SD). A "negative" small study may simply be underpowered (a type II error).
  • Multiple comparisons inflate type I error: with 20 independent tests at α = 0.05, about one will be "significant" by chance. Use a Bonferroni correction (α/number of tests).
  • Standard error of the mean: SEM = SD/√n. 95% CI for a mean = mean ± 1.96 × SEM. The CI narrows as n increases.
  • Interpreting a CI: for a ratio (RR, OR, HR), a 95% CI that includes 1 means p > 0.05 (not significant). For a difference (of means, or ARR), a CI that includes 0 means not significant. If the 95% CIs of two groups do not overlap, the difference is significant. If they overlap, it may or may not be.
  • Normal distribution: ±1 SD contains 68%, ±2 SD 95% (more exactly ±1.96 SD), ±3 SD 99.7%. Each tail beyond 2 SD contains about 2.5%. In a positive (right) skew, mean > median > mode (the tail pulls the mean toward it; example: income). In a negative skew, mean < median < mode. The median is robust to outliers.
  • Precision vs accuracy: precision is reliability or reproducibility; random error reduces it, and a larger n improves it. Accuracy is validity, closeness to the truth; systematic error (bias) reduces it. Inter-rater reliability is measured with the κ statistic.
  • Correlation (r from −1 to +1) shows association, not causation. r² is the proportion of variance explained.
TestUseExample
Two-sample (unpaired) t-testCompares the means of 2 independent groups (continuous outcome)Mean HbA1c on drug vs placebo
Paired t-testThe same subjects measured twice, or matched pairsBP before and after a diet in the same patients
ANOVACompares the means of 3 or more groupsMean LDL with 3 different statins
Chi-square (χ²)Compares proportions of categorical variables% with MI in smokers vs nonsmokers. Use Fisher exact test when expected cell counts are small (<5).
Pearson correlationTwo continuous variables, linear relationshipHeight vs weight. Spearman is the nonparametric (rank-based) version.
Mann–Whitney U / WilcoxonNonparametric equivalents of the unpaired and paired t-testsSkewed data
Linear / logistic regressionContinuous / binary outcome with several predictors (adjusts for confounders)Logistic regression gives an adjusted OR
Kaplan–Meier, log-rank, CoxTime-to-event (survival) analysisCox gives the HR

sections.heading: 12. Epidemiology: prevention and screening
sections.html:
LevelGoalExamples
PrimaryPrevent the disease from occurringVaccination, seat belts, smoking cessation, statin in a patient without ASCVD, folic acid, HIV PrEP
SecondaryDetect early, asymptomatic disease and reduce morbidityScreening: mammography, Pap/HPV testing, colonoscopy, BP screening, LDCT for lung cancer
TertiaryReduce complications of established diseaseCardiac rehabilitation, diabetic foot care, statin after MI, physiotherapy after stroke
QuaternaryProtect patients from overmedicalizationDeprescribing; avoiding unnecessary imaging

Good screening criteria (Wilson–Jungner): an important disease with a detectable preclinical phase, effective early treatment, an acceptable and accurate test (high sensitivity first, then a confirmatory test with high specificity), and cost-effectiveness. Screening is evaluated by its effect on disease-specific mortality, because of lead-time and length-time bias.

USPSTF recommendation (average risk; current as of 2025–2026)Who
Breast cancer: mammography every 2 years (B, 2024 update)Women 40–74
Cervical cancer21–29: cytology every 3 years. 30–65: cytology every 3 years, primary hrHPV every 5 years, or co-testing every 5 years. Stop at 65 after adequate negative screening.
Colorectal cancer45–75 (45–49 is grade B; 50–75 grade A). Colonoscopy every 10 years, FIT yearly, and other options. 76–85: individualize.
Lung cancer: annual low-dose CT50–80 with ≥20 pack-years who currently smoke or quit within 15 years
Abdominal aortic aneurysm: one-time ultrasoundMen 65–75 who have ever smoked (≥100 cigarettes)
Osteoporosis: DXAWomen ≥65, and younger postmenopausal women at increased risk
Prostate cancer: PSAMen 55–69: individual shared decision (C). ≥70: do not screen (D).
HIV / hepatitis CHIV 15–65 (everyone, at least once); HCV 18–79 once
Prediabetes / type 2 diabetesAdults 35–70 with overweight or obesity
HypertensionAdults ≥18 (confirm outside the office: ambulatory or home BP)
Chlamydia / gonorrheaSexually active women ≤24, and older women at increased risk
Depression; anxietyDepression: adolescents 12–18 and all adults. Anxiety: adults ≤64 and children 8–18.
Intimate partner violenceWomen of reproductive age (with referral to support services)

Reportable diseases: the physician reports to the local or state health department (which reports to the CDC); the patient's consent is not required. Examples: HIV/AIDS, TB, syphilis, gonorrhea, chlamydia, hepatitis A/B/C, measles, mumps, rubella, pertussis, meningococcal disease, salmonellosis/shigellosis, Lyme disease, rabies, anthrax, and other potential bioterrorism agents. Outbreak investigation: confirm the diagnosis and the outbreak, write a case definition, find cases (epidemic curve), generate hypotheses, test them (usually with a case–control study), then put control measures in place. A point-source epidemic curve has a single sharp peak.

sections.heading: 13. Ethics: core principles and US law
sections.html:
PrincipleMeaningExam application
AutonomyRespect a competent patient's right to decideA competent adult may refuse any treatment, including life-saving treatment (a Jehovah's Witness refusing blood, a refused amputation)
BeneficenceAct in the patient's best interestAutonomy generally outweighs beneficence when the patient has capacity
Nonmaleficence"First, do no harm"Weigh risks against benefits; doctrine of double effect (opioids for dyspnea or pain at the end of life are acceptable even if they might hasten death, because the intent is symptom relief)
JusticeFair distribution of resources; treat patients equallyDo not refuse care based on insurance status, HIV status, race or other characteristics. EMTALA requires a medical screening exam and stabilization in the emergency department regardless of ability to pay.

Informed consent

  • Elements: a discussion of the diagnosis, the nature of the procedure, its risks, benefits and alternatives (including no treatment), in language the patient understands (with a professional interpreter if needed). The decision must be voluntary (free of coercion), and the patient must have decision-making capacity. Consent can be withdrawn at any time. The physician performing the procedure (or a qualified team member) obtains it; a signature alone is not consent.
  • Exceptions: (1) Emergency with implied consent: an unconscious or incapacitated patient, no surrogate available, and delay would cause serious harm. (2) The patient waives the right to be informed ("Just do whatever you think is best, doctor"). (3) Therapeutic privilege: withholding information when disclosure itself would cause severe, immediate harm. This is very rare; it is almost never the answer, and family wishes alone do not justify it. (4) Lack of capacity, in which case a surrogate gives consent.
  • Research: an IRB approves the study, and participants give informed consent and can withdraw at any time without penalty. The Belmont Report principles are respect for persons, beneficence, and justice.

Decision-making capacity

CapacityCompetence
A clinical judgment made by any physician (a psychiatry consult is not required, but it helps in difficult cases). It is decision-specific and can fluctuate (delirium, intoxication).A legal determination made by a judge. An incompetent person has a court-appointed guardian.

The patient must be able to: (1) communicate a choice (consistently); (2) understand the relevant information; (3) appreciate how it applies to their own situation; and (4) reason about the options in a way consistent with their values. A psychiatric diagnosis, dementia, or a choice the doctor disagrees with does not by itself mean incapacity. Intoxication, delirium, severe depression with hopelessness that distorts reasoning, or psychosis whose delusions bear on the decision can remove capacity. Before calling a decision "irrational," check whether it fits the patient's values.

Minors (under 18 in most states)

  • A parent or legal guardian consents. Exceptions where the minor consents alone (state laws vary; the USMLE convention is): emergencies; emancipated minors (married, in the military, financially independent and living apart, or a parent themselves, for their own care; a pregnant minor consents for her prenatal care and her child's care); and condition-specific care: contraception, STI testing and treatment (including HIV in most states), prenatal care, and substance-use treatment. Many states also allow minors to consent to outpatient mental health care.
  • Abortion: laws vary greatly by state since the 2022 Dobbs decision. Many states require parental consent or notification with a judicial bypass option. USMLE questions focus on counseling and confidentiality rather than specific state law.
  • Keep the adolescent's information confidential as allowed by law, and encourage (but do not require) parental involvement. Interview adolescents alone for part of the visit (HEADSS history).
  • When parents refuse life-saving treatment for a child (for example, a transfusion for the child of Jehovah's Witnesses): in an emergency, treat. If time allows, seek a court order or child protective services involvement. Parents may refuse non-urgent, non-life-threatening care, and they may refuse vaccines (counsel, document, and keep caring for the child).

Confidentiality and HIPAA

  • HIPAA Privacy Rule: protects identifiable health information (PHI). It permits disclosure without the patient's authorization for treatment, payment and health care operations, public health reporting, and legal requirements. Disclose the "minimum necessary." Patients have a right to access and get copies of their own records (generally within 30 days; the physician may not refuse because a bill is unpaid) and to request corrections. Never discuss patients in elevators or cafeterias, or leave detailed voicemails.
  • Family and friends: share information only with the patient's permission. If the patient is present and does not object, sharing is fine. If the patient is incapacitated, share what is in their best interest. Answer "I need your permission to discuss your care with your family."
  • Exceptions to confidentiality (disclosure is required or permitted):
    • Serious, foreseeable harm to an identifiable third party: the Tarasoff duty to protect, by warning the intended victim and/or notifying the police (and considering hospitalization).
    • A patient at imminent risk of suicide: involuntary hold.
    • Child abuse and elder abuse: mandatory reporting on reasonable suspicion; proof is not needed. Report to CPS or Adult Protective Services.
    • Reportable infectious diseases: to the public health department.
    • Gunshot and stab wounds (most states).
    • Impaired drivers (seizures, dementia): reporting laws vary by state. Counsel the patient not to drive and follow the state's law; some states, such as California, mandate physician reporting.
    • Partner notification for HIV/STIs: encourage the patient to tell partners. Health departments do anonymous partner notification. If the patient refuses, the physician may notify the at-risk partner or the health department, depending on state law.
  • Intimate partner violence in adults: generally not mandatory to report (a few states have exceptions). Ask privately, document, assess safety, give resources and a safety plan, and respect the patient's choice.

Advance directives and surrogate decision-making

InstrumentWhat it isKey point
Living willA written statement of which treatments the patient would want or refuse if incapacitatedBinding. Follow it even if the family disagrees.
Durable power of attorney for health care (health care proxy / agent)Names the person who makes decisions if the patient loses capacityRanks above next of kin (including the spouse). The agent uses substituted judgment: what the patient would have wanted, not what the agent wants.
POLST / MOLSTPortable, actionable medical orders for seriously ill patients (CPR, intubation, scope of treatment)Followed by EMS and across settings
DNR / DNI orderNo CPR / no intubationDoes not mean "do not treat": antibiotics, surgery, dialysis and ICU care can continue. DNR orders are reconsidered (not automatically suspended) around surgery.
Oral advance directiveThe patient's clearly stated prior wishes (for example, to the physician)Valid if informed, specific and repeated. Document it.

Surrogate hierarchy if there is no designated agent (it varies by state, but in general): court-appointed guardian → spouse/domestic partner → adult children → parents → adult siblings → other relatives or close friends. Several adult children may need to reach a consensus. The surrogate uses substituted judgment (the patient's values) first. If the patient's wishes are unknown, the surrogate uses the best-interest standard. If the family disagrees or there is a conflict, involve an ethics consultation (after first trying to talk it through). If there is no surrogate and no emergency, involve a court-appointed guardian or follow the institution's process.

  • Withholding and withdrawing treatment are ethically and legally equivalent. Artificial nutrition and hydration are medical treatments that can be refused.
  • Medical aid in dying (physician-assisted death: the patient self-administers a prescribed lethal medication) is legal in about a dozen jurisdictions (for example, Oregon, Washington, California, Colorado, Vermont, New Jersey, and the District of Columbia). Euthanasia (the physician administers it) is illegal in every US state. When a patient asks, first explore their reasons: depression, pain, fear of being a burden.
  • Brain death is legal death. Mechanical support may be discontinued; the family is informed compassionately but does not consent to the declaration. Notify the organ procurement organization; the treating physician does not request donation.
  • Futile treatment: physicians are not obliged to provide physiologically futile interventions. Follow the institutional policy, which includes an ethics consultation.
  • Hospice: Medicare eligibility requires a prognosis of 6 months or less if the disease runs its usual course, and the patient chooses comfort-focused care. Palliative care can be given at any stage, alongside curative treatment.

Other high-yield ethics scenarios (USMLE "best response" logic)

ScenarioBest approach
The family asks you not to tell the patient a cancer diagnosisExplore their reasons and concerns. Then ask the patient how much they want to know and who should be involved. A competent patient has the right to know, and also the right to decline information or delegate it to family.
A patient demands an unnecessary test or antibioticsExplore the patient's concerns and expectations, explain why it is not indicated, and offer an appropriate plan. Do not order it just to please the patient, and do not dismiss them.
Non-adherence to medicationAsk non-judgmentally about barriers (cost, side effects, beliefs, complexity), then simplify the regimen.
Medical errorDisclose promptly and honestly, even if there was no harm (when the error reached the patient): what happened, an apology, the consequences, and what will prevent it in the future. Report it through the institution's safety system. Near misses that never reached the patient are reported internally; disclosing them is not required. Never alter records.
An impaired or incompetent colleague (alcohol on the breath, a surgeon with tremor)Patient safety comes first: remove the colleague from patient care now if there is immediate risk, then report to a supervisor (department chair, chief of staff) or the state physician health program. Do not ignore it, and do not only "talk to them privately."
Gifts from patientsA small, sentimental gift can be accepted. Decline cash or large gifts, and gifts that change the relationship.
Gifts from industryAvoid gifts other than modest items that benefit patients or education. Payments are publicly reported under the Sunshine Act (Open Payments). Disclose conflicts of interest.
Romantic relationship with a patientNever with a current patient. It is unethical with a former patient if the doctor uses trust or knowledge gained in the relationship, and always for psychiatrists. If a patient behaves seductively, set boundaries and use a chaperone. Transfer care if it continues.
Treating yourself or family membersAvoid, except in emergencies or for minor short-term problems.
Conscientious objection (for example, to contraception)You may decline to personally provide a service, but you must inform the patient and refer them in a timely way, and you must not obstruct care. In an emergency, you must provide care.
Patient with limited EnglishUse a professional medical interpreter (in person, by phone, or by video). Do not use family members, especially children, or untrained staff. Title VI of the Civil Rights Act applies.
A patient becomes angry about waitingAcknowledge and apologize for the wait ("I'm sorry you had to wait. I can see that you're frustrated."), then refocus on their care. Do not be defensive or blame others.
A patient asks for your opinion ("What would you do?")Explore their values and give a recommendation grounded in their goals. It is acceptable to give a professional recommendation.
A patient leaving against medical adviceAssess capacity. If the patient has capacity, explain the risks, offer alternatives and follow-up, document, and leave the door open to return. The patient cannot be restrained.
Suspected child abuse when the parents want to leaveReport to CPS. A hospital hold is possible if the child is in danger.
Elder neglect or financial exploitationReport to Adult Protective Services (mandatory in most states).
MalpracticeRequires the "4 Ds": Duty, Dereliction (breach of the standard of care), Damage, and Direct causation. It is civil law, decided on a preponderance of the evidence. The most common cause of lawsuits is poor communication.
Exam trap: answers that "refer to the ethics committee," "obtain a court order," "consult the hospital lawyer," or "call psychiatry to assess capacity" are usually wrong as the first step. The USMLE wants you to talk to the patient or family first, explore, clarify and educate. Choose escalation only after direct communication has failed, or in true emergencies (such as an emergent transfusion for a child).

sections.heading: 14. Communication skills
sections.html:
FrameworkSteps
SPIKES (breaking bad news)Setting: private, seated, uninterrupted, support people present if the patient wishes. Perception: "What is your understanding of why we did the test?" Invitation: "How much detail would you like?" Knowledge: give a warning shot ("I'm afraid I have bad news"), then speak plainly, in small chunks, without jargon. Emotions: pause, use silence, respond with empathy. Strategy and summary: next steps and follow-up.
NURSE (responding to emotion)Name the emotion, Understand, Respect, Support, Explore
Motivational interviewing (stages of change: precontemplation → contemplation → preparation → action → maintenance → relapse)OARS: Open-ended questions, Affirmations, Reflective listening, Summarizing. Elicit the patient's own reasons for change, roll with resistance, and support self-efficacy. In precontemplation, raise awareness without pushing.
Teach-back"To make sure I explained it clearly, can you tell me how you'll take this medicine?" This checks understanding and is essential with low health literacy.
Interview techniqueBegin with open-ended questions, then move to closed ones. Use facilitation, reflection and summarization, and avoid leading questions. Take sexual history in a non-judgmental, inclusive way ("Do you have sex with men, women, or both?"). Ask about the pronouns a patient uses.

sections.heading: 15. Patient safety and quality improvement
sections.html:
ConceptKey points
Swiss cheese modelHarm happens when holes in several layers of defense line up. Look for system failures, not individual blame.
Active vs latent errorsActive error: at the "sharp end," by the frontline worker (giving the wrong drug). Latent error: at the "blunt end," a system design flaw (look-alike vials stored together, understaffing).
Error vs adverse event vs near missAn adverse event is harm from medical care; it may or may not involve an error. A near miss is an error caught before it reached the patient.
Sentinel eventAn unexpected event causing death or serious harm (wrong-site surgery, a retained foreign object). It requires a root cause analysis (Joint Commission). "Never events" are serious, preventable events that should never happen.
Root cause analysis (RCA)Retrospective: after the event, a team finds the system causes (fishbone/Ishikawa diagram, the "5 whys").
Failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA)Prospective: identifies the ways a process could fail before it is put in place, and prioritizes them.
Just cultureDistinguishes human error (console the person), at-risk behavior (coach them) and reckless behavior (discipline). Non-punitive reporting increases reporting.
Hierarchy of interventions (strongest to weakest)Forcing functions and physical constraints (enteral connectors that cannot fit IV lines), automation and computerized order entry with alerts, standardization and simplification (removing concentrated KCl from wards), checklists and double checks, and finally education, training, policies and warnings (weakest).
PDSA cyclePlan (aim, prediction), Do (a small-scale test), Study (analyze the data), Act (adopt, adapt, or abandon). The Model for Improvement asks three questions: What are we trying to accomplish? How will we know a change is an improvement? What changes can we make?
Quality measures (Donabedian)Structure: resources (nurse-to-patient ratio, EHR). Process: what is done (% of patients with diabetes who get an annual HbA1c or foot exam). Outcome: the result for patients (mortality, HbA1c control, infection rate). Balancing measure: unintended effects elsewhere (faster discharges vs readmission rates).
Data toolsRun chart and control chart (variation over time: common-cause vs special-cause); Pareto chart (the 80/20 rule, where the few largest causes are targeted first); fishbone diagram; process map (flowchart).
Communication toolsI-PASS handoffs (Illness severity, Patient summary, Action list, Situation awareness/contingency, Synthesis by receiver); SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation); closed-loop communication and read-back of verbal orders and critical lab values; surgical "time-out" (Universal Protocol); WHO surgical safety checklist.
Medication safetyMedication reconciliation at every transition of care. Avoid dangerous abbreviations: "U" (write "units"), trailing zeros ("1.0 mg" can be misread as 10 mg; write "1 mg"), and a missing leading zero (write "0.5 mg," not ".5 mg"). Watch for look-alike/sound-alike drugs (use tall-man lettering).
Cognitive biases in diagnosisAnchoring (sticking with the initial impression), availability (a recent memorable case), premature closure, confirmation bias, framing, diagnostic momentum, and the posterior probability error. Counter them with a deliberate differential diagnosis and a "diagnostic time-out."
Human factorsFatigue, alarm fatigue, interruptions, and workload. Duty-hour limits (ACGME): 80 hours per week averaged over 4 weeks.
Infection prevention bundlesCLABSI: hand hygiene, maximal barrier precautions, chlorhexidine skin antisepsis, avoiding the femoral site, and daily review of whether the line is still needed. CAUTI: remove catheters early.
High-yield: when asked for the "best way to prevent recurrence" of an error, pick the system-level fix that is strongest in the hierarchy (a forcing function or standardization) over "retrain staff" or "discipline the nurse." When asked "what kind of measure is X?", ask whether X counts what was done (a process measure) or what happened to the patient (an outcome measure).

title: Step 1 · General Pathology, Hematology & Oncology
meta: Exam: Step 1 · Systems covered: General principles of pathology (cell injury, inflammation, repair, neoplasia), Blood & lymphoreticular system, Heme/Onc pharmacology · Approx study time: 4–5 days (notes 2.5 days + questions/review 2 days)

sections.heading: Overview
sections.html:
From NEET PG to USMLE

  • Mechanism over list. NEET PG asks "which is a feature of X"; USMLE gives a vignette and asks the step behind the finding (e.g., not "hepcidin rises in ACD" but "the patient's low serum iron despite high ferritin is due to internalization of which transporter?" → ferroportin).
  • Drug names. USMLE uses US generic names: acetaminophen (not paracetamol), epinephrine (not adrenaline), alteplase/tenecteplase, apixaban/rivaroxaban, enoxaparin. Brand names are rarely used in stems.
  • Units. Hb in g/dL, MCV in fL (μm³), platelets as /mm³ (e.g., 250,000/mm³), ferritin in ng/mL, bilirubin in mg/dL, creatinine in mg/dL, calcium in mg/dL (normal 8.5–10.5). Memorize the US lab reference sheet provided on the exam, but do not depend on it for speed.
  • Classification. WHO 5th edition (2022) / ICC terminology is now used in USMLE-style resources: "AML with PML::RARA" (APL), "B-lymphoblastic leukemia," "plasma cell myeloma." FAB "M3" still appears in older teaching — know both.
  • Ethnicity clues. US vignettes use ancestry as a probabilistic clue: sickle cell (African American), α-thal trait with cis deletion (Southeast Asian), β-thal (Mediterranean, South Asian), G6PD (African, Mediterranean). For an Indian graduate, note that β-thal trait and iron deficiency coexist commonly — USMLE usually gives a "clean" single diagnosis.
  • Transfusion and anticoagulation practice follows US norms: DOACs (apixaban) are first-line for most VTE and nonvalvular AF; warfarin is reserved for mechanical valves, antiphospholipid syndrome, and severe CKD scenarios; reversal agents (idarucizumab, andexanet alfa, 4-factor PCC) are tested.

sections.heading: 1. Cellular adaptation and injury
sections.html:
AdaptationDefinitionClassic examples
Hypertrophy↑ cell size (↑ structural proteins); permanent cells (cardiac, skeletal muscle) can only do thisLVH in hypertension; skeletal muscle with exercise
Hyperplasia↑ cell number (labile/stable cells)Endometrial hyperplasia (unopposed estrogen, ↑ risk of carcinoma); BPH (not premalignant)
Atrophy↓ size/number via ubiquitin–proteasome degradation and autophagyDenervation, ↓ blood supply, ↓ endocrine stimulation, pressure (hydronephrosis)
MetaplasiaOne differentiated cell type replaced by another (reprogramming of stem cells); reversibleBarrett esophagus (squamous → columnar with goblet cells); bronchial squamous metaplasia in smokers; vitamin A deficiency → keratomalacia; myositis ossificans (mesenchymal)
DysplasiaDisordered growth (loss of polarity, pleomorphism, ↑ N:C ratio); reversible but premalignantCIN, Barrett with dysplasia

Cell injury: reversible vs irreversible

Reversible (↓ ATP)Irreversible (membrane damage)
Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase failure → cellular swelling (earliest visible change), hydropic changePlasma membrane damage → enzyme leak (troponin, CK-MB, ALT/AST)
↑ Anaerobic glycolysis → ↓ pH → nuclear chromatin clumpingMitochondrial membrane damage → cytochrome c release; large amorphous (flocculent) Ca²⁺-rich mitochondrial densities
Ribosome detachment from RER → ↓ protein synthesisLysosomal membrane rupture → autolysis
Membrane blebbing, myelin figures, fatty changeNuclear: pyknosis (condensation) → karyorrhexis (fragmentation) → karyolysis (dissolution)

Hypoxia/ischemia: most vulnerable cells — neurons (3–5 min; hippocampal CA1 pyramidal cells, Purkinje cells, cortical layers 3, 5, 6 → laminar necrosis), myocardium (subendocardium, 20–40 min for irreversibility), renal proximal tubule (straight segment) and medullary thick ascending limb, hepatocytes zone 3 (centrilobular). Watershed areas: ACA/MCA and MCA/PCA borders; splenic flexure (SMA/IMA) and rectosigmoid (Sudeck point).

Free radical injury: generated by radiation (hydrolysis of water → hydroxyl radical, the most damaging), drug metabolism (acetaminophen → NAPQI; CCl₄ → CCl₃•), Fenton reaction (Fe²⁺ + H₂O₂ → •OH; hemochromatosis, Wilson Cu), oxidative burst, reperfusion. Damage: lipid peroxidation, protein oxidation, DNA breaks. Defense: superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione peroxidase (needs reduced glutathione, regenerated by NADPH from G6PD), vitamins A, C, E.

Ischemia–reperfusion injury: restoring flow → burst of ROS, Ca²⁺ influx (contraction band necrosis in myocardium), neutrophil and complement influx. Explains rising troponin and arrhythmias after PCI or thrombolysis.

Pathologic calcification

DystrophicMetastatic
Serum Ca²⁺/phosphateNormalElevated (hypercalcemia, hyperphosphatemia — CKD, hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D toxicity, sarcoidosis, milk-alkali)
TissueDamaged/necrotic tissueNormal tissue, especially interstitium of lungs, kidneys (nephrocalcinosis), gastric mucosa, systemic arteries (all lose acid → alkaline interstitium)
ExamplesAtherosclerotic plaques, damaged/aortic valves (calcific aortic stenosis), TB caseation, fat necrosis, psammoma bodies (Papillary thyroid, Serous ovarian cystadenocarcinoma, Meningioma, Mesothelioma), CREST calcinosisCalciphylaxis in end-stage renal disease

sections.heading: 2. Necrosis and apoptosis
sections.html:
TypeMechanism / appearanceClassic sites
CoagulativeProtein denaturation > enzymatic digestion; cell outlines ("ghost cells") preserved; eosinophilic cytoplasmIschemic infarct of any solid organ except brain (heart, kidney, spleen); wedge-shaped
LiquefactiveEnzymatic digestion (neutrophil or microglial enzymes) → fluidBrain infarct, abscess, pancreatic pseudocyst contents
CaseousCoagulative + liquefactive; cheesy, granular, acellular center ringed by granulomaTB, systemic fungi (Histoplasma, Coccidioides), Nocardia
Fat (enzymatic)Lipase releases fatty acids → bind Ca²⁺ (saponification) → chalky white, basophilic on H&EAcute pancreatitis (peripancreatic fat)
Fat (traumatic)Trauma to adipose; no lipase; can calcify → mimic carcinoma on mammogramBreast
FibrinoidImmune complex deposition or plasma protein leak in vessel walls; bright pinkMalignant hypertension, vasculitis (PAN), preeclampsia, rheumatic nodules
GangrenousDry = coagulative ischemia of a limb; wet = superimposed infection (liquefactive)Distal limbs (diabetes, PAD), GI tract

Apoptosis

ATP-dependent programmed death without inflammation. Morphology: cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation (pyknosis), membrane blebbing, apoptotic bodies, eosinophilic cytoplasm; DNA laddering (fragments in multiples of ~180 bp) on gel. Effector caspases (3, 6, 7) cleave cytoskeleton and activate endonucleases. Phosphatidylserine flips to the outer leaflet → "eat-me" signal for macrophages.

PathwayTriggerKey moleculesExam hooks
Intrinsic (mitochondrial)DNA damage, growth factor withdrawal, hypoxia, misfolded proteinsp53 → ↑ BAX/BAK (pro-apoptotic, form pores) vs BCL-2/BCL-xL (anti-apoptotic, block cytochrome c release); cytochrome c + APAF-1 → apoptosome → caspase-9t(14;18) BCL-2 overexpression → follicular lymphoma; venetoclax (BCL-2 inhibitor) for CLL/AML; endometrial shedding; thymocyte deletion
Extrinsic (death receptor)Fas ligand (CD95L) binds Fas (CD95); TNF binds TNFR1FADD → caspase-8 → caspase-3Negative selection of thymocytes; defective Fas → autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome (ALPS, ↑ double-negative CD4⁻CD8⁻ T cells)
Cytotoxic T/NK cellsTarget with viral or tumor antigen on MHC IPerforin + granzyme B → directly activates caspasesViral hepatitis Councilman bodies (apoptotic hepatocytes)
High-yield: Other regulated death pathways — necroptosis (RIPK1/RIPK3/MLKL; caspase-independent, inflammatory), pyroptosis (inflammasome → caspase-1 → IL-1β and gasdermin pores), ferroptosis (iron-dependent lipid peroxidation). Autophagy is a survival mechanism under nutrient deprivation (lipofuscin = residual bodies, "wear-and-tear" pigment).

sections.heading: 3. Inflammation
sections.html:
Acute inflammation

Innate response (minutes–days); neutrophil-predominant; triggered by PAMPs (LPS → TLR4/CD14; flagellin → TLR5; dsRNA → TLR3) and DAMPs (uric acid, ATP, HMGB1) via toll-like receptors and the NLRP3 inflammasome.

  • Vascular phase: transient arteriolar vasoconstriction → vasodilation (histamine, PGI₂, PGE₂, NO) → ↑ permeability (histamine, bradykinin, LTC₄/D₄/E₄, C3a/C5a) by endothelial contraction in postcapillary venules → exudate (protein-rich, specific gravity > 1.020) → stasis.
  • Cellular phase: margination → rolling → tight adhesion → transmigration → chemotaxis → phagocytosis → killing (Figure 1).
  • Outcomes: resolution (lipoxins, resolvins, IL-10, TGF-β), abscess, fibrosis, or chronic inflammation.
[[figure:ch04-fig01]]

Phagocyte killing and defects

Oxygen-dependent killing: NADPH oxidase (O₂ → O₂⁻; respiratory burst) → superoxide dismutase (→ H₂O₂) → myeloperoxidase (H₂O₂ + Cl⁻ → HOCl, bleach). Oxygen-independent: lysozyme, major basic protein, defensins.

DisorderDefectClinical cluesLab
Chronic granulomatous diseaseNADPH oxidase (X-linked CYBB/gp91phox most common)Recurrent infections with catalase-positive organisms (S. aureus, Burkholderia cepacia, Serratia, Nocardia, Aspergillus); granulomasAbnormal dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow cytometry (↓ fluorescence); nitroblue tetrazolium stays colorless. Tx: TMP-SMX + itraconazole prophylaxis, IFN-γ, HSCT
Myeloperoxidase deficiencyMPOUsually asymptomatic; Candida infections in diabeticsNormal DHR (burst intact)
Chédiak–HigashiLYST (lysosomal trafficking)Partial albinism, peripheral neuropathy, recurrent pyogenic infections, bleedingGiant granules in neutrophils, pancytopenia

Mediators

MediatorSourceActions
HistamineMast cells, basophils, plateletsArteriolar dilation, venular permeability (immediate transient response)
BradykininKallikrein cleaves HMWKPermeability, vasodilation, pain; degraded by ACE (ACE-inhibitor angioedema; C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency → hereditary angioedema)
PGI₂, PGD₂, PGE₂, PGF₂αCOX pathwayVasodilation, ↑ permeability (with others); PGE₂ → fever and pain; PGI₂ inhibits platelets
TXA₂Platelets (COX-1)Vasoconstriction, platelet aggregation (blocked by aspirin)
LTB₄5-lipoxygenaseNeutrophil chemotaxis
LTC₄, D₄, E₄ (cysteinyl)5-lipoxygenaseBronchoconstriction, vasoconstriction, permeability (zileuton blocks 5-LOX; montelukast blocks receptor)
C3a, C5aComplementAnaphylatoxins (mast cell degranulation); C5a also chemotactic. C3b = opsonin; C5b-9 = MAC
IL-1, TNF-α, IL-6MacrophagesFever (via PGE₂ in hypothalamus), acute-phase response (IL-6 → hepatocytes), endothelial activation; TNF → cachexia, septic shock
IL-8 (CXCL8)Macrophages, endotheliumNeutrophil chemotaxis
Nitric oxideiNOS in macrophages, eNOSVasodilation, microbicidal
High-yield: Acute-phase reactants (IL-6 driven). Up: CRP (opsonin), ferritin, fibrinogen (↑ ESR via rouleaux), hepcidin, serum amyloid A, haptoglobin, procalcitonin, complement. Down ("negative"): albumin, transferrin, transthyretin (prealbumin). So in inflammation, TIBC (≈ transferrin) is low.

Chronic inflammation and granulomas

Mononuclear cells (macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells), tissue destruction, and attempted repair (fibrosis, angiogenesis). Causes: persistent infection, autoimmunity, foreign material. Granuloma formation: macrophage presents antigen on MHC II → Th1 cell; macrophage IL-12 → Th1 differentiation; Th1 IFN-γ → macrophages become epithelioid cells and fuse into Langhans (peripheral horseshoe nuclei) or foreign-body giant cells; TNF-α maintains granulomas (anti-TNF therapy → reactivation TB — screen with IGRA before starting). Noncaseating: sarcoidosis, Crohn disease, berylliosis, cat-scratch (stellate), foreign body, GPA; caseating: TB, fungi.

sections.heading: 4. Tissue repair and wound healing
sections.html:
PhaseTimeKey events and mediators
Inflammatory0–3 daysPlatelet plug, fibrin; neutrophils (day 1–2) then macrophages (day 2–3), PDGF, TGF-β
ProliferativeDay 3 – weeksGranulation tissue (fibroblasts, new capillaries via VEGF/FGF, type III collagen); epithelialization; myofibroblast wound contraction
Remodeling (maturation)1 week – 6+ monthsType III → type I collagen (metalloproteinases need zinc); tensile strength ≈ 70–80% of original at 3 months and never fully regained
  • Cell types: labile (continuously dividing: skin, GI mucosa, bone marrow, hair follicles) · stable/quiescent (G0, can re-enter: hepatocytes, PCT cells, fibroblasts) · permanent (neurons, cardiac and skeletal muscle, RBCs, lens) → repair by scar.
  • Growth factors: VEGF (angiogenesis), FGF-2 (angiogenesis, fibroblast), PDGF (fibroblast/smooth muscle chemotaxis and growth), TGF-β (fibrosis, collagen synthesis, anti-inflammatory), EGF (epithelial), metalloproteinases (remodeling).
  • Impairments: vitamin C deficiency (prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase cofactor → weak collagen triple helix; perifollicular hemorrhage, corkscrew hairs, gum bleeding), zinc deficiency (metalloproteinase cofactor; also dysgeusia, acrodermatitis), copper deficiency (lysyl oxidase cross-linking), glucocorticoids, diabetes, infection (most common cause of delayed healing), ischemia, foreign body.
  • Abnormal scars: hypertrophic — excess, parallel collagen confined to wound borders, often regresses; keloid — excess disorganized type I and III collagen extending beyond borders, earlobes/chest/shoulders, more common in people with darker skin, recurs after excision.

sections.heading: 5. Amyloidosis
sections.html:
Misfolded proteins form β-pleated sheet fibrils that deposit extracellularly. Congo red → apple-green birefringence under polarized light. Tissue diagnosis: abdominal fat pad aspirate, rectal or target-organ biopsy; mass spectrometry or immunohistochemistry types the protein (critical for therapy).

TypePrecursor proteinSettingClues / treatment
AL (primary)Ig light chain (λ > κ)Plasma cell dyscrasia (myeloma, MGUS)Nephrotic syndrome, restrictive cardiomyopathy (low-voltage ECG + thick walls), macroglossia, periorbital purpura ("raccoon eyes"), carpal tunnel, hepatomegaly, neuropathy. Tx: daratumumab–bortezomib–cyclophosphamide–dexamethasone, ASCT
AA (secondary)Serum amyloid A (acute-phase reactant)Chronic inflammation: RA, IBD, bronchiectasis, osteomyelitis, familial Mediterranean feverKidney most common (nephrotic). Tx: control the underlying disease (colchicine for FMF)
ATTR wild-type (senile systemic)Normal transthyretinOlder men (> 70)HFpEF/restrictive cardiomyopathy, bilateral carpal tunnel, lumbar spinal stenosis, biceps tendon rupture; Tc-99m PYP scan uptake; Tx: tafamidis (TTR stabilizer)
ATTR hereditaryMutant transthyretin (e.g., V122I common in African Americans)ADCardiomyopathy and/or familial amyloid polyneuropathy; Tx: tafamidis, patisiran/vutrisiran (siRNA), inotersen
Aβ2Mβ2-microglobulinLong-term hemodialysisCarpal tunnel, shoulder arthropathy (not filtered by dialysis membranes)
AβAmyloid precursor protein (APP, chr 21)Alzheimer disease, cerebral amyloid angiopathyLobar hemorrhage in elderly; early Alzheimer in Down syndrome
AIAPPAmylinType 2 diabetesIslet deposits
ACal (localized)CalcitoninMedullary thyroid carcinomaAmyloid stroma in tumor
AANFAtrial natriuretic factorIsolated atrial amyloid (aging)Usually incidental
Exam trap: An elderly man with HFpEF, low-voltage ECG, and a history of bilateral carpal tunnel release has normal serum free light chains → think wild-type ATTR, not AL. Always exclude AL (serum/urine immunofixation + free light chains) before calling it ATTR.

sections.heading: 6. Neoplasia
sections.html:
Definitions and behavior

  • Neoplasm: monoclonal, autonomous proliferation (X-inactivation studies: G6PD isoform in leiomyoma = monoclonal). Benign: well differentiated, slow, encapsulated, no metastasis. Malignant: anaplasia, invasion, metastasis.
  • Carcinoma in situ: full-thickness dysplasia, intact basement membrane. Invasion requires loss of E-cadherin (cell–cell), collagenases (MMPs; type IV collagen of basement membrane), laminin and integrin binding.
  • Grade = degree of differentiation (histology). Stage = TNM extent (spread) — stage has more prognostic value. Metastasis (M) is the single most important prognostic factor in most solid tumors.
  • Routes: carcinomas → lymphatics (except renal cell carcinoma → renal vein, HCC → hepatic vein, follicular thyroid and choriocarcinoma → hematogenous); sarcomas → hematogenous.
  • Most common metastatic sites: brain (lung > breast > melanoma > RCC > GI; multiple well-circumscribed lesions at gray–white junction), liver (colon > stomach > pancreas > breast > lung), bone (prostate, breast > lung, thyroid, kidney). Metastases are more common than primary tumors in brain, liver, and bone.
  • Bone lesions: lytic — myeloma, RCC, thyroid, NSCLC, melanoma; blastic — prostate, SCLC, breast (mixed), Hodgkin lymphoma.

Hallmarks of cancer (with drug targets)

HallmarkMechanismExample / drug
Self-sufficiency in growth signalsOncogenic receptor tyrosine kinases, RAS, MYCHER2 amplification (trastuzumab); EGFR mutation (osimertinib)
Insensitivity to anti-growth signalsLoss of RB, p16 (CDKN2A), TGF-β pathway (SMAD4)CDK4/6 inhibitors (palbociclib) in ER⁺ breast cancer
Evasion of apoptosisBCL-2 overexpression, TP53 lossVenetoclax
Limitless replicationTelomerase reactivation (TERT)—
Sustained angiogenesisVEGF, FGF; VHL loss → HIF-1α stabilizationBevacizumab, sunitinib
Invasion and metastasisE-cadherin loss (CDH1; diffuse gastric, lobular breast), MMPs—
Immune evasionPD-L1 expression, ↓ MHC IPembrolizumab, nivolumab (PD-1); ipilimumab (CTLA-4)
Reprogrammed metabolismWarburg effect: aerobic glycolysis (basis of FDG-PET)IDH1/2 mutation → 2-hydroxyglutarate (ivosidenib, enasidenib)
Genomic instabilityMismatch repair (Lynch) or BRCA (homologous recombination) defectsPARP inhibitors (olaparib) for BRCA; MSI-high → checkpoint inhibitor response

Oncogenes (gain of function; one allele sufficient)

GeneProductAssociated tumors

sections.heading: 7. Hematopoiesis and blood cells
sections.html:
• Sites: yolk sac (weeks 3–8) → liver (weeks 6–birth; main site in midgestation) → spleen (weeks 10–28) → bone marrow (week 18 onward; sole site after birth). "Young Liver Synthesizes Blood." Extramedullary hematopoiesis recurs in liver/spleen in myelofibrosis and severe hemolysis (β-thal major → "chipmunk" facies, crew-cut skull).
  • Lineages: hematopoietic stem cell (CD34⁺) → common myeloid progenitor (→ erythrocytes, megakaryocytes, granulocytes, monocytes, mast cells) and common lymphoid progenitor (→ B, T, NK cells).
  • Growth factors: EPO (renal peritubular interstitial cells; hypoxia → HIF), TPO (liver), G-CSF (filgrastim), GM-CSF (sargramostim), IL-3, IL-5 (eosinophils), IL-7 (lymphoid).
  • Hemoglobin switching: embryonic (ζ₂ε₂, Gower) → HbF (α₂γ₂; higher O₂ affinity because it binds 2,3-BPG poorly) → HbA (α₂β₂, ~97% adult) and HbA₂ (α₂δ₂, ~2.5%). β-chain disorders appear at ~6 months as HbF falls.
CellKey features
RBCBiconcave, 120-day life span, glycolysis only (no mitochondria), HMP shunt for NADPH; Cl⁻/HCO₃⁻ exchanger (band 3); reticulocytes (bluish, RNA) circulate 1 day
PlateletMegakaryocyte fragment, 8–10 days; α-granules (vWF, fibrinogen, fibronectin, PF4), dense granules (ADP, Ca²⁺, serotonin); ~1/3 sequestered in spleen
NeutrophilMultilobed nucleus; specific granules (lactoferrin, lysozyme, ALP), azurophilic (MPO, elastase); hypersegmented (≥ 5–6 lobes) in B12/folate deficiency; band forms ↑ in acute infection ("left shift")
Monocyte → macrophageKidney-shaped nucleus; CD14; activated by IFN-γ; LPS binds CD14/TLR4
EosinophilBilobed, major basic protein; ↑ in "PACCMAN": parasites (invasive helminths), asthma, Churg–Strauss (EGPA), chronic adrenal insufficiency, myeloid neoplasms, allergy, neoplasm (Hodgkin)
BasophilHistamine, heparin, LTs; ↑ in CML (basophilia is a clue)
Mast cellTissue; IgE (FcεRI) cross-linking → degranulation; tryptase marker; cromolyn stabilizes
LymphocyteB (CD19, CD20, CD21 = EBV receptor), T (CD3, CD4/CD8), NK (CD16, CD56)
Plasma cell"Clock-face" chromatin, perinuclear Golgi halo, CD138

sections.heading: 8. Anemias
sections.html:
First step: MCV and reticulocyte response. Reticulocyte production index (RPI) = corrected retic % (retic % × Hct/45) ÷ maturation factor (1 at Hct 45, 1.5 at 35, 2 at 25, 2.5 at 15). RPI > 2 → adequate marrow response (hemolysis/blood loss); < 2 → hypoproliferative.

[[figure:ch04-fig02]]

Microcytic anemias

DisorderMechanismKey findingsTreatment
Iron deficiencyBlood loss (menses; GI loss in men and postmenopausal women = colon cancer until proven otherwise), ↓ intake, ↓ absorption (celiac, gastrectomy, PPI), ↑ demand (pregnancy). Iron absorbed as Fe²⁺ in duodenum via DMT1; exported by ferroportin↓ ferritin (most sensitive and specific; < 30 ng/mL), ↑ TIBC, ↓ saturation, ↑ RDW (earliest), ↑ free erythrocyte protoporphyrin, thrombocytosis; pica (pagophagia), koilonychia, angular cheilitis, glossitis. Plummer–Vinson: + esophageal websOral ferrous sulfate (every-other-day dosing improves absorption by ↓ hepcidin surge); IV iron if intolerance or malabsorption; find the source (colonoscopy/EGD)
Anemia of chronic disease (inflammation)IL-6 → ↑ hepcidin → ferroportin internalized and degraded → iron trapped in macrophages/enterocytes; ↓ EPO response↓ serum iron, ↓ TIBC, normal/↑ ferritin; usually normocyticTreat underlying disease; ESA in CKD
α-thalassemiaGene deletion (4 α genes, chr 16)1 deleted: silent carrier; 2: trait (cis in Asians → risk of Hb Barts offspring; trans in Africans); 3: HbH disease (β₄, Heinz-like inclusions); 4: Hb Barts (γ₄) → hydrops fetalisTrait: none (avoid iron); HbH: transfusions as needed, folate
β-thalassemiaPoint mutations (splice site, promoter) chr 11 → ↓ (β⁺) or absent (β⁰) β-chains; excess α-chains precipitate → ineffective erythropoiesisMinor: ↑ HbA₂ (> 3.5%), mild microcytosis, ↑ RBC count. Major: symptoms at 6 months, ↑↑ HbF, hepatosplenomegaly, bone expansion, iron overloadMajor: chronic transfusion + chelation (deferoxamine, deferasirox, deferiprone), luspatercept, HSCT; gene therapy (betibeglogene)
Sideroblastic anemiaDefect in heme synthesis: X-linked ALAS2 (most common congenital), alcohol, lead, vitamin B6 deficiency (isoniazid), copper deficiency, zinc excess, MDS↑ iron, ↑ ferritin, ↓ TIBC, ↑ saturation; ringed sideroblasts; basophilic stipplingPyridoxine (B6 is ALA synthase cofactor); remove toxin
Lead poisoningInhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase → ↑ ALA, ↑ protoporphyrin (zinc protoporphyrin); also inhibits rRNA degradationCoarse basophilic stippling, lead lines on gums (Burton) and metaphyses, encephalopathy, wrist/foot drop, abdominal colic; old paint (pre-1978 housing), batteries, ammunition, ayurvedic remediesSuccimer (children, mild); dimercaprol + CaEDTA (severe/encephalopathy); remove source
[[figure:ch04-fig03]]
Exam trap: In a patient with RA or IBD, ferritin can be "normal" (e.g., 60 ng/mL) despite true iron deficiency because ferritin rises with inflammation. Ferritin < 100 ng/mL with transferrin saturation < 20% suggests combined iron deficiency + ACD; soluble transferrin receptor is ↑ in iron deficiency but normal in pure ACD.

Macrocytic anemias

Folate deficiencyVitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency
CausesPoor diet (alcohol use disorder, elderly), pregnancy, hemolysis (↑ demand), drugs (methotrexate, TMP, phenytoin), stores last ~3 monthsPernicious anemia (anti-intrinsic factor and anti-parietal cell antibodies; ↑ gastric cancer risk), gastrectomy, terminal ileal disease (Crohn, resection), Diphyllobothrium latum, strict vegan diet, metformin, PPIs, nitrous oxide; stores last years
Homocysteine↑↑
Methylmalonic acidNormal↑ (B12 is cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase)
Neurologic findingsNoneSubacute combined degeneration (dorsal columns, lateral corticospinal tracts, peripheral nerves) from abnormal myelin; dementia
TreatmentOral folic acidIM or high-dose oral B12. Folate alone corrects the anemia but NOT (and may unmask/worsen) the neurologic damage

Orotic aciduria: AR deficiency of UMP synthase → megaloblastic anemia refractory to B12/folate, orotic acid crystals in urine, no hyperammonemia (vs OTC deficiency) → treat with uridine triacetate.

Normocytic, hypoproliferative anemias

  • Aplastic anemia: pancytopenia + hypocellular fatty marrow; causes — T-cell–mediated autoimmune (most), drugs (chloramphenicol, carbamazepine, benzene, alkylators), viruses (parvovirus B19, EBV, HIV, seronegative hepatitis), Fanconi anemia (DNA repair, short stature, absent thumbs/radii, café-au-lait). Tx: HSCT (young) or ATG + cyclosporine + eltrombopag.
  • Pure red cell aplasia: thymoma, parvovirus B19 (aplastic crisis in chronic hemolysis — sickle cell, HS; retic count near zero), Diamond–Blackfan (congenital, macrocytic, triphalangeal thumbs).
  • CKD: ↓ EPO → normocytic; burr cells; treat with ESA (epoetin, darbepoetin) once iron repleted; target Hb ~10–11 g/dL (higher targets ↑ stroke and thrombosis).
  • Myelophthisic anemia: marrow replaced by tumor, fibrosis, granulomas → leukoerythroblastic smear (nucleated RBCs, immature myeloid cells, teardrops).

sections.heading: 10. Hemostasis and the coagulation cascade
sections.html:
Primary hemostasis (platelet plug): endothelial injury → transient vasoconstriction (endothelin) → vWF binds exposed subendothelial collagen → platelets adhere via GpIb → activation (ADP via P2Y12, TXA₂, thrombin via PAR-1) → shape change, granule release → GpIIb/IIIa binds fibrinogen → aggregation. Secondary hemostasis (fibrin): tissue factor–VIIa initiates; thrombin amplifies (activates V, VIII, XI, XIII, platelets) → fibrin cross-linked by XIIIa.

[[figure:ch04-fig05]]

Interpreting coagulation tests

DisorderPlatelet countBleeding time / PFAPTaPTTNotes
Hemophilia A / BNNN↑Mixing study corrects (unless inhibitor)
von Willebrand diseaseN↑NN or ↑↓ vWF:Ag, ↓ ristocetin cofactor activity
Vitamin K deficiency / warfarinNN↑ (first)N or ↑Factor VII has shortest half-life (~6 h)

DIC↓↑↑↑↓ fibrinogen, ↑ D-dimer, schistocytes

Aspirin / uremiaN↑NNUremia: dysfunctional platelets (desmopressin helps)

Bleeding disorders

  • Platelet-type bleeding: mucocutaneous — petechiae, epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia, bleeding immediately after surgery. Coagulation-factor bleeding: deep — hemarthroses, muscle hematomas, delayed bleeding after procedures.
  • Hemophilia A (factor VIII, X-linked; ~1/3 de novo), B (factor IX, Christmas disease), C (factor XI, AR, Ashkenazi Jewish). Tx: recombinant factor; emicizumab (bispecific antibody that bridges IXa and X, mimicking VIIIa) for hemophilia A prophylaxis; desmopressin for mild hemophilia A; gene therapy (valoctocogene, etranacogene). Inhibitors → bypassing agents (recombinant VIIa, aPCC).
  • von Willebrand disease (most common inherited bleeding disorder, AD; type 1 = quantitative). vWF carries and stabilizes factor VIII. Tx: desmopressin (releases vWF from endothelial Weibel–Palade bodies), vWF concentrate, antifibrinolytics (aminocaproic acid, TXA), OCPs for menorrhagia. Acquired vWD: aortic stenosis (Heyde syndrome — angiodysplasia + GI bleed), MPNs, Wilms tumor.
  • Vitamin K deficiency: newborns (sterile gut, poor placental transfer, low breast milk K → give IM vitamin K at birth), antibiotics, malabsorption (fat-soluble), warfarin.
  • Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP): IgG anti-GpIIb/IIIa → splenic destruction. Children: post-viral, self-limited. Adults: women, chronic, associated with SLE, HIV, HCV, H. pylori. Diagnosis of exclusion. Tx (if bleeding or platelets < 30,000/mm³): glucocorticoids, IVIG (fast rise, before surgery), anti-D, TPO receptor agonists (romiplostim, eltrombopag), rituximab, splenectomy.
  • DIC: widespread activation of coagulation → consumption of platelets and factors. Causes: sepsis (gram-negative), trauma, obstetric (abruptio, amniotic fluid embolism, retained fetus), APL, adenocarcinoma, snake bites, transfusion reaction. Tx: treat cause; replace platelets/cryoprecipitate/FFP if bleeding.

Thrombotic microangiopathies

TTPHUS (typical, STEC)Atypical HUS
Mechanism↓ ADAMTS13 (usually acquired autoantibody) → ultra-large vWF multimers → platelet microthrombiShiga toxin (E. coli O157:H7, Shigella) damages renal endotheliumComplement dysregulation (factor H, I, MCP mutations)
ClinicalAdults (women); MAHA + thrombocytopenia ± fever, neuro changes, renal involvement (pentad seen in a minority)Children; bloody diarrhea → MAHA, thrombocytopenia, AKINo diarrhea; recurrent
TreatmentUrgent plasma exchange + glucocorticoids, caplacizumab (anti-vWF A1 domain), rituximab. Avoid platelet transfusion.Supportive (fluids, dialysis); avoid antibiotics and antimotility agentsEculizumab/ravulizumab
Exam trap: "MAHA + thrombocytopenia + normal PT/aPTT" = TTP/HUS. "MAHA + thrombocytopenia + prolonged PT/aPTT + low fibrinogen" = DIC. Do not wait for ADAMTS13 results before starting plasma exchange if TTP is suspected (PLASMIC score helps).

Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)

Type II HIT: IgG against heparin–platelet factor 4 (PF4) complexes → Fc receptor platelet activation → thrombocytopenia (> 50% fall) and thrombosis (venous > arterial), typically 5–10 days after starting heparin (sooner with recent exposure). Risk: UFH > LMWH; surgical > medical patients. Evaluate with 4T score → anti-PF4 ELISA → serotonin release assay. Management: stop all heparin (including flushes), start non-heparin anticoagulant (argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux, or a DOAC); do not start warfarin until platelets recover (> 150,000/mm³) because of venous limb gangrene risk; no platelet transfusion.

Thrombophilias (hypercoagulable states)

Virchow triad: stasis, endothelial injury, hypercoagulability.

Antiphospholipid syndromeLupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2-glycoprotein IArterial + venous thrombosis, recurrent pregnancy loss, ↑ aPTT; Tx warfarin (DOACs inferior, especially triple-positive)
HyperhomocysteinemiaEndothelial damage; MTHFR, B6/B12/folate deficiencyArterial + venous thrombosis
AcquiredMalignancy, pregnancy, estrogen, immobility, surgery, nephrotic syndrome, PNH, MPNs, HIT

sections.html:

ReactionTimingMechanismFeatures / prevention
Febrile nonhemolytic (most common)1–6 hCytokines from donor WBCs accumulated in stored blood; recipient anti-HLA antibodiesFever, chills; prevent with leukoreduction
AllergicMinutes–2 hType I hypersensitivity to donor plasma proteinsUrticaria, pruritus; antihistamines
AnaphylacticMinutesRecipient with IgA deficiency has anti-IgA antibodiesHypotension, bronchospasm, angioedema; epinephrine; future: washed or IgA-deficient products
