Massive transfusion: hypocalcemia (citrate chelates Ca²⁺ → perioral paresthesia, QT prolongation), hyperkalemia, hypothermia, dilutional coagulopathy. CMV-negative or leukoreduced products for transplant/neonates.

sections.heading: 12. White cell disorders and hematologic malignancies
sections.html:
Non-neoplastic leukocyte changes

  • Neutrophilia: bacterial infection, glucocorticoids (demargination; also ↓ eosinophils and lymphocytes), epinephrine, lithium. Leukemoid reaction (WBC > 50,000/mm³, left shift, ↑ LAP score/Döhle bodies, toxic granulation) vs CML (↓ LAP, basophilia, BCR::ABL1).
  • Neutropenia: < 1500/mm³; drugs (clozapine, carbamazepine, PTU/methimazole, TMP-SMX, chemotherapy), viral infection, Felty syndrome, ethnic (Duffy-null) neutropenia. Febrile neutropenia (ANC < 500 + fever) = emergency → empiric antipseudomonal β-lactam (cefepime, piperacillin–tazobactam).
  • Lymphocytosis: viral (EBV atypical "Downey" cells), pertussis, CLL. Lymphopenia: HIV, glucocorticoids, DiGeorge, SCID, radiation.
  • Infectious mononucleosis: EBV infects B cells (CD21); atypical lymphocytes are reactive CD8⁺ T cells; heterophile (Monospot) +; avoid contact sports (splenic rupture); amoxicillin rash.

Leukemias

TypeAgeKey featuresMarkers / geneticsTreatment / prognosis
B-ALL (lymphoblastic)Children (peak 2–5 y; most common childhood cancer); Down syndrome ↑ risk (after age 5)Abrupt pancytopenia (fatigue, infections, bleeding), bone pain, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly; CNS and testicular sanctuary sites; > 20% blastsTdT⁺ (nuclear), CD10, CD19, CD22, PAX5. Good: t(12;21), hyperdiploidy. Poor: t(9;22), KMT2A (11q23) in infantsMulti-agent chemo with intrathecal MTX; CAR-T (anti-CD19), blinatumomab (CD19/CD3 BiTE); ~90% cure in children
T-ALLAdolescent malesMediastinal (thymic) mass → SVC syndrome, airway compressionTdT⁺, cytoplasmic CD3, CD2, CD5, CD7, ± CD1a; NOTCH1Chemo; nelarabine
AMLAdults (median ~68 y); Down syndrome (acute megakaryoblastic, < 5 y)Pancytopenia; ≥ 20% myeloblasts; Auer rods (MPO⁺ crystallized granules); gum infiltration and skin (monocytic types); leukostasis if very high WBCMPO⁺, CD13, CD33, CD34, CD117. Risk factors: prior alkylators/topo II inhibitors, radiation, benzene, MDS, MPN. FLT3-ITD (poor; midostaurin, gilteritinib), NPM1 (favorable), IDH1/2 (ivosidenib/enasidenib)"7 + 3" (cytarabine + daunorubicin); venetoclax + azacitidine in older/unfit; allo-HSCT
APL (AML with PML::RARA)Adults (~40 y)DIC (granules release tissue factor) is the presenting emergency; many Auer rods (faggot cells)t(15;17); CD33⁺, often CD34⁻, HLA-DR⁻ATRA + arsenic trioxide (induce differentiation); start ATRA on suspicion; watch for differentiation syndrome (fever, edema, pulmonary infiltrates → dexamethasone); excellent prognosis
CLL / small lymphocytic lymphoma> 60 y; most common adult leukemia in USOften asymptomatic lymphocytosis; smudge cells; lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly; warm AIHA, ITP, hypogammaglobulinemia (infections); Richter transformation to DLBCLCD5⁺, CD19, CD20 (dim), CD23⁺, CD200; del(13q) good; del(17p)/TP53 poor; unmutated IGHV poorWatch and wait if early; BTK inhibitors (ibrutinib, acalabrutinib, zanubrutinib), venetoclax + obinutuzumab
Hairy cell leukemiaMiddle-aged menMassive splenomegaly, pancytopenia (monocytopenia), "dry tap" (marrow fibrosis), no lymphadenopathy; cells with hair-like cytoplasmic projectionsTRAP⁺, CD11c, CD25, CD103, annexin A1; BRAF V600ECladribine or pentostatin (purine analogs); excellent response; vemurafenib if refractory
CML45–85 yMarked leukocytosis with full spectrum of myeloid maturation, basophilia, thrombocytosis, splenomegaly; ↓ LAP; chronic → accelerated → blast crisis (AML or ALL)t(9;22) Philadelphia chromosome, BCR::ABL1 constitutive tyrosine kinaseImatinib, dasatinib, nilotinib, bosutinib; ponatinib or asciminib (allosteric) for T315I
Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphomaJapan, Caribbean, West AfricaHypercalcemia (lytic bone lesions), cutaneous lesions, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly; "flower cells"HTLV-1; CD4⁺, CD25⁺Poor prognosis

Myelodysplastic syndromes

Clonal stem-cell disorder with ineffective hematopoiesis → cytopenias in an older adult with hypercellular marrow and dysplasia: pseudo-Pelger–Huët neutrophils (bilobed, hypogranular), ringed sideroblasts, micromegakaryocytes; < 20% blasts (≥ 20% = AML). Causes: de novo, prior chemo/radiation. Del(5q) → macrocytic anemia, normal/↑ platelets, responds to lenalidomide. Tx: supportive, ESA, luspatercept, azacitidine/decitabine (hypomethylating), HSCT.

Lymphomas

Hodgkin lymphomaNon-Hodgkin lymphoma
SpreadContiguous; localized to a single group (often cervical/mediastinal)Noncontiguous; multiple peripheral nodes; extranodal involvement common
CellReed–Sternberg cells (CD15⁺, CD30⁺, PAX5 weak, CD45⁻, CD20⁻ in classic) in a reactive backgroundMostly B cells (85%); some T/NK
B symptomsCommon (fever, night sweats, > 10% weight loss); Pel–Ebstein fever; alcohol-induced node pain; pruritusLess common
AssociationsBimodal (20s and > 55); EBVHIV/immunosuppression, autoimmune disease (Sjögren → MALT), H. pylori, HCV, EBV, HTLV-1

Hodgkin subtypeFeatures
Nodular sclerosis (most common, ~70%)Young women, mediastinal mass; lacunar cells; collagen bands; excellent prognosis
Mixed cellularityOlder men, EBV, eosinophils (IL-5 from RS cells), many RS cells; intermediate prognosis

Lymphocyte-depletedElderly, HIV, worst prognosis
Nodular lymphocyte-predominant (not "classic")"Popcorn" (LP) cells: CD20⁺, CD45⁺, CD15⁻, CD30⁻; indolent
NHL subtypeTypical patientGenetics / markersKey features
Diffuse large B-cell (most common NHL)Older adults (any age)BCL2, BCL6 rearrangements; "double-hit" (MYC + BCL2) = high-gradeRapidly enlarging mass, aggressive but curable (R-CHOP ~60%); may arise from CLL/follicular
FollicularAdultst(14;18) IGH::BCL2; CD10⁺, BCL2⁺Painless, waxing–waning lymphadenopathy; indolent, incurable; transforms to DLBCL
BurkittChildren/young adults; endemic (Africa, EBV, jaw), sporadic (abdomen/ileocecal), HIVt(8;14) MYC; CD10⁺, Ki-67 ~100%"Starry sky" (tingible-body macrophages among sheets of lymphocytes); fastest-growing tumor → tumor lysis syndrome
Mantle cellOlder ment(11;14) CCND1; CD5⁺, CD23⁻, cyclin D1⁺, SOX11Aggressive, GI involvement (lymphomatous polyposis)
Marginal zone / MALTChronic inflammation: H. pylori (stomach), Sjögren (parotid), Hashimoto (thyroid)t(11;18) BIRC3::MALT1Gastric MALT often regresses with H. pylori eradication
Primary CNS lymphomaHIV (CD4 < 50), EBVB cellSingle ring-enhancing lesion (vs multiple in toxoplasmosis); high-dose MTX
Adult T-cellHTLV-1CD4⁺See above
Mycosis fungoides / Sézary syndromeAdultsCD4⁺ skin-homing T cellsPatches/plaques → tumors; Pautrier microabscesses; Sézary: erythroderma + circulating cerebriform cells
Anaplastic large cellChildren/young adults; breast implant-associated (ALK⁻)t(2;5) NPM1::ALK; CD30⁺Hallmark horseshoe-shaped nuclei
Extranodal NK/T-cell, nasal typeEast Asia, Latin AmericaEBVDestructive midline facial lesion
Enteropathy-associated T-cellCeliac diseaseT cellSmall bowel
High-yield: Tumor lysis syndrome (Burkitt, ALL, high-WBC leukemias after chemo): ↑ K⁺, ↑ phosphate, ↑ uric acid, ↓ Ca²⁺ (precipitates with phosphate) → AKI and arrhythmia. Prevent with aggressive IV fluids + allopurinol (xanthine oxidase inhibitor) or rasburicase (recombinant urate oxidase; converts uric acid → allantoin; contraindicated in G6PD deficiency → hemolysis and methemoglobinemia).
[[figure:ch04-fig06]]

Plasma cell disorders

DisorderDefinitionKey features
Plasma cell (multiple) myeloma≥ 10% clonal marrow plasma cells (or plasmacytoma) + myeloma-defining event: CRAB (hyperCalcemia, Renal failure, Anemia, Bone lytic lesions) or ≥ 60% plasma cells, free light chain ratio ≥ 100, > 1 focal MRI lesionAge > 60, more common in African Americans. Back pain/pathologic fractures (osteoclast activation via RANKL, IL-6); "punched-out" lytic lesions (whole-body low-dose CT; bone scan is negative because lesions are lytic); M spike (IgG > IgA) on SPEP; Bence Jones proteins (light chains) in urine → "myeloma kidney" (cast nephropathy), AL amyloid; rouleaux; infections (functional hypogammaglobulinemia — leading cause of death); ↑ total protein with normal albumin (↑ protein gap); hyperviscosity (rare). Tx: bortezomib–lenalidomide–dexamethasone ± daratumumab (anti-CD38), autologous SCT; bisphosphonates/denosumab; CAR-T (anti-BCMA)
MGUSM protein < 3 g/dL, < 10% plasma cells, no CRABMost common plasma cell disorder (~3% over age 50); progresses ~1%/year to myeloma or related disorder → monitor only
Smoldering myelomaM protein ≥ 3 g/dL or 10–59% plasma cells, no myeloma-defining event~10%/year progression early; observe (high-risk: clinical trials/lenalidomide)
Waldenström macroglobulinemiaIgM M spike + lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma in marrowMYD88 L265P; hyperviscosity (blurred vision, headache, retinal "sausage" veins, epistaxis), peripheral neuropathy, cold agglutinins, cryoglobulinemia; no lytic bone lesions. Tx: plasmapheresis for hyperviscosity, rituximab-based, BTK inhibitors
Solitary plasmacytomaSingle lesion (bone or extramedullary)Radiation
POEMSPolyneuropathy, Organomegaly, Endocrinopathy, M protein (λ), Skin changes↑ VEGF; sclerotic bone lesions

Myeloproliferative neoplasms

Clonal proliferation of mature myeloid cells; all can progress to myelofibrosis or AML; ↑ uric acid (gout) from cell turnover; thrombosis and bleeding.

MPNGeneticsFindingsTreatment
Polycythemia veraJAK2 V617F (~95%), JAK2 exon 12↑ RBC mass with low EPO (vs secondary polycythemia: ↑ EPO — hypoxia, RCC, testosterone); often ↑ WBC and platelets; aquagenic pruritus (mast cell histamine), erythromelalgia (burning hands/feet — aspirin-responsive), plethora, Budd–Chiari, splenomegalyPhlebotomy (Hct < 45%), low-dose aspirin, hydroxyurea or interferon if high risk; ruxolitinib (JAK1/2 inhibitor)
Essential thrombocythemiaJAK2 (~55%), CALR (~25%), MPLPlatelets > 450,000/mm³ (exclude reactive: iron deficiency, inflammation, asplenia); thrombosis and bleeding (acquired vWD if platelets > 1 million); diagnosis of exclusionAspirin; hydroxyurea or anagrelide if high risk
Primary myelofibrosisJAK2, CALR, MPLMegakaryocyte-derived PDGF/TGF-β → marrow fibrosis → "dry tap"; teardrop cells, leukoerythroblastic smear; massive splenomegaly (extramedullary hematopoiesis)Ruxolitinib, fedratinib, momelotinib, allo-HSCT
CMLBCR::ABL1See leukemiasTKIs
Systemic mastocytosisKIT D816VFlushing, urticaria pigmentosa (Darier sign), ↑ tryptase, peptic ulcers (histamine → gastric acid)Midostaurin, avapritinib, antihistamines

Histiocytoses

Langerhans cell histiocytosis: clonal proliferation of immature dendritic (Langerhans) cells; BRAF V600E in ~50–60% (MAPK pathway — now considered a myeloid neoplasm). Cells: S-100⁺, CD1a⁺, langerin (CD207)⁺; Birbeck granules ("tennis racket" rod-shaped on EM). Presentations: lytic skull lesions in a child, diabetes insipidus (pituitary stalk), exophthalmos, seborrheic-like rash, otitis; adults: smoking-related pulmonary LCH (upper-lobe cysts and nodules). Historical eponyms: Letterer–Siwe (infant multisystem), Hand–Schüller–Christian (lytic skull + DI + exophthalmos), eosinophilic granuloma (solitary bone lesion with eosinophils, good prognosis). Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH): uncontrolled macrophage/T-cell activation — fever, hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, very high ferritin, ↑ triglycerides, ↓ fibrinogen, ↑ soluble IL-2 receptor; familial (perforin, PRF1) or triggered by EBV/malignancy; Tx: etoposide + dexamethasone, HSCT.

sections.html:
Anticoagulants

DrugMechanismMonitoringKey toxicitiesReversal
Unfractionated heparin (IV/SC)Binds antithrombin → ↑ 1000× activity; inactivates IIa and Xa equally (long chains bridge AT and thrombin)aPTT or anti-XaBleeding, HIT, osteoporosis (long term), hyperkalemia (↓ aldosterone)Protamine sulfate (positively charged; complete)
LMWH (enoxaparin, dalteparin)AT-mediated; Xa > IIaUsually none; anti-Xa in renal failure, obesity, pregnancyLess HIT; renally clearedProtamine (partial)
FondaparinuxPentasaccharide; AT-mediated, Xa onlyNoneRenal clearance; no HITNone specific
Direct thrombin inhibitors: argatroban (hepatic), bivalirudin (renal; PCI), dabigatran (oral)Bind thrombin directlyaPTT (argatroban/bivalirudin)Bleeding; dabigatran dyspepsiaIdarucizumab (dabigatran); dialysis
Direct Xa inhibitors: apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxabanBind free and clot-bound XaNone routineBleeding (apixaban least GI bleeding)Andexanet alfa (decoy Xa); 4-factor PCC
WarfarinInhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1) → ↓ γ-carboxylation of glutamate residues on II, VII, IX, X, C, SPT/INR (goal 2–3; 2.5–3.5 for some mechanical mitral valves)Bleeding, teratogen (nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses — use LMWH in pregnancy), skin necrosis (protein C deficiency), many CYP2C9 interactions; genotype variability (VKORC1, CYP2C9)Vitamin K (slow); 4-factor PCC (fast) or FFP
High-yield: Warfarin interactions — ↑ INR with CYP2C9 inhibitors (amiodarone, fluconazole, metronidazole, TMP-SMX, acute alcohol); ↓ INR with inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St. John's wort, chronic alcohol) and vitamin K–rich foods. Bridge with heparin when starting warfarin for acute thrombosis (≥ 5 days and INR ≥ 2 for 24 h).

Antiplatelet agents

ClassDrugsMechanismNotes
COX inhibitorAspirinIrreversibly acetylates COX-1 and COX-2 → ↓ TXA₂ for platelet life span (7–10 days)↑ bleeding time; GI ulcers, tinnitus, Reye syndrome in children, AERD (Samter triad); salicylate toxicity → respiratory alkalosis + AG metabolic acidosis
P2Y12 (ADP receptor) blockersClopidogrel, prasugrel (irreversible prodrugs); ticagrelor (reversible, not prodrug); cangrelor (IV)Block ADP-induced GpIIb/IIIa expressionClopidogrel needs CYP2C19 activation (poor metabolizers ↓ effect); ticagrelor dyspnea; prasugrel contraindicated with prior stroke/TIA; ticlopidine → TTP, neutropenia
GpIIb/IIIa inhibitorsAbciximab, eptifibatide, tirofibanBlock fibrinogen bindingPCI/ACS; thrombocytopenia
PDE-3 inhibitorsCilostazol, dipyridamole↑ cAMP in platelets; vasodilationCilostazol for claudication; contraindicated in HF
PAR-1 antagonistVorapaxarBlocks thrombin receptor on plateletsPrior MI/PAD; bleeding

Thrombolytics and hemostatic agents

  • Thrombolytics (alteplase, reteplase, tenecteplase): convert plasminogen → plasmin (fibrin-specific). Used in acute ischemic stroke (within 4.5 h), STEMI without timely PCI, massive (hemodynamically unstable) PE. ↑ PT/aPTT, no change in platelet count. Contraindications: active bleeding, prior hemorrhagic stroke, ischemic stroke within 3 months, recent intracranial surgery, severe uncontrolled hypertension. Reversal: aminocaproic acid or TXA (lysine analogs inhibiting plasminogen activation), cryoprecipitate.
  • Desmopressin (V2 agonist): ↑ vWF and factor VIII release — mild hemophilia A, vWD type 1, uremic bleeding. Hyponatremia risk.
  • Hematopoietic agents: epoetin/darbepoetin (CKD, chemo anemia; ↑ thrombosis, HTN), filgrastim/pegfilgrastim (G-CSF; bone pain), romiplostim/eltrombopag (TPO receptor agonists), hydroxyurea (ribonucleotide reductase inhibitor; ↑ HbF), deferoxamine/deferasirox (iron chelators).

Chemotherapy and the cell cycle

title: Step 1 · Cardiovascular, Respiratory & Renal Systems
meta: Exam: Step 1 · Systems covered: Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Renal/Urinary (embryology, anatomy, histology, physiology, pathology, pharmacology) · Approx study time: 5–6 days (2 days cardio, 1.5 days respiratory, 2 days renal, half-day questions/review)

sections.heading: Overview
sections.html:
From NEET PG to USMLE

  • Mechanism over recall. NEET PG asks "drug of choice for X". Step 1 asks "a patient starts drug X and develops Y — which change in GFR / PV loop / ion current explains it?" For every fact below, be able to draw the curve and predict the direction of change.
  • Graphs are tested directly. Expect pressure–volume loops, Wiggers diagrams, O2–Hb curves, flow–volume loops and Starling curves as images. Practise reading them, not just memorising.
  • US drug names. US uses generic names in vignettes: albuterol (= salbutamol), acetaminophen (= paracetamol), epinephrine (= adrenaline), furosemide, hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ), chlorthalidone, metoprolol succinate. Brand names occasionally appear in Step 2/3 only.
  • Units. US labs use mg/dL: creatinine (normal ~0.6–1.2 mg/dL; divide µmol/L by 88.4), BUN (not urea; BUN ≈ urea ÷ 2.14 when both in mg/dL), glucose mg/dL (mmol/L × 18), calcium mg/dL (mmol/L × 4).
  • Acid–base is a calculation sport. Always compute anion gap, Winter's formula, and delta–delta. Step 1 loves "mixed" disorders.
  • Guidelines show up even on Step 1 pharmacology: heart failure "four pillars" (ARNI/ACEi/ARB + evidence-based β-blocker + MRA + SGLT2 inhibitor), GINA (ICS-formoterol reliever rather than SABA alone), GOLD (LABA + LAMA), KDIGO (SGLT2 inhibitors in CKD). Indian teaching often lags on these.
  • Epidemiology differs. Rheumatic heart disease is common in India but rare in the US; in US vignettes the most common cause of aortic stenosis is age-related calcific (or bicuspid valve in younger patients), and the most common cause of MR is mitral valve prolapse/degenerative disease. Diabetes is the #1 cause of ESRD in the US.

sections.heading: Cardiac embryology
sections.html:
The heart begins as paired endocardial tubes (lateral plate splanchnic mesoderm) that fuse into a single heart tube by week 3; it beats by ~day 22, making the cardiovascular system the first functional organ system. Cardiac looping (week 4) establishes left–right orientation and requires dynein (defects → dextrocardia, as in Kartagener syndrome). Neural crest cells migrate into the outflow tract to form the aorticopulmonary (conotruncal) septum.

Embryonic structureAdult derivative
Truncus arteriosusAscending aorta and pulmonary trunk
Bulbus cordisSmooth outflow parts of both ventricles (conus arteriosus of RV, aortic vestibule of LV)
Primitive ventricleTrabeculated parts of left and right ventricles
Primitive atriumTrabeculated parts of both atria (auricles)
Left horn of sinus venosusCoronary sinus
Right horn of sinus venosusSmooth part of right atrium (sinus venarum)
Right common cardinal + right anterior cardinal veinsSuperior vena cava
Primitive pulmonary veinSmooth part of left atrium
Endocardial cushionsAV septum, membranous IV septum, AV (mitral/tricuspid) valves, contribute to outflow septation

Atrial septation: septum primum grows toward the endocardial cushions (closing ostium primum); perforations form ostium secundum; septum secundum grows to the right of septum primum, leaving the foramen ovale. After birth, ↑ LA pressure pushes septum primum against septum secundum (functional closure → anatomic fusion). Patent foramen ovale = failure of fusion (25% of adults; paradoxical emboli). Ostium secundum ASD = excess resorption of septum primum or deficient septum secundum (most common ASD). Ostium primum ASD = endocardial cushion defect (Down syndrome).

Ventricular septation: muscular septum grows up from the floor; the membranous part forms last from the endocardial cushions + aorticopulmonary septum → membranous VSD is the most common VSD (and VSD is the most common congenital heart defect overall).

Outflow tract: neural crest → spiral aorticopulmonary septum. Failure to spiral → D-transposition of the great arteries; failure to form/divide → persistent truncus arteriosus; anterosuperior (skewed) displacement of the infundibular septum → tetralogy of Fallot.

Aortic (pharyngeal) archDerivative
1stPart of maxillary artery
2ndStapedial and hyoid arteries
3rdCommon carotid and proximal internal carotid arteries
4thLeft: aortic arch; Right: proximal right subclavian artery
6thProximal pulmonary arteries; left 6th → ductus arteriosus
High-yield: Recurrent laryngeal nerves hook under the 6th arch on the left (ligamentum arteriosum) but under the 4th arch on the right (right subclavian, because right 5th/6th distal parts regress). Hence left recurrent laryngeal palsy with aortic arch aneurysm or massive LA enlargement (Ortner syndrome).

Fetal circulation

Oxygenated blood from the placenta travels in the umbilical vein (highest fetal PO2 ≈ 30 mmHg, ~80% saturated) → ductus venosus (bypasses liver) → IVC → RA → foramen ovale → LA → LV → aorta → head and upper limbs. SVC blood → RA → RV → pulmonary trunk → ductus arteriosus (high pulmonary vascular resistance in fetus) → descending aorta → umbilical arteries → placenta. Fetal Hb (α2γ2) binds 2,3-BPG poorly → higher O2 affinity.

At birth: first breath → ↓ pulmonary vascular resistance → ↑ LA pressure (closes foramen ovale); ↑ PO2 and ↓ prostaglandins (placental loss) → ductus arteriosus closes. Indomethacin/ibuprofen (or acetaminophen) promote PDA closure; alprostadil (PGE1) keeps it open in ductal-dependent lesions.

Fetal structurePostnatal remnant
Ductus arteriosusLigamentum arteriosum
Ductus venosusLigamentum venosum
Foramen ovaleFossa ovalis
Umbilical arteriesMedial umbilical ligaments (proximal parts → superior vesical arteries)
Umbilical veinLigamentum teres hepatis (in falciform ligament)
Allantois → urachusMedian umbilical ligament
NotochordNucleus pulposus

sections.heading: Cardiac anatomy
sections.html:
• Most anterior chamber: right ventricle (injured in parasternal stab wounds). Most posterior: left atrium — enlargement (mitral stenosis) compresses the esophagus (dysphagia) and left recurrent laryngeal nerve (hoarseness). TEE views the LA best.
  • Coronary dominance is defined by which artery gives the posterior descending artery (PDA): right-dominant ~85%, left-dominant ~8%, codominant ~7%.
  • RCA → SA nodal artery (~60%), AV nodal artery (~80–90%), right marginal (RV), PDA (in right-dominant). Inferior MI (RCA) → bradycardia/AV block, RV infarct, posteromedial papillary muscle rupture.
  • LAD → anterior 2/3 of IV septum, anterior LV wall, apex, anterolateral papillary muscle (also LCX). Most commonly occluded artery.
  • LCX → lateral and posterior LV walls; obtuse marginal branches.
  • Posteromedial papillary muscle has a single supply (PDA) → more vulnerable to rupture than the anterolateral one (dual LAD + LCX supply).
  • Coronary blood flow to the LV peaks in early diastole (systolic compression of intramyocardial vessels). Tachycardia shortens diastole → ↓ perfusion while ↑ demand. Venous drainage: coronary sinus → RA.
  • Pericardium: fibrous + serous (parietal and visceral); innervated by phrenic nerve (C3–C5) → pericarditis pain referred to shoulder/trapezius ridge.

sections.heading: Cardiac and vascular histology
sections.html:
• Cardiomyocytes: striated, single central nucleus, branched, joined by intercalated discs (gap junctions [connexins] for electrical coupling; desmosomes for mechanical coupling). Rich in mitochondria; depend on oxidative metabolism (fatty acids). Terminally differentiated — injury heals by fibrosis (scar), not regeneration.
  • T-tubules at Z lines (dyads, vs triads in skeletal muscle). Contraction requires Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release: L-type Ca2+ current triggers ryanodine receptor (RyR2) opening.
  • Atrial myocytes contain granules of ANP; ventricular myocytes release BNP on stretch.
  • Arteries: intima (endothelium), media (smooth muscle; elastic lamellae in elastic arteries like aorta), adventitia (vasa vasorum). Arterioles are the main site of resistance; capillaries the main site of exchange (largest total cross-sectional area → slowest velocity); veins contain ~2/3 of blood volume (capacitance).
  • Purkinje fibers: larger, pale cells (glycogen-rich, few myofibrils) — fastest conduction.

sections.heading: Cardiac physiology — key equations
sections.html:
ParameterEquation / definitionExam notes
Cardiac outputCO = SV × HR; Fick: CO = V̇O2 ÷ (CaO2 − CvO2)Early exercise ↑ CO mainly via HR and SV; late exercise mainly via HR. Very high HR (e.g. VT) ↓ diastolic filling → ↓ CO.
Mean arterial pressureMAP = CO × TPR ≈ DBP + ⅓(SBP − DBP)At normal HR, ~⅔ of the cycle is diastole.
Pulse pressureSBP − DBP; ∝ SV, ∝ 1/arterial compliance↑ in aortic regurgitation, hyperthyroidism, aging (stiff aorta), exercise; ↓ in AS, cardiogenic shock, tamponade, advanced HF.
Stroke volumeSV = EDV − ESVDetermined by preload, afterload, contractility.
Ejection fractionEF = SV ÷ EDV (normal ≥ 55%)Index of contractility; ↓ in systolic HF, normal in HFpEF.
Resistance (Poiseuille)R = ΔP ÷ Q = 8ηL ÷ πr4Halving radius ↑ resistance 16-fold. Viscosity ↑ in polycythemia, hyperproteinemia (myeloma), hereditary spherocytosis.
Series vs parallelSeries: RT = R1 + R2…; Parallel: 1/RT = 1/R1 + 1/R2…Organs are in parallel — removing one organ (e.g. nephrectomy) ↑ total resistance.
Wall tension (Laplace)Wall stress = (P × r) ÷ (2 × wall thickness)Dilated ventricle ↑ wall stress → ↑ O2 demand; concentric hypertrophy is compensation that normalizes wall stress.
Capillary fluid exchange (Starling)Jv = Kf[(Pc − Pi) − σ(πc − πi)]Edema: ↑ Pc (HF), ↓ πc (nephrotic, cirrhosis), ↑ Kf (burns, sepsis), ↑ πi / lymphatic block (filariasis, node dissection).

Preload, afterload, contractility

  • Preload ≈ EDV (venous return). ↑ by volume, venoconstriction, exercise, AV fistula, slower HR. Venodilators (nitroglycerin) ↓ preload.
  • Afterload ≈ aortic pressure / wall stress during ejection. ↑ by hypertension, AS, vasoconstriction. Arteriolar dilators (hydralazine) ↓ afterload; ACEi/ARBs ↓ both.
  • Contractility (inotropy) ↑ by catecholamines (β1 → Gs → cAMP → PKA → phosphorylates L-type Ca2+ channels and phospholamban → ↑ SERCA activity → bigger SR stores), digoxin (↑ intracellular Na+ → ↓ Na+/Ca2+ exchange → ↑ intracellular Ca2+), ↑ HR (Bowditch/treppe effect). ↓ by β-blockers, non-DHP Ca2+ channel blockers, acidosis, hypoxia/hypercapnia, systolic HF, loss of myocardium (MI).
  • Myocardial O2 demand ↑ with ↑ afterload, ↑ contractility, ↑ HR, ↑ ventricular diameter (wall tension). Myocardium already extracts ~75% of delivered O2 at rest → ↑ demand must be met by ↑ flow (coronary vasodilation via adenosine, NO, ↓ O2).
[[figure:ch05-fig01]]

Pressure–volume loop

The LV pressure–volume loop runs counter-clockwise: (1) filling along the EDPVR from mitral opening to mitral closing; (2) isovolumetric contraction (both valves closed); (3) ejection after the aortic valve opens; (4) isovolumetric relaxation after the aortic valve closes. Loop width = stroke volume; area = stroke work. The slope of the end-systolic pressure–volume relationship (ESPVR) reflects contractility.

[[figure:ch05-fig02]]

Cardiac cycle (Wiggers diagram)

  • Isovolumetric contraction — between mitral closure (S1) and aortic opening; highest O2 consumption phase.
  • Rapid then reduced ejection — aortic valve open; aortic pressure tracks LV pressure.
  • Isovolumetric relaxation — aortic closure (S2, dicrotic notch on aortic tracing) to mitral opening.
  • Rapid filling (S3 if ventricle dilated/volume overloaded), reduced filling (diastasis), atrial systole (S4 if ventricle stiff; ~20–30% of filling at rest, more important in elderly/LVH; lost in AF).
[[figure:ch05-fig03]]

Heart sounds and splitting

FindingMechanismAssociations
S3 (early diastole)Rapid filling into a compliant/dilated ventricleNormal in children, pregnancy, athletes; pathologic in dilated HF, MR, AR, high output states
S4 (late diastole)Atrial kick into a stiff ventricleLVH (HTN, AS, HCM), acute MI; always abnormal in adults; absent in AF
Physiologic split S2Inspiration → ↑ venous return to right heart and ↑ pulmonary capacitance → P2 laterNormal
Wide splitDelayed RV emptying (normal pattern exaggerated)Pulmonic stenosis, RBBB
Fixed splitL→R shunt keeps RV volume high regardless of respirationASD
Paradoxical splitDelayed LV emptying → P2 before A2; split narrows on inspirationSevere AS, LBBB, RV pacing

Jugular venous pulse: a wave = RA contraction (absent in AF; cannon a waves when RA contracts against a closed tricuspid valve — complete heart block, VT, AV dissociation); c = RV contraction bulging tricuspid valve; x descent = atrial relaxation + downward pull of TV (lost in TR → giant c–v wave); v = RA filling against closed TV; y descent = RA emptying into RV (steep in constrictive pericarditis; blunted in tamponade). Kussmaul sign (JVP rises on inspiration): constrictive pericarditis, restrictive cardiomyopathy, RV infarct, tricuspid stenosis.

Murmurs

Maneuvers are a favorite second-order question. Rules: right-sided murmurs ↑ on inspiration (Carvallo sign). ↑ venous return (squatting, passive leg raise) ↑ most murmurs. ↓ venous return (standing, Valsalva strain phase) ↓ most murmurs except hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (louder) and MVP (click earlier, murmur longer). ↑ afterload (sustained handgrip) ↑ MR, AR, VSD; ↓ HCM (larger LV cavity); ↓ AS murmur (smaller gradient). ↓ afterload (amyl nitrite) does the opposite.

[[figure:ch05-fig04]]

Cardiac action potentials and conduction

PhaseVentricular myocyte / PurkinjePacemaker (SA, AV node)
0 — upstrokeFast voltage-gated Na+ channels (INa)L-type Ca2+ channels (slow upstroke → slow AV conduction)
1 — initial repolarizationNa+ channels inactivate; transient outward K+ (Ito)Absent
2 — plateauL-type Ca2+ influx balanced by K+ efflux; Ca2+ triggers CICR → contractionAbsent
3 — repolarizationDelayed rectifier K+ (IKr, IKs); Ca2+ channels closeK+ efflux
4 — diastoleStable resting potential (~−90 mV) via inward rectifier IK1Spontaneous depolarization: "funny" current If (HCN channels; mixed Na+/K+, net Na+ in) + T-type Ca2+. Slope sets heart rate.
[[figure:ch05-fig05]]
  • Conduction velocity: Purkinje > atria > ventricles > AV node. Pacemaker hierarchy: SA > AV > His–Purkinje/ventricle.
  • AV nodal delay (~100 ms) allows ventricular filling; it is the site acted on by adenosine, β-blockers, non-DHP CCBs, digoxin, vagal maneuvers.
  • Refractory periods: effective refractory period covers phases 0–3; class IA/III drugs lengthen it (antiarrhythmic) and the QT (pro-torsades).

ECG essentials

Interval / findingNormalAbnormal & causes
PR interval120–200 ms>200 ms: 1st-degree AV block. Short PR + delta wave: WPW (bundle of Kent).
QRS<120 msWide: bundle branch block, ventricular rhythm, hyperkalemia, TCA/class I toxicity.
QTc≲440 ms (men), ≲460 ms (women)Long QT: ↓K+, ↓Mg2+, ↓Ca2+; drugs (class IA/III, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, haloperidol, TCAs, ondansetron, methadone); congenital (Romano–Ward AD; Jervell–Lange-Nielsen AR + sensorineural deafness). Short QT: hypercalcemia, digoxin.
ST elevation localization—V1–V2 septal; V1–V4 anterior (LAD); I, aVL, V5–V6 lateral (LCX/diagonal); II, III, aVF inferior (RCA); ST depression V1–V3 with tall R = posterior (PDA); V4R = RV infarct.
RhythmKey featuresNotes
Atrial fibrillationIrregularly irregular, no P wavesRisk of LA appendage thrombus → stroke; CHA2DS2-VASc guides anticoagulation; rate control (β-blocker, diltiazem) or rhythm control.
Atrial flutterSawtooth flutter waves ~300/min, often 2:1 block (ventricular rate ~150)Macro-reentry around tricuspid annulus; catheter ablation definitive.
Mobitz I (Wenckebach)Progressive PR lengthening then dropped QRSAV nodal, usually benign (high vagal tone, drugs, inferior MI).
Mobitz IISudden dropped QRS without PR changeInfranodal (His–Purkinje); may progress to complete block → pacemaker.
3rd-degree (complete) blockP waves and QRS independent (AV dissociation); cannon a wavesLyme carditis, inferior MI, drugs, degeneration; pacemaker.
WPWShort PR, delta wave, wide QRSOrthodromic AVRT; with AF avoid AV nodal blockers (adenosine, β-blockers, CCBs, digoxin) → use procainamide or cardioversion.
Torsades de pointesPolymorphic VT with twisting axis, long QT baselineIV magnesium sulfate; correct K+; stop QT-prolonging drugs; overdrive pacing/isoproterenol.
Brugada syndromePseudo-RBBB with coved ST elevation V1–V3AD, SCN5A loss-of-function; more common in Asian men; ICD for sudden death prevention.

Autonomic and reflex control

  • Carotid sinus baroreceptors (CN IX → nucleus tractus solitarius) respond to ↑ and ↓ BP; aortic arch (CN X) responds mainly to ↑ BP. Hypotension → ↓ firing → ↑ sympathetic, ↓ vagal tone. Carotid massage ↑ firing → ↑ AV node refractoriness → terminates some SVTs.
  • Cushing reaction: ↑ ICP → cerebral ischemia → ↑ sympathetic → hypertension → baroreceptor-mediated bradycardia; plus irregular respirations (triad).
  • Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid > aortic bodies) sense ↓ PaO2 (<60 mmHg), ↑ PaCO2, ↓ pH; central chemoreceptors (medulla) sense CSF pH changes from PaCO2 (do not respond directly to PaO2).
  • Organ blood flow autoregulation: heart (adenosine, NO, CO2, ↓O2), brain (PaCO2/pH — hyperventilation ↓ ICP transiently), kidneys (myogenic + tubuloglomerular feedback), lungs (hypoxia → vasoconstriction, unique), skeletal muscle (local metabolites during exercise; sympathetic at rest), skin (sympathetic/thermoregulation).
Normal pressures (mmHg)Value
Right atrium (≈ CVP)<5
Right ventricle25/5
Pulmonary artery25/10 (mean ~15)
Pulmonary capillary wedge (≈ LA pressure, ≈ LVEDP)<12
Left ventricle130/10
Aorta130/90
Exam trap: PCWP overestimates LV end-diastolic pressure in mitral stenosis (PCWP > LVEDP), and is normal in isolated right heart failure, pulmonary hypertension from lung disease, and noncardiogenic pulmonary edema (ARDS, PCWP <18).

sections.html:
Congenital heart disease

LesionKey featuresAssociations / management
Right-to-left shunts (early cyanosis, "blue babies")
Tetralogy of FallotPulmonary infundibular stenosis (determines severity), RVH ("boot-shaped" heart), overriding aorta, VSD. "Tet spells" relieved by squatting (↑ SVR → ↓ R→L shunt). Harsh systolic ejection murmur at LUSB (from RVOT obstruction).22q11 deletion; anterosuperior displacement of infundibular septum. Surgical repair.
D-Transposition of great arteriesAorta from RV, pulmonary trunk from LV → parallel circulations; incompatible with life without mixing (PDA, ASD, VSD). "Egg on a string" CXR.Maternal diabetes. PGE1 to keep PDA open, balloon atrial septostomy, arterial switch.
Persistent truncus arteriosusSingle outflow vessel; almost always with VSD22q11 deletion
Tricuspid atresiaNo tricuspid valve, hypoplastic RV; needs ASD + VSDLeft axis deviation on ECG
TAPVRPulmonary veins drain to systemic venous circulation; needs ASD/PFO—
Ebstein anomalyApical displacement of tricuspid leaflets → "atrialized" RV, TR, RA enlargementMaternal lithium; WPW association
Left-to-right shunts (acyanotic; late cyanosis if Eisenmenger)
VSD (most common)Holosystolic murmur LLSB; small ones often close spontaneously; louder murmur = smaller defectDown, FAS, congenital rubella; large → surgical closure
ASDFixed split S2, pulmonic flow murmur; paradoxical emboli; O2 step-up in RASecundum (most common) vs primum (Down)
PDAContinuous "machine-like" murmur; wide pulse pressure; Eisenmenger → differential cyanosis (lower body blue, clubbing of toes not fingers)Congenital rubella, prematurity, high altitude. NSAIDs close; PGE1 keeps open.
AVSD (endocardial cushion defect)Primum ASD + inlet VSD + common AV valveDown syndrome
Obstructive
Coarctation of aortaNarrowing near ductus/ligamentum arteriosum; arm HTN, weak/delayed femoral pulses (brachiofemoral delay), rib notching from intercostal collaterals, "3 sign" on CXR. Severe neonatal (preductal) form → ductal-dependent lower body perfusion.Turner syndrome, bicuspid aortic valve; ↑ risk of berry aneurysms, aortic dissection, HF
High-yield: Eisenmenger syndrome = uncorrected L→R shunt → pulmonary arterial hypertension → RVH → shunt reversal (R→L) → late cyanosis, clubbing, polycythemia. Once established, defect closure is contraindicated. Other associations: Williams syndrome → supravalvular aortic stenosis; Marfan → MVP, aortic root dilation/AR, dissection; Noonan → pulmonic stenosis; Friedreich ataxia → HCM; congenital rubella → PDA, pulmonary artery stenosis.

Hypertension and arteriosclerosis

  • Definition (2017 ACC/AHA, retained in the 2025 AHA/ACC guideline): elevated 120–129/<80; stage 1 130–139 or 80–89; stage 2 ≥140 or ≥90 mmHg. Hypertensive emergency = severe BP (typically ≥180/120) with acute end-organ damage (encephalopathy, papilledema, AKI, MI, dissection, pulmonary edema).
  • Primary (essential) ~90%. Secondary: renal parenchymal disease, renovascular (fibromuscular dysplasia — young women, "string of beads"; atherosclerotic — older smokers), primary aldosteronism (most common endocrine cause; hypokalemia, ↓ renin), obstructive sleep apnea, pheochromocytoma, Cushing, coarctation, hyperthyroidism, drugs (NSAIDs, decongestants, OCPs, stimulants).
  • Hyaline arteriolosclerosis (pink homogeneous wall thickening): benign HTN, diabetes (also efferent arteriole). Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis ("onion-skinning"): malignant HTN; may show fibrinoid necrosis. Mönckeberg medial calcific sclerosis: medial calcification, radial/femoral arteries, does not narrow lumen, "pipestem" on x-ray; falsely elevated BP and ankle-brachial index.

Atherosclerosis

Disease of elastic and large/medium muscular arteries. Sequence: endothelial injury/dysfunction (HTN, smoking, hyperglycemia, turbulent flow at branch points) → LDL enters intima and is oxidized → monocytes adhere (VCAM-1) and become macrophages → uptake of oxidized LDL via scavenger receptors → foam cells → fatty streak → cytokines/PDGF/FGF recruit smooth muscle from media → collagen fibrous cap over necrotic lipid core (cholesterol clefts) → complex atheroma (calcification, ulceration, thrombosis). Vulnerable plaques have thin caps and large lipid cores (rupture → ACS), not necessarily the tightest stenosis.

Most common sites: abdominal aorta > coronary arteries > popliteal > carotid > circle of Willis. Risk factors: modifiable (smoking, HTN, dyslipidemia, diabetes, obesity, inactivity) and non-modifiable (age, male sex, postmenopausal state, family history of premature ASCVD, ↑ Lp(a)).

Aortic disease

ConditionMechanism / features
Abdominal aortic aneurysmAtherosclerosis + transmural inflammation and MMP-mediated degradation of media; infrarenal; risk: smoking (strongest), male, age >65, family history. Pulsatile mass; rupture → hypotension, flank/back pain. USPSTF: one-time ultrasound screening for men 65–75 who have ever smoked.
Thoracic aortic aneurysmCystic medial degeneration (Marfan [fibrillin-1], Loeys–Dietz, Ehlers–Danlos vascular type), bicuspid aortic valve, HTN; historically tertiary syphilis (obliterative endarteritis of vasa vasorum → "tree bark" intima).
Aortic dissectionIntimal tear → blood dissects through media. Risk: HTN (most common), connective tissue disease, bicuspid valve, cocaine, pregnancy. Sudden tearing chest pain radiating to back, unequal arm BPs, mediastinal widening; can cause AR, tamponade, MI (RCA), stroke. Stanford A (ascending) → emergency surgery; B (descending only) → medical (IV β-blocker first to ↓ HR and dP/dt, then vasodilator).

Ischemic heart disease

SyndromePathologyECG / markers
Stable anginaFixed stenosis ≳70%; chest pain with exertion, relieved by rest/nitroglycerinST depression during stress (subendocardial ischemia)
Vasospastic (Prinzmetal) anginaCoronary vasospasm at rest; triggers smoking, cocaine, amphetamines, triptans, coldTransient ST elevation. Treat CCBs, nitrates; avoid nonselective β-blockers.
Unstable anginaPlaque rupture + non-occlusive thrombus; rest pain or crescendo pattern± ST depression/T inversion; troponin normal
NSTEMISubendocardial necrosis (inner third most vulnerable — farthest from epicardial vessels, highest wall stress)ST depression; ↑ troponin
STEMITransmural infarct from occlusive thrombusST elevation, later Q waves; ↑ troponin

Cardiac troponin I/T rises within ~3–4 h, peaks ~24–48 h, stays elevated 7–10 days (most sensitive/specific). CK-MB normalizes in 48–72 h → useful for detecting reinfarction. Coronary steal (adenosine, regadenoson, dipyridamole) diverts flow from stenotic beds during pharmacologic stress testing.

Time after MIGross / microscopicComplications
0–24 hNo gross change → dark mottling; wavy fibers, early coagulative necrosis (4–12 h); contraction band necrosis if reperfused; edema, hemorrhageVentricular arrhythmia (most common cause of early death), cardiogenic shock, acute HF
1–3 daysHyperemic border; extensive necrosis with neutrophil infiltrationFibrinous (peri-infarction) pericarditis — friction rub
3–14 daysYellow-tan, soft center with red border; macrophages then granulation tissue — wall weakestFree wall rupture → tamponade; papillary muscle rupture (posteromedial, RCA) → acute MR; IV septal rupture (L→R shunt, O2 step-up in RV); LV pseudoaneurysm
2 weeks – monthsGray-white collagen scarTrue ventricular aneurysm (dyskinetic wall, persistent ST elevation, mural thrombus), chronic HF, arrhythmia, Dressler syndrome (autoimmune pericarditis weeks later)
Exam trap: RV infarction (inferior STEMI + hypotension + clear lungs + JVD) is preload-dependent — give IV fluids and avoid nitrates/diuretics.

Cardiomyopathies

TypeCausesFeatures
Dilated (most common)Idiopathic/genetic (TTN truncation), alcohol, wet beriberi (thiamine), Coxsackie B myocarditis, cocaine, Chagas (T. cruzi), doxorubicin (dose-dependent; dexrazoxane protects), trastuzumab (usually reversible), peripartum, hemochromatosis, sarcoidosis, thyrotoxicosis, tachycardia-induced, Takotsubo (stress, apical ballooning, often reversible)Systolic dysfunction, eccentric hypertrophy (sarcomeres added in series), S3, MR/TR from annular dilation; "balloon" heart on imaging
Hypertrophic (HCM)~60% familial AD; sarcomere genes — β-myosin heavy chain (MYH7), myosin-binding protein C (MYBPC3); Friedreich ataxiaAsymmetric septal hypertrophy, myofiber disarray, diastolic dysfunction; systolic anterior motion of mitral leaflet → dynamic LVOT obstruction + MR; S4; syncope, sudden cardiac death in young athletes (ventricular arrhythmia). Treat β-blocker or verapamil, mavacamten/aficamten (cardiac myosin inhibitors) for obstructive HCM, ICD if high risk; avoid volume depletion, vasodilators, diuretics. Concentric hypertrophy (sarcomeres added in parallel).
Restrictive / infiltrativeAmyloidosis (AL; transthyretin — wild-type in elderly men or V122I variant in Black patients), sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis, Löffler endocarditis (eosinophilic), endomyocardial fibrosis, post-radiationDiastolic dysfunction, normal-size ventricles with thick walls, biatrial enlargement, Kussmaul sign. Amyloid: low-voltage ECG despite thick walls; sarcoid: conduction block, VT

Heart failure

  • HFrEF (EF ≤40%), HFmrEF (41–49%), HFpEF (≥50%; HTN, obesity, elderly women, diabetes).
  • Neurohormonal activation (RAAS, sympathetic, ADH) initially compensates but drives remodeling — the basis of mortality-reducing therapy. BNP/NT-proBNP released by stretched ventricles (useful to rule out HF in dyspnea; falsely ↑ in CKD and degraded by neprilysin — NT-proBNP is preferred for monitoring on sacubitril).
  • Left HF: pulmonary congestion, orthopnea (↑ venous return supine), paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, crackles, S3, "heart failure cells" (hemosiderin-laden alveolar macrophages).
  • Right HF: most commonly due to left HF; isolated RHF = cor pulmonale (lung disease, PE, pulmonary HTN). JVD, hepatomegaly ("nutmeg liver", centrilobular congestion → cardiac cirrhosis), peripheral edema, ascites.
  • High-output HF: severe anemia, thyrotoxicosis, AV fistula, wet beriberi, Paget disease of bone, pregnancy.

Shock

TypeCVP / RAPCWPCOSVRClinical clue
Hypovolemic↓↓↓↑Hemorrhage, burns, vomiting; cold, clammy
Cardiogenic↑↑↓↑MI, arrhythmia, acute MR; pulmonary edema
Obstructive↑↑ (tamponade) or ↓/normal (PE, tension PTX)↓↑Tamponade: equalized diastolic pressures; PE: RV strain
Distributive — septic, anaphylactic↓↓↑ (early)↓Warm, flushed, bounding pulses, tachycardia
Distributive — neurogenic↓↓↓↓Spinal cord injury above T6; warm, bradycardic

Mixed venous O2 saturation (SvO2) is ↓ in hypovolemic/cardiogenic shock (↑ extraction) and ↑ in septic shock and cyanide poisoning (impaired tissue O2 use).

Valvular disease

LesionCauses (US)Findings
Aortic stenosisAge-related calcific (>70 y); bicuspid valve (presents ~50–60 y); RHD (with mitral involvement)Crescendo–decrescendo SEM at RUSB → carotids; pulsus parvus et tardus; soft/absent A2, paradoxical split; LVH, S4. Symptoms: syncope, angina, dyspnea (HF) — each markedly ↓ survival without valve replacement. Heyde syndrome (angiodysplasia GI bleed + acquired vWF deficiency); schistocytes.
Aortic regurgitationAortic root dilation (HTN, Marfan, ankylosing spondylitis, syphilis), bicuspid valve, endocarditis, RHDEarly diastolic decrescendo blowing murmur at LSB (sit forward, end-expiration); wide pulse pressure, bounding "water-hammer" pulse, head bobbing, nail-bed pulsation; Austin Flint mid-diastolic rumble (regurgitant jet impairs anterior mitral leaflet).
Mitral regurgitationMVP/myxomatous degeneration, ischemic papillary dysfunction/rupture, LV dilation, RHD, endocarditisHolosystolic blowing murmur at apex → axilla; S3; ↑ with handgrip, squatting
Mitral valve prolapseMyxomatous degeneration (Marfan, Ehlers–Danlos, ADPKD); most common valvular lesionMid-systolic click + late systolic murmur; click earlier with ↓ preload (standing, Valsalva)
Mitral stenosisAlmost always rheumatic heart diseaseOpening snap + mid-diastolic rumble at apex (left lateral decubitus); LA enlargement → AF, thrombus, dysphagia, hoarseness; pulmonary HTN; hemoptysis
Tricuspid regurgitationRV dilation, IV drug use endocarditis, carcinoid (with pulmonic stenosis), EbsteinHolosystolic LLSB murmur ↑ on inspiration; pulsatile liver, giant v waves

Rheumatic fever and endocarditis

Acute rheumatic fever: weeks after group A streptococcal pharyngitis (not skin infection); molecular mimicry (anti-M protein antibodies cross-react with cardiac myosin, valve, joint, brain) — type II hypersensitivity. Major Jones criteria: migratory polyarthritis, pancarditis, subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum, Sydenham chorea. Histology: Aschoff bodies (granulomas with giant cells) and Anitschkow cells ("caterpillar" nuclei). Acute → MR; chronic → MS (fusion of commissures, "fish-mouth" valve). Treat penicillin; secondary prophylaxis with benzathine penicillin.

OrganismSetting
S. aureusMost common overall; acute, destructive; IV drug users (tricuspid), normal valves, prosthetic valves
Viridans streptococci (S. sanguinis, S. mutans)Subacute; previously damaged valves; dental procedures; dextran helps fibrin–platelet adhesion
S. gallolyticus (formerly bovis)Associated with colorectal neoplasia → colonoscopy
EnterococcusGU/GI procedures, elderly men
Coagulase-negative staphylococci (S. epidermidis)Prosthetic valves, devices (biofilm)
Culture-negativeHACEK, Coxiella, Bartonella, prior antibiotics
NonbacterialLibman–Sacks (SLE, antiphospholipid; vegetations on both sides of valve); nonbacterial thrombotic (marantic) endocarditis in malignancy (mucinous adenocarcinoma, e.g. pancreas) and hypercoagulable states

Signs: fever, new murmur, Roth spots (retinal hemorrhage with pale center), Osler nodes (painful finger pads — immune complex), Janeway lesions (painless palms/soles — septic microemboli), splinter hemorrhages, glomerulonephritis, septic emboli (lungs in right-sided disease), anemia. Diagnosis by modified Duke criteria (blood cultures + echo).

Pericardial disease and cardiac tumors

  • Acute pericarditis: sharp pleuritic chest pain relieved by sitting forward, friction rub, diffuse ST elevation with PR depression. Causes: idiopathic/viral (Coxsackie B), uremia, post-MI/Dressler, SLE/RA, TB, malignancy, radiation. Treat NSAIDs + colchicine (↓ recurrence).
  • Cardiac tamponade: Beck triad (hypotension, JVD, muffled heart sounds), tachycardia, pulsus paradoxus (>10 mmHg inspiratory SBP fall — also in severe asthma/COPD, OSA, croup), electrical alternans, equalization of diastolic pressures, absent y descent. Treat pericardiocentesis.
  • Constrictive pericarditis: TB (developing world), post-radiation/surgery (US); Kussmaul sign, pericardial knock, steep y descent, pericardial calcification.
  • Tumors: metastases most common overall. Myxoma — most common primary in adults, usually LA (attached to fossa ovalis), "ball-valve" obstruction, tumor plop, syncope, constitutional symptoms (IL-6), gelatinous with myxoid stroma. Rhabdomyoma — most common in children, ventricular, associated with tuberous sclerosis (often regresses).

Vasculitides

Vessel sizeDiseaseDistinguishing featuresTreatment
LargeGiant cell (temporal) arteritisAge >50, women; unilateral headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, vision loss (ophthalmic artery); polymyalgia rheumatica; ↑ ESR; segmental granulomatous inflammation with giant cells (skip lesions → biopsy may be negative)High-dose glucocorticoids immediately (do not wait for biopsy); tocilizumab steroid-sparing
Takayasu arteritisWomen <40, Asian; "pulseless disease" (weak upper-limb pulses, arm claudication, BP difference); granulomatous thickening of aortic arch and branchesGlucocorticoids
MediumPolyarteritis nodosaHepatitis B association; renal (HTN), mesenteric, nerve (mononeuritis multiplex), skin; spares lungs; transmural fibrinoid necrosis in different stages; microaneurysms ("rosary") on angiography; ANCA negativeGlucocorticoids, cyclophosphamide; antivirals if HBV
Kawasaki diseaseAsian children <5 y; fever ≥5 days + bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, polymorphous rash, cervical lymphadenopathy, strawberry tongue/cracked lips, hand–foot erythema/edema then desquamation; coronary artery aneurysms (thrombosis/MI)IVIG + aspirin (an exception to the Reye syndrome rule); echocardiography
Buerger disease (thromboangiitis obliterans)Heavy smokers, young men; segmental thrombosing vasculitis of distal limbs; claudication, Raynaud, ulcers, autoamputation; superficial migratory thrombophlebitisSmoking cessation
SmallGranulomatosis with polyangiitisUpper airway (sinusitis, saddle nose, otitis), lungs (nodules, cavities, hemoptysis), kidneys (pauci-immune RPGN); necrotizing granulomas; PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA)Glucocorticoids + rituximab or cyclophosphamide
Microscopic polyangiitisLung + kidney, palpable purpura; no granulomas, no nasopharyngeal disease; MPO-ANCA (p-ANCA)As above
Eosinophilic GPA (Churg–Strauss)Asthma, sinusitis, peripheral eosinophilia, mononeuritis multiplex, cardiac involvement; granulomas; MPO-ANCA (~40%); ↑ IgEGlucocorticoids; mepolizumab
IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura)Most common childhood systemic vasculitis; often after URI; palpable purpura on buttocks/legs, arthralgia, abdominal pain (intussusception risk), IgA nephropathy-like GNSupportive; steroids for severe disease
Cryoglobulinemic vasculitisHepatitis C; purpura, arthralgia, GN (MPGN pattern), ↓ C4Treat HCV
Behçet syndrome (variable vessel)HLA-B51; recurrent oral + genital aphthous ulcers, uveitis, erythema nodosum, pathergy; "Silk Road" populationsGlucocorticoids, colchicine, apremilast
High-yield: Vascular tumors — strawberry (infantile) hemangioma (appears in first weeks, grows, regresses by ~5–7 y; propranolol for complicated lesions); cherry angioma (adults, benign); pyogenic granuloma (bleeds, pregnancy); cystic hygroma (Turner); glomus tumor (painful, under nail); Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8, HIV); angiosarcoma (vinyl chloride, arsenic, Thorotrast; post-mastectomy lymphedema); bacillary angiomatosis (Bartonella in HIV — neutrophilic infiltrate distinguishes it from Kaposi).

sections.heading: Cardiovascular pharmacology
sections.html:
Antihypertensives

US first-line classes: thiazide-type diuretic (chlorthalidone preferred for long half-life), ACE inhibitor or ARB, dihydropyridine CCB. The 2025 AHA/ACC guideline favors a target <130/80 mmHg for most adults and two-drug single-pill combinations for stage 2 HTN. β-Blockers are not first-line for uncomplicated HTN in the US.

ComorbidityPreferred agent(s)
HFrEFARNI/ACEi/ARB + evidence-based β-blocker + MRA (+ SGLT2i); avoid non-DHP CCBs
Diabetes or CKD with albuminuriaACEi or ARB (↓ intraglomerular pressure); add SGLT2i
PregnancyLabetalol, nifedipine, methyldopa; IV hydralazine/labetalol for severe range. ACEi/ARB/aliskiren contraindicated.
Black patients without CKD/HFThiazide or CCB as initial therapy
BPHα1-blocker as add-on (not monotherapy)
Post-MI, angina, AF rate controlβ-blocker
Hypertensive emergencyIV nicardipine, clevidipine, labetalol, esmolol; nitroprusside (cyanide toxicity with prolonged use); fenoldopam (D1 agonist — ↑ renal perfusion, natriuresis). Lower MAP ≤25% in first hour (except dissection: target SBP <120 rapidly).
Drug classMechanismKey adverse effects / notes
ACE inhibitors (-pril)↓ Ang II and aldosterone; ↑ bradykinin; efferent arteriolar dilationCough, angioedema (bradykinin — contraindicated in C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency/previous angioedema), hyperkalemia, ↑ creatinine (rise ≤30% acceptable), teratogen (renal tubular dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, skull hypoplasia); avoid in bilateral renal artery stenosis
ARBs (-sartan)AT1 receptor blockadeAs ACEi but little cough; angioedema much rarer
AliskirenDirect renin inhibitorHyperkalemia; don't combine with ACEi/ARB in diabetes
Sacubitril/valsartan (ARNI)Neprilysin inhibition (↑ ANP/BNP, bradykinin) + ARBHypotension, hyperkalemia, angioedema; 36-hour washout after stopping an ACEi
DHP CCBs (amlodipine, nifedipine, nicardipine, clevidipine)Block vascular smooth muscle L-type Ca2+ channelsPeripheral edema (precapillary dilation), flushing, headache, reflex tachycardia (short-acting nifedipine), gingival hyperplasia
Non-DHP CCBs (verapamil, diltiazem)Cardiac L-type channels: ↓ AV conduction, contractilityBradycardia, AV block, worsen HFrEF, constipation (verapamil), ↑ digoxin levels (verapamil)
Hydralazine↑ cGMP → arteriolar dilationReflex tachycardia (give with β-blocker; avoid alone in angina), fluid retention (give with diuretic), drug-induced lupus (slow acetylators). With isosorbide dinitrate ↓ mortality in self-identified Black patients with HFrEF.
MinoxidilOpens KATP channels → hyperpolarizes smooth muscleHypertrichosis (topical for alopecia), pericardial effusion, reflex tachycardia, fluid retention
Clonidine, methyldopaCentral α2 agonists ↓ sympathetic outflowClonidine: rebound HTN on abrupt withdrawal, sedation, dry mouth. Methyldopa: Coombs-positive hemolytic anemia, safe in pregnancy
α1-blockers (prazosin, doxazosin, terazosin)↓ arteriolar and venous tone; ↓ prostate smooth muscle toneFirst-dose orthostatic hypotension, dizziness
NitroprussideReleases NO → ↑ cGMP (arterial + venous)Cyanide toxicity (treat sodium thiosulfate/hydroxocobalamin)

Antianginal therapy

  • Goal: ↓ myocardial O2 demand (↓ HR, contractility, wall tension, afterload).
  • Nitrates (nitroglycerin, isosorbide mono-/dinitrate): NO → ↑ cGMP → venodilation (↓ preload, main antianginal effect) ± coronary dilation. AE: headache, flushing, reflex tachycardia (add β-blocker), orthostatic hypotension, tolerance (need a nitrate-free interval — "Monday disease" in industrial exposure). Contraindicated with PDE-5 inhibitors (severe hypotension) and in RV infarction or severe AS.
  • β-blockers: ↓ HR and contractility, ↑ diastolic perfusion time. Avoid in vasospastic angina (unopposed α constriction) and cocaine chest pain in the acute phase (classic teaching).
  • Ranolazine: inhibits late Na+ current → ↓ intracellular Ca2+ loading; no effect on HR/BP; prolongs QT; constipation, dizziness.
  • Ivabradine: blocks If (HCN) in SA node → ↓ HR without ↓ contractility; luminous phenomena (phosphenes), bradycardia; indicated for HFrEF in sinus rhythm with HR ≥70 on maximally tolerated β-blocker.

β-Blocker specifics

  • β1-selective: atenolol, bisoprolol, esmolol (ultrashort, IV), metoprolol, nebivolol (also ↑ NO), betaxolol, acebutolol. Safer (not absolutely safe) in asthma/COPD and diabetes.
  • Nonselective β: propranolol, nadolol, timolol, pindolol. Propranolol: thyroid storm, essential tremor, migraine prophylaxis, infantile hemangioma; nadolol/propranolol: variceal bleeding prophylaxis.
  • α + β: carvedilol, labetalol. Intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (partial agonists): pindolol, acebutolol — avoid post-MI/HF.
  • HFrEF mortality benefit: only carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol.
  • AE: bradycardia, AV block, bronchospasm, masked hypoglycemia, fatigue, erectile dysfunction, worsening of acute decompensated HF. Overdose: IV glucagon (↑ cAMP independent of β receptor), high-dose insulin euglycemia therapy, atropine, calcium.

Antiarrhythmics (Vaughan Williams)

ClassDrugsMechanism & effectUsesToxicity
IAQuinidine, procainamide, disopyramideModerate Na+ block + K+ block → ↑ AP duration, ↑ ERP, ↑ QTAtrial and ventricular arrhythmias; procainamide for WPW with AF and stable wide-complex tachycardiaTorsades; quinidine — cinchonism (tinnitus, headache), thrombocytopenia, diarrhea; procainamide — drug-induced lupus (anti-histone); disopyramide — HF, anticholinergic
IBLidocaine, mexiletineWeak Na+ block, preferential for depolarized/ischemic tissue; ↓ AP durationVentricular arrhythmias post-MI; digoxin-induced arrhythmiasCNS toxicity (paresthesias, tremor, seizures), cardiovascular depression
ICFlecainide, propafenoneStrong Na+ block, marked use-dependence; prolongs QRS; little AP duration changeSVTs and AF in structurally normal hearts ("pill-in-the-pocket")Proarrhythmic; contraindicated in structural/ischemic heart disease (CAST trial ↑ mortality)
IIMetoprolol, esmolol, propranolol, atenolol↓ cAMP → ↓ If and Ca2+ currents → ↓ phase 4 slope; ↑ PRRate control of AF/flutter, SVT, post-MI, VT preventionSee β-blockers; treat overdose with glucagon
IIIAmiodarone, sotalol, dofetilide, ibutilide, dronedaroneK+ channel block → ↑ AP duration, ↑ ERP, ↑ QTAF (rhythm control), VT/VF (amiodarone)Sotalol/dofetilide/ibutilide — torsades (sotalol also β-blocks). Amiodarone (has class I–IV actions; torsades uncommon): pulmonary fibrosis, hepatotoxicity, hypo- or hyperthyroidism (iodine-rich, inhibits peripheral T4→T3), corneal microdeposits, optic neuropathy, blue-gray skin, photosensitivity, neuropathy, CYP inhibition (↑ warfarin, digoxin). Monitor PFTs, LFTs, TFTs.
IVVerapamil, diltiazemL-type Ca2+ block in nodal tissue → ↓ conduction velocity, ↑ ERP, ↑ PRRate control of AF, prevention of nodal re-entryConstipation, flushing, edema, bradycardia, AV block, HF
OtherAdenosineA1 receptor → ↑ K+ efflux, ↓ Ca2+ current in AV node; half-life ~10 sDrug of choice to terminate PSVT (AVNRT); diagnostic in narrow-complex tachycardiaFlushing, chest pain, dyspnea, sense of doom, transient asystole; effect blocked by theophylline/caffeine, potentiated by dipyridamole
OtherMagnesium sulfateStabilizes membranesTorsades de pointes; digoxin toxicityHyporeflexia, hypotension

Heart failure drugs

DrugMortality benefit in HFrEF?Notes
ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan), or ACEi/ARBYes (ARNI preferred over ACEi)↓ afterload and remodeling
β-blockers (carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol)YesStart low when euvolemic; not during acute decompensation with shock
MRA (spironolactone, eplerenone)YesHyperkalemia; spironolactone gynecomastia (eplerenone more selective)
SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin)Yes (also ↓ hospitalization in HFpEF)Benefit independent of diabetes
Hydralazine + isosorbide dinitrateYes in self-identified Black patients; alternative if ACEi/ARB/ARNI not tolerated—
Loop diureticsNo (symptom relief)Relieve congestion
DigoxinNo (↓ hospitalizations)Symptomatic HFrEF, AF rate control
Ivabradine↓ HF hospitalizationSinus rhythm, HR ≥70 on max β-blocker
Inotropes: dobutamine (β1), milrinone (PDE-3 inhibitor → ↑ cAMP → inotropy + vasodilation)No (may ↑ mortality long-term)Acute decompensation, cardiogenic shock, bridge

Digoxin: inhibits Na+/K+-ATPase → ↑ intracellular Na+ → reduced Na+/Ca2+ exchanger extrusion of Ca2+ → ↑ SR Ca2+ → ↑ contractility; also ↑ vagal tone (↓ AV conduction). Renally cleared, narrow therapeutic index. Toxicity: nausea/vomiting, anorexia, confusion, blurred/yellow vision, arrhythmias (atrial tachycardia with AV block, bidirectional VT, PVCs), hyperkalemia in acute overdose (poor prognostic sign). Risk ↑ with renal failure, hypokalemia (less K+ competing at the pump), hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia, and drugs that ↓ clearance or displace it (verapamil, amiodarone, quinidine, dronedarone). Antidote: digoxin immune Fab; correct K+ and Mg2+ (IV calcium for hyperkalemia was traditionally discouraged in digoxin toxicity; Fab is the definitive treatment). ECG: scooped ("Salvador Dalí") ST depression is a digoxin effect, not toxicity.

Lipid-lowering drugs

DrugMechanismMain lipid effectAdverse effects
Statins (atorvastatin, rosuvastatin, simvastatin, pravastatin)Inhibit HMG-CoA reductase → ↓ hepatic cholesterol → ↑ LDL receptor expression↓↓↓ LDL; ↓ TG; small ↑ HDL; ↓ mortality in ASCVDMyalgia/myopathy, rhabdomyolysis (↑ with fibrates [esp. gemfibrozil], niacin, CYP3A4 inhibitors with simvastatin/lovastatin/atorvastatin), hepatotoxicity (↑ transaminases), small ↑ diabetes risk; teratogenic
EzetimibeBlocks NPC1L1 cholesterol absorption at brush border↓ LDL (~20%)Rare ↑ LFTs, diarrhea
PCSK9 inhibitors — evolocumab, alirocumab (mAbs); inclisiran (siRNA, twice yearly)Prevent LDL receptor degradation↓↓↓ LDL (~50–60%); ↓ Lp(a) modestlyInjection-site reactions, nasopharyngitis
Bempedoic acidInhibits ATP-citrate lyase (upstream of HMG-CoA reductase); prodrug activated in liver, not muscle↓ LDL (~20%)↑ uric acid/gout, tendon rupture; little myalgia
Bile acid sequestrants (cholestyramine, colestipol, colesevelam)Bind bile acids → liver diverts cholesterol to bile acid synthesis↓ LDL; ↑ TGGI upset, ↓ absorption of fat-soluble vitamins and drugs (digoxin, warfarin, thyroxine); avoid in hypertriglyceridemia
Fibrates (fenofibrate, gemfibrozil)PPAR-α activation → ↑ lipoprotein lipase, ↑ HDL synthesis↓↓↓ TGMyopathy (with statins), cholesterol gallstones (inhibit cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase)
NiacinInhibits lipolysis in adipose (hormone-sensitive lipase) → ↓ hepatic VLDL synthesis↑↑ HDL, ↓ LDL, ↓ TGFlushing (prostaglandin-mediated; ↓ with aspirin), hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia (gout), hepatotoxicity; no outcome benefit added to statins
Omega-3 (icosapent ethyl)↓ hepatic VLDL production↓ TGAF, bleeding
High-yield: Pancreatitis risk rises when TG >1000 mg/dL — treat with fibrate first. Familial hypercholesterolemia (LDL receptor mutation, AD): LDL ≥190, tendon xanthomas (Achilles), premature MI → high-intensity statin ± ezetimibe ± PCSK9 inhibitor.
