sections.heading: Respiratory embryology
sections.html:
The lung bud (respiratory diverticulum) arises from the ventral foregut endoderm in week 4; the tracheoesophageal septum separates it from the esophagus. Endoderm → airway epithelium and glands; splanchnic mesoderm → cartilage, smooth muscle, connective tissue, vessels.

StageWeeksEventsRelated defects
Embryonic4–7Lung bud → trachea, bronchial buds, lobar/segmental bronchiTracheoesophageal fistula, tracheal atresia
Pseudoglandular5–17Conducting airways down to terminal bronchioles; no gas exchange possibleCongenital diaphragmatic hernia → pulmonary hypoplasia
Canalicular16–25Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, capillary invasion; type I/II pneumocytes appear (surfactant ~week 20+); respiration possible ~week 24–25Limit of viability
Saccular26 – birthTerminal sacs, thinning of blood–air barrier; surfactant ↑Neonatal RDS if premature
Alveolar36 weeks – ~8 yearsTrue alveoli multiply (~20–70 million at birth → ~300–400 million in adult)—
  • Tracheoesophageal fistula: most common form = proximal esophageal atresia + distal TE fistula → polyhydramnios (fetus can't swallow amniotic fluid), drooling, choking/cyanosis with first feeds, gastric air bubble, NG tube coils in pouch. Associated with VACTERL. H-type (isolated fistula) → recurrent aspiration pneumonia.
  • Congenital diaphragmatic hernia: usually left posterolateral (Bochdalek) defect from failed pleuroperitoneal fold fusion → abdominal contents in thorax → pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension; scaphoid abdomen.
  • Pulmonary hypoplasia also follows oligohydramnios (Potter sequence — bilateral renal agenesis, ARPKD, posterior urethral valves).
  • Bronchogenic cyst: abnormal budding of foregut; mediastinal/hilar, fluid-filled; may compress airway or become infected.
  • Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (NRDS): surfactant deficiency → ↑ alveolar surface tension → atelectasis, ↓ compliance, V/Q mismatch, R→L shunting. Risk: prematurity, maternal diabetes (fetal insulin inhibits surfactant synthesis), C-section without labor (no stress cortisol surge). Lecithin:sphingomyelin ratio <1.5 predicts NRDS (≥2.0 mature). CXR: diffuse ground-glass, air bronchograms. Prevention: antenatal betamethasone/dexamethasone (24–34 weeks). Treatment: CPAP, exogenous surfactant. Complications of O2 therapy: retinopathy of prematurity, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, intraventricular hemorrhage; hypoxemia keeps PDA open.

sections.heading: Respiratory anatomy and histology
sections.html:
• Right lung 3 lobes; left lung 2 lobes + lingula (homolog of right middle lobe). Right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical → aspirated foreign bodies go right. Supine: posterior segment of RUL or superior segment of RLL. Upright: basal segments of RLL. Lying on right side: right middle lobe/posterior RUL.
  • Pulmonary artery relation to bronchus at hilum: right artery anterior to right main bronchus; left artery superior to left main bronchus.
  • Diaphragm innervated by phrenic nerves (C3–C5): irritation → referred shoulder pain; injury → paradoxical elevation of hemidiaphragm. Structures passing through: IVC at T8 (caval hiatus, central tendon), esophagus + vagal trunks at T10, aorta + thoracic duct + azygos at T12. Carotid bifurcation at C4; trachea bifurcates at T4 (sternal angle).
  • Conducting zone (nose → terminal bronchioles): anatomic dead space (~150 mL), warms/humidifies/filters air. Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium → cuboidal in bronchioles. Cartilage and submucosal glands end with bronchi; goblet cells end at terminal bronchioles; airway smooth muscle extends to terminal bronchioles (sparse beyond). Most airway resistance is in medium-sized bronchi (not small airways, which are numerous and in parallel).
  • Respiratory zone (respiratory bronchioles → alveolar ducts → alveoli): gas exchange. Cilia end at respiratory bronchioles; alveolar macrophages clear debris.
  • Type I pneumocytes: ~97% of alveolar surface; thin, gas exchange; very sensitive to injury. Type II pneumocytes: cuboidal, lamellar bodies, secrete surfactant (dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine = lecithin), serve as progenitors for type I and II cells after injury. Club (Clara) cells: nonciliated, dome-shaped cells in bronchioles; secrete a component of surfactant, detoxify via CYP450, progenitor cells.
  • Surfactant ↓ surface tension (especially in small alveoli as they shrink), preventing collapse (Laplace: collapsing pressure = 2T/r) and ↑ compliance; produced from ~week 20, adequate ~week 35.

sections.heading: Respiratory physiology
sections.html:
Lung volumes and mechanics

[[figure:ch05-fig06]]
  • Dead space: physiologic VD = anatomic + alveolar dead space. Bohr: VD = VT × (PaCO2 − PeCO2) ÷ PaCO2. Apex of healthy lung is the main source of alveolar dead space. Minute ventilation = VT × RR; alveolar ventilation = (VT − VD) × RR → rapid shallow breathing wastes ventilation.
  • PaCO2 ∝ CO2 production ÷ alveolar ventilation — the single best index of ventilation (halving VA doubles PaCO2).
  • Compliance = ΔV/ΔP. ↑ in emphysema (loss of elastic tissue) and normal aging; ↓ in pulmonary fibrosis, edema, pneumonia, ARDS, NRDS, obesity/kyphoscoliosis (chest wall). Hysteresis: inflation and deflation curves differ because of surface tension.
  • Elastic recoil of lung pulls inward; chest wall springs outward. In emphysema, ↓ recoil → ↑ FRC (barrel chest); in fibrosis, ↑ recoil → ↓ FRC. Radial traction keeps small airways open — lost in emphysema → dynamic airway collapse on expiration (air trapping, pursed lips create auto-PEEP).
  • Flow–volume loops: obstructive — scooped ("coved") expiratory limb, shifted to higher volumes; restrictive — narrow tall loop at lower volumes; fixed upper airway obstruction (tracheal stenosis) — flattened inspiratory and expiratory limbs; variable extrathoracic (vocal cord paralysis) — flattened inspiratory limb; variable intrathoracic (tumor) — flattened expiratory limb.

Oxygen and carbon dioxide transport

O2 content CaO2 = (1.34 × Hb × SaO2) + (0.003 × PaO2); normal ~20 mL O2/dL. O2 delivery = CO × CaO2. Hemoglobin shows positive cooperativity (sigmoid curve) between T (taut, low affinity) and R (relaxed, high affinity) states; myoglobin (monomer) has a hyperbolic curve and very high affinity.

[[figure:ch05-fig07]]
ConditionHbPaO2SaO2 (true)O2 content
Anemia↓NormalNormal↓
Polycythemia↑NormalNormal↑
CO poisoningNormalNormal↓ (pulse oximetry falsely normal)↓
MethemoglobinemiaNormalNormal↓ (SpO2 ~85% regardless of PaO2)↓
Hypoxemic lung diseaseNormal (↑ if chronic)↓↓↓
  • Carbon monoxide: binds Hb ~200–250× more avidly than O2; left shift; also inhibits complex IV. Headache, dizziness, cherry-red skin (late), bilateral globus pallidus necrosis. Sources: furnaces, car exhaust, fires (often with cyanide). Treat 100% O2 (shortens CO-Hb half-life from ~5 h to ~1 h) or hyperbaric O2.
  • Methemoglobinemia: Fe3+ cannot bind O2; causes: nitrites/nitrates (well water), dapsone, topical anesthetics (benzocaine, lidocaine), primaquine, congenital cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency. Chocolate-brown blood, cyanosis unresponsive to O2, "saturation gap". Treat methylene blue (contraindicated in G6PD deficiency → ascorbic acid/exchange transfusion). Intentional induction (nitrites) is used for cyanide poisoning.
  • Cyanide: inhibits cytochrome c oxidase → lactic acidosis, ↑ venous O2 (bright-red venous blood), bitter almond odor. Treat hydroxocobalamin (forms cyanocobalamin) or nitrites + sodium thiosulfate.
  • CO2 transport: ~70% as HCO3− (carbonic anhydrase in RBCs; Cl− shift), ~20–25% carbaminohemoglobin, ~5% dissolved. Haldane effect: in the lungs, oxygenation of Hb promotes release of H+ and CO2. Bohr effect: in tissues, ↑ H+/CO2 ↓ Hb O2 affinity → O2 unloading.

Pulmonary circulation and V/Q

  • Low-pressure, high-compliance system. Hypoxic vasoconstriction diverts blood from poorly ventilated alveoli (opposite of systemic vessels); chronic generalized hypoxia (COPD, altitude, OSA) → pulmonary hypertension → cor pulmonale.
  • Perfusion-limited gases (O2 normally, CO2, N2O): equilibrate early along capillary; uptake ↑ only by ↑ flow. Diffusion-limited (CO; O2 in fibrosis, emphysema, strenuous exercise, altitude): don't equilibrate. DLCO measures diffusion capacity (↓ emphysema, ILD, PE, anemia, pulmonary HTN; ↑ alveolar hemorrhage, polycythemia, asthma sometimes).
  • Zones of the upright lung: both ventilation and perfusion are greatest at the base, but perfusion increases more steeply → V/Q highest at apex (~3) (wasted ventilation; high PAO2 → reactivation TB favors apex) and lowest at base (~0.6). Exercise recruits apical capillaries → more uniform V/Q.
  • V/Q = 0 (shunt): airway obstruction, consolidation, atelectasis, intracardiac R→L shunt — supplemental O2 does not correct hypoxemia well. V/Q = ∞ (dead space): blood flow obstruction (PE), ↑ alveolar pressure — O2 improves PaO2.
  • Pulmonary vascular resistance is lowest at FRC (↑ at high volumes from compression of alveolar vessels and at low volumes from narrowing of extra-alveolar vessels).

Alveolar gas equation and causes of hypoxemia

PAO2 = FiO2(Patm − PH2O) − PaCO2/R ≈ 0.21 × (760 − 47) − PaCO2/0.8 ≈ 150 − PaCO2/0.8 at sea level on room air. A–a gradient = PAO2 − PaO2; normal ~10–15 mmHg (↑ with age, roughly age/4 + 4).

MechanismA–a gradientCorrects with 100% O2?Examples
↓ Inspired PO2NormalYesHigh altitude
HypoventilationNormalYesOpioid/benzodiazepine overdose, neuromuscular disease, obesity hypoventilation, chest wall disease
V/Q mismatch (most common)↑YesCOPD, asthma, pneumonia, PE
Diffusion limitation↑YesInterstitial lung disease, emphysema
Right-to-left shunt↑No (little)ARDS, lobar consolidation, intracardiac shunt, pulmonary AVM

Hypoxemia = ↓ PaO2; hypoxia = ↓ O2 delivery to tissue (↓ CO, hypoxemia, anemia, CO poisoning); ischemia = loss of blood flow.

Adaptations: altitude and exercise

High altitudeExercise
Acute: ↓ PaO2 → peripheral chemoreceptors → hyperventilation → ↓ PaCO2 → respiratory alkalosis (acute mountain sickness; acetazolamide prophylaxis promotes HCO3− excretion)
Chronic: ↑ EPO → ↑ Hct; ↑ 2,3-BPG (right shift); ↑ mitochondria; renal HCO3− excretion; hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction → pulmonary HTN, RVH; HAPE (nifedipine), HACE (dexamethasone)		↑ O2 consumption and CO2 production matched by ↑ ventilation → arterial PaO2 and PaCO2 unchanged; ↑ venous PCO2, ↓ venous PO2; ↑ pulmonary blood flow (recruitment), more uniform V/Q; pH ↓ only in strenuous exercise (lactate)

Control of breathing: dorsal respiratory group (medulla) — inspiration; ventral group — forced expiration; pneumotaxic center (upper pons) — shortens inspiration, ↑ rate; apneustic center (lower pons) — prolongs inspiration. Chronic CO2 retainers (severe COPD) have blunted central CO2 drive; high-flow O2 can worsen hypercapnia (mainly by worsening V/Q matching via release of hypoxic vasoconstriction and the Haldane effect, rather than only by "loss of hypoxic drive") — titrate to SpO2 88–92%.

sections.heading: Respiratory pathology
sections.html:
Obstructive lung diseases

Hallmark: FEV1/FVC <0.70 (post-bronchodilator, GOLD), air trapping (↑ RV, FRC, TLC), V/Q mismatch.

DiseasePathologyClinical clues
Chronic bronchitisHypertrophy/hyperplasia of submucosal mucous glands (Reid index >50%), goblet cell metaplasia; small airway inflammationProductive cough ≥3 months/year for ≥2 consecutive years; smokers; hypoxemia + hypercapnia, cyanosis, cor pulmonale ("blue bloater")
Emphysema — centriacinarDestruction of respiratory bronchioles; protease (neutrophil/macrophage elastase) > antiprotease; upper lobesSmoking; dyspnea, ↓ DLCO, barrel chest, pursed-lip breathing, hyperresonance, "pink puffer"
Emphysema — panacinarEntire acinus; lower lobesα1-antitrypsin deficiency (PiZZ, SERPINA1): early emphysema (worse with smoking) + liver disease (misfolded protein retained in hepatocyte ER → PAS+, diastase-resistant globules → cirrhosis, HCC)
Emphysema — paraseptalDistal acinus near pleura; apical blebsSpontaneous pneumothorax in tall young adults
AsthmaType I hypersensitivity; Th2 cytokines (IL-4 → IgE class switch, IL-5 → eosinophils, IL-13 → mucus); smooth muscle hypertrophy, goblet cell hyperplasia, thickened basement membrane; Curschmann spirals (shed epithelium in mucus plugs), Charcot–Leyden crystals (eosinophil galectin-10)Episodic wheeze, cough (night/exercise), triggers; reversible obstruction (↑ FEV1 ≥12% and ≥200 mL after bronchodilator); methacholine challenge for hyperresponsiveness; pulsus paradoxus in severe attacks; normal/high DLCO
Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory diseaseCOX inhibition shunts arachidonic acid → 5-lipoxygenase → ↑ cysteinyl leukotrienesAsthma + nasal polyps + NSAID sensitivity; leukotriene modifiers, aspirin desensitization
BronchiectasisPermanent dilation of bronchi from chronic necrotizing infection + impaired clearanceCopious purulent sputum, recurrent infections, hemoptysis, clubbing; "tram-track"/signet-ring sign on CT. Causes: cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener — dynein arm defect, situs inversus, infertility, sinusitis), allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (central bronchiectasis in asthma/CF), obstruction, MAC, immunodeficiency
High-yield: Cystic fibrosis — AR, CFTR gene on chromosome 7; most common mutation F508del (misfolding → ER retention → proteasomal degradation). ↓ Cl− secretion into airway/GI lumen + ↑ Na+ (and water) reabsorption → thick secretions; in sweat glands CFTR reabsorbs Cl− → ↑ sweat Cl− (≥60 mmol/L diagnostic). Nasal transepithelial potential difference is more negative. Presents with meconium ileus, failure to thrive, pancreatic insufficiency (ADEK deficiency), recurrent S. aureus (childhood) then Pseudomonas infections, nasal polyps, male infertility (bilateral absence of vas deferens), CF-related diabetes. Treatment: airway clearance, dornase alfa (DNase), hypertonic saline, azithromycin, inhaled tobramycin, pancreatic enzymes, CFTR modulators (elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor; vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor; ivacaftor alone for gating mutations such as G551D).

Restrictive lung diseases

Hallmark: ↓ TLC, ↓ FVC, FEV1/FVC normal or ↑ (>0.8).

  • Poor breathing mechanics (extrapulmonary) — normal A–a gradient and DLCO: neuromuscular (ALS, myasthenia gravis, Guillain–Barré, polio), chest wall (kyphoscoliosis, morbid obesity, ankylosing spondylitis), pleural disease.
  • Interstitial lung diseases (pulmonary) — ↑ A–a gradient, ↓ DLCO, ↑ recoil.
ILDKey features
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosisOlder male smokers; repeated alveolar injury → aberrant repair (TGF-β) → fibroblastic foci; usual interstitial pneumonia pattern — subpleural, basal, temporally heterogeneous fibrosis, honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis; dry "Velcro" crackles, clubbing. Treat pirfenidone (anti-TGF-β) or nintedanib (tyrosine kinase inhibitor); steroids not helpful
SarcoidosisUS: Black women; immune-mediated noncaseating granulomas (CD4 Th1); bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, reticular opacities, erythema nodosum, lupus pernio, anterior uveitis, Bell palsy, cardiac (heart block), hypercalcemia/hypercalciuria (macrophage 1α-hydroxylase → ↑ calcitriol), ↑ ACE; Löfgren syndrome (erythema nodosum + hilar adenopathy + arthritis + fever; good prognosis). Treat glucocorticoids if symptomatic
Hypersensitivity pneumonitisType III/IV reaction to inhaled organic antigens (farmer's lung — thermophilic actinomycetes; bird fancier's lung); poorly formed granulomas; cough, dyspnea, fever hours after exposure; chronic → fibrosis. Remove exposure
Drug-inducedAmiodarone, bleomycin, busulfan, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin, checkpoint inhibitors; radiation
Pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosisYoung adult smokers; upper-lobe nodules and cysts; Birbeck granules, CD1a+, S-100+, langerin (CD207)+
Connective tissue diseaseSystemic sclerosis (NSIP pattern; most common cause of death), RA, polymyositis/dermatomyositis (anti-Jo-1)

Pneumoconioses

DiseaseExposureLocationDistinguishing features
AsbestosisShipbuilding, roofing, plumbing, insulation, brake liningsLower lobesCalcified pleural plaques (most common lesion; benign marker of exposure), ferruginous (asbestos) bodies — golden-brown beaded rods, Prussian-blue positive. Bronchogenic carcinoma is the most common cancer (synergy with smoking); mesothelioma risk ↑ (not smoking-related)
SilicosisSandblasting, foundries, mining, quarrying, stone countertopsUpper lobesFibrotic nodules; "eggshell" calcification of hilar nodes; silica impairs macrophage phagolysosome function → ↑ TB risk; ↑ lung cancer
Coal workers' pneumoconiosisCoal dustUpper lobesCoal macules; progressive massive fibrosis; Caplan syndrome (RA + pneumoconiosis with intrapulmonary nodules). Anthracosis (asymptomatic carbon pigment) is common in city dwellers
BerylliosisAerospace, electronics, nuclear industriesUpper lobes (diffuse)Type IV hypersensitivity → noncaseating granulomas (mimics sarcoidosis; beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test); ↑ lung cancer; steroid-responsive

Mesothelioma: malignant pleural tumor; recurrent hemorrhagic pleural effusions, pleural thickening encasing the lung; histology — psammoma bodies; markers calretinin, cytokeratin 5/6, WT-1 positive (adenocarcinoma is TTF-1/CEA positive instead); BAP1 loss.

Vascular, acute and pleural disorders

  • Pulmonary embolism: Virchow triad (stasis, endothelial injury, hypercoagulability); most from proximal deep leg veins. Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia (sinus tachycardia is the most common ECG finding; S1Q3T3 classic but uncommon), hypoxemia with ↑ A–a gradient and respiratory alkalosis, hemoptysis, RV strain. Infarcts are hemorrhagic, wedge-shaped (dual blood supply usually protects). Imaging: CT pulmonary angiography; V/Q scan if contrast contraindicated. Wells score + D-dimer (low pretest probability). Lines of Zahn (alternating platelet/fibrin and RBC layers) identify antemortem thrombi. Treat anticoagulation (DOAC, LMWH); thrombolysis for massive PE with shock.
  • Other emboli: fat (long-bone fracture, liposuction → hypoxemia, confusion, petechial rash 1–3 days later), air (decompression, central line), amniotic fluid (during/after delivery → DIC, cardiovascular collapse), septic, tumor.
  • ARDS (Berlin definition): onset within 1 week of insult, bilateral opacities, not fully explained by cardiac failure/overload, PaO2/FiO2 ≤300 on PEEP ≥5 (mild 201–300, moderate 101–200, severe ≤100). Causes: sepsis (most common), pneumonia, aspiration, trauma, pancreatitis, transfusion (TRALI), drowning. Pathogenesis: neutrophil-mediated endothelial and type I pneumocyte injury → protein-rich exudate → diffuse alveolar damage with hyaline membranes → R→L shunt; later organizing/fibrotic phase. Treat cause; low tidal-volume ventilation (≈6 mL/kg ideal body weight), plateau pressure ≤30 cmH2O, PEEP, prone positioning.
  • Pulmonary hypertension (mean PA pressure >20 mmHg at rest, per 2022 ESC/ERS; older definition ≥25): Group 1 PAH (BMPR2 mutation — loss of antiproliferative signaling; drugs/toxins such as methamphetamine and anorexigens; connective tissue disease; HIV; portopulmonary; congenital shunt; schistosomiasis); Group 2 left heart disease (most common); Group 3 lung disease/hypoxia (COPD, ILD, OSA, altitude); Group 4 chronic thromboembolic (potentially curable by endarterectomy); Group 5 multifactorial (sarcoidosis, myeloproliferative, metabolic). Histology: medial hypertrophy, intimal fibrosis, plexiform lesions. Loud P2, RV heave, cor pulmonale.
  • Sleep apnea: OSA — obesity, large neck, tonsillar hypertrophy (children); daytime somnolence, morning headaches, HTN, AF, pulmonary HTN, ↑ EPO; diagnose polysomnography; CPAP, weight loss (tirzepatide FDA-approved for moderate–severe OSA with obesity), hypoglossal nerve stimulator. Central sleep apnea — Cheyne–Stokes breathing in HF, opioids. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome — BMI ≥30 with awake PaCO2 >45 mmHg.
Pleural effusionMechanismCauses
Transudate↑ hydrostatic or ↓ oncotic pressure; protein-poorHF (most common overall), cirrhosis (hepatic hydrothorax), nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminemia
Exudate (Light's criteria: any of — pleural/serum protein >0.5; pleural/serum LDH >0.6; pleural LDH >⅔ upper limit of normal serum LDH)↑ vascular permeability; protein-richPneumonia (parapneumonic, empyema — pH <7.2 or glucose <60 → drain), malignancy, TB (lymphocytic, ↑ adenosine deaminase), PE, RA (very low glucose), SLE, pancreatitis (↑ amylase)
ChylothoraxThoracic duct injury/obstructionTrauma, surgery, lymphoma; milky, TG >110 mg/dL
Exam findingPercussionFremitusBreath soundsTrachea
Pleural effusionDull↓↓Away (if large)
Atelectasis (obstruction)Dull↓↓Toward
Simple pneumothoraxHyperresonant↓↓Midline/toward
Tension pneumothoraxHyperresonant↓↓Away + hypotension, JVD → needle decompression then chest tube
Consolidation (lobar pneumonia)Dull↑Bronchial, egophony, whispered pectoriloquyMidline

Lung cancer

Leading cause of cancer death in the US. Metastases to the lung (breast, colon, prostate, kidney…) are more common than primary lung cancer. USPSTF (2021): annual low-dose CT for adults aged 50–80 with ≥20 pack-years who currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years. Presentations: cough, hemoptysis, weight loss, post-obstructive pneumonia, SVC syndrome (facial plethora, distended neck veins), Pancoast (superior sulcus) tumor → Horner syndrome (sympathetic chain), C8–T1 brachial plexus pain, hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal), hemidiaphragm paralysis (phrenic), pleural/pericardial effusion. Lung cancer commonly metastasizes to adrenals, brain, bone, liver.

TypeLocationHistology / markersAssociations
Adenocarcinoma (most common overall; most common in nonsmokers and women)PeripheralGlands, mucin, TTF-1+, napsin A+; adenocarcinoma in situ — lepidic growth along alveolar walls ("ground-glass")EGFR (osimertinib), ALK (alectinib), ROS1, KRAS G12C (sotorasib), BRAF, RET, MET mutations; hypertrophic osteoarthropathy, clubbing
Squamous cell carcinomaCentral (hilar), may cavitateKeratin pearls, intercellular bridges; p40/p63+Strong smoking link; PTHrP → hypercalcemia
Small cell carcinomaCentralSmall round blue cells, scant cytoplasm, nuclear molding, crush artifact; neuroendocrine (Kulchitsky) — chromogranin A, synaptophysin, CD56, NSEStrong smoking link; MYC amplification; ectopic ACTH (Cushing), SIADH, Lambert–Eaton (anti-presynaptic P/Q-type Ca2+ channel), anti-Hu paraneoplastic encephalomyelitis, cerebellar degeneration; treated with chemoradiation ± immunotherapy, not surgery
Large cell carcinomaPeripheralPleomorphic giant cells, no glandular/squamous differentiationSmoking; poor prognosis
Bronchial carcinoidCentral or peripheral; may cause obstructionNests of neuroendocrine cells, chromogranin+, low gradeNot smoking related; occasionally carcinoid syndrome

From NEET PG to USMLE: current asthma/COPD strategy

  • GINA no longer recommends SABA-only treatment for adults/adolescents: preferred reliever is as-needed low-dose ICS–formoterol (Track 1), with maintenance-and-reliever therapy (MART) at Steps 3–5. US NAEPP (2020) similarly endorses ICS-formoterol SMART from step 3.
  • GOLD: initial therapy for group A — a bronchodilator; groups B and E — LABA + LAMA; add ICS (triple therapy) for exacerbations with blood eosinophils ≥300 cells/µL; azithromycin or roflumilast for frequent exacerbators. Interventions with mortality benefit: smoking cessation, long-term O2 for resting hypoxemia (PaO2 ≤55 mmHg or SaO2 ≤88%, or ≤59 mmHg/89% with cor pulmonale or polycythemia), and in selected patients triple inhaled therapy, home NIV for chronic hypercapnia, lung volume reduction surgery and pulmonary rehabilitation after hospitalization.
  • COPD exacerbation: SABA ± SAMA, systemic glucocorticoids (5 days), antibiotics if sputum purulence ↑, noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation for hypercapnic respiratory acidosis.

sections.heading: Renal embryology
sections.html:
• Pronephros (week 4) — degenerates. Mesonephros — interim kidney in first trimester; mesonephric (Wolffian) duct later forms male genital ducts. Metanephros — permanent kidney, appears week 5; nephrogenesis continues until ~32–36 weeks (premature infants have fewer nephrons).
  • Ureteric bud (outgrowth of mesonephric duct) → ureter, renal pelvis, calyces, collecting ducts. Metanephric mesenchyme (blastema) → glomerulus through DCT (Bowman capsule, PCT, loop, DCT). Reciprocal induction is required; failure → renal agenesis or multicystic dysplastic kidney.
  • Ureteropelvic junction is the last part to canalize → most common cause of fetal hydronephrosis.
  • Potter sequence: oligohydramnios (bilateral renal agenesis, ARPKD, posterior urethral valves in males) → fetal compression → flat face, low-set ears, retrognathia, limb deformities (clubfeet), and pulmonary hypoplasia (cause of death).
  • Horseshoe kidney: inferior poles fuse and ascent is trapped beneath the inferior mesenteric artery; functions normally; ↑ risk of hydronephrosis (UPJ obstruction), stones, infection, Wilms tumor; associated with Turner syndrome and trisomies 13, 18, 21.
  • Multicystic dysplastic kidney: abnormal ureteric bud–mesenchyme interaction → nonfunctional cystic kidney (usually unilateral, contralateral kidney hypertrophies). Duplex collecting system: bifid ureteric bud → vesicoureteral reflux and/or obstruction. Posterior urethral valves: membrane in posterior urethra of males → bilateral hydronephrosis, distended bladder.

sections.heading: Renal anatomy and histology
sections.html:
• Kidneys retroperitoneal at T12–L3; right kidney lower (liver). Left renal vein receives left adrenal and left gonadal veins and passes between the SMA and aorta (nutcracker syndrome → hematuria, left varicocele). Left kidney preferred for living donor transplant (longer vein).
  • Renal blood flow: renal artery → segmental → interlobar → arcuate → interlobular (cortical radiate) → afferent arteriole → glomerulus → efferent arteriole → peritubular capillaries / vasa recta (medulla; low flow → vulnerable to ischemia; papillary necrosis).
  • Ureters pass under the uterine artery and vas deferens ("water under the bridge") — at risk in hysterectomy (ligation of uterine vessels). Ureteral narrowing (common stone impaction): UPJ, crossing the iliac vessels at pelvic brim, ureterovesical junction (narrowest).
  • Glomerular filtration barrier: fenestrated endothelium (size barrier) → glomerular basement membrane (type IV collagen; heparan sulfate gives negative charge) → podocyte foot processes with slit diaphragm (nephrin, podocin). Loss of the charge barrier → selective albuminuria (minimal change disease).
  • Juxtaglomerular apparatus: JG (granular) cells — modified smooth muscle of afferent arteriole that secrete renin; macula densa — NaCl sensor in the distal TAL/early DCT; extraglomerular mesangial cells.
  • PCT cells have a dense apical brush border and abundant mitochondria (most vulnerable to toxic injury). EPO is made by peritubular interstitial fibroblast-like cells.

sections.heading: Renal physiology
sections.html:
Body fluids

Total body water ≈ 60% of body weight (lower in women, elderly, obesity): intracellular ⅔ (40% of weight), extracellular ⅓ (20%) — of which interstitial ¾ and plasma ¼. Plasma volume measured with radiolabeled albumin; ECF with inulin or mannitol. Plasma osmolality ≈ 2[Na+] + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8 (≈ 285–295 mOsm/kg). Osmolal gap >10 suggests unmeasured osmoles (methanol, ethylene glycol, ethanol, isopropyl alcohol).

Clearance, GFR and renal plasma flow

QuantityFormulaNotes
ClearanceCx = (Ux × V̇) ÷ PxCx < GFR → net reabsorption; Cx > GFR → net secretion; Cx = GFR → neither (inulin)
GFRCinulin (gold standard); creatinine clearance (slightly overestimates — creatinine is secreted)Normal ~100–125 mL/min; eGFR by CKD-EPI 2021 equation (race-free in the US)

Exam trap: In bilateral renal artery stenosis, heart failure, or volume depletion, GFR depends on Ang II-mediated efferent constriction — ACEi/ARB (and NSAIDs on the afferent side) can precipitate AKI. The "triple whammy" = ACEi/ARB + diuretic + NSAID.

Tubular handling

  • Glucose: freely filtered; reabsorbed in PCT by SGLT2 (bulk) and SGLT1. Glycosuria begins at plasma glucose ~180–200 mg/dL (threshold); all transporters saturated at Tm ~375 mg/min. "Splay" reflects nephron heterogeneity. Normal pregnancy lowers the threshold (↑ GFR) → glycosuria.
  • Amino acids: PCT Na+-dependent transporters. Hartnup disease (neutral amino acids, tryptophan → niacin deficiency/pellagra-like rash). Cystinuria (cystine, ornithine, lysine, arginine → hexagonal cystine stones; cyanide–nitroprusside test).
  • Urea: ~50% reabsorbed passively; ADH ↑ urea transporters in the inner medullary collecting duct → contributes to medullary osmotic gradient.
  • PAH and many drugs (penicillin, uric acid, methotrexate, diuretics) are secreted by PCT organic anion transporters (probenecid inhibits).

Hypermagnesemia↓ deep tendon reflexes (first sign), lethargy, bradycardia, hypotension, respiratory depression, cardiac arrestMagnesium sulfate for preeclampsia (antidote: calcium gluconate), renal failure, laxatives/antacids
HypophosphatemiaMuscle weakness (diaphragm), hemolysis, rhabdomyolysis, osteomalacia/ricketsRefeeding syndrome (insulin drives PO43−, K+, Mg2+ into cells), hyperparathyroidism, Fanconi, X-linked hypophosphatemia (↑ FGF23)
HyperphosphatemiaMetastatic calcification, hypocalcemiaCKD, tumor lysis, rhabdomyolysis, hypoparathyroidism
High-yield: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes → IV calcium gluconate first (stabilizes cardiac membranes; does not lower K+), then shift K+ into cells (insulin + glucose, β2-agonist, bicarbonate if acidotic), then remove it (loop diuretics, potassium binders — patiromer, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate — or hemodialysis).

sections.heading: Acid–base physiology
sections.html:
Henderson–Hasselbalch: pH = 6.1 + log([HCO3−] ÷ (0.03 × PaCO2)). Normal: pH 7.35–7.45, PaCO2 35–45 mmHg, HCO3− 22–28 mEq/L, anion gap 8–12 (lower it ~2.5 for every 1 g/dL fall in albumin below 4). The kidney reabsorbs filtered HCO3− (mainly PCT, via carbonic anhydrase) and regenerates new HCO3− by excreting titratable acid (H2PO4−) and NH4+ (the adaptable component; PCT glutamine metabolism ↑ in acidosis, ↓ by hyperkalemia).

[[figure:ch05-fig10]]
  • Mixed disorders to recognize: salicylate toxicity (respiratory alkalosis + HAGMA); vomiting in DKA (HAGMA + metabolic alkalosis — delta–delta >2); COPD on diuretics (chronic respiratory acidosis + metabolic alkalosis); septic shock with tachypnea (lactic acidosis + respiratory alkalosis).
  • Urine anion gap (UNa + UK − UCl) in NAGMA: negative in diarrhea (kidney appropriately excretes NH4Cl), positive in distal (type 1) and type 4 RTA (impaired NH4+ excretion).
  • Toxic alcohols: methanol → formic acid → optic papillitis/blindness; ethylene glycol → glycolic and oxalic acids → AKI with calcium oxalate crystals. Both: HAGMA + ↑ osmolal gap; treat fomepizole (alcohol dehydrogenase inhibitor) ± dialysis.
Renal tubular acidosisDefectSerum K+Urine pHCauses / associations
Type 1 (distal)α-intercalated cells cannot secrete H+ → no new HCO3−, ↓ NH4+ excretion↓>5.5 (cannot acidify)Sjögren, RA, SLE, amphotericin B, lithium, analgesic nephropathy, obstruction, hereditary (AE1); calcium phosphate stones (alkaline urine, hypocitraturia, bone buffering → hypercalciuria). Treat alkali (citrate)
Type 2 (proximal)↓ PCT HCO3− reabsorption (lowered threshold)↓<5.5 once serum HCO3− falls below threshold (alkaline early)Fanconi syndrome, acetazolamide, multiple myeloma, tenofovir; hypophosphatemic rickets/osteomalacia. Needs large alkali doses
Type 4 (hyperkalemic)Hypoaldosteronism or aldosterone resistance → hyperkalemia ↓ PCT ammoniagenesis↑<5.5 (can acidify, but little buffer)Diabetic nephropathy (hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism — most common), ACEi/ARB, NSAIDs, heparin, calcineurin inhibitors, trimethoprim, K+-sparing diuretics, adrenal insufficiency, obstruction. Treat fludrocortisone, K+ restriction, loop diuretic

sections.html:
Urine casts and sediment

FindingMeaning
RBC casts, dysmorphic RBCsGlomerulonephritis (nephritic), malignant hypertension
WBC castsTubulointerstitial inflammation: acute pyelonephritis, acute interstitial nephritis, transplant rejection
Muddy brown granular casts, renal tubular epithelial cell castsAcute tubular necrosis
Fatty casts, oval fat bodies ("Maltese cross" under polarized light)Nephrotic syndrome
Waxy (broad) castsAdvanced CKD (dilated, atrophic tubules)
Hyaline castsNonspecific (Tamm–Horsfall protein); concentrated urine, dehydration, normal
Dipstick heme + but no RBCsMyoglobinuria (rhabdomyolysis) or hemoglobinuria (intravascular hemolysis)

Glomerular diseases

[[figure:ch05-fig11]]
DiseaseLight microscopyImmunofluorescenceElectron microscopyClinical pearls
Post-streptococcal GNHypercellular, neutrophilsGranular ("lumpy-bumpy") IgG, IgM, C3Subepithelial humpsNephritogenic GAS; 2–4 weeks after pharyngitis, 3–6 weeks after impetigo; ↑ ASO/anti-DNase B; ↓ C3 (normalizes in ~8 weeks); children recover, adults may progress
IgA nephropathy (Berger)Mesangial proliferationMesangial IgA (galactose-deficient IgA1 immune complexes)Mesangial depositsMost common GN worldwide; episodic gross hematuria concurrent with or 1–3 days after mucosal infection; normal C3; renal-limited form of IgA vasculitis
Rapidly progressive (crescentic) GNCrescents (fibrin, parietal epithelial cells, monocytes/macrophages) in Bowman spaceLinear (anti-GBM); granular (immune complex: PSGN, SLE, IgA); none (pauci-immune ANCA)VariesRenal failure over weeks–months; Goodpasture — young men (and older women), smoking/hydrocarbons trigger lung hemorrhage, type II hypersensitivity; treat plasmapheresis + steroids + cyclophosphamide
Diffuse proliferative GN"Wire looping" of capillariesGranular ("full house" in SLE)Subendothelial depositsLupus class IV — most common and severe lupus nephritis; ↓ C3/C4; can be nephrotic too
MPGN type I / C3 glomerulopathy (DDD)"Tram-track" GBM splitting (mesangial interposition)Granular (type I); C3 only (DDD)Subendothelial (I); intramembranous dense ribbons (DDD)Type I: HBV, HCV, cryoglobulins; DDD: C3 nephritic factor (stabilizes C3 convertase) → persistently ↓ C3
Alport syndromeVariableNegativeThinning/splitting of GBM ("basket-weave")X-linked COL4A5 most commonly; hematuria, sensorineural deafness, anterior lenticonus
Minimal change diseaseNormalNegativeDiffuse effacement of podocyte foot processesMost common nephrotic in children; triggers: infection, immunization, Hodgkin lymphoma, NSAIDs; >90% remit with glucocorticoids
FSGSSegmental sclerosis and hyalinosisUsually negative (nonspecific IgM/C3 in sclerotic areas)EffacementCommon cause of primary nephrotic syndrome in US adults, especially Black adults (APOL1 risk alleles); secondary — HIV (collapsing), heroin, sickle cell, obesity, reduced nephron mass, interferon; progresses to ESRD
Membranous nephropathyDiffuse capillary wall and GBM thickeningGranular IgG, C3 along GBMSubepithelial deposits with "spike and dome" GBM projectionsPrimary — anti-PLA2R (~70–80%); secondary — SLE (class V), HBV/HCV, solid tumors, NSAIDs, penicillamine, gold; highest risk of thrombosis (renal vein) among nephrotic diseases
Diabetic glomerulopathyMesangial expansion, GBM thickening, nodular sclerosis (Kimmelstiel–Wilson), efferent > afferent hyaline arteriolosclerosisLinear nonspecific IgG trappingGBM thickeningNonenzymatic glycation + hyperfiltration; earliest sign moderately ↑ albuminuria (30–300 mg/g); ACEi/ARB, SGLT2i, finerenone, GLP-1 RA slow progression
AmyloidosisMesangial and capillary-wall amorphous pink depositsκ/λ restriction in ALRandomly arranged nonbranching fibrilsAL (plasma cell dyscrasia), AA (RA, IBD, chronic osteomyelitis, familial Mediterranean fever); Congo red apple-green birefringence
Exam trap: Timing separates PSGN from IgA nephropathy: hematuria weeks after a sore throat with low C3 = PSGN; hematuria within days of a sore throat with normal C3 = IgA nephropathy. Low complement in nephritic syndrome narrows the list to PSGN, lupus nephritis, MPGN/C3 glomerulopathy, cryoglobulinemia, and endocarditis-associated GN.

Acute kidney injury

KDIGO definition: ↑ serum creatinine ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 h, or ≥1.5× baseline within 7 days, or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥6 h.

ParameterPrerenalIntrinsic (ATN)Postrenal
Urine osmolality (mOsm/kg)>500<350 (isosthenuric ~300)<350
Urine Na+ (mEq/L)<20>40>40 (variable early)
FENa<1%>2%>2% (may be <1% early)
BUN:Cr>20 (↑ urea reabsorption with ↓ flow)<15Varies (often >15)
SedimentBland, hyaline castsMuddy brown granular castsBland ± hematuria
CausesHypovolemia, HF, cirrhosis (hepatorenal), NSAIDs/ACEi in volume-dependent statesIschemia, nephrotoxins, AIN, GNBPH, stones (bilateral or single kidney), pelvic tumors, neurogenic bladder, catheter obstruction
  • Acute tubular necrosis — most common cause of intrinsic AKI. Ischemic: the proximal straight tubule (S3) and medullary TAL are most vulnerable (high ATP demand in a relatively hypoxic outer medulla). Nephrotoxic: PCT injury from aminoglycosides, vancomycin, cisplatin, IV contrast, amphotericin, myoglobin (rhabdomyolysis — crush injury, statins, seizures, prolonged immobilization), hemoglobin, light chains (myeloma cast nephropathy), uric acid (tumor lysis), ethylene glycol (calcium oxalate crystals). Phases: initiation → maintenance (oliguria, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, volume overload, uremia) → recovery (polyuria; risk of hypokalemia, hypovolemia).
  • Acute interstitial nephritis — drug hypersensitivity (type I/IV) 1–2 weeks after exposure: β-lactams, PPIs, NSAIDs, sulfonamides (incl. diuretics), rifampin, allopurinol; also infections and autoimmune disease (Sjögren, sarcoidosis). Fever, rash, eosinophilia, sterile pyuria/WBC casts ± urine eosinophils. Stop drug ± glucocorticoids. Can progress to papillary necrosis.
  • Renal papillary necrosis — sloughed papillae → gross hematuria, flank pain, proteinuria. Causes: sickle cell disease/trait, acute pyelonephritis, analgesic (NSAID) nephropathy, diabetes, obstruction.
  • Diffuse cortical necrosis — acute generalized infarction of both cortices from vasospasm + DIC; obstetric catastrophes (placental abruption), septic shock.
  • Contrast-associated AKI — Cr rises 24–48 h after contrast, usually reversible; prevention = isotonic IV fluids in high-risk patients.

Chronic kidney disease

Definition (KDIGO): GFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² or markers of damage (albuminuria ≥30 mg/g, sediment, imaging, biopsy) for >3 months. Staged by GFR (G1–G5) and albuminuria (A1–A3). Most common causes in the US: diabetes, then hypertension. Consequences:

  • Anemia — normocytic, ↓ EPO (treat ESA after iron repletion; HIF-PH inhibitor daprodustat for dialysis patients).
  • CKD–mineral and bone disorder — ↓ PO43− excretion → hyperphosphatemia + ↑ FGF23 + ↓ 1α-hydroxylase → ↓ calcitriol → hypocalcemia → secondary hyperparathyroidism → renal osteodystrophy (osteitis fibrosa cystica, adynamic bone disease, osteomalacia), vascular calcification, calciphylaxis. Treat phosphate binders (sevelamer, lanthanum, calcium acetate), calcitriol/analogs, cinacalcet (calcimimetic).
  • Metabolic acidosis (initially NAGMA, later HAGMA), hyperkalemia, hypertension, volume overload, accelerated atherosclerosis (leading cause of death), uremic platelet dysfunction (bleeding; desmopressin), uremic pericarditis, encephalopathy/asterixis, pruritus, neuropathy.
  • Slowing progression: BP control, ACEi/ARB if albuminuric, SGLT2 inhibitors (KDIGO 2024: most adults with CKD and eGFR ≥20), finerenone (nonsteroidal MRA) in T2D with albuminuria, semaglutide in T2D-CKD, avoid nephrotoxins, dose-adjust drugs.
  • Urgent dialysis indications: refractory acidosis, electrolytes (refractory hyperkalemia), intoxication (dialyzable: lithium, salicylates, methanol, ethylene glycol, metformin-associated lactic acidosis, theophylline), refractory volume overload, uremic complications (pericarditis, encephalopathy, bleeding).
  • Acquired cystic kidney disease in long-term dialysis → ↑ risk of RCC.

Nephrolithiasis

StoneFrequency / X-rayCrystalUrine pHCausesTreatment/prevention
Calcium oxalateMost common (~75–80%); radiopaqueEnvelope (dihydrate) or dumbbell/needle (monohydrate)Any (often low)Idiopathic hypercalciuria, hypocitraturia, enteric hyperoxaluria (Crohn disease, bariatric surgery — fat binds Ca2+, leaving oxalate free for absorption), ethylene glycol, excess vitamin C, primary hyperoxaluriaFluids, thiazides (↓ urinary Ca2+), potassium citrate, low sodium and low animal protein diet, normal dietary calcium (restricting Ca2+ ↑ oxalate absorption)
Calcium phosphateRadiopaqueWedge-shaped prismsHigh (>7)Distal (type 1) RTA, primary hyperparathyroidism, carbonic anhydrase inhibitorsThiazides, treat cause
Ammonium magnesium phosphate (struvite)~15%; radiopaque; staghorn calculi"Coffin lid" rectangular prismsHigh (urease splits urea → NH3)Urease-positive organisms: Proteus, Klebsiella, S. saprophyticus, UreaplasmaEradicate infection, surgical removal of stone (nidus for infection)
Uric acid~5–10%; radiolucent (visible on CT/ultrasound)Rhomboid or rosettes, yellow-brownLow (<5.5)Gout, tumor lysis/high cell turnover (leukemia, myeloproliferative), chronic diarrhea/ileostomy (acidic, concentrated urine), metabolic syndromeAlkalinize urine (potassium citrate), fluids, allopurinol/febuxostat
Cystine~1%; faintly radiopaque; may be staghornHexagonalLowCystinuria (AR; PCT dibasic amino acid transporter defect); childrenFluids, alkalinize urine, chelating agents (tiopronin, penicillamine)

Presentation: colicky flank pain radiating to the groin, hematuria, nausea. Noncontrast CT is the most sensitive imaging; ultrasound in pregnancy/children. Stones ≤10 mm often pass — medical expulsive therapy with tamsulosin; urgent decompression if obstruction + infection.

Urinary tract infection and pyelonephritis

  • Cystitis: dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain; leukocyte esterase (WBCs) and nitrite (gram-negative Enterobacterales reduce nitrate) positive; E. coli (P fimbriae for pyelonephritis), S. saprophyticus (young sexually active women), Klebsiella, Proteus (alkaline urine), Enterococcus, Pseudomonas (nosocomial/catheter).
  • Acute pyelonephritis: fever, flank pain, CVA tenderness, nausea; WBC casts; ascending infection (cortex, relative sparing of glomeruli/vessels); risk — VUR, obstruction, pregnancy, diabetes. Complications: perinephric abscess, papillary necrosis, urosepsis.
  • Chronic pyelonephritis: recurrent episodes (VUR, obstruction) → coarse asymmetric corticomedullary scars over blunted calyces; tubules filled with eosinophilic casts resembling thyroid follicles ("thyroidization"). Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis: foamy macrophages, often with Proteus staghorn stone — mimics tumor.

Cystic kidney diseases

DiseaseGeneticsFeatures
Autosomal dominant PKDPKD1 (chromosome 16, polycystin-1, ~85%, more severe) or PKD2 (chromosome 4, polycystin-2)Bilateral massively enlarged cystic kidneys in adults; flank pain, hematuria, hypertension (↑ renin), recurrent UTIs/stones, progressive CKD. Extrarenal: hepatic cysts (most common), berry aneurysms (subarachnoid hemorrhage), MVP, colonic diverticulosis. Treat BP control (ACEi/ARB) and tolvaptan (V2 antagonist slows cyst growth in rapidly progressive disease)
Autosomal recessive PKDPKHD1 (chromosome 6, fibrocystin)Infancy; bilateral enlarged kidneys with radially arranged collecting-duct cysts; oligohydramnios → Potter sequence; congenital hepatic fibrosis → portal hypertension; systemic hypertension; often need transplant
Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease (medullary cystic kidney disease)UMOD, MUC1Small shrunken kidneys, tubulointerstitial fibrosis, poor concentrating ability, hyperuricemia/gout (UMOD), progressive CKD
Medullary sponge kidneyUsually sporadicCystic dilation of medullary collecting ducts ("paintbrush" on urography); nephrocalcinosis, calcium stones, hematuria, UTIs; usually good prognosis
Simple cystsAcquired, ↑ with ageVery common; thin smooth wall, anechoic on ultrasound; benign (vs complex cysts with septa/solid parts → evaluate for RCC)

Renal and urinary tract tumors

TumorKey features
Renal cell carcinoma (clear cell)Most common renal malignancy in adults; men 50–70; risk: smoking, obesity, hypertension, acquired cystic kidney disease, von Hippel–Lindau (VHL loss on chromosome 3p → ↑ HIF → ↑ VEGF). Arises from PCT epithelium; polygonal clear cells rich in lipid and glycogen; golden-yellow mass. Classic triad (hematuria, flank mass, flank pain) is uncommon. Paraneoplastic: EPO (polycythemia), PTHrP (hypercalcemia), renin, ACTH, hepatic dysfunction (Stauffer syndrome). Invades renal vein → IVC; left varicocele that does not decompress when supine (left gonadal vein drains to left renal vein). Hematogenous mets to lung, bone. Resistant to conventional chemo/radiation → resection, immune checkpoint inhibitors, VEGF-TKIs, HIF-2α inhibitor (belzutifan) for VHL tumors
Papillary / chromophobe RCCPapillary — MET (hereditary), trisomy 7/17; chromophobe — intercalated cells, perinuclear halos, Birt–Hogg–Dubé
Renal oncocytomaBenign; from collecting-duct intercalated cells; large eosinophilic cells packed with mitochondria (no perinuclear clearing); central stellate scar on imaging; often resected because it mimics RCC
AngiomyolipomaBenign; blood vessels + smooth muscle + fat (fat-density on CT); bilateral/multiple in tuberous sclerosis (TSC1/TSC2); risk of hemorrhage when large; mTOR inhibitors (everolimus)
Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma)Most common renal malignancy in young children (2–4 y); triphasic: blastema, stroma, epithelium (embryonic glomerular structures); large unilateral flank mass that does not cross the midline (vs neuroblastoma), hematuria, hypertension (renin). Loss-of-function WT1 (11p13) or WT2 cluster (11p15). Syndromes: WAGR (Wilms, aniridia [PAX6], genitourinary anomalies, range of developmental delays — 11p13 deletion), Denys–Drash (Wilms, early-onset nephrotic syndrome from diffuse mesangial sclerosis, 46,XY DSD — WT1 mutation), Beckwith–Wiedemann (macroglossia, organomegaly, hemihyperplasia, omphalocele, neonatal hypoglycemia — 11p15). Excellent prognosis with nephrectomy + chemotherapy
Urothelial (transitional cell) carcinomaMost common tumor of the urinary tract (bladder > renal pelvis/ureter); painless gross hematuria in older adults; field effect → multifocal recurrence. Risk: smoking (strongest), aromatic amines (aniline dyes, rubber, leather), cyclophosphamide, phenacetin, aristolochic acid. Two pathways: low-grade papillary (FGFR3, recurs) vs flat carcinoma in situ (p53, invasive). BCG intravesical for CIS/non-muscle-invasive disease
Squamous cell carcinoma of bladderChronic irritation: Schistosoma haematobium (Middle East, Africa), long-term catheters, chronic cystitis, stones
Adenocarcinoma of bladderUrachal remnant (dome of bladder), bladder exstrophy, cystitis glandularis

title: Step 1 · Gastrointestinal, Endocrine & Reproductive Systems
meta: Exam: Step 1 · Systems covered: Gastrointestinal, Endocrine, Reproductive (embryology → anatomy → histology → physiology → pathology → pharmacology) · Approx study time: 5–6 days (2 days GI, 2 days endocrine, 1–2 days reproductive) + 45 practice questions

sections.heading: Overview
sections.html:
From NEET PG to USMLE

  • Mechanism over list. NEET PG asks "which is the most common site of carcinoid?"; Step 1 asks why the patient with carcinoid develops a pellagra-like rash (tryptophan diverted to serotonin → niacin deficiency) and why flushing appears only after liver metastasis (first-pass hepatic MAO inactivation of serotonin).
  • Epidemiology flips. In the US, esophageal adenocarcinoma (Barrett) outnumbers squamous cell carcinoma; Addison disease is usually autoimmune, not tuberculous; gallstones are mostly cholesterol stones; the most common cause of hypothyroidism is Hashimoto (iodine deficiency is the worldwide answer).
  • Renamed entities you must recognize: NAFLD/NASH → MASLD/MASH (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, 2023); central/nephrogenic diabetes insipidus → AVP deficiency / AVP resistance (2022); "sessile serrated adenoma" → sessile serrated lesion. Older names still appear in vignettes.
  • US drug landscape: ranitidine was withdrawn (2020, NDMA contamination) — famotidine is the US H2 blocker; domperidone is not FDA approved (metoclopramide is the US prokinetic, with a boxed warning for tardive dyskinesia); first-line H. pylori therapy in treatment-naive US patients is bismuth quadruple therapy (ACG 2024), with vonoprazan-based regimens as alternatives.
  • Lab units: glucose in mg/dL (126 mg/dL ≈ 7.0 mmol/L), calcium mg/dL (normal 8.4–10.2), bilirubin mg/dL (1 mg/dL ≈ 17 µmol/L), hCG mIU/mL.
  • Integrated stems: one vignette often tests embryology + anatomy + drug (e.g., MEN2A thyroid nodule → screen for pheochromocytoma before surgery → α-blockade before β-blockade).
============================ GASTROINTESTINAL ============================

sections.heading: GI Anatomy
sections.html:
Retroperitoneal organs

Retroperitoneal structures (injury → retroperitoneal hematoma, posterior pain, flank ecchymosis): adrenal glands, aorta & IVC, duodenum (parts 2–4), pancreas (all except tail, which lies in the splenorenal ligament), ureters, ascending & descending colon, kidneys, esophagus (thoracic/abdominal part posteriorly), rectum (mid/lower). Intraperitoneal: stomach, 1st part of duodenum (first ~2 cm), jejunum, ileum, cecum, appendix, transverse & sigmoid colon, liver, spleen, pancreatic tail.

RectumSuperior rectal ↔ middle & inferior rectalAnorectal varices (distinct from hemorrhoids)

TIPS shunts portal vein → hepatic vein; lowers portal pressure but can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy (ammonia bypasses the liver).

Pectinate (dentate) lineAbove (endoderm, hindgut)Below (ectoderm)
Artery / veinSuperior rectal a. (IMA) / superior rectal v. → IMV → portalInferior rectal a. (internal pudendal) / inferior rectal v. → internal pudendal → internal iliac → IVC
NerveVisceral (painless)Somatic: inferior rectal branch of pudendal (painful)
LymphInternal iliac nodesSuperficial inguinal nodes
LesionsInternal hemorrhoids (painless bleeding), adenocarcinomaExternal hemorrhoids (painful when thrombosed), anal fissure (posterior midline, pain with defecation), squamous cell carcinoma (HPV)

Hernias

HerniaPath / defectKey facts
Indirect inguinalThrough deep (internal) ring, lateral to inferior epigastric vessels, within spermatic cord (internal spermatic fascia)Patent processus vaginalis; most common hernia in both sexes; infants, males; can reach scrotum
Direct inguinalThrough Hesselbach triangle (inferior epigastric vessels laterally, lateral border of rectus abdominis medially, inguinal ligament inferiorly), medial to inferior epigastric vesselsWeak transversalis fascia; older men; covered by external spermatic fascia only
FemoralBelow inguinal ligament through femoral canal, lateral to pubic tubercle, medial to femoral veinMore common in women (but indirect inguinal still most common hernia in women); highest risk of incarceration/strangulation
Sliding hiatalGE junction displaced above diaphragmMost common hiatal hernia; "hourglass stomach"; GERD
ParaesophagealGE junction in normal position; fundus herniates alongsideRisk of volvulus/strangulation; usually repaired
Congenital diaphragmaticDefective pleuroperitoneal membrane (Bochdalek, posterolateral, left)Scaphoid abdomen, bowel sounds in chest, pulmonary hypoplasia drives mortality
High-yield: "MDs don't LIe" — Medial to inferior epigastrics = Direct; Lateral = Indirect. The inferior epigastric vessels are the landmark surgeons see laparoscopically.

sections.html:
RegionDistinguishing histology
LayersMucosa (epithelium, lamina propria, muscularis mucosae) → submucosa (Meissner plexus: secretion, blood flow) → muscularis externa (inner circular, outer longitudinal; Auerbach/myenteric plexus between them: motility) → serosa (intraperitoneal) or adventitia (retroperitoneal)
EsophagusNonkeratinized stratified squamous; upper 1/3 skeletal muscle, lower 1/3 smooth muscle
StomachFundus/body: parietal cells (HCl, intrinsic factor), chief cells (pepsinogen), ECL cells (histamine); antrum: G cells (gastrin), D cells (somatostatin); mucous cells throughout
DuodenumVilli, microvilli, Brunner glands in submucosa (alkaline mucus; hypertrophy with peptic ulcer disease)
JejunumTallest villi, prominent plicae circulares ("feathery" on imaging)
IleumPeyer patches (lamina propria/submucosa; M cells sample antigen; IgA plasma cells), most goblet cells of small bowel
ColonCrypts but no villi, abundant goblet cells; taeniae coli, haustra
Liver lobule zonesZone 1 (periportal): highest O₂; viral hepatitis, ingested toxins (cocaine). Zone 2: yellow fever. Zone 3 (centrilobular): lowest O₂, highest CYP450 → ischemia ("shock liver"), acetaminophen, alcohol, halothane; first to show alcoholic damage
Other liver cellsKupffer cells (sinusoidal macrophages); hepatic stellate (Ito) cells store vitamin A and become myofibroblasts in fibrosis; bile canaliculi between hepatocytes

sections.heading: GI Physiology
sections.html:
GI hormones and secretory products

Hormone (cell, site)Main actionsStimulated by / inhibited byClinical link
Gastrin (G cells, antrum & duodenum)↑ H⁺ (mainly via ECL histamine), ↑ mucosal growth, ↑ motility↑ peptides/amino acids, distension, vagus (via GRP), alkaline pH; ↓ acid (pH <1.5), somatostatin↑↑ in Zollinger-Ellison, atrophic gastritis, PPI use
Somatostatin (D cells)Universal "off": ↓ acid, ↓ pepsinogen, ↓ pancreatic & biliary secretion, ↓ gastrin, ↓ insulin/glucagon↑ acid; ↓ vagusOctreotide: varices, carcinoid, VIPoma, acromegaly
CCK (I cells, duodenum/jejunum)↑ pancreatic enzymes, gallbladder contraction, relax sphincter of Oddi, ↓ gastric emptying↑ fatty acids, amino acidsPostprandial biliary colic after fatty meals
Secretin (S cells, duodenum)↑ pancreatic HCO₃⁻, ↓ gastric acid, ↑ bile flow↑ acid, fatty acids in duodenumSecretin paradoxically raises gastrin in gastrinoma
GIP (K cells, duodenum/jejunum)↑ insulin (incretin), ↓ acid↑ glucose, fat, amino acidsOral glucose → more insulin than IV glucose (incretin effect); tirzepatide is a GIP/GLP-1 agonist
GLP-1 (L cells, ileum/colon)↑ glucose-dependent insulin, ↓ glucagon, ↓ gastric emptying, satiety↑ nutrients; degraded by DPP-4GLP-1 agonists, DPP-4 inhibitors
Motilin (M cells, small bowel)Migrating motor complexes in fasting state↑ fastingErythromycin is a motilin agonist (prokinetic)
VIP (enteric neurons)↑ intestinal water/electrolyte secretion, relax smooth muscle/sphinctersDistension, vagusVIPoma: watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, achlorhydria
Nitric oxideSmooth muscle relaxation incl. LES—Loss of NO/VIP inhibitory neurons → achalasia
Ghrelin (stomach)↑ appetite, ↑ GH secretion↑ fasting; ↓ food↑ in Prader-Willi; ↓ after sleeve gastrectomy

Gastric acid regulation (parietal cell)

Three stimulants converge on the apical H⁺/K⁺-ATPase: ACh (M3, Gq → ↑Ca²⁺), gastrin (CCK-B, Gq) and histamine (H2, Gs → ↑cAMP). Gastrin acts mostly indirectly by releasing histamine from ECL cells. Somatostatin and prostaglandins (Gi) inhibit. Because the pump is the final common step, PPIs suppress acid regardless of stimulus. Vagotomy removes ACh; atropine blocks it. Phases: cephalic (~30%, vagal), gastric (~60%, distension + peptides), intestinal (~10%).

Pancreatic exocrine secretion and digestion

NutrientDigestionAbsorption
CarbohydrateSalivary/pancreatic amylase → oligosaccharides; brush-border disaccharidases (lactase, sucrase, maltase)Glucose & galactose: SGLT1 (Na⁺-coupled); fructose: GLUT5 (facilitated); all exit via GLUT2. Only monosaccharides absorbed
ProteinPepsin; trypsinogen activated by duodenal enteropeptidase (enterokinase) → trypsin activates other zymogensAmino acids, di- and tripeptides (PepT1, H⁺-coupled)
FatLipase + colipase, emulsified by bile acids → micellesInto enterocyte → chylomicrons (apoB-48, requires MTTP) → lacteals; medium-chain TGs go directly to portal blood
MicronutrientSiteNotes
IronDuodenumFe³⁺ reduced to Fe²⁺ (duodenal cytochrome b), apical DMT1 → basolateral ferroportin (blocked by hepcidin)
FolateSmall bowel (jejunum)Deficiency develops in months
Vitamin B12Terminal ileumReleased from haptocorrin (R-binder) by pancreatic proteases → binds intrinsic factor → ileal receptor (cubilin); deficiency after ileal resection, Crohn, pernicious anemia, pancreatic insufficiency, Diphyllobothrium, metformin, PPIs
Bile acidsTerminal ileum (~95% recycled)Loss → bile acid diarrhea, cholesterol gallstones, fat malabsorption

Bile: bile acids (cholic, chenodeoxycholic; rate-limiting enzyme cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase), phospholipids, cholesterol, conjugated bilirubin, water, HCO₃⁻. Conjugation with glycine/taurine makes them water-soluble.

Salivary secretion: hypotonic (ducts reabsorb Na⁺/Cl⁻), stimulated by both parasympathetic (more volume) and sympathetic (more protein) — atropine causes dry mouth.

Bilirubin metabolism and jaundice

[[figure:ch06-fig02]]
Hereditary hyperbilirubinemiaDefectBilirubinFeatures / treatment
Gilbert syndrome↓ UGT1A1 activity (promoter TA-repeat variant); mild ↓ uptakeUnconjugated, mild (<3–4 mg/dL)Jaundice with fasting, stress, illness, exertion; benign; normal CBC and LFTs; irinotecan toxicity risk
Crigler-Najjar type IAbsent UGT1A1 (AR)Unconjugated, very high (often >20)Kernicterus in neonates; phototherapy, plasmapheresis, liver transplant; no response to phenobarbital
Crigler-Najjar type IIMarkedly ↓ UGT1A1Unconjugated, moderateResponds to phenobarbital (induces UGT)
Dubin-JohnsonDefective MRP2 (canalicular export)ConjugatedGrossly black liver (epinephrine-metabolite pigment); benign
RotorDefective hepatic uptake/storage (OATP1B1 + 1B3)ConjugatedMilder, liver not black; benign
Exam trap: "Dark urine" means conjugated bilirubin. A hemolytic patient with jaundice has normally coloured urine for bilirubin (but ↑ urobilinogen). Gilbert is the answer when an otherwise well young adult turns yellow during a fast (Ramadan, exam stress, gastroenteritis) with normal hemoglobin, haptoglobin and transaminases.

sections.heading: GI Pathology
sections.html:
Oral cavity, salivary glands and esophagus

ConditionMechanism / pathologyKey clue
Pleomorphic adenomaBenign mixed tumor, parotid (most common salivary tumor)Painless mobile mass; recurs if incompletely excised; facial nerve palsy suggests malignancy
Warthin tumorCystic tumor with germinal centers; smokersBilateral parotid masses
Mucoepidermoid carcinomaMost common malignant salivary tumorMucinous + squamous cells
AchalasiaLoss of inhibitory (NO/VIP) neurons in myenteric plexus → incomplete LES relaxation, ↑ LES tone, aperistalsis; secondary: Chagas (T. cruzi), pseudoachalasia (cardia cancer)Dysphagia to solids and liquids from the start; "bird's beak" barium swallow; manometry is diagnostic; ↑ SCC risk
Systemic sclerosis (CREST)Smooth-muscle atrophy/fibrosis → ↓ LES tone, ↓ peristalsisGERD + dysphagia, Raynaud, sclerodactyly
Esophageal spasm / hypercontractileUncoordinated contractionsChest pain mimicking angina; "corkscrew" esophagus
Eosinophilic esophagitisTh2 allergic (foods); ≥15 eosinophils/hpfAtopic young man with food impaction; rings ("trachealization") and furrows; not responsive to PPI alone in many; topical steroids, elimination diet, dupilumab
Infectious esophagitisCandida (white pseudomembranes), HSV-1 (punched-out ulcers), CMV (linear ulcers, intranuclear inclusions)Immunosuppressed (HIV)
Pill esophagitisBisphosphonates, doxycycline, KCl, NSAIDs, ironTake with water, stay upright 30 min
Plummer-VinsonEsophageal web + iron deficiency anemia + glossitis/cheilosis↑ SCC risk
Zenker diverticulumFalse (pulsion) diverticulum through Killian triangle (cricopharyngeal dysfunction)Elderly; halitosis, regurgitation of undigested food, neck gurgling
Mallory-Weiss syndromeMucosal laceration at GE junction from retchingAlcohol, bulimia; hematemesis, no pneumomediastinum
Boerhaave syndromeTransmural rupture (distal, left posterolateral)Severe chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema, Hamman crunch; water-soluble contrast study
Esophageal varicesPortal hypertension (left gastric → azygos)Painless massive hematemesis; octreotide + endoscopic banding + antibiotics (ceftriaxone)
GERDTransient LES relaxation; worse with hiatal hernia, obesity, pregnancy, smoking, sclerodermaHeartburn, chronic cough, hoarseness, asthma, dental erosions
Barrett esophagusIntestinal metaplasia: nonciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells replacing squamous in distal esophagusPrecursor of adenocarcinoma; surveillance endoscopy
Esophageal cancerSquamous cell carcinomaAdenocarcinoma
LocationUpper/middle 2/3Lower 1/3 (GE junction)
Risk factorsAlcohol, tobacco, very hot drinks, achalasia, caustic injury, nitrosamines, Plummer-Vinson, betel nutGERD → Barrett, obesity, tobacco
EpidemiologyMost common worldwide (incl. India, "Asian esophageal cancer belt")Most common in the US

Stomach

ConditionMechanism / features
Acute erosive gastritisNSAIDs (↓ PGE₂ → ↓ mucus/HCO₃⁻, ↓ blood flow), alcohol, uremia, chemotherapy. Curling ulcer: burns → hypovolemia → mucosal ischemia. Cushing ulcer: brain injury → ↑ vagal tone → ↑ acid
Chronic autoimmune (type A) gastritisT-cell destruction of parietal cells in body/fundus; anti-parietal cell & anti-intrinsic factor antibodies; achlorhydria → ↑ gastrin → ECL hyperplasia → gastric carcinoid; pernicious anemia; ↑ adenocarcinoma risk
H. pylori (type B) gastritisMost common; urease → ammonia; begins in antrum; ↑ risk peptic ulcer, adenocarcinoma, MALT lymphoma (may regress after eradication). Diagnose: urea breath test, stool antigen, biopsy (urease, histology)
Ménétrier diseaseHyperplasia of foveolar (surface mucous) cells, ↑ TGF-α; giant rugae, protein-losing gastropathy (edema), atrophy of parietal cells
Gastric adenocarcinoma, intestinal typeH. pylori, nitrosamines (smoked foods, Japan/Korea), blood group A, atrophic gastritis; lesser curvature, ulcerated mass with heaped margins
Gastric adenocarcinoma, diffuse typeSignet-ring cells, loss of E-cadherin (CDH1), linitis plastica ("leather bottle"); not linked to H. pylori
Metastatic signsVirchow node (left supraclavicular), Sister Mary Joseph nodule (periumbilical), Krukenberg tumor (bilateral ovaries), Blumer shelf; paraneoplastic acanthosis nigricans, Leser-Trélat sign
GISTInterstitial cells of Cajal; KIT (CD117) or PDGFRA activating mutation, DOG1+; imatinib
Peptic ulcerGastric ulcerDuodenal ulcer
PainWorse with meals → weight lossBetter with meals → weight gain; nocturnal
H. pylori~70%~90%
Mechanism↓ mucosal protection (NSAIDs, H. pylori)↑ acid and/or ↓ HCO₃⁻; ZES if multiple/distal
MalignancyMust biopsy margins (can be ulcerated cancer)Almost never malignant
ComplicationsLesser curvature bleed → left gastric arteryPosterior → GDA bleed; anterior → perforation (free air, pain referred to shoulder)

Malabsorption and small bowel disorders

DisorderMechanismDiagnosis / key findings
Celiac diseaseGluten (gliadin) deamidated by tissue transglutaminase → presented on HLA-DQ2/DQ8 → T-cell injury, mostly distal duodenum/proximal jejunumIgA anti-tTG (check total IgA — celiac is associated with IgA deficiency), anti-endomysial, deamidated gliadin; biopsy: villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, intraepithelial lymphocytosis. Iron deficiency, osteoporosis, dermatitis herpetiformis; ↑ risk enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma. D-xylose test abnormal
Lactase deficiencyPrimary (age-related, common in non-Europeans) or secondary to mucosal injuryOsmotic diarrhea, ↑ stool osmotic gap, ↓ stool pH, positive hydrogen breath test; villi normal in primary
Pancreatic insufficiencyChronic pancreatitis, CF, obstructing cancerSteatorrhea, fat-soluble vitamin and B12 deficiency, ↓ fecal elastase, normal D-xylose test (absorption needs no enzymes)
Whipple diseaseTropheryma whipplei (gram +) in macrophagesOlder man: arthralgia, diarrhea, weight loss, cardiac, neuro (oculomasticatory myorhythmia); PAS+ foamy macrophages in lamina propria; ceftriaxone then TMP-SMX
Tropical sprueProbably infectious; after residence in tropics (incl. India)Megaloblastic anemia (folate/B12); responds to tetracycline + folate
AbetalipoproteinemiaAR MTTP mutation → no apoB-48/apoB-100 lipoproteinsInfant failure to thrive, steatorrhea, acanthocytes, lipid-laden enterocytes, ataxia, retinitis pigmentosa (vitamin E deficiency)
Small intestinal bacterial overgrowthStasis (blind loop, diabetes, scleroderma)Bloating; ↓ B12 with ↑ folate (bacteria make folate); breath test
Short bowel / ileal resection↓ bile acid recyclingBile acid diarrhea, steatorrhea, B12 deficiency, gallstones, oxalate stones

Stool osmotic gap = 290 − 2(stool Na⁺ + K⁺). Gap >125 mOsm/kg → osmotic diarrhea (lactose, laxatives); <50 → secretory (cholera, VIPoma, carcinoid). Secretory diarrhea persists with fasting.

Inflammatory bowel disease

FeatureCrohn diseaseUlcerative colitis
LocationMouth to anus; terminal ileum most common; skip lesions; rectum often spared; perianal diseaseRectum always involved, extends proximally in continuous fashion; backwash ileitis
DepthTransmural → fistulas, strictures, abscessesMucosa/submucosa
Gross / imagingCobblestoning, linear ulcers, creeping fat, "string sign"Pseudopolyps, friable mucosa, loss of haustra ("lead pipe"), toxic megacolon
MicroscopyNoncaseating granulomas, lymphoid aggregatesCrypt abscesses (neutrophils), crypt distortion
ImmunologyTh1/Th17; NOD2; ASCA antibodiesTh2-like; p-ANCA
SmokingWorsensParadoxically protective
Specific complicationsCalcium oxalate stones, gallstones, B12 deficiency, malabsorption, fistulas (enterovesical → pneumaturia)PSC, toxic megacolon, higher CRC risk (pancolitis, duration)
SurgeryNot curative (recurs at anastomosis)Proctocolectomy is curative

Shared extraintestinal manifestations: erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, episcleritis/uveitis, peripheral arthritis (tracks bowel activity), axial spondyloarthritis (HLA-B27; independent of bowel activity), aphthous ulcers. Microscopic colitis (collagenous/lymphocytic): older women, chronic watery diarrhea, normal-appearing mucosa, linked to NSAIDs, PPIs, SSRIs; budesonide. IBS (Rome IV): recurrent abdominal pain ≥1 day/week for 3 months related to defecation and change in stool frequency/form; no alarm features.

Other small bowel and colon disorders

ConditionKey points
AppendicitisObstruction (fecalith in adults, lymphoid hyperplasia in children); periumbilical pain (visceral T10) → McBurney point (parietal peritoneum); psoas/obturator/Rovsing signs
DiverticulosisFalse diverticula (mucosa + submucosa) where vasa recta penetrate; sigmoid; low fiber, ↑ intraluminal pressure. Commonest cause of painless hematochezia in older adults
DiverticulitisLLQ pain, fever, leukocytosis; CT; complications abscess, perforation, colovesical fistula (pneumaturia, fecaluria). Selected immunocompetent patients with uncomplicated disease may be managed without antibiotics (AGA/ACP)
AngiodysplasiaDilated submucosal vessels, cecum/right colon, elderly; associated with aortic stenosis (Heyde: acquired vWF deficiency), ESRD
IntussusceptionIleocolic; 6 months–3 years; lead point (Meckel, lymphoid hyperplasia after viral infection/rotavirus vaccine, adult tumor); colicky pain, "currant jelly" stool, sausage-shaped mass, US "target sign"; air/contrast enema
VolvulusMidgut (infants, malrotation) or sigmoid (elderly, constipated; "coffee bean" sign); cecal (younger)
Acute mesenteric ischemiaSMA embolus (AF) or thrombosis; pain out of proportion to exam, ↑ lactate, "currant jelly" stool late
Chronic mesenteric ischemia"Intestinal angina": postprandial pain, food fear, weight loss
Ischemic colitisWatershed (splenic flexure, rectosigmoid), elderly after hypotension; thumbprinting
Small bowel obstructionAdhesions (most common in adults), hernias, tumors; air-fluid levels
Ileus / OgilvieHypomotility without obstruction: postoperative, hypokalemia, opioids; colonic pseudo-obstruction in hospitalized patients (neostigmine)
Necrotizing enterocolitisPremature, formula-fed; pneumatosis intestinalis, portal venous gas
Hemorrhoids / fissureSee pectinate line table above

Colonic polyps and polyposis syndromes

PolypFeaturesMalignant potential
HyperplasticMost common non-neoplastic, small, rectosigmoid; serrated surfaceVery low
Inflammatory pseudopolypRegenerating mucosa in IBDNone (but IBD itself ↑ risk)
Hamartomatous (juvenile, Peutz-Jeghers)Normal tissue, disordered architectureSolitary juvenile polyp: none; syndromes: ↑
Adenomatous (tubular → tubulovillous → villous)Neoplastic; risk rises with size >1 cm, villous histology, high-grade dysplasia. Villous adenoma may cause secretory diarrhea with hypokalemiaYes (chromosomal instability pathway)
Sessile serrated lesionRight colon, flat; BRAF mutation, CpG island methylator phenotype (MLH1 silencing → MSI)Yes (serrated pathway; interval cancers)
SyndromeGene / inheritanceHallmarks
Familial adenomatous polyposisAPC (5q), ADHundreds–thousands of adenomas; ~100% CRC by 40–50 without prophylactic colectomy; duodenal/periampullary adenomas; CHRPE
Gardner syndromeAPCFAP + osteomas (mandible/skull), desmoid tumors, epidermoid cysts, supernumerary/impacted teeth
Turcot syndromeAPC or mismatch repairPolyposis + brain tumors (medulloblastoma with APC; glioblastoma with MMR)
MUTYH-associated polyposisMUTYH, ARAttenuated polyposis; consider when no parental history
Lynch syndrome (HNPCC)MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, EPCAM, ADFew polyps, rapid progression, proximal CRC at young age, microsatellite instability; endometrial (most common extracolonic), ovarian, gastric, small bowel, urothelial, sebaceous skin tumors (Muir-Torre)
Peutz-JeghersSTK11, ADHamartomatous polyps throughout GI tract (intussusception), mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation of lips/buccal mucosa/hands; ↑ breast, pancreatic, colorectal, gonadal (Sertoli cell, sex-cord tumor with annular tubules) cancers
Juvenile polyposisSMAD4, BMPR1A, ADMany juvenile polyps; SMAD4 overlaps with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia
Cowden (PTEN hamartoma)PTEN, ADHamartomas, trichilemmomas; breast, follicular thyroid, endometrial cancer

Colorectal cancer

Adenoma–carcinoma sequence (chromosomal instability, ~80%): loss of APC (normal mucosa → at-risk mucosa; ↑ β-catenin/Wnt) → KRAS activation (adenoma) → loss of TP53 and 18q (SMAD4/DCC) (carcinoma). Microsatellite instability (~15%): mismatch repair loss (Lynch germline, or sporadic MLH1 promoter hypermethylation via serrated pathway); right-sided, mucinous, lymphocyte-rich, responsive to immune checkpoint inhibitors. NSAIDs/aspirin inhibit COX-2 and reduce adenoma formation.

Right (proximal) colonLeft (distal) colon
GrowthExophytic, bleeding massInfiltrating, "napkin-ring"/"apple-core" lesion
PresentationIron deficiency anemia, fatigue, occult blood (older man with IDA = colonoscopy)Change in bowel habits, thin stools, hematochezia, obstruction

Associations: Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis biotype I) bacteremia/endocarditis and Clostridium septicum infection → colonoscopy. CEA is for monitoring recurrence, not screening. USPSTF (2021): average-risk screening ages 45–75 (colonoscopy every 10 y, FIT yearly, stool DNA-FIT every 1–3 y, CT colonography or flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 y); individualize 76–85. Family history of CRC in a first-degree relative <60: start at 40 or 10 years before the relative's diagnosis, colonoscopy every 5 y.

Carcinoid (neuroendocrine) tumors of the GI tract: small bowel (ileum) and appendix are classic sites; carcinoid syndrome requires hepatic metastases (see Endocrine).

Liver: patterns of injury

PatternLabsTypical causes
Hepatocellular↑↑ AST/ALT (ALT > AST in viral, MASLD; AST:ALT >2:1 in alcohol — AST is mitochondrial and alcohol causes pyridoxal-phosphate deficiency lowering ALT)Viral hepatitis, drugs, ischemia (AST/ALT in thousands, rapid fall), autoimmune, Wilson
Cholestatic↑↑ ALP + ↑ GGT (confirms hepatic source), ↑ conjugated bilirubinObstruction, PBC, PSC, drugs (anabolic steroids, OCPs, amoxicillin-clavulanate)
Synthetic failure↑ PT/INR (not corrected by vitamin K), ↓ albuminCirrhosis, fulminant failure

Viral hepatitis

VirusGenome / familyTransmissionChronicity & features
HAVssRNA (+), picornavirusFecal-oral (travel, shellfish)Never chronic; IgM anti-HAV = acute; vaccine
HBVPartially double-stranded DNA, hepadnavirus, uses reverse transcriptaseParenteral, sexual, perinatalChronic in ~90% of infected neonates vs <5% of adults; HCC even without cirrhosis (integration); polyarteritis nodosa, membranous nephropathy
HCVssRNA (+), flavivirus; no proofreading → envelope variation, no vaccineIV drug use (most common in US), transfusion before 1992Chronic in majority (~75%); cirrhosis, HCC; mixed cryoglobulinemia, MPGN, porphyria cutanea tarda, lichen planus. Cure with DAAs (≥95%)
HDVDefective ssRNA, needs HBsAg coatParenteralCoinfection (with acute HBV) vs superinfection (on chronic HBV; worse, more chronicity)
HEVssRNA (+), hepevirusFecal-oral, waterborne (Indian subcontinent epidemics), undercooked porkFulminant hepatitis with high mortality in pregnant women; chronic in transplant recipients

Screening (US): USPSTF recommends one-time HCV screening for all adults 18–79; CDC (2023) recommends HBV screening (HBsAg, anti-HBs, total anti-HBc) at least once for all adults ≥18.

[[figure:ch06-fig03]]
HBsAgAnti-HBsHBeAgAnti-HBcInterpretation
+−+IgMAcute infection, highly infectious
−−−IgMWindow period
−+−IgGRecovered, immune (natural infection)
−+−−Vaccinated (anti-HBs alone)
+ (>6 mo)−+IgGChronic, high replication
+ (>6 mo)−−IgGChronic, low replication (inactive carrier) — or precore mutant if HBV DNA high

HCV drugs (pan-genotypic regimens): sofosbuvir (NS5B polymerase inhibitor, nucleotide analog) + velpatasvir (NS5A inhibitor); glecaprevir (NS3/4A protease inhibitor) + pibrentasvir (NS5A). Check for HBV coinfection before DAAs — HBV reactivation risk. HBV drugs: tenofovir, entecavir (nucleos(t)ide RT inhibitors), peginterferon-α.

Other liver diseases

DiseaseMechanismClues / diagnosis / treatment
Alcohol-associated liver diseaseSteatosis (↑ NADH/NAD⁺ → ↑ glycerol-3-P, ↓ fatty acid oxidation) → hepatitis → cirrhosisAlcoholic hepatitis: Mallory-Denk bodies (intermediate filaments), neutrophils, zone 3 injury, AST:ALT >2:1, fever, tender hepatomegaly
MASLD / MASH (formerly NAFLD/NASH)Insulin resistance → hepatic steatosis ± steatohepatitisObesity, T2DM; ALT > AST; most common chronic liver disease in US; resmetirom (THR-β agonist, 2024) for MASH with fibrosis
Autoimmune hepatitisT-cell mediatedYoung women; type 1 ANA + anti-smooth muscle (anti-actin); type 2 anti-LKM1 (children); ↑ IgG; interface hepatitis with plasma cells; steroids ± azathioprine
Hereditary hemochromatosisHFE C282Y (AR) → inappropriately low hepcidin → ↑ ferroportin → ↑ duodenal absorption and macrophage release↑ ferritin, ↑ transferrin saturation (>45%), ↓ TIBC; "bronze diabetes," cirrhosis, HCC, restrictive→dilated cardiomyopathy, hypogonadism, 2nd/3rd MCP arthropathy (CPPD); Prussian blue stain; phlebotomy; chelation (deferoxamine, deferasirox) for transfusional overload
Wilson diseaseATP7B (chr 13, AR) → ↓ copper incorporation into ceruloplasmin and ↓ biliary excretion↓ ceruloplasmin, ↑ 24-h urinary copper, ↑ hepatic copper; Kayser-Fleischer rings; putamen degeneration (tremor, dysarthria, parkinsonism), psychiatric symptoms, Coombs-negative hemolysis, Fanconi syndrome; penicillamine or trientine (chelators), zinc (↓ absorption)
α1-antitrypsin deficiencyMisfolded PiZ protein retained in hepatocyte ERPAS+, diastase-resistant globules; cirrhosis + panacinar (lower-lobe) emphysema
Primary biliary cholangitisAutoimmune lymphocytic, granulomatous destruction of intrahepatic small bile ductsMiddle-aged woman, pruritus, fatigue, ↑ ALP, antimitochondrial antibody; Sjögren, Hashimoto; xanthomas, osteoporosis; ursodiol; add-on PPAR agonists (elafibranor, seladelpar)
Primary sclerosing cholangitisConcentric "onion-skin" fibrosis of intra- and extrahepatic ductsYoung man with UC; p-ANCA; "beaded" ducts on MRCP; ↑ cholangiocarcinoma, gallbladder cancer and CRC risk
Budd-Chiari syndromeHepatic vein thrombosis (polycythemia vera, pregnancy, OCPs, HCC, PNH)Painful hepatomegaly, ascites, centrilobular congestion ("nutmeg liver"), no JVD (distinguishes from right heart failure)
Reye syndromeAspirin in viral illness (influenza, varicella) → mitochondrial injury, ↓ β-oxidationChildren: microvesicular steatosis, hypoglycemia, vomiting, encephalopathy, ↑ ammonia; avoid aspirin <18 y except Kawasaki
Hepatic encephalopathy↑ NH₃ (shunting, ↓ urea cycle) → astrocyte glutamine swelling; triggers: GI bleed, infection, hypokalemia/alkalosis, sedatives, constipation, TIPSAsterixis; lactulose (colonic acidification traps NH₄⁺) + rifaximin
Cirrhosis complicationsPortal hypertension, hypoalbuminemia, hyperestrinism (↓ hepatic metabolism)Ascites (SAAG ≥1.1), SBP (PMN ≥250/mm³; ceftriaxone), hepatorenal syndrome (terlipressin + albumin), spider angiomas, palmar erythema, gynecomastia, testicular atrophy
Liver tumorKey features
Hemangioma (cavernous)Most common benign; peripheral nodular enhancement with centripetal fill-in; do not biopsy (bleeding)
Focal nodular hyperplasiaYoung women, central stellate scar; no malignant potential
Hepatic adenomaOCPs, anabolic steroids, glycogen storage disease; risk of rupture/bleeding (especially in pregnancy); β-catenin-mutated subtype can transform
Hepatocellular carcinomaCirrhosis of any cause, HBV (even without cirrhosis), HCV, alcohol, MASLD, hemochromatosis, α1AT, Wilson, aflatoxin (Aspergillus, TP53 codon 249 mutation); ↑ AFP; arterial-phase enhancement with washout on CT/MRI is diagnostic in cirrhosis (biopsy often unnecessary); spreads hematogenously, portal vein invasion (portal vein thrombosis) or hepatic vein invasion → Budd-Chiari
AngiosarcomaVinyl chloride, arsenic, Thorotrast
MetastasesMost common malignant liver tumors (GI, breast, lung)

Gallbladder and biliary tract

ConditionKey points

Biliary colicTransient cystic duct obstruction; postprandial RUQ pain <6 h; normal labs
Acute cholecystitisPersistent cystic duct obstruction → inflammation; RUQ pain >6 h, fever, Murphy sign, leukocytosis; ultrasound (wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid); HIDA scan shows non-filling of gallbladder if US equivocal. Acalculous form in critically ill (stasis, ischemia)
CholedocholithiasisStone in CBD → ↑ ALP, ↑ conjugated bilirubin; may cause pancreatitis
