Pancreas

ConditionKey points
Acute pancreatitisPremature trypsin activation → autodigestion. Causes: gallstones and alcohol (most common), hypertriglyceridemia (>1000 mg/dL), hypercalcemia, post-ERCP, drugs (azathioprine, valproate, didanosine, thiazides, protease inhibitors), trauma, mumps, scorpion sting, PRSS1/SPINK1. Diagnosis = 2 of 3: epigastric pain radiating to back, lipase (or amylase) ≥3× ULN, imaging. Complications: pseudocyst (fibrous/granulation wall, no epithelium, ≥4 weeks), walled-off necrosis, hypocalcemia (fat saponification), ARDS, DIC, splenic vein thrombosis; Cullen (periumbilical) and Grey Turner (flank) signs = retroperitoneal hemorrhage. Treatment: goal-directed (moderate) fluid resuscitation with lactated Ringer, analgesia, early oral/enteral feeding; cholecystectomy during the same admission for gallstone pancreatitis
Chronic pancreatitisAlcohol (adults), CF (children); calcifications on CT, chain-of-lakes duct; triad of pain, steatorrhea, diabetes (type 3c); ↓ fecal elastase; ↑ adenocarcinoma risk
Pancreatic adenocarcinomaSmoking (strongest modifiable risk), chronic pancreatitis, diabetes, obesity, BRCA2, Peutz-Jeghers, Lynch; KRAS (~90%), CDKN2A (p16), TP53, SMAD4. Head (~2/3): painless obstructive jaundice + Courvoisier sign (palpable nontender gallbladder), weight loss, new-onset diabetes, migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau sign); CA 19-9 for monitoring; Whipple procedure if resectable
Cystic neoplasmsIPMN (communicates with duct, mucin; older), mucinous cystic neoplasm (body/tail, ovarian-type stroma, women), serous cystadenoma (glycogen-rich, benign, "sunburst" calcification)

sections.html:
Hypothalamic–pituitary axes

Hypothalamic hormonePituitary targetEnd-organ / feedbackNotes
CRHACTH (from POMC, along with MSH, β-endorphin)Cortisol → ↓ CRH, ↓ ACTHCircadian: peak early morning; stress ↑
TRHTSH, ↑ prolactinT4/T3 → ↓ TRH, ↓ TSHPrimary hypothyroidism → ↑ TRH → hyperprolactinemia
GnRH (pulsatile)FSH, LHSex steroids, inhibin (↓ FSH)Continuous GnRH (leuprolide) suppresses LH/FSH; prolactin ↓ GnRH
GHRH (↑) / somatostatin (↓)GHIGF-1 (liver) → ↓ GH (↑ somatostatin)GH ↑ in sleep, hypoglycemia, exercise, ghrelin; ↓ by glucose, obesity
Dopamine (↓, tonic)ProlactinProlactin → ↑ dopamineStalk compression or D2 antagonists → ↑ prolactin (all other anterior hormones fall)
ADH, oxytocin (made in hypothalamus)Released from posterior pituitaryOsmolality (ADH), suckling/cervical stretch (oxytocin)ADH: V2 (Gs, aquaporin-2 insertion, collecting duct), V1 (Gq, vasoconstriction)

Anterior pituitary cell types: acidophils (GH, prolactin) and basophils (FSH, LH, ACTH, TSH). TSH, LH, FSH and hCG share an identical α subunit; the β subunit confers specificity (so very high hCG can stimulate the TSH receptor). Receptor signaling: cAMP — FSH, LH, ACTH, TSH, CRH, hCG, ADH-V2, PTH, calcitonin, glucagon, GHRH; IP₃ (Gq) — GnRH, oxytocin, ADH-V1, TRH, histamine-H1, angiotensin II, gastrin; intracellular receptors — steroids, T3/T4, vitamin D; receptor tyrosine kinase — insulin, IGF-1, FGF, PDGF; JAK/STAT (nonreceptor TK) — GH, prolactin, cytokines, EPO, G-CSF, thrombopoietin; cGMP — ANP/BNP, NO.

[[figure:ch06-fig04]]

Steroid hormone synthesis and congenital adrenal hyperplasia

[[figure:ch06-fig05]]
High-yield: CAH logic in two questions — (1) Is blood pressure high? (11β or 17α: DOC excess) (2) Are androgens high? (21-OH or 11β: virilization; 17α: no sex steroids). Newborn screening measures 17-OH progesterone. Treatment: glucocorticoid replacement (suppresses ACTH) ± fludrocortisone for salt wasters.

Thyroid physiology

Iodide enters follicular cells via the Na⁺/I⁻ symporter (blocked by perchlorate, pertechnetate), moves to colloid via pendrin, and is oxidized and organified onto tyrosines of thyroglobulin by thyroid peroxidase (TPO), which also couples MIT + DIT → T3 and DIT + DIT → T4 (TPO is blocked by methimazole and PTU). Thyroglobulin is endocytosed and proteolyzed to release mostly T4. 5′-deiodinase converts T4 → active T3 peripherally (blocked by PTU, propranolol, glucocorticoids, amiodarone, iodinated contrast); inner-ring (5-) deiodination gives inactive reverse T3 (↑ in sick euthyroid). Wolff-Chaikoff effect: excess iodide transiently blocks organification; Jod-Basedow: iodine load causes hyperthyroidism in iodine-deficient nodular glands.

T3 actions (nuclear receptor): ↑ Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase → ↑ BMR and heat; ↑ β1 receptors → ↑ HR, contractility; brain maturation (cretinism); bone growth with GH; ↑ glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, lipolysis; ↓ LDL (↑ LDL receptors). TBG rises with estrogen (pregnancy, OCPs): total T4 ↑, free T4 normal, TSH normal. TBG falls with androgens, nephrotic syndrome, liver failure.

[[figure:ch06-fig06]]

Calcium, PTH and vitamin D

[[figure:ch06-fig07]]

Insulin and glucagon

Insulin release: glucose enters β cells via GLUT2 → glycolysis → ↑ ATP/ADP → closes K⁺-ATP channels (SUR1/Kir6.2; target of sulfonylureas) → depolarization → voltage-gated Ca²⁺ influx → exocytosis. Proinsulin → insulin + C-peptide (marker of endogenous secretion). Insulin receptor is a tyrosine kinase → PI3K/Akt (metabolic; GLUT4 translocation in skeletal muscle and adipose) and RAS/MAPK (growth). Insulin-independent glucose uptake: brain (GLUT1/3), RBCs (GLUT1), liver/β cells/kidney/intestine (GLUT2), cornea, placenta. Insulin also drives K⁺ into cells (Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase), ↑ glycogen, lipid and protein synthesis, ↓ lipolysis, ↓ ketogenesis, ↓ glucagon.

Glucagon (α cells; Gs → cAMP, liver): ↑ glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, ketogenesis, lipolysis. Stimulated by hypoglycemia, amino acids (protein meal), epinephrine; inhibited by insulin, glucose, somatostatin, GLP-1. Counter-regulatory hormones to hypoglycemia: glucagon (first), epinephrine, then cortisol and GH.

sections.heading: Endocrine Pathology
sections.html:
Pituitary and hypothalamus

DisorderKey points
Prolactinoma (most common functional pituitary adenoma)Women: amenorrhea, galactorrhea, infertility (prolactin inhibits GnRH); men: ↓ libido, ED, later mass effect. Other causes of ↑ prolactin to exclude: pregnancy, hypothyroidism, D2 antagonists (antipsychotics, metoclopramide), methyldopa, verapamil, stalk compression (usually <150 ng/mL), CKD. Treat with D2 agonists (cabergoline, bromocriptine) even for macroadenomas
Acromegaly / gigantismGH adenoma (GNAS activating mutation in ~40%); large hands/feet, jaw, frontal bossing, macroglossia, sweating, HTN, insulin resistance, cardiomyopathy (main cause of death), OSA, colon polyps. Screen IGF-1; confirm with failure of GH suppression after oral glucose. Transsphenoidal surgery; octreotide/lanreotide, pegvisomant (GH receptor antagonist), cabergoline
Nonfunctioning macroadenomaMass effect: bitemporal hemianopia (optic chiasm), headache, hypopituitarism (GH, LH/FSH lost first), mild ↑ prolactin
Pituitary apoplexyHemorrhage into adenoma: sudden headache, ophthalmoplegia (cavernous sinus CN III, IV, VI), visual loss, acute adrenal insufficiency → emergent glucocorticoids
Sheehan syndromePostpartum pituitary infarction after severe hemorrhage (gland enlarged in pregnancy, lactotroph hyperplasia); failure to lactate first, then amenorrhea, cold intolerance, adrenal insufficiency
Empty sellaHerniated arachnoid flattens pituitary; often idiopathic, obese women; usually normal function
Kallmann syndromeFailed GnRH neuron migration from olfactory placode (KAL1/ANOS1); anosmia + hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (↓ GnRH, FSH, LH, sex steroids)
Central DI (AVP deficiency)Nephrogenic DI (AVP resistance)Primary polydipsiaSIADH
CausesIdiopathic/autoimmune, trauma, surgery, craniopharyngioma, histiocytosis, hypoxic encephalopathyLithium, demeclocycline, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia, AVPR2 (X-linked) or AQP2 mutationsPsychiatric, hypothalamic thirst lesionSmall cell lung cancer, CNS disease, pulmonary disease, drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine, cyclophosphamide, vincristine), pain/nausea, post-op
Serum Na⁺ / osm↑ / ↑↑ / ↑↓ or low-normal↓ / ↓ (euvolemic)
Urine osmLow (<300)LowLow; concentrates with water deprivationInappropriately high (>100), urine Na⁺ >40
Water deprivation → desmopressinLittle rise → rises >50% after desmopressinLittle rise → minimal changeConcentrates normally—
TreatmentDesmopressinTreat cause, thiazides, amiloride (lithium), NSAIDs, low-solute dietBehavioralFluid restriction, salt tablets; hypertonic saline if severe/symptomatic; vaptans (conivaptan, tolvaptan), demeclocycline. Correct ≤8–10 mEq/L in 24 h (osmotic demyelination)

Copeptin (stable AVP surrogate) after hypertonic saline or arginine stimulation is increasingly used to distinguish DI from primary polydipsia.

Thyroid disorders

Hyperthyroid causeMechanismDistinguishing features
Graves diseaseType II hypersensitivity: thyroid-stimulating IgG (TSI) against TSH receptor; also activates orbital/pretibial fibroblasts → glycosaminoglycan depositionDiffuse goiter with bruit, exophthalmos, pretibial myxedema, thyroid acropachy; diffuse ↑ RAIU; women 20–40
Toxic multinodular goiter / toxic adenomaAutonomous nodules (activating TSH receptor mutations)Older patients; patchy or single hot nodule; no ophthalmopathy; Jod-Basedow after iodine load
Subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditisPost-viral granulomatous inflammationPainful, tender thyroid, fever, ↑ ESR; hyper → hypo → euthyroid; ↓ RAIU; NSAIDs, β-blockers
Painless (silent) and postpartum thyroiditisLymphocytic (variant of Hashimoto)Nontender; anti-TPO +; within 1 year postpartum; ↓ RAIU; β-blockers only
Factitious thyrotoxicosisExogenous T4↓ RAIU, small gland, low thyroglobulin
Struma ovarii, hCG-mediated (mole, choriocarcinoma), TSH-omaEctopic or non-thyroidal stimulusStruma: ↓ neck RAIU; TSH-oma: ↑ TSH with ↑ FT4

Thyroid storm (precipitated by surgery, infection, iodine, childbirth): fever, tachyarrhythmia (AF), delirium, vomiting/diarrhea, high-output HF. Treat: β-blocker (propranolol), PTU (blocks synthesis + peripheral conversion), then iodine ≥1 hour after thionamide (prevents new hormone release; given earlier it would fuel synthesis), glucocorticoids (↓ conversion; covers relative adrenal insufficiency), supportive cooling (acetaminophen, not aspirin — salicylates displace T4 from TBG).

Hypothyroid causeFeatures
Hashimoto thyroiditis (most common in iodine-sufficient regions)Anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin; HLA-DR3/DR5; lymphocytic infiltrate with germinal centers, Hürthle (oncocytic) cells; painless goiter; may have early transient hyperthyroidism ("hashitoxicosis"); ↑ risk of primary thyroid B-cell lymphoma (MALT/DLBCL) — rapidly enlarging gland
Iodine deficiency (most common worldwide)Endemic goiter, cretinism
Congenital hypothyroidismThyroid dysgenesis/dyshormonogenesis; newborn screening; pot belly, pallor, puffy face, protruding umbilicus/hernia, macroglossia, prolonged jaundice, poor feeding → intellectual disability if untreated
Riedel thyroiditisIgG4-related fibrosis extending beyond gland, rock-hard "woody" thyroid; mimics anaplastic cancer
Drug-inducedAmiodarone (iodine + direct toxicity; also causes hyperthyroidism), lithium (↓ release), thionamides, checkpoint inhibitors
ClinicalCold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, bradycardia, menorrhagia, myxedema (GAG deposition), delayed relaxation of reflexes, hyperlipidemia, ↑ CK, hyponatremia; myxedema coma: IV levothyroxine + hydrocortisone
Thyroid cancerFeatures
Papillary (~80%)Best prognosis; ionizing radiation in childhood; RET/PTC rearrangements, BRAF V600E; papillae, Orphan Annie eye (empty-appearing) nuclei, nuclear grooves and pseudoinclusions, psammoma bodies; lymphatic spread to cervical nodes
FollicularRAS, PAX8–PPARγ; diagnosed by capsular/vascular invasion (cannot be distinguished from adenoma on FNA); hematogenous spread (bone, lung)
MedullaryC cells → calcitonin (tumor marker; deposits as amyloid in stroma), CEA; sporadic or RET (MEN2A/2B, familial MTC); prophylactic thyroidectomy in RET carriers
AnaplasticElderly; rapidly enlarging mass invading trachea/esophagus; TP53; dismal prognosis
LymphomaArises in Hashimoto

Thyroid nodule approach: TSH first. Low TSH → radionuclide scan (a "hot" hyperfunctioning nodule is rarely malignant; treat hyperthyroidism). Normal/high TSH → ultrasound → FNA if size/sonographic features warrant (microcalcifications, hypoechoic, irregular margins, taller-than-wide).

Adrenal disorders

DisorderKey points
Cushing syndromeCauses: exogenous glucocorticoids (most common), pituitary ACTH adenoma (Cushing disease; most common endogenous), ectopic ACTH (small cell lung cancer, bronchial carcinoid; marked hypokalemia, hyperpigmentation, rapid onset), adrenal adenoma/carcinoma/nodular hyperplasia. Features: central obesity, moon face, buffalo hump, wide purple striae, proximal myopathy, HTN, hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, immunosuppression, skin thinning, hirsutism, depression. Work-up: Figure 4
Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison)US: autoimmune (anti-21-hydroxylase; APS-1 with AIRE, APS-2 with thyroid disease + T1DM); worldwide: TB; also HIV/CMV, metastases, hemorrhage (anticoagulants, Waterhouse-Friderichsen from meningococcemia), adrenoleukodystrophy. ↓ cortisol + ↓ aldosterone → hypotension, hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, non-AG metabolic acidosis, hypoglycemia, eosinophilia; ↑ ACTH/MSH → hyperpigmentation (buccal mucosa, palmar creases). Diagnosis: low AM cortisol, ↑ ACTH, no rise after cosyntropin stimulation. Treat hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone; stress dosing
Secondary/tertiary adrenal insufficiencyPituitary/hypothalamic disease or withdrawal of chronic steroids; ↓ ACTH → no hyperpigmentation, no hyperkalemia (aldosterone preserved via RAAS); hyponatremia can still occur (cortisol deficiency → ↑ ADH)
Adrenal crisisShock, abdominal pain, vomiting in a patient with known/unknown AI under stress → IV hydrocortisone (or dexamethasone if testing needed) + saline
Primary hyperaldosteronismBilateral adrenal hyperplasia (most common) or aldosterone-producing adenoma (Conn); HTN, hypokalemia (often normal K⁺ in modern series), metabolic alkalosis, low renin, no edema (aldosterone escape via ANP/pressure natriuresis). Screen: plasma aldosterone:renin ratio; confirm with salt-loading suppression test; adrenal CT + adrenal venous sampling. Adenoma → laparoscopic adrenalectomy; hyperplasia → spironolactone/eplerenone
Secondary hyperaldosteronism↑ renin: renal artery stenosis (fibromuscular dysplasia, atherosclerosis), HF, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, diuretics, renin-secreting tumor
PheochromocytomaChromaffin cell tumor; ~30–40% hereditary (MEN2, VHL, NF1, SDHx paraganglioma syndromes); episodic headache, sweating, tachycardia, HTN, pallor, anxiety. Diagnosis: plasma free or 24-h urine fractionated metanephrines, then imaging. Treat: α-blockade first (phenoxybenzamine, irreversible; or doxazosin) for 10–14 days, then β-blocker, then surgery — β-blockade first leaves α-vasoconstriction unopposed → hypertensive crisis
NeuroblastomaMost common adrenal tumor in children (<4 y); neural crest; abdominal mass that may cross the midline, MYCN amplification (poor prognosis), ↑ urinary HVA and VMA, Homer-Wright rosettes, opsoclonus-myoclonus, "raccoon eyes" (periorbital metastases); usually normotensive
Adrenal incidentalomaTest all for cortisol excess (1-mg dex) and pheochromocytoma; aldosterone if hypertensive/hypokalemic; >4 cm or suspicious imaging → resection

Diabetes mellitus

FeatureType 1Type 2
MechanismT-cell mediated destruction of β cells (type IV hypersensitivity); autoantibodies to GAD65, insulin, IA-2, ZnT8Insulin resistance (obesity, ↑ free fatty acids, inflammation) + progressive β-cell dysfunction; islet amyloid (amylin) deposition
GeneticsHLA-DR3/DR4 (DQ2/DQ8); weaker concordance in twins (~50%)Strong (~90% twin concordance), polygenic
Insulin / C-peptide↓↓Variable (↑ early, ↓ late)
Acute complicationDKAHyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (enough insulin to prevent ketosis)

Diagnosis (ADA): HbA1c ≥6.5%, fasting plasma glucose ≥126 mg/dL, 2-h glucose ≥200 mg/dL on 75-g OGTT, or random glucose ≥200 mg/dL with classic symptoms (asymptomatic results need confirmation). Prediabetes: A1c 5.7–6.4%, FPG 100–125, 2-h 140–199. USPSTF: screen adults 35–70 with overweight/obesity.

DKA: insulin deficiency + ↑ glucagon → lipolysis → hepatic ketogenesis (β-hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate) → anion-gap metabolic acidosis, Kussmaul respiration, fruity breath, abdominal pain, osmotic diuresis. Serum K⁺ is often high (insulin deficiency, acidosis shifts) despite total-body K⁺ depletion. Treat: isotonic fluids, IV insulin (only after K⁺ ≥3.3 mEq/L), K⁺ replacement, add dextrose when glucose ~200–250 and continue insulin until the gap closes. Complication: cerebral edema (children), hypokalemia, mucormycosis. HHS: glucose often >600, osmolality >320, profound dehydration and altered mental status, minimal ketosis.

Chronic complications: nonenzymatic glycation (AGEs) → large-vessel atherosclerosis (MI is the leading cause of death), hyaline arteriolosclerosis, glomerular basement membrane thickening and Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules (nodular glomerulosclerosis), efferent arteriole hyalinization → hyperfiltration (ACE inhibitors/ARBs and SGLT2 inhibitors slow nephropathy); aldose reductase → sorbitol accumulation in cells lacking sorbitol dehydrogenase (Schwann cells, lens, retina, kidney) → neuropathy, cataracts, retinopathy (microaneurysms → neovascularization). Other: gastroparesis, foot ulcers, Charcot joints, necrobiosis lipoidica.

MEN syndromes and neuroendocrine tumors

SyndromeGeneComponents
MEN1 (Wermer)MEN1 (menin, tumor suppressor), ADParathyroid hyperplasia (most common, first), pancreatic/duodenal NETs (gastrinoma → ZES, insulinoma, VIPoma, glucagonoma), pituitary adenoma (prolactinoma); also angiofibromas, collagenomas
MEN2A (Sipple)RET (receptor tyrosine kinase, gain of function), ADMedullary thyroid carcinoma (~100%), pheochromocytoma, parathyroid hyperplasia; cutaneous lichen amyloidosis, Hirschsprung
MEN2BRET (often M918T)Medullary thyroid carcinoma (aggressive, early — thyroidectomy in first year of life), pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas (lips, tongue, GI ganglioneuromatosis), marfanoid habitus; no hyperparathyroidism
TumorProductFeatures
Carcinoid (well-differentiated NET)Serotonin, histamine, kallikreinCarcinoid syndrome requires bypass of hepatic first-pass metabolism (liver metastases, or primary in bronchus/ovary): episodic flushing, watery diarrhea, bronchospasm, right-sided valve fibrosis (tricuspid regurgitation, pulmonic stenosis; left valves spared because lung MAO degrades serotonin). ↑ urinary 5-HIAA. Niacin deficiency (pellagra) from tryptophan diversion. Octreotide; telotristat (tryptophan hydroxylase inhibitor) for diarrhea. Carcinoid crisis with anesthesia → octreotide
InsulinomaInsulinWhipple triad (hypoglycemia symptoms, low glucose, relief with glucose); fasting hypoglycemia with ↑ insulin, ↑ C-peptide and ↑ proinsulin, negative sulfonylurea screen. 72-h fast. Exogenous insulin: ↑ insulin, ↓ C-peptide. Sulfonylurea: ↑ insulin, ↑ C-peptide, positive drug screen
Gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison)GastrinRefractory, multiple, or distal duodenal/jejunal ulcers, diarrhea (acid inactivates lipase), thick gastric folds; "gastrinoma triangle"; fasting gastrin markedly ↑ with low gastric pH; secretin stimulation → paradoxical ↑ gastrin; check Ca²⁺ for MEN1
VIPomaVIPWatery diarrhea, hypokalemia, achlorhydria (WDHA); secretory (persists with fasting)
GlucagonomaGlucagonNecrolytic migratory erythema, diabetes, DVT, weight loss, depression, glossitis
SomatostatinomaSomatostatinDiabetes, cholelithiasis, steatorrhea, achlorhydria

sections.heading: Reproductive Embryology
sections.html:
Sex determination: SRY on Yp → testis-determining factor → gonad becomes testis. Sertoli cells secrete anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) → regression of paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts. Leydig cells secrete testosterone → mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts form epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, ejaculatory duct. DHT (via 5α-reductase) forms external genitalia and prostate. Without SRY/AMH/testosterone: Müllerian ducts form fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix and upper third of vagina; lower vagina from the urogenital sinus; Wolffian remnants persist as Gartner duct cysts.

Indifferent structureMaleFemale
Genital tubercle (DHT)Glans penis, corpus cavernosum/spongiosumGlans clitoris, vestibular bulbs
Urogenital sinusProstate, bulbourethral (Cowper) glands, bladderLower vagina, Skene and Bartholin glands, bladder, urethra
Urogenital (urethral) foldsVentral shaft (penile urethra)Labia minora
Labioscrotal swellingsScrotumLabia majora
GubernaculumAnchors testis in scrotumOvarian ligament + round ligament of uterus
Processus vaginalisTunica vaginalis (patent → indirect hernia, hydrocele)Obliterated (canal of Nuck)

Hypospadias: failure of urethral folds to fuse → ventral meatus; more common, associated with cryptorchidism and inguinal hernia. Epispadias: faulty positioning of genital tubercle → dorsal meatus; associated with bladder exstrophy. Müllerian anomalies: septate uterus (incomplete resorption of septum; recurrent pregnancy loss), bicornuate uterus (incomplete fusion), uterus didelphys (complete fusion failure), Müllerian agenesis (Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser: 46,XX, normal ovaries and secondary sex characteristics, absent uterus/upper vagina → primary amenorrhea).

sections.heading: Reproductive Anatomy
sections.html:
LigamentContentsClinical point
Infundibulopelvic (suspensory ligament of ovary)Ovarian artery and veinUreter lies close — risk of injury when ligating ovarian vessels; ovarian torsion twists this pedicle
Cardinal (transverse cervical)Uterine artery and veinUreter passes under uterine artery ("water under the bridge") — injury during hysterectomy
Round ligament of uterusArtery of SampsonExits deep inguinal ring → labia majora
Broad ligamentOvaries, tubes, round ligamentsMesosalpinx, mesovarium, mesometrium
Ovarian ligament—Ovary to uterine horn (gubernacular remnant)

Gonadal venous drainage: left gonadal vein → left renal vein (90° angle, compressible between SMA and aorta → left varicocele; a new left varicocele in an older man may signal renal cell carcinoma invading the left renal vein); right gonadal vein → IVC. Lymphatics: ovaries/testes → para-aortic nodes; scrotum, vulva, lower vagina → superficial inguinal; body of uterus/cervix/upper vagina → external/internal iliac nodes. Erection = parasympathetic (pelvic splanchnics, NO → cGMP); emission = sympathetic (hypogastric); ejaculation = visceral and somatic (pudendal) — "Point, Squeeze, Shoot."

Histology: vagina — stratified squamous, nonkeratinized; ectocervix — stratified squamous; endocervix — simple columnar; transformation zone (squamocolumnar junction) is the site of dysplasia; uterus — simple columnar with tubular glands; fallopian tube — ciliated columnar (ciliary dysfunction in Kartagener → infertility, ectopic risk); ovary surface — simple cuboidal.

sections.heading: Reproductive Physiology
sections.html:
Spermatogenesis and male hormonal control

StagePloidy / chromosomesNotes
Spermatogonium2N, 46 (diploid)Stem cells at basement membrane; mitosis from puberty
Primary spermatocyte4N DNA, 46 chromosomesEnters meiosis I
Secondary spermatocyte2N DNA, 23 chromosomesMeiosis II
Spermatid1N, 23Spermiogenesis: acrosome (Golgi), flagellum (axoneme from centriole), loss of cytoplasm
Spermatozoon1NFull cycle ~2–2.5 months; capacitation occurs in female tract
CellStimulusSecretes / function
Sertoli (seminiferous tubule)FSHAndrogen-binding protein (keeps intratubular testosterone high), inhibin B (↓ FSH), AMH; tight junctions = blood–testis barrier; supports spermatogenesis; temperature-sensitive (↓ sperm in cryptorchidism/varicocele)
Leydig (interstitium)LHTestosterone (→ ↓ LH via GnRH feedback); temperature-insensitive — testosterone often normal in cryptorchidism

Exogenous testosterone/anabolic steroids → ↓ GnRH/LH/FSH → testicular atrophy, ↓ intratesticular testosterone → azoospermia (infertility). Testosterone actions: Wolffian differentiation, spermatogenesis, ↑ muscle, libido, epiphyseal closure (via aromatization to estrogen), ↑ hematocrit. DHT: external genitalia, prostate growth, male-pattern baldness, sebaceous glands.

Oogenesis: primary oocytes are formed in utero and arrested in prophase I until ovulation (completing meiosis I with the LH surge); the secondary oocyte is arrested in metaphase II until fertilization. Nondisjunction risk rises with maternal age (long prophase arrest).

Menstrual cycle

[[figure:ch06-fig08]]
EventMechanism
Follicle selectionFSH rise at end of prior cycle recruits follicles; FSH → granulosa aromatase converts theca-derived androgens (LH-driven) into estradiol ("two-cell, two-gonadotropin"); dominant follicle has most FSH receptors and survives falling FSH
LH surgeEstradiol >~200 pg/mL for ~2 days → positive feedback; ovulation; meiosis I completes; Mittelschmerz (midcycle pain)
Luteal phaseCorpus luteum (LH-dependent) secretes progesterone + estradiol → secretory endometrium, thick cervical mucus, ↑ temperature; inhibin A ↓ FSH
MenstruationWithout hCG the corpus luteum regresses (~day 24–28) → progesterone withdrawal → spiral artery constriction, endometrial shedding; FSH rises again
Cycle length variabilityDue to the follicular phase; luteal phase is constant ~14 days
MenopauseFollicle depletion → ↓ estradiol, ↓ inhibin → ↑ FSH (best marker), ↑ LH; mean age ~51; hot flashes, vaginal atrophy, osteoporosis, ↑ CVD risk. Primary ovarian insufficiency if <40 years (Turner, fragile X premutation, autoimmune, chemotherapy)

Pregnancy and lactation physiology

Fertilization in the ampulla; implantation in posterior uterine wall ~day 6 after fertilization; syncytiotrophoblast secretes hCG (detectable in serum ~8 days after fertilization, doubles ~every 48 h early, peaks ~8–10 weeks) which maintains the corpus luteum until the placenta takes over progesterone production at ~8–10 weeks. Placenta: syncytiotrophoblast makes hCG, hPL (human placental lactogen: insulin resistance, lipolysis → glucose for fetus), progesterone, estriol (needs fetal adrenal DHEA-S + fetal liver; low estriol in trisomy 21/18 screening); cytotrophoblast is the stem layer.

SystemNormal change in pregnancy
HematologicPlasma volume ↑ ~45% > RBC mass ↑ ~25% → dilutional anemia; leukocytosis; hypercoagulable (↑ fibrinogen, factors VII, VIII, X, vWF; ↓ protein S) → VTE risk highest postpartum
CardiovascularCO ↑ 30–50% (↑ SV then ↑ HR), ↓ SVR (progesterone, NO, placental shunt), BP nadir in 2nd trimester; supine hypotension (IVC compression) — position left lateral; benign flow murmur, S3 may be normal
RespiratoryProgesterone → ↑ tidal volume and minute ventilation → compensated respiratory alkalosis (PaCO₂ ~30 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ ~18–21); ↓ FRC (elevated diaphragm); ↑ O₂ consumption
RenalGFR ↑ ~50% → ↓ BUN and creatinine (Cr 0.9 may be abnormal); glucosuria; hydronephrosis/ureteral dilation (progesterone, compression) → pyelonephritis risk
Endocrine↑ TBG (↑ total T4), hCG weakly stimulates TSH receptor (1st-trimester ↓ TSH); ↑ prolactin (estrogen-driven lactotroph hyperplasia; pituitary enlarges); ↑ cortisol/CBG; insulin resistance (hPL, cortisol, progesterone) in 2nd–3rd trimester
GI / hepatic↓ LES tone (GERD), ↓ motility (constipation), gallbladder stasis (gallstones), ↑ ALP (placental), ↓ albumin

Lactation: prolactin drives milk production but high estrogen/progesterone block its action during pregnancy; delivery of the placenta (progesterone withdrawal) allows lactation. Suckling → ↑ prolactin (↓ dopamine) and oxytocin (milk let-down; myoepithelial contraction). Prolactin suppresses GnRH → lactational amenorrhea. Breast milk lacks adequate vitamin D and iron for infants (supplement vitamin D 400 IU/day); colostrum is rich in IgA.

sections.heading: Reproductive Pathology
sections.html:
Disorders of sex development and chromosomal disorders

DisorderKaryotype / defectPhenotypeHormones
Klinefelter syndrome47,XXY (meiotic nondisjunction); Barr bodyTall, eunuchoid, small firm testes, gynecomastia, infertility (azoospermia), ↓ body hair, learning difficulties; ↑ breast cancer, germ cell tumors, autoimmune disease↑ FSH, ↑ LH, ↓ testosterone, ↓ inhibin B, ↑ estradiol (seminiferous tubule dysgenesis + Leydig dysfunction)
Turner syndrome45,X (often paternal X lost) or mosaic; no Barr bodyShort stature (SHOX), streak ovaries → primary amenorrhea (most common cause), webbed neck, cystic hygroma, lymphedema of hands/feet, shield chest, bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation, horseshoe kidney, hypothyroidism; normal intelligence↑ FSH, ↑ LH, ↓ estrogen (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism); Y material → gonadoblastoma risk
Double Y (47,XYY)Paternal nondisjunctionTall, severe acne, normal fertility, ↑ ADHD/autism riskNormal
Androgen insensitivity syndrome46,XY, defective androgen receptor (X-linked)Female external genitalia, blind-ending vagina, no uterus or tubes (AMH works), testes in labia/inguinal canal (remove after puberty — malignancy risk), breast development, scant pubic/axillary hair↑ testosterone, ↑ estrogen (aromatized), ↑ LH (no feedback)
5α-reductase deficiency46,XY, ARAmbiguous/female-appearing external genitalia at birth; normal internal male ducts; virilization at puberty (↑ testosterone, type 1 isozyme)Normal testosterone and LH, ↓ DHT, ↑ testosterone:DHT ratio
Aromatase deficiencyEither karyotypeXX: ambiguous genitalia at birth, maternal virilization during pregnancy (fetal androgens cross placenta), primary amenorrhea; both sexes tall (no epiphyseal closure)↑ androgens, ↓ estrogen, ↑ FSH/LH
Ovotesticular DSD46,XX or 46,XYBoth ovarian and testicular tissueVariable
Kallmann syndromeSee pituitary sectionDelayed puberty + anosmia↓ GnRH, FSH, LH, sex steroids
Exam trap: AIS vs Müllerian agenesis — both present as primary amenorrhea with absent uterus and a blind vaginal pouch. Pubic/axillary hair and karyotype separate them: MRKH (46,XX) has normal hair and normal female testosterone; AIS (46,XY) has scant hair and male-range testosterone.

Ovary

ConditionKey points
Polycystic ovary syndrome↑ LH:FSH, hyperinsulinemia/insulin resistance → ↑ theca androgen production + ↓ SHBG → hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne), anovulation (oligomenorrhea, infertility), polycystic ovaries ("string of pearls"); obesity, acanthosis nigricans, MASLD, OSA, T2DM. Rotterdam: 2 of 3 (oligo/anovulation, hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries) after excluding mimics (TSH, prolactin, 17-OHP). Chronic unopposed estrogen → endometrial hyperplasia/carcinoma. Tx: weight loss, combined OCPs (cycle control, ↓ androgens), spironolactone (hirsutism), metformin; letrozole is first-line for ovulation induction (clomiphene alternative)
Functional cystsFollicular (most common; hyperestrinism), corpus luteum (hemorrhage), theca lutein (bilateral; high hCG — mole, choriocarcinoma, multiple gestation)
Ovarian torsionTwisting of infundibulopelvic ligament; sudden unilateral pain, vomiting; ovarian mass (dermoid) is a lead point; Doppler; laparoscopic detorsion
Ovarian neoplasmFeaturesMarker
Surface epithelial tumors (most common; older women) — risk ↑ with BRCA1/2, Lynch, nulliparity, endometriosis (endometrioid, clear cell); ↓ with OCPs, multiparity, breastfeeding, tubal ligation/salpingectomy
Serous cystadenoma / borderline / high-grade serous carcinomaCiliated tubal-type epithelium; high-grade serous (most common malignant ovarian tumor) arises often from tubal fimbriae (STIC), TP53, BRCA; psammoma bodies; bilateralCA-125 (monitoring; not screening)
Mucinous cystadenoma/carcinomaLarge multiloculated cysts; pseudomyxoma peritonei is usually from appendiceal primaryCEA, CA 19-9
Endometrioid, clear cell carcinomaAssociated with endometriosis; endometrioid may coexist with endometrial carcinomaCA-125
Brenner tumorBladder-like (urothelial) epithelium with "coffee-bean" nuclei; usually benign—
Germ cell tumors (young women, adolescents)
Mature cystic teratoma (dermoid)Most common ovarian tumor in women <30; hair, teeth, sebum; torsion; struma ovarii (thyroid tissue → hyperthyroidism); rare squamous transformation—
Immature teratomaImmature neuroectoderm; malignant±AFP
DysgerminomaOvarian counterpart of seminoma: sheets of "fried egg" cells; radiosensitive; Turner/gonadal dysgenesisLDH, ±hCG, PLAP
Yolk sac (endodermal sinus) tumorAggressive; children/young women; Schiller-Duval bodies (glomeruloid)AFP
Choriocarcinoma (non-gestational)Syncytio- and cytotrophoblast, no villi; hemorrhagic; theca lutein cysts, hyperthyroidismhCG
Sex cord–stromal tumors
Granulosa cell tumorMost common malignant stromal tumor; estrogen → precocious puberty (juvenile type), endometrial hyperplasia/carcinoma and postmenopausal bleeding (adult type, FOXL2); Call-Exner bodies (follicle-like rosettes around eosinophilic material), coffee-bean nucleiInhibin, estradiol
Sertoli-Leydig cell tumorAndrogens → virilization (deep voice, clitoromegaly, hirsutism); Reinke crystals (Leydig)Testosterone
Fibroma / thecomaFibroma: bundles of spindle fibroblasts; Meigs syndrome = fibroma + ascites + right pleural effusion (resolves after resection). Thecoma: estrogen-secreting, postmenopausal—
Metastatic — Krukenberg tumor: bilateral, mucin-secreting signet-ring cells, usually from diffuse gastric cancer (also breast, colon)

USPSTF recommends against ovarian cancer screening (CA-125/ultrasound) in average-risk women. BRCA carriers: risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy after childbearing (BRCA1 ~35–40 y; BRCA2 ~40–45 y).

Uterus and cervix

ConditionKey points
EndometriosisEndometrial glands and stroma outside the uterus (retrograde menstruation, metaplasia, lymphatic spread): ovary ("chocolate cyst," endometrioma), pelvic peritoneum (powder-burn lesions), uterosacral ligaments. Cyclic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, dyschezia, infertility; normal-sized uterus, nodular uterosacral ligaments. Diagnosis: laparoscopy (definitive). Tx: NSAIDs, continuous OCPs/progestins, GnRH agonists or antagonists (elagolix, relugolix combination), surgery
AdenomyosisEndometrial tissue within myometrium; multiparous women 40s; dysmenorrhea, heavy bleeding, uniformly enlarged, soft, "boggy" tender uterus; hysterectomy definitive
Leiomyoma (fibroid)Most common tumor in women; Black women; estrogen-sensitive (grow in pregnancy, shrink after menopause); well-circumscribed whorled smooth muscle; heavy menstrual bleeding, pressure, infertility, iron deficiency; does not progress to leiomyosarcoma. Tx: OCPs/levonorgestrel IUD, GnRH analogs (preoperative), myomectomy, uterine artery embolization, hysterectomy
LeiomyosarcomaArises de novo; postmenopausal; rapidly enlarging single mass with necrosis/hemorrhage, high mitoses
Endometrial hyperplasiaUnopposed estrogen (obesity — adipose aromatase, PCOS, estrogen-only HRT, tamoxifen, granulosa cell tumor, early menarche/late menopause, nulliparity); atypia is the key predictor of carcinoma; abnormal uterine bleeding
Endometrial carcinoma (most common gynecologic cancer in US)Endometrioid (estrogen-dependent, from hyperplasia, perimenopausal; PTEN, MSI/Lynch, KRAS, CTNNB1) vs serous (older, atrophic endometrium, TP53, psammoma bodies, aggressive). Presents with postmenopausal bleeding → transvaginal US (stripe >4 mm) or endometrial biopsy. OCPs and smoking ↓ risk (smoking ↑ most other cancers)
Asherman syndromeIntrauterine adhesions after D&C/infection → secondary amenorrhea, infertility; no withdrawal bleed to progesterone or estrogen-progesterone challenge
Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia → cervical carcinomaHigh-risk HPV 16, 18 (also 31, 33, 45...): E6 degrades p53, E7 binds/inactivates Rb (releases E2F). Koilocytes (wrinkled "raisin" nuclei, perinuclear halo). CIN 1→3 (reversible) → invasive squamous cell carcinoma (most common) or adenocarcinoma (HPV 18). Risk: early sexual debut, multiple partners, smoking, HIV/immunosuppression. Invasion lateral → ureteral obstruction → hydronephrosis, renal failure (common cause of death)

Cervical screening (USPSTF 2018; ACOG concurs): ages 21–29 cytology every 3 years; 30–65 primary HPV every 5 years, co-testing every 5 years, or cytology every 3 years. Stop at >65 with adequate negative prior screening; not needed after hysterectomy for benign disease. (A 2024 USPSTF draft favors primary HPV testing from 30 and allows self-collected samples.) HPV vaccine (9-valent) routinely at 11–12 (can start at 9), catch-up through 26; shared decision 27–45.

Vulva/vagina: Bartholin cyst/abscess (obstructed duct, lateral posterior introitus); lichen sclerosus (thin "parchment" skin, postmenopausal, slight ↑ SCC risk); lichen simplex chronicus (no ↑ risk); vulvar SCC (HPV-related younger, or lichen sclerosus-related older); extramammary Paget disease (intraepithelial adenocarcinoma, PAS+); clear cell adenocarcinoma of vagina (DES exposure in utero); sarcoma botryoides (embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, girls <4, "grape-like" mass, desmin+).

Breast

Benign lesionKey points
Fibrocystic changesCyclic bilateral tenderness/lumpiness, premenopausal; nonproliferative (cysts, fibrosis) — no ↑ risk; proliferative without atypia (ductal hyperplasia, sclerosing adenosis) — slight ↑; atypical ductal/lobular hyperplasia — ↑ risk ~4–5×
FibroadenomaMost common breast tumor <35; small, rubbery, mobile, well-circumscribed; estrogen-sensitive (grows in pregnancy); biphasic (stroma + ducts)
Phyllodes tumorOlder (~50s); large, rapidly growing, "leaf-like" stromal projections; may be malignant; wide excision
Intraductal papillomaMost common cause of bloody nipple discharge; small subareolar tumor in lactiferous duct
Fat necrosisAfter trauma/surgery; calcified, irregular mass mimicking cancer; saponification, foamy macrophages
Acute mastitisBreastfeeding, S. aureus through nipple fissure; continue breastfeeding/pumping; dicloxacillin or cephalexin
Periductal mastitis / duct ectasiaPeriductal: smokers, squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts, subareolar abscess. Duct ectasia: older multiparous women, green-brown discharge, plasma cells
Gynecomastia↑ estrogen:androgen ratio: puberty, old age, Klinefelter, cirrhosis, hyperthyroidism, testicular tumors (Leydig, choriocarcinoma/hCG), drugs (spironolactone, ketoconazole, cimetidine, digoxin, GnRH analogs, antiandrogens, marijuana, anabolic steroids)
Breast cancerFeatures
Risk factorsAge, ↑ lifetime estrogen exposure (early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, first pregnancy >30, obesity in postmenopausal women, estrogen–progestin HRT), alcohol, chest radiation, atypical hyperplasia, BRCA1 (triple-negative, medullary-like, ovarian), BRCA2 (male breast, pancreas, prostate), TP53 (Li-Fraumeni), PTEN, CDH1, PALB2
DCISMalignant cells confined by basement membrane; microcalcifications on mammogram; comedo subtype has central necrosis
Paget disease of the nippleEczematous, ulcerated nipple; intraepidermal adenocarcinoma cells with halo; underlying DCIS or invasive carcinoma
Invasive ductal carcinoma (no special type)Most common (~75%); firm, fixed, stellate mass; desmoplasia
Invasive lobular carcinomaLoss of E-cadherin (CDH1) → discohesive cells in single file; often bilateral/multicentric, ER+; metastasizes to unusual sites (peritoneum, GI, ovaries)
Inflammatory carcinomaTumor emboli in dermal lymphatics → erythema, warmth, peau d'orange; mistaken for mastitis; poor prognosis
OthersMucinous (older, good prognosis), medullary pattern/tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (BRCA1), tubular (good prognosis)
PrognosisTNM stage (axillary node status most important in early disease); receptors: ER/PR+ (endocrine therapy, best prognosis), HER2 (ERBB2) amplified (trastuzumab — cardiotoxicity, ↓ LVEF), triple-negative (young, Black women, BRCA1, worst)

USPSTF (2024): biennial screening mammography for women 40–74.

Testis, scrotum and prostate

ConditionKey points
CryptorchidismUndescended testis (often unilateral, inguinal); ↓ spermatogenesis (temperature), normal testosterone; ↑ germ cell tumor risk (also in contralateral testis); orchiopexy by 6–18 months
Testicular torsionBell-clapper deformity (inadequate gubernacular fixation); acute severe pain, high-riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex, no relief with elevation; surgical detorsion + bilateral orchiopexy within 6 h
Epididymitis<35: C. trachomatis, N. gonorrhoeae; older: E. coli; pain relieved by elevation (Prehn sign), cremasteric reflex present

HydroceleFluid in tunica vaginalis (patent processus vaginalis in infants); transilluminates
BPHHyperplasia of transition/periurethral zone (DHT-dependent); not premalignant; α1-blockers, 5α-reductase inhibitors, tadalafil
Prostate adenocarcinomaPeripheral zone (posterior lobe, palpable on DRE); ↑ PSA; osteoblastic bone metastases (lumbar spine, ↑ ALP); USPSTF: individual decision for PSA at 55–69
Testicular tumorFeaturesMarkers
Germ cell tumors (~95%), 15–35 y; painless firm mass that does not transilluminate; scrotal US → radical inguinal orchiectomy (never transscrotal biopsy: changes lymphatic drainage to inguinal nodes). Retroperitoneal (para-aortic) node spread
SeminomaMost common; older (~35–40); homogeneous, large cells with clear cytoplasm ("fried egg"), lymphocytic stroma; late spread; very radio- and chemosensitive; excellent prognosisPLAP; hCG ↑ in some (syncytiotrophoblastic cells); AFP never elevated
Embryonal carcinomaHemorrhagic, necrotic mass; often painful; usually part of mixed tumors; aggressive±hCG, ±AFP

Non-germ cell

Sertoli cell tumorUsually benign; Peutz-Jeghers, Carney—

Pregnancy complications

ConditionMechanism / features
Ectopic pregnancyMost often ampulla of fallopian tube; risk: prior ectopic, PID/chlamydia (tubal scarring), tubal surgery, IUD in situ (if pregnancy occurs), smoking, IVF. Amenorrhea + abdominal pain + vaginal bleeding; hCG above discriminatory zone (~3500 mIU/mL) without intrauterine pregnancy on TVUS; hCG rises <~35–50% in 48 h. Methotrexate (stable, unruptured, hCG low) or salpingostomy/salpingectomy; ruptured → surgery. Arias-Stella reaction in endometrium
Spontaneous abortionLoss <20 weeks; most first-trimester losses are chromosomal (trisomy 16 commonest; 45,X); recurrent: antiphospholipid syndrome, uterine septum, parental translocation, uncontrolled diabetes/thyroid disease
Placenta previaPlacenta over/near internal os; painless third-trimester bleeding; prior C-section, multiparity, advanced maternal age; no digital cervical exam; TVUS; cesarean
Placental abruptionPremature separation; painful bleeding, tender hypertonic uterus, fetal distress; hypertension/preeclampsia, cocaine, smoking, trauma; DIC (tissue factor release)
Placenta accreta spectrumDefective decidua basalis → villi attach to (accreta), invade (increta) or penetrate (percreta) myometrium; prior C-section + previa is the highest risk; postpartum hemorrhage → cesarean hysterectomy
Vasa previaFetal vessels over os; painless bleeding with rupture of membranes + fetal bradycardia (fetal blood loss)
PreeclampsiaNew HTN (≥140/90) after 20 weeks + proteinuria (≥300 mg/24 h, P:C ≥0.3) or end-organ dysfunction (platelets <100,000, Cr >1.1 or doubled, transaminases 2× ULN, pulmonary edema, new headache/visual symptoms). Mechanism: abnormal trophoblast invasion → failed spiral artery remodeling → placental ischemia → ↑ sFlt-1 (binds VEGF/PlGF) and soluble endoglin → endothelial dysfunction. Fibrinoid necrosis of placental vessels. Risk: nulliparity, prior preeclampsia, chronic HTN, diabetes, CKD, autoimmune disease (APS, SLE), multifetal gestation, obesity, molar pregnancy (<20 wk). Low-dose aspirin (81 mg) from 12 weeks for high-risk women. Treat: delivery (definitive; at ≥37 wk without severe features, ≥34 wk with severe features), antihypertensives (labetalol, nifedipine, hydralazine) for severe-range BP ≥160/110, magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis with severe features
Eclampsia / HELLPEclampsia: seizures (MgSO₄ treats and prevents). HELLP: hemolysis (schistocytes), elevated liver enzymes, low platelets — deliver. Complications: hepatic subcapsular hematoma, DIC, stroke (leading cause of death), PRES
Gestational diabeteshPL and other diabetogenic hormones; screen 24–28 weeks (1-h 50-g glucose challenge then 3-h 100-g OGTT, or 75-g 2-h OGTT). Fetal hyperinsulinemia → macrosomia (shoulder dystocia), neonatal hypoglycemia, polycythemia, hyperbilirubinemia, RDS (insulin ↓ surfactant). Diet first; insulin preferred pharmacotherapy (metformin, glyburide cross placenta). Pregestational diabetes: caudal regression, transposition of great arteries, neural tube defects
Hydatidiform moleComplete: 46,XX (or XY), entirely paternal (empty ovum + duplicated sperm, or dispermy), no fetal parts, diffuse villous edema and trophoblast proliferation, p57 negative, hCG ↑↑↑, "snowstorm"/"cluster of grapes" US, uterus large for dates, hyperemesis, early preeclampsia, hyperthyroidism, theca lutein cysts; ~15–20% → gestational trophoblastic neoplasia. Partial: 69,XXX/XXY (two sperm + normal ovum), fetal parts present, p57 positive, lower hCG and malignant risk. Tx: suction curettage, serial hCG until undetectable; contraception during follow-up
Gestational choriocarcinomaAfter mole, abortion or normal pregnancy; hemorrhagic, no villi; early hematogenous spread to lung ("cannonball"); very chemosensitive (methotrexate)
Amniotic fluid abnormalitiesPolyhydramnios (>8 cm AFI ~>24): esophageal/duodenal atresia, anencephaly (impaired swallowing), maternal diabetes, fetal anemia, multiple gestation. Oligohydramnios (AFI <5): bilateral renal agenesis, posterior urethral valves, placental insufficiency, ROM → Potter sequence (pulmonary hypoplasia, flat face, limb deformities)
Postpartum hemorrhageUterine atony (most common: overdistension, prolonged labor, chorioamnionitis, MgSO₄) → bimanual massage, oxytocin, then methylergonovine (avoid in HTN), carboprost (avoid in asthma), misoprostol, tranexamic acid; retained placenta, lacerations, coagulopathy
Amniotic fluid embolismDuring labor/delivery: sudden dyspnea, hypotension, hypoxia, DIC; lanugo/squames in pulmonary vessels

title: Step 1 · Nervous System, Behavioral Science/Psychiatry, Musculoskeletal & Skin
meta: Exam: Step 1 · Neurology, special senses, psychiatry, neuro/psych pharmacology, musculoskeletal, rheumatology, dermatology · Approx study time: 5–6 days

sections.heading: Overview
sections.html:
From NEET PG to USMLE

  • Localization over lists. NEET PG asks "which tract carries vibration?"; USMLE gives a patient with a left-sided tongue deviation, right hemiparesis and right loss of vibration, and asks which artery is occluded. Always reason: symptom → tract/nucleus → level → side → vessel.
  • US drug names. Learn the generic names US-style: acetaminophen (not paracetamol), levetiracetam, lamotrigine, carbidopa-levodopa, donepezil, haloperidol, olanzapine, lurasidone, methotrexate, adalimumab. Brand names are rarely tested on Step 1, but stems may mention them.
  • DSM-5-TR criteria are tested precisely. Duration thresholds (e.g., schizophreniform 1–6 months, GAD ≥ 6 months, PTSD > 1 month, MDD ≥ 2 weeks) decide the answer. ICD-style diagnoses used in Indian textbooks (e.g., "neurosis") are not used.
  • Behavioral science is a whole discipline. Defense mechanisms, developmental milestones, sleep physiology and learning theory appear far more often than in Indian exams. They are cheap marks if memorized.
  • Mechanism of drug toxicity matters. You will be asked why clozapine causes agranulocytosis or why valproate is teratogenic (folate antagonism → neural tube defects), not just that it does.
  • Rheumatology is antibody- and HLA-driven. Expect anti-CCP, anti-dsDNA, anti-Jo-1, anti-centromere, HLA-B27, HLA-DR4 associations and the biologics' targets (TNF-α, IL-6R, IL-17A, CTLA-4, CD20).
======================= NEURO EMBRYOLOGY =======================

======================= CELLS =======================

sections.heading: Neural cells, injury and the blood–brain barrier
sections.html:
CellFunctionMarker / pathology
AstrocyteBBB support (foot processes), K⁺ buffering, glycogen, scar (gliosis)GFAP; astrocytoma, glioblastoma
MicrogliaCNS macrophagesHIV reservoir
OligodendrocyteCNS myelin; one cell myelinates many axonsDestroyed in MS, PML (JC virus); "fried egg" oligodendroglioma

Neuronal injury: Red neurons (eosinophilic cytoplasm, pyknotic nucleus) appear 12–24 h after irreversible ischemia. Axonal injury distal to a cut → Wallerian degeneration; the cell body shows central chromatolysis (swelling, peripheral nucleus, dispersed Nissl). Most vulnerable to hypoxia: hippocampal CA1 pyramidal cells, neocortex layers 3, 5, 6 (laminar necrosis), cerebellar Purkinje cells, watershed areas.

Blood–brain barrier: tight junctions of nonfenestrated endothelium + basement membrane + astrocyte foot processes. Absent at circumventricular organs: area postrema (chemoreceptor trigger zone → vomiting), OVLT (osmosensing), subfornical organ, neurohypophysis, median eminence.

======================= SPINAL CORD =======================

sections.heading: Spinal cord: tracts and lesions
sections.html:
The spinal cord ends at L1–L2 (conus medullaris) in adults; lumbar puncture is done at L3–L5 (iliac crest level ≈ L4). Layers penetrated: skin → supraspinous ligament → interspinous ligament → ligamentum flavum → epidural space → dura → arachnoid → subarachnoid space (CSF).

TractModality1st-order neuron → synapseDecussation
Dorsal column–medial lemniscusFine touch, vibration, proprioceptionDRG → ascends ipsilaterally (fasciculus gracilis = legs, medial; cuneatus = arms, lateral) → nucleus gracilis/cuneatus (medulla)Medulla (internal arcuate fibers) → medial lemniscus → VPL → cortex
Spinothalamic (anterolateral)Pain, temperature (lateral); crude touch (anterior)DRG → dorsal horn (substantia gelatinosa)Spinal cord, within 1–2 segments (anterior white commissure) → VPL
Lateral corticospinalVoluntary motorUMN in precentral gyrus (Betz cells) → internal capsule (posterior limb) → cerebral peduncle → pyramidsCaudal medulla (pyramidal decussation) → synapse on anterior horn LMN
Dorsal/ventral spinocerebellarUnconscious proprioceptionClarke nucleus (dorsal)Dorsal: ipsilateral (inferior cerebellar peduncle)

Somatotopy: in the lateral corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts, sacral fibers are lateral, cervical fibers medial (so central cord lesions spare sacral sensation — "sacral sparing"). In the dorsal column it is the reverse: cervical lateral (cuneatus), sacral medial (gracilis).

======================= BRAINSTEM AND CN =======================

sections.heading: Brainstem and cranial nerves
sections.html:
Motor nuclei lie medial, sensory nuclei lateral. Motor CN whose nuclei lie medially are the factors of 12 (except I and II): CN III, IV, VI, XII (III, VI and XII exit ventrally near the midline; IV exits dorsally). Medulla holds CN IX, X, XI (nucleus ambiguus), XII; pons holds V, VI, VII, VIII; midbrain III, IV. CN I and II are CNS outgrowths (myelinated by oligodendrocytes — hence optic neuritis in MS).

Ischemic stroke pathology timeline: 12–24 h red neurons → 24–72 h neutrophils → 3–5 d microglia/macrophages → 1–2 wk reactive gliosis and vascular proliferation → > 2 wk glial scar / liquefactive necrosis with cystic cavity. Tissue plasminogen activator (alteplase or tenecteplase) within 4.5 h of last-known-well if no contraindication; mechanical thrombectomy for large-vessel occlusion up to 24 h in selected patients. Secondary prevention: antiplatelet (aspirin, clopidogrel), statin, BP control; carotid endarterectomy for symptomatic stenosis ≥ 70% (consider ≥ 50%).

Intracranial hemorrhage

[[figure:ch07-fig04]]

Intraparenchymal hemorrhage: hypertension (Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysms of lenticulostriates → basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, cerebellum), cerebral amyloid angiopathy (lobar, recurrent, elderly; β-amyloid in vessel walls), anticoagulation, AVM, tumor, hemorrhagic conversion of ischemic stroke. Saccular (berry) aneurysm risk: ADPKD, Ehlers–Danlos, Marfan, coarctation, smoking, hypertension. SAH complications: rebleeding, vasospasm, hydrocephalus (impaired CSF resorption), hyponatremia (SIADH or cerebral salt wasting).

Sensory receptors: Meissner (fine touch, glabrous skin, rapidly adapting), Pacinian (vibration, pressure, deep, rapidly adapting), Merkel (pressure, deep static touch, slowly adapting), Ruffini (stretch, slowly adapting), free nerve endings (pain, temperature; Aδ fast myelinated, C slow unmyelinated). Hearing: Weber lateralizes to the affected ear in conductive loss and to the normal ear in sensorineural loss. Rinne: air > bone normally and in sensorineural; bone > air in conductive loss. Noise-induced loss starts at 4000 Hz; presbycusis affects high frequencies (base of cochlea). Cholesteatoma: keratinizing squamous epithelium in middle ear, painless otorrhea. Vertigo: BPPV (otoliths in semicircular canal, Dix–Hallpike, Epley maneuver), vestibular neuritis (constant days), Ménière (endolymphatic hydrops: vertigo + tinnitus + low-frequency sensorineural loss + aural fullness).

Anesthetics and neuromuscular blockers

ClassKey points
Inhaled (sevoflurane, desflurane, isoflurane, N₂O)Low blood/gas solubility → fast induction & recovery (N₂O, desflurane). High lipid solubility → high potency, low MAC. ↓ cerebral metabolic rate but ↑ cerebral blood flow. Halothane → hepatotoxicity; methoxyflurane → nephrotoxicity; enflurane → seizures. Malignant hyperthermia (RYR1 mutation) with any volatile + succinylcholine → dantrolene
IV: propofolPotentiates GABAA; rapid; hypotension; propofol infusion syndrome
IV: ketamineNMDA antagonist; dissociative; ↑ BP, bronchodilation (good in asthma, shock); emergence hallucinations. Esketamine nasal spray for treatment-resistant depression
IV: etomidateGABAA; hemodynamically stable; adrenal suppression (11β-hydroxylase)
IV: dexmedetomidineCentral α2 agonist; sedation without respiratory depression
Local anestheticsBlock Na⁺ channels from inside (cytoplasmic side); enter in uncharged form → infected (acidic) tissue needs more. Small, myelinated fibers blocked first: pain > temperature > touch > pressure. Esters (one i: procaine, tetracaine, cocaine, benzocaine) vs amides (two i's: lidocaine, bupivacaine). Bupivacaine cardiotoxicity → lipid emulsion. Benzocaine → methemoglobinemia
Succinylcholine (depolarizing)Persistent nicotinic depolarization: phase I (no fade, potentiated by AChE inhibitors) → phase II. Hyperkalemia (burns, crush, denervation), malignant hyperthermia, prolonged paralysis with pseudocholinesterase deficiency
Nondepolarizing (rocuronium, vecuronium, cisatracurium)Competitive nicotinic antagonists; reversed by neostigmine (+ glycopyrrolate) or sugammadex (encapsulates rocuronium/vecuronium). Cisatracurium: Hofmann elimination (organ-independent)

Opioids

Agonists at μ (morphine, fentanyl, oxycodone, hydromorphone, methadone), δ, κ receptors → open K⁺ channels, close Ca²⁺ channels → ↓ neurotransmitter release. Toxicity: miosis (no tolerance), constipation (no tolerance), respiratory depression, sedation; serotonin syndrome risk with meperidine, tramadol, methadone + SSRIs. Meperidine → normeperidine seizures. Partial agonist: buprenorphine (high affinity — precipitates withdrawal in a patient on full agonist; used with naloxone for OUD). Mixed agonist-antagonist: butorphanol, nalbuphine (κ agonist). Antagonists: naloxone (overdose), naltrexone (alcohol and opioid use disorder maintenance), methylnaltrexone (peripheral; opioid constipation). Loperamide, diphenoxylate: antidiarrheal. Dextromethorphan: NMDA antagonist antitussive. Tramadol: weak μ agonist + SNRI; lowers seizure threshold.

Learning theory and development

Classical conditioning: a natural reflex elicited by a learned stimulus (Pavlov). Operant conditioning: positive/negative reinforcement ↑ behavior (add a reward / remove an aversive stimulus); punishment ↓ behavior; extinction = no reinforcement. Variable-ratio reinforcement (slot machines) is most resistant to extinction. Transference (patient → physician) vs countertransference (physician → patient).

Sleep physiology

[[figure:ch07-fig06]]

Sleep is initiated by the VLPO nucleus of the hypothalamus (GABA, galanin) inhibiting arousal centers; wakefulness is maintained by orexin (hypocretin) from the lateral hypothalamus. Serotonin (raphe) initiates sleep; ↓ NE and ↑ ACh (pons) during REM. Benzodiazepines ↓ N3 and REM (useful for night terrors, sleepwalking); alcohol, barbiturates and TCAs ↓ REM. Depression: ↓ REM latency, ↑ REM density, ↓ N3, early-morning awakening.

Suicide risk factors (SAD PERSONS): sex (male completes more; female attempts more), age, depression, previous attempt (strongest predictor), ethanol/drugs, rational thinking loss, sickness, organized plan, no spouse, social support lacking. Firearms are the most common method in the US.

AntidepressantMechanismKey adverse effects / uses

Muscle physiology

Action potential → T-tubule DHP receptor (L-type, voltage sensor) mechanically coupled to ryanodine receptor (RyR1) on sarcoplasmic reticulum → Ca²⁺ release → binds troponin C → tropomyosin moves → myosin binds actin → power stroke. ATP binding releases myosin from actin (rigor mortis when ATP absent). Sarcomere: A band constant; H band and I band shorten. Type I fibers: slow, red, oxidative (postural; ↑ with endurance training). Type II: fast, white, glycolytic (↑ with weight training). Smooth muscle: Ca²⁺–calmodulin → myosin light-chain kinase; NO → ↑ cGMP → myosin light-chain phosphatase → relaxation.

Epidermis layers (deep → superficial, "Californians Like Girls in String Bikinis"): stratum basale (stem cells, melanocytes), spinosum (desmosomes; Langerhans cells), granulosum (keratohyalin granules), lucidum (palms/soles only), corneum (anucleate keratin). Subtypes: superficial spreading (most common), nodular, lentigo maligna, acral lentiginous (palms, soles, nails — most common in darker skin)

title: Mock Exam A · Step 1 (2 blocks × 40 questions, 60 minutes per block)
meta: Exam: Step 1 · Mixed disciplines and systems, weighted per the USMLE Step 1 content outline · 2 hours of testing + 30–60 minutes of review

sections.heading: Instructions
sections.html:
How to take this mock

  • Sit each block in one go with a timer: 60 minutes for 40 questions (about 90 seconds per question, the real Step 1 pace). Take a 10–15 minute break between blocks if you like, as you would on test day.
  • No notes, no First Aid, no phone, no searching. Do not open any "Show answer" panel until the whole block is finished.
  • Write your answers on a sheet (1–80), then score yourself against the answer key at the end. Your percent correct is (number right ÷ 80) × 100.
  • Interpretation: ≥70%: comfortable for this level of material, keep doing timed blocks. 60–69%: borderline, keep working, focus on your weakest systems and repeat a mock in 2–3 weeks. <60%: postpone your exam date and rebuild content before more testing.
  • NEET PG habit to break: Step 1 rarely asks for the name of the disease. It asks for the mechanism, the next link in the chain, or the lab value that follows. Identify the diagnosis first, then ask "what is the question really testing?"
  • Review every question, including the ones you got right. Read the "why not" line for every distractor, and log each miss by topic so you can see which systems need more work.

title: Step 2 CK · Internal Medicine I: Cardiology, Pulmonology & Critical Care, Nephrology
meta: Exam: Step 2 CK · Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Critical Care, Renal/Electrolytes · Approx study time: 4–5 days (notes) + 1 day (questions)

sections.heading: Overview
sections.html:
From NEET PG to USMLE

  • CK wants the next step, not the textbook list. NEET PG asks "drug of choice". CK asks what you do now for this patient: stabilise (ABCs, shock, cardioversion), then test, then treat. In an unstable patient, the answer is almost never "get a CT".
  • Use US guideline names and numbers. These are ACC/AHA (cardiology), GINA and GOLD (asthma and COPD), IDSA/ATS (pneumonia), KDIGO (kidney), Surviving Sepsis Campaign (SSC) and USPSTF (screening). Several changed in 2025–2026. This chapter follows the 2025 ACC/AHA guidelines for ACS and hypertension, the 2026 ACC/AHA dyslipidemia guideline, the 2026 SSC update and GOLD 2026/2027. Where NBME questions may still reflect older logic, a note says so.
  • Drug names are generic, with US brands in passing. Sacubitril-valsartan (Entresto), apixaban (Eliquis), rivaroxaban (Xarelto), ticagrelor (Brilinta), dapagliflozin (Farxiga), empagliflozin (Jardiance), budesonide-formoterol (Symbicort), tiotropium (Spiriva).
  • Units differ. Creatinine is in mg/dL (1 mg/dL ≈ 88 µmol/L). BUN is in mg/dL (urea mmol/L × 2.8 ≈ BUN mg/dL). Glucose is in mg/dL (mmol/L × 18). Cholesterol is in mg/dL (mmol/L × 38.7).
  • Warfarin is less often the answer than in Indian practice. DOACs are preferred for AF and VTE. The main exceptions where warfarin is still the answer: mechanical valves, moderate–severe (often rheumatic) mitral stenosis and antiphospholipid syndrome. Rheumatic MS is common in your patients from India, so learn it cold.
  • US-specific systems. Recognise these terms: "door-to-balloon" targets, rapid response and code teams, ICU "bundles", and telemetry admission versus observation.
===================== CARDIOLOGY =====================

sections.heading: 1. Chest pain: the first 10 minutes
sections.html:
Every adult with possible ischemic chest pain gets a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of arrival and a high-sensitivity troponin (hs-cTn). Repeat the troponin at 1–3 h depending on the assay. Run through the life-threatening differential in parallel: ACS, aortic dissection, PE, tension pneumothorax, tamponade and esophageal rupture (Boerhaave). Low-risk patients (for example HEART score 0–3 with negative serial hs-troponin) can be discharged with outpatient follow-up. This follows the 2021 AHA/ACC chest pain guideline.

Clue in stemThinkNext best step
Pressure-like pain, diaphoresis, ST elevationSTEMIActivate cath lab; aspirin; primary PCI
Tearing pain to back, pulse/BP differential >20 mm Hg, wide mediastinum, AR murmurAortic dissectionCT angiography (TEE if unstable); IV β-blocker; no antithrombotics
Pleuritic pain, tachycardia, hypoxia, recent immobilisationPEWells → D-dimer or CTPA
Sharp pain better leaning forward, diffuse ST↑ + PR↓, friction rubPericarditisNSAID + colchicine
Hypotension, JVD, muffled sounds, pulsus paradoxus >10TamponadeEcho → pericardiocentesis
Retching, then chest pain, subcutaneous emphysemaBoerhaaveCT or water-soluble contrast esophagram; surgery
Absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation, hypotensionTension pneumothoraxNeedle decompression (do not wait for CXR), then chest tube
Young patient, cocaine use, chest painCoronary vasospasm or MIBenzodiazepines, aspirin, nitrates, CCB; avoid β-blockers acutely

Stable chest pain with no known CAD (2021 guideline):

  • Low risk: no testing is needed.
  • Intermediate–high risk: either anatomic or functional testing is acceptable. Anatomic means CCTA, which is favoured if age is under 65 and the patient is not on optimal therapy. Functional means stress imaging.

Choosing the stress test:

  • Can exercise and has an interpretable ECG: exercise ECG.
  • Cannot exercise: pharmacologic stress, either dobutamine echo or a vasodilator (regadenoson or adenosine) with nuclear MPI.
  • LBBB or paced rhythm: vasodilator MPI, because exercise or dobutamine causes false septal defects.
  • Baseline ST depression ≥1 mm, LVH with strain, digoxin or WPW: add imaging (echo or MPI) to exercise.
  • Severe bronchospasm: avoid adenosine and regadenoson; use dobutamine echo.
  • Before testing: hold caffeine 12–24 h before vasodilator stress.

sections.heading: 2. Acute coronary syndromes (2025 ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI guideline)
sections.html:
STEMI ECG: new ST elevation at the J point in ≥2 contiguous leads. The threshold is ≥1 mm in most leads. In V2–V3 it is ≥2 mm (men ≥40 y), ≥2.5 mm (men <40 y) or ≥1.5 mm (women).

STEMI-equivalents:

  • Posterior MI: ST depression in V1–V3 with tall R waves. Confirm with ST elevation in V7–V9.
  • LBBB with Sgarbossa criteria: concordant ST elevation ≥1 mm, or concordant ST depression in V1–V3.
  • de Winter T waves.
  • Left main or multivessel ischemia: diffuse ST depression with ST elevation in aVR, together with ongoing ischemia.

Wellens syndrome (deep or biphasic T waves in V2–V3, pain-free) means a critical proximal LAD stenosis. Arrange early angiography and do not stress test.

[[figure:ch08-fig01]]
ComponentKey points (2025 ACS guideline)
Aspirin162–325 mg chewed, then 75–100 mg daily indefinitely
P2Y12 inhibitorTicagrelor or prasugrel preferred over clopidogrel if PCI. Prasugrel is contraindicated with prior stroke/TIA and generally avoided at age ≥75 or weight <60 kg. Use clopidogrel with fibrinolysis or when a strong agent cannot be used. DAPT for ≥12 months if bleeding risk is not high. In selected patients, it is reasonable to stop aspirin after ≥1 month and continue ticagrelor alone.
AnticoagulantUFH (PCI), enoxaparin, or bivalirudin. Fondaparinux is not used alone for PCI (catheter thrombosis).
LipidsHigh-intensity statin for all. Recheck lipids at 4–8 weeks. If LDL is ≥70 mg/dL on maximal statin, add ezetimibe, a PCSK9 mAb or another nonstatin (Class 1). It is reasonable to add one if LDL is 55–69 (2a).
β-blockerOral, within 24 h, unless HF, low output, risk of cardiogenic shock, PR >240 ms or 2°/3° AV block, or active asthma/cocaine. Avoid IV β-blocker in a patient at risk of shock.
RAAS inhibitorACEi/ARB if EF ≤40%, HTN, DM or CKD. Add an MRA (eplerenone) if EF ≤40% with HF or DM.
RevascularisationMultivessel disease in a stable patient: complete revascularisation of significant non-culprit lesions, during the same procedure or staged. Cardiogenic shock: culprit-only PCI; routine multivessel PCI is harmful. CABG is preferred for left main or complex 3-vessel disease (especially with DM).
OtherO2 only if SpO2 <90%. Do not use routine morphine (it delays P2Y12 absorption). NSAIDs are contraindicated. Refer to cardiac rehab before discharge. Transfusing to Hb ~10 g/dL is reasonable in anemic ACS without active bleeding.

Absolute contraindications to fibrinolysis:

  • Any prior intracranial hemorrhage
  • Known cerebral vascular lesion (AVM) or malignant intracranial neoplasm
  • Ischemic stroke within 3 months (except acute stroke within 4.5 h)
  • Suspected aortic dissection
  • Active bleeding (not menses) or bleeding diathesis
  • Significant closed-head or facial trauma within 3 months
  • Intracranial or intraspinal surgery within 2 months
  • Severe uncontrolled HTN not responsive to therapy

Signs that fibrinolysis has failed: <50% ST resolution at 60–90 min, ongoing pain or instability. Send for rescue PCI.

Post-MI complicationTimingClueManagement
Arrhythmia (VF, AV block)First 24–48 hInferior MI: bradycardia and AV block (RCA → AV node)ACLS; atropine or pacing
RV infarctionWith inferior MIHypotension, clear lungs, JVD, ST↑ V4R; nitrates cause a BP crashIV fluids; avoid nitrates and diuretics; PCI
Papillary muscle rupture2–7 dAcute severe MR, flash pulmonary edema; posteromedial muscle (single PDA supply, inferior MI)Afterload reduction, IABP/MCS, emergency surgery
Ventricular septal rupture3–5 dNew holosystolic murmur with thrill, O2 step-up RA→RVEmergency surgery
Free wall rupture5–14 dSudden tamponade, PEAPericardiocentesis, surgery

Exam trap: A patient with an inferior STEMI becomes hypotensive after sublingual nitroglycerin. The answer is an IV normal saline bolus. Furosemide, morphine and further nitrates are all wrong. RV infarction is preload-dependent.

sections.heading: 3. Stable (chronic) coronary disease (2023 AHA/ACC CCD guideline)
sections.html:
• Mortality and event reduction:
    • Aspirin 75–100 mg, or clopidogrel if aspirin is not tolerated
    • High-intensity statin
    • BP <130/80
    • SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA if DM (and SGLT2i if HF or CKD)
    • Smoking cessation, cardiac rehab, influenza vaccine
    • β-blockers are clearly indicated if EF ≤40% or MI within the past year
  • Angina relief:
    • First line: SL nitroglycerin PRN, plus a β-blocker or CCB
    • Add-on: long-acting nitrate or ranolazine
    • Never combine nitrates with PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil within 24 h, tadalafil within 48 h)
  • Revascularisation: for symptoms refractory to medical therapy. It improves survival in significant left main disease and multivessel disease with reduced EF (prefer CABG, especially with DM). In stable patients with preserved EF, PCI relieves angina but does not reduce death or MI (ISCHEMIA trial).

sections.heading: 4. Heart failure (2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA)
sections.html:
Stages. ACC/AHA stages: A (at risk), B (structural disease without symptoms), C (symptomatic), D (advanced). NYHA class I–IV describes symptoms within stages C/D. Classify by EF:

  • HFrEF: ≤40%
  • HFmrEF: 41–49%
  • HFpEF: ≥50%
  • HFimpEF: EF previously ≤40%, now >40%. Continue GDMT.

Diagnosis: BNP/NT-proBNP (lower in obesity, higher in CKD and with sacubitril for BNP) and TTE.

HFrEF "four pillars" (all improve mortality)Details / cautions
ARNI sacubitril-valsartan (preferred). ACEi, or ARB if ACEi is not tolerated.Preferred for NYHA II–III. Switching from an ACEi needs a 36-hour washout (angioedema risk). Contraindicated with prior angioedema and in pregnancy.
Evidence-based β-blocker (carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol)Start when euvolemic and stable. Do not start in cardiogenic shock or "cold and wet" HF.
MRA (spironolactone, eplerenone)Use if eGFR >30 and K <5.0. Monitor K. Gynecomastia with spironolactone: switch to eplerenone.
SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin)Benefit with or without diabetes. Caution: euglycemic DKA and genital mycotic infection.
  • Add-ons in HFrEF:
    • Hydralazine + isosorbide dinitrate for self-identified Black patients with NYHA III–IV on optimal GDMT (mortality benefit), or for anyone who cannot take ACEi/ARB/ARNI (e.g., because of AKI or hyperkalemia)
    • Ivabradine if EF ≤35%, in sinus rhythm, with HR ≥70 on maximal β-blocker
    • Digoxin reduces hospitalisation but not mortality
    • Loop diuretics relieve symptoms only
    • IV iron if iron-deficient
  • Devices:
    • ICD (primary prevention): EF ≤35% with NYHA II–III despite ≥3 months of GDMT, ≥40 days after MI, and expected survival >1 year
    • CRT: EF ≤35%, sinus rhythm, LBBB with QRS ≥150 ms, NYHA II–ambulatory IV
  • Drugs to avoid in HFrEF:
    • Non-dihydropyridine CCBs (diltiazem, verapamil)
    • Thiazolidinediones
    • NSAIDs
    • Saxagliptin
    • Class IC antiarrhythmics and dronedarone
  • HFmrEF and HFpEF:
    • SGLT2i (2a)
    • Diuretics for congestion
    • Control BP and AF; treat obesity
    • ARNI, ARB or MRA may be considered (2b), especially at the lower end of the EF range
  • Acute decompensated HF:
    • Warm and wet (most common): IV loop diuretic (IV dose ≥ home oral dose); vasodilator (nitroglycerin) if hypertensive; NIPPV for respiratory distress
    • Cold and wet: inotrope (dobutamine or milrinone) ± mechanical support
    • Cold and dry: cautious fluids
    • Continue β-blocker unless the patient is in shock or has marked hypotension
CardiomyopathyKey featuresManagement
Hypertrophic (HCM)Autosomal dominant sarcomere mutation (β-myosin heavy chain, myosin-binding protein C). Systolic murmur ↑ with Valsalva/standing, ↓ with squat/handgrip. Exertional syncope, sudden death in athletes.Avoid dehydration, diuretics and vasodilators. β-blocker (first line) or non-DHP CCB. Mavacamten (cardiac myosin inhibitor) for symptomatic obstructive HCM. Septal myectomy or alcohol ablation. ICD if high risk. Screen first-degree relatives with echo/ECG.
DilatedIdiopathic, alcohol, postpartum, doxorubicin, Chagas, tachycardia-induced, myocarditisGDMT; treat cause
RestrictiveAmyloid (transthyretin [ATTR]: older men, carpal tunnel, low voltage despite thick walls; diagnose with Tc-PYP scan), sarcoid, hemochromatosisTafamidis or acoramidis for ATTR; treat cause
TakotsuboPostmenopausal woman, emotional stress, apical ballooning, normal coronariesSupportive; GDMT until recovery

sections.heading: 5. Arrhythmias
sections.html:
Atrial fibrillation (2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS)

AF is managed on three tracks at once: stroke prevention, rate control and rhythm control. Treat risk factors too: weight loss, OSA, alcohol, HTN.

CHA₂DS₂-VAScPoints
C: CHF or LV dysfunction1
H: Hypertension1
A₂: Age ≥752
D: Diabetes1
S₂: prior Stroke/TIA/thromboembolism2
V: Vascular disease (MI, PAD, aortic plaque)1
A: Age 65–741
Sc: Sex category female1

Anticoagulation thresholds:

  • Score ≥2 in men or ≥3 in women: anticoagulate (Class 1)
  • 1 in men or 2 in women: reasonable to anticoagulate
  • 0 in men or 1 in women: no therapy
  • Aspirin is not an acceptable substitute

The 2024 ESC guideline uses CHA₂DS₂-VA, which drops sex, with a threshold of ≥2. The US 2023 guideline still uses CHA₂DS₂-VASc. Scores apply to atrial flutter too.

  • Choice of anticoagulant: DOAC (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran) is preferred over warfarin. Warfarin (INR 2–3) is required for a mechanical valve or moderate–severe mitral stenosis. In ESRD on dialysis, warfarin or apixaban is used.
  • Bleeding risk: HAS-BLED identifies modifiable bleeding risks. It is not a reason to withhold anticoagulation.
  • Left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO, e.g., Watchman): for patients with a contraindication to long-term anticoagulation.
  • Reversal agents: dabigatran → idarucizumab; factor Xa inhibitors → andexanet alfa or 4-factor PCC; warfarin → vitamin K + 4F-PCC.
[[figure:ch08-fig02]]

Rhythm-control drugs:

  • No structural heart disease: flecainide or propafenone ("pill-in-the-pocket", combined with an AV-nodal blocker)
  • CAD: sotalol, dofetilide or amiodarone (dronedarone is also an option)
  • HFrEF: amiodarone or dofetilide
  • Amiodarone monitoring: TSH, LFTs, PFTs/CXR and eye exam

Other arrhythmias

RhythmKey ECGManagement
Atrial flutterSawtooth waves II/III/aVF, ~150 bpm (2:1)As AF (anticoagulation, rate control); cavotricuspid isthmus ablation is curative
Multifocal atrial tachycardia≥3 P-wave morphologies; COPDTreat the lung disease and hypoxia; correct K/Mg; verapamil or β1-blocker if needed
AVNRT / AVRT (SVT)Regular narrow-complex tachycardia, 150–250Vagal maneuvers → adenosine 6 mg then 12 mg rapid IV push → IV diltiazem/β-blocker; unstable → synchronized cardioversion. Long term: ablation.
WPWShort PR, delta waveSymptomatic: ablation. AF with pre-excitation: procainamide or ibutilide, or cardioversion.
Monomorphic VTWide regular tachycardiaPulseless → defibrillate. Unstable with a pulse → synchronized cardioversion. Stable → amiodarone, procainamide or sotalol.
Torsades de pointesPolymorphic VT with long QTIV magnesium 2 g; overdrive pacing or isoproterenol; defibrillate if pulseless; stop QT-prolonging drugs
Mobitz I (Wenckebach)Progressive PR prolongationUsually benign; no pacing if asymptomatic
Mobitz II / 3° AV blockDropped QRS without PR change / AV dissociationPermanent pacemaker (even if asymptomatic); temporary pacing if unstable
BrugadaCoved ST↑ V1–V2, RBBB-likeICD if syncope or arrest; avoid fever and triggering drugs

ACLS essentials (AHA)

  • High-quality CPR:
    • Rate 100–120/min; depth 2–2.4 in (5–6 cm) with full recoil
    • Minimal interruptions (<10 s); 30:2 without an advanced airway
    • With an advanced airway: 1 breath every 6 s with continuous compressions
    • End-tidal CO₂ <10 mm Hg means poor CPR. A sudden rise to >40 suggests return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC).
  • Bradycardia with poor perfusion:
    • First: atropine 1 mg IV every 3–5 min (max 3 mg)
    • If atropine fails: transcutaneous pacing or dopamine 5–20 µg/kg/min or epinephrine 2–10 µg/min infusion
    • Atropine often fails in Mobitz II or 3° block with a wide escape rhythm and in heart transplant patients; pace early
    • β-blocker overdose → glucagon; CCB overdose → calcium + high-dose insulin
  • Tachycardia with a pulse:
    • Unstable (hypotension, altered mental status, shock, ischemic chest pain, acute HF) → synchronized cardioversion
    • Stable narrow regular → vagal maneuvers → adenosine
    • Stable wide regular monomorphic → adenosine is acceptable if SVT with aberrancy is suspected; otherwise amiodarone or procainamide
    • Never give AV-nodal blockers for irregular wide-complex tachycardia (pre-excited AF)
  • Post-ROSC care:
    • 12-lead ECG; emergent cath if STEMI
    • Avoid hypotension (SBP ≥90, MAP ≥65)
    • SpO₂ 92–98%
    • Targeted temperature management with active fever prevention (≤37.5 °C) for comatose patients
[[figure:ch08-fig03]]
High-yield: In VF, epinephrine comes after the 2nd shock and amiodarone after the 3rd. In PEA and asystole, give epinephrine as soon as possible and never shock. Hyperkalemic arrest: give calcium + bicarbonate. Suspected PE in arrest: consider thrombolysis.

Prosthetic valves:

  • Mechanical: lifelong warfarin. INR target 2.5 for an aortic valve without risk factors; 3.0 for mitral, or aortic with risk factors. Add aspirin 75–100 mg if bleeding risk is low. DOACs are contraindicated.
