sections.heading: 7. Hypertension (2025 AHA/ACC guideline)
sections.html:
CategorySBPDBPAction
Normal<120and<80Reassess yearly
Elevated120–129and<80Lifestyle
Stage 1130–139or80–89Drug + lifestyle if clinical CVD, DM, CKD, or PREVENT 10-y CVD risk ≥7.5%. Otherwise lifestyle for 3–6 months, then drug if still ≥130/80.
Stage 2≥140or≥90Drug + lifestyle; start two first-line agents, ideally as a single-pill combination
  • Diagnosis and goal:
    • Confirm with home or ambulatory BP monitoring (white-coat and masked HTN)
    • Target <130/80 for most adults; encourage SBP <120 if tolerated
    • The 2025 guideline replaced the Pooled Cohort Equations with PREVENT, and the stage 1 threshold moved from ASCVD ≥10% to PREVENT ≥7.5%
  • First-line drug classes:
    • Thiazide-type diuretic (chlorthalidone, indapamide, HCTZ)
    • ACEi or ARB (never both together)
    • Long-acting DHP CCB (amlodipine)
  • Compelling indications:
    • ACEi/ARB: albuminuric CKD or DM
    • β-blocker: HFrEF, post-MI, angina, AF rate control
    • Labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa in pregnancy; ACEi/ARB are teratogenic
  • Workup for all hypertensives: BMP, lipid panel, A1c, TSH, ECG and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (new for all in 2025).
  • Resistant HTN: BP above goal on 3 drugs, including a diuretic, at optimal doses.
    • Confirm adherence and rule out white-coat effect
    • Screen everyone for primary aldosteronism with the aldosterone/renin ratio; you need not stop most drugs except MRAs
    • Add spironolactone as the 4th drug
    • Look for OSA, renal artery stenosis and NSAID use
    • Renal denervation may be considered (2b)
  • Secondary-HTN clues:
    • Hypokalemia: hyperaldosteronism
    • Flash pulmonary edema, or Cr rising >30% after ACEi: renal artery stenosis (fibromuscular dysplasia in young women; atherosclerosis in older smokers)
    • Episodic headache, sweating, palpitations: pheochromocytoma (plasma free metanephrines)
    • Upper-limb HTN, rib notching: coarctation
    • Snoring: OSA
  • Hypertensive emergency (BP usually >180/120 with acute end-organ damage):
    • Admit to ICU and use IV titratable agents: nicardipine, clevidipine, labetalol, esmolol, nitroprusside
    • Lower BP by ≤25% in the first hour, then to 160/100–110 over the next 2–6 h, then to normal over 24–48 h
    • Exceptions: aortic dissection (SBP <120 and HR ≤60 within 20 min, β-blocker first); severe preeclampsia (labetalol, hydralazine, nifedipine); acute ischemic stroke (<185/110 before thrombolysis, otherwise permissive up to 220/120)
    • Agent by setting: phentolamine for pheochromocytoma or cocaine; nitroglycerin for ACS or pulmonary edema
    • Hypertensive urgency (no organ damage): oral agents and outpatient follow-up; do not drop BP rapidly

sections.heading: 8. Lipids (2026 ACC/AHA multisociety dyslipidemia guideline)
sections.html:
The 2026 guideline brought back LDL-C goals. It replaced the Pooled Cohort Equations with PREVENT-ASCVD (ages 30–79). It recommends measuring Lp(a) once in every adult and using CAC to reclassify uncertain cases.

IntensityLDL reductionRegimens
High≥50%Atorvastatin 40–80 mg; rosuvastatin 20–40 mg
Moderate30–49%Atorvastatin 10–20; rosuvastatin 5–10; simvastatin 20–40; pravastatin 40–80
Low<30%Simvastatin 10; pravastatin 10–20
  • Statin myopathy: check CK if there are symptoms. Stop the statin if CK >10× ULN with symptoms. Otherwise rechallenge with a different statin or lower dose.
  • Statin-associated liver changes: transaminases <3× ULN are not a reason to stop.
  • Triglycerides ≥500 mg/dL (and especially ≥1,000): fibrate to prevent pancreatitis. For residual risk with TG 150–499 on a statin, icosapent ethyl.
  • USPSTF 2022: statin for ages 40–75 with ≥1 risk factor and 10-y risk ≥10% (B), or 7.5–<10% (C).
Exam trap: Older question banks use the 2018 "four statin benefit groups" and treat by intensity without goals. Under 2026 logic, if a post-MI patient on atorvastatin 80 mg has LDL ≥70 (or even ≥55), the answer is "add ezetimibe". It is never "switch to a fibrate" and never "no change".

sections.heading: 9. Syncope (2017 ACC/AHA/HRS)
sections.html:
Every patient gets a history, exam (including orthostatic vitals) and ECG. Further testing depends on what you suspect.

TypeCluesWorkup / management
Reflex (vasovagal, situational, carotid sinus)Prodrome (warmth, nausea), trigger (standing, pain, micturition, cough), quick recoveryReassure, counter-pressure maneuvers, fluids/salt. Tilt-table only if recurrent and unclear.
OrthostaticSBP drop ≥20 or DBP ≥10 within 3 min of standing; volume loss, drugs (α-blockers, diuretics), autonomic failure (Parkinson, DM)Stop offending drugs, fluids; midodrine or fludrocortisone
Cardiac: arrhythmicNo prodrome, palpitations, supine or exertional, abnormal ECG (bifascicular block, long QT, Brugada, WPW, Mobitz II), family history of sudden deathAdmit with telemetry. Holter (daily symptoms), event monitor (weekly), implantable loop recorder (infrequent).
Cardiac: structuralExertional; murmur (AS, HCM); PE; dissectionTTE, then treat the lesion
High-yield: Exertional syncope is cardiac until proven otherwise. Get an echo. Do not order head CT, EEG or carotid duplex unless there are focal neuro signs or seizure features.

sections.heading: 10. Pericardial disease
sections.html:
ConditionFindingsManagement
Acute pericarditis≥2 of: pleuritic pain better leaning forward, friction rub, diffuse ST↑ + PR↓, effusion. Viral/idiopathic most common; uremic; post-MI; TB (common in India); autoimmune.NSAID (ibuprofen) or high-dose aspirin + colchicine for 3 months, exercise restriction. Steroids only if NSAIDs are contraindicated (they raise recurrence). Admit if high risk: fever >38 °C, large effusion, tamponade, troponin↑, immunosuppressed, anticoagulated, no response at 1 week. Uremic pericarditis → dialysis.
Cardiac tamponadeBeck triad (hypotension, JVD, muffled heart sounds); pulsus paradoxus >10 mm Hg; electrical alternans; echo shows RA/RV diastolic collapseIV fluids as a bridge; urgent pericardiocentesis. Avoid diuretics, nitrates and positive-pressure ventilation if possible.
Constrictive pericarditisKussmaul sign (JVP rises on inspiration), pericardial knock, ascites/edema; calcification on CT (TB, radiation, post-surgical)Diuretics; pericardiectomy

sections.heading: 11. Infective endocarditis (2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria)
sections.html:
• Major criteria:
    • Microbiologic: a typical organism in ≥2 separate blood cultures (S. aureus, viridans streptococci, S. gallolyticus, HACEK, E. faecalis, and others), or positive Coxiella serology (phase I IgG >1:800)
    • Imaging: vegetation, abscess, perforation or new valvular regurgitation on echo or cardiac CT, or abnormal PET/CT activity around a prosthetic valve
    • New surgical evidence also counts
  • Minor criteria:
    • Predisposition (prior IE, prosthetic valve, IV drug use, congenital heart disease)
    • Fever ≥38.0 °C
    • Vascular phenomena (emboli, Janeway lesions, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial hemorrhage, conjunctival hemorrhage)
    • Immunologic phenomena (Osler nodes, Roth spots, glomerulonephritis, positive RF)
    • Microbiologic evidence that falls short of major
  • Definite IE: 2 major, or 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor.

Workup and treatment:

  • Draw 3 sets of blood cultures before antibiotics (from separate sites).
  • Echo: TTE first. Go to TEE for a prosthetic valve, for suspicion of abscess, when TTE is non-diagnostic, and in essentially all S. aureus bacteremia.
  • Empiric native-valve therapy: vancomycin + ceftriaxone (or + cefepime/gentamicin per institution). For a prosthetic valve, add gentamicin and rifampin once the organism is known.
  • Duration is usually 4–6 weeks. Partial oral step-down is acceptable in selected stable left-sided IE (POET trial).
SettingOrganismNote
IV drug use, tricuspid valve, septic pulmonary emboliS. aureusMSSA: nafcillin/oxacillin or cefazolin. MRSA: vancomycin or daptomycin.
Recent dental work, subacute courseViridans streptococciPenicillin G or ceftriaxone
Bacteremia + colon cancerS. gallolyticus (bovis)Colonoscopy
GU procedure, older manEnterococcusAmpicillin + ceftriaxone (or gentamicin)
Early prosthetic valve (<1 y)S. epidermidis, S. aureusVancomycin + rifampin + gentamicin
Culture-negativeHACEK, Coxiella, Bartonella (homeless, lice)Serologies

Indications for early surgery:

  • HF caused by valve dysfunction (most common)
  • Uncontrolled infection: abscess, new heart block, persistent bacteremia >5–7 days on appropriate therapy, fungal or highly resistant organisms
  • Recurrent emboli with a persistent vegetation, or a large mobile vegetation (>10 mm) on the left side

Prophylaxis (amoxicillin 2 g, 30–60 min before dental procedures that manipulate gingiva or perforate mucosa) is given only to patients with:

  • A prosthetic valve or prosthetic repair material (including TAVR)
  • Prior IE
  • Unrepaired cyanotic CHD, repaired CHD with a residual defect, or within 6 months of complete repair
  • A cardiac transplant with valvulopathy

Not for MVP, bicuspid valve, rheumatic heart disease without prosthesis, or HCM.

sections.heading: 12. Peripheral artery disease and the aorta
sections.html:
ABIInterpretation

PAD management:

  • Smoking cessation
  • High-intensity statin
  • Single antiplatelet (aspirin or clopidogrel). Low-dose rivaroxaban 2.5 mg BID + aspirin lowers major limb and CV events.
  • BP control and foot care
  • Supervised exercise therapy (first line for claudication)
  • Cilostazol for claudication (contraindicated in HF)
  • Revascularise for lifestyle-limiting claudication despite therapy, or for chronic limb-threatening ischemia (rest pain, ulcer, gangrene)

Acute limb ischemia (6 Ps: pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia; often embolic from AF):

  • Give an immediate IV heparin bolus and infusion, then perform urgent revascularisation (catheter thrombolysis or surgical embolectomy).
  • Motor loss or sensory loss beyond the toes means an immediately threatened limb: emergent surgery.
  • After reperfusion, watch for compartment syndrome.
Aortic conditionKey points
DissectionRisk factors: HTN (most common), Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos, bicuspid valve, cocaine, pregnancy. Stanford A (ascending) → emergency surgery. Stanford B (descending only) → medical therapy; TEVAR if complicated (malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain or HTN). Imaging: CTA if stable; TEE if unstable or contrast contraindicated. Medical: IV esmolol or labetalol first (HR ≤60), then add nicardipine or nitroprusside if SBP is still >120. A vasodilator alone causes reflex tachycardia and propagates the tear. No anticoagulants or thrombolytics.
AAAUSPSTF: one-time ultrasound for men 65–75 who ever smoked (≥100 cigarettes) (B); selective for never-smoking men (C); not for women who never smoked (D). Repair if ≥5.5 cm (men), ≥5.0 cm (women), growth >0.5 cm in 6 months (or ≥1 cm/yr), or symptoms. EVAR or open repair. Surveillance ultrasound every 2–3 y for 3.0–3.9 cm and yearly for 4.0–4.9 cm. Rupture triad: pain, hypotension, pulsatile mass. If unstable, go straight to the OR.

sections.heading: 13. Pulmonary function tests (PFTs)
sections.html:
Read PFTs in this order:

  1. Is FEV₁/FVC low? A post-bronchodilator ratio <0.70 (or below the lower limit of normal) means obstruction.
  2. If there is obstruction, is there a bronchodilator response? ATS/ERS 2022 defines it as a rise >10% of the predicted value in FEV₁ or FVC. The older definition was ≥12% and 200 mL from baseline.
  3. If FVC is low with a normal ratio, check TLC. TLC <80% predicted confirms restriction.
  4. Then use DLCO to locate the problem.
[[figure:ch08-fig04]]

sections.heading: 14. Asthma (GINA 2025)
sections.html:
GINA no longer recommends SABA-only treatment in adults and adolescents, because it raises the risk of severe exacerbation. GINA describes two tracks:

  • Track 1 (preferred): the reliever is as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol (budesonide-formoterol). Steps 3–5 use the same inhaler for maintenance and reliever therapy (MART).
  • Track 2: the reliever is a SABA. It is used only together with ICS, whether "ICS whenever SABA is taken" or daily ICS.

The US NAEPP 2020 update also endorses SMART at steps 3–4.

StepTypical patientTrack 1 (preferred)Track 2
1–2Symptoms <4–5 days/weekAs-needed low-dose ICS-formoterolStep 1: ICS whenever SABA is used. Step 2: daily low-dose ICS + PRN SABA.
3Symptoms most days or waking ≥1/weekLow-dose maintenance ICS-formoterol (MART)Low-dose ICS-LABA + PRN SABA
4Daily symptoms, waking ≥1/week, low lung functionMedium-dose MARTMedium/high-dose ICS-LABA
5Uncontrolled despite step 4Add LAMA (tiotropium); phenotype and refer. Biologics: anti-IgE (omalizumab), anti-IL-5 (mepolizumab, reslizumab), anti-IL-5R (benralizumab), anti-IL-4Rα (dupilumab), anti-TSLP (tezepelumab). Low-dose oral steroid is a last resort.Same

Before stepping up:

  • Check inhaler technique and adherence first.
  • Look for triggers: GERD, allergic rhinitis, β-blockers, NSAIDs (aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, AERD).
  • Step down after 3 months of good control.

Exacerbation:

  • Initial treatment: SABA (repeated or continuous), ipratropium for severe attacks, systemic corticosteroids (prednisone 40–50 mg for 5–7 days) and O₂ to SpO₂ 93–95%.
  • Severe or refractory attack: add IV magnesium sulfate 2 g.
  • Danger signs: silent chest, drowsiness, inability to speak, and a normal or rising PaCO₂. A normal PaCO₂ in an attack means the patient is tiring. Prepare for intubation.
  • Ventilating the asthmatic: use a low RR, low tidal volume and long expiratory time to avoid auto-PEEP (permissive hypercapnia).

sections.heading: 15. COPD (GOLD 2026; GOLD 2027 noted)
sections.html:
Diagnosis: post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC <0.70 with symptoms or exposure. Screen for α1-antitrypsin deficiency once in every COPD patient, especially if young, a non-smoker or with basal emphysema.

Spirometric severity (GOLD 1–4) by FEV₁ % predicted:

  • GOLD 1: ≥80
  • GOLD 2: 50–79
  • GOLD 3: 30–49
  • GOLD 4: <30
GOLD groupDefinitionInitial therapy
A0–1 moderate exacerbation (not hospitalised) and mMRC 0–1 / CAT <10A bronchodilator. GOLD 2027 prefers a LAMA.
B0–1 moderate exacerbation and mMRC ≥2 / CAT ≥10LABA + LAMA (single inhaler)
E≥2 moderate exacerbations or ≥1 leading to hospitalisationLABA + LAMA. Use LABA + LAMA + ICS if blood eosinophils ≥300/µL.
  • Follow-up escalation for exacerbations on LABA + LAMA:
    • Eosinophils ≥100: add ICS (triple therapy)
    • Eosinophils ≥300 with chronic bronchitis on triple therapy: dupilumab (or mepolizumab)
    • Otherwise: roflumilast (FEV₁ <50% with chronic bronchitis) or azithromycin (preferably in former smokers; check QT and hearing)
    • ICS-LABA alone (without LAMA) is not encouraged in COPD. ICS raises pneumonia risk.
  • What reduces mortality:
    • Smoking cessation (varenicline is most effective; combination NRT)
    • Long-term O₂ if PaO₂ ≤55 mm Hg or SaO₂ ≤88% at rest, or PaO₂ 56–59 with cor pulmonale, edema or Hct >55%. Use ≥15 h/day.
    • Triple therapy in frequent exacerbators
    • NIV for chronic hypercapnia after hospitalisation
    • Pulmonary rehab after an exacerbation
    • Lung volume reduction in selected patients
  • Vaccines: influenza, COVID-19, pneumococcal, RSV (per ACIP age and risk criteria) and Tdap.
  • Acute exacerbation:
    • SABA ± SAMA
    • Prednisone 40 mg for 5 days
    • Antibiotics if sputum purulence plus increased dyspnea or sputum volume, or if ventilated: amoxicillin-clavulanate, doxycycline or a macrolide; cover Pseudomonas if risk
    • Controlled O₂ to SpO₂ 88–92%
    • NIPPV (BiPAP) if pH ≤7.35 and PaCO₂ ≥45 mm Hg. Intubate if NIV fails, or with coma, hemodynamic instability or inability to protect the airway.
Exam trap: Giving 100% non-rebreather O₂ to a CO₂ retainer worsens hypercapnia. V/Q mismatch and the Haldane effect matter more than loss of hypoxic drive. Titrate to 88–92%.

sections.heading: 16. Pneumonia (IDSA/ATS 2019, with 2023 updates on steroids)
sections.html:
Where to treat: decide the site of care with the PSI (preferred) or CURB-65, plus clinical judgement. CURB-65 scores 1 point each for:

  • Confusion
  • BUN >19 mg/dL (urea >7 mmol/L)
  • RR ≥30
  • BP: SBP <90 or DBP ≤60
  • Age ≥65

Score 0–1: outpatient. Score 2: admit. Score ≥3: consider ICU.

Severe CAP: 1 major criterion (septic shock needing vasopressors, or respiratory failure needing mechanical ventilation) or ≥3 minor criteria. Minor criteria:

  • RR ≥30
  • PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤250
  • Multilobar infiltrates
  • Confusion
  • BUN ≥20
  • WBC <4,000
  • Platelets <100,000
  • Temperature <36 °C
  • Hypotension needing aggressive fluids
SettingEmpiric regimen
Outpatient, healthy, no recent antibioticsAmoxicillin 1 g TID, or doxycycline, or macrolide (only if local pneumococcal macrolide resistance is <25%)
Outpatient with comorbidities (heart, lung, liver, renal disease, DM, alcoholism, cancer, asplenia)Amoxicillin-clavulanate or cefpodoxime/cefuroxime + macrolide or doxycycline, or respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) alone
Inpatient, non-severeβ-lactam (ceftriaxone, ampicillin-sulbactam) + macrolide, or respiratory FQ alone
Inpatient, severe (ICU)β-lactam + macrolide, or β-lactam + respiratory FQ
MRSA risk (prior respiratory MRSA, or recent hospitalisation + IV antibiotics with local risk factors)Add vancomycin or linezolid. Obtain cultures and nasal MRSA PCR; a negative PCR supports stopping.
Pseudomonas risk (prior respiratory isolate, structural lung disease, recent IV antibiotics)Piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime, ceftazidime, meropenem or imipenem
HAP (≥48 h after admission) / VAPAntipseudomonal β-lactam ± MRSA coverage (vancomycin/linezolid) based on risk and local antibiogram. Use a second antipseudomonal agent if high mortality risk. Treat 7 days.
  • Duration: ≥5 days and until clinically stable (normal vitals, eating, normal mentation).
  • Steroids: hydrocortisone is suggested in severe CAP (2023 data, the CAPE COD trial; not in influenza).
  • Aspiration: no routine anaerobic coverage unless there is a lung abscess or empyema.
  • Follow-up imaging: a routine follow-up CXR is not needed. Repeat imaging only if symptoms persist or the patient qualifies for lung cancer screening.
  • Atypical organisms:
    • Legionella: hyponatremia, diarrhea, high fever, contact with water systems. Test with urinary antigen.
    • Mycoplasma: young patient, cold agglutinins, bullous myringitis.

sections.heading: 17. Pulmonary embolism
sections.html:
Wells score (PE likely if >4). Points:

  • Clinical signs of DVT: 3
  • PE is the most likely diagnosis: 3
  • HR >100: 1.5
  • Immobilisation ≥3 days or surgery within 4 weeks: 1.5
  • Prior VTE: 1.5
  • Hemoptysis: 1
  • Cancer: 1

PERC is applied only when the clinician's pretest probability is low (<15%). If all 8 criteria are met, no testing is needed:

  1. Age <50
  2. HR <100
  3. SaO₂ ≥95%
  4. No hemoptysis
  5. No estrogen use
  6. No prior VTE
  7. No unilateral leg swelling
  8. No surgery or trauma requiring hospitalisation within 4 weeks

Age-adjusted D-dimer: after age 50, the cutoff is age × 10 µg/L.

[[figure:ch08-fig05]]
Risk classDefinitionTreatment
High risk (massive)SBP <90 for ≥15 min, needs pressors, or cardiac arrestUFH + systemic thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg over 2 h). If contraindicated or failed: catheter-directed therapy or surgical embolectomy. ECMO if refractory.
Intermediate (submassive)Normotensive but RV dysfunction on echo/CT ± troponin/BNP↑Anticoagulate and monitor. Rescue thrombolysis if the patient decompensates (routine lytics: more bleeding, no mortality benefit). PE response team.
Low risksPESI 0, no RV strainDOAC; consider early discharge or outpatient treatment
  • Choosing an anticoagulant:
    • DOAC first line. Apixaban and rivaroxaban need no parenteral lead-in. Dabigatran and edoxaban need ≥5 days of heparin first.
    • Cancer: apixaban, edoxaban, rivaroxaban or LMWH. Prefer LMWH or apixaban for GI/GU luminal cancers because of bleeding risk.
    • Pregnancy: LMWH; warfarin is teratogenic and DOACs are avoided.
    • Antiphospholipid syndrome (especially triple-positive): warfarin, not DOAC.
    • Severe CKD (CrCl <15–30): UFH, then warfarin.
  • Duration:
    • Provoked by a major transient risk factor (surgery): 3 months.
    • Unprovoked, or a persistent risk factor: ≥3 months, then consider indefinite therapy (reduced-dose apixaban or rivaroxaban is an option) if bleeding risk is low.
    • Active cancer: as long as the cancer is active.
  • IVC filter: only for acute VTE with an absolute contraindication to anticoagulation (e.g., active bleeding, recent neurosurgery), or recurrence despite therapeutic anticoagulation. Remove it when anticoagulation can start.
  • Thrombophilia testing: not routine after a provoked VTE.
  • Occult cancer screening after unprovoked VTE: age-appropriate screening only.

sections.heading: 18. Interstitial lung disease and sarcoidosis
sections.html:
EntityCluesDiagnosisManagement
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosisMan >60, ex-smoker, insidious dyspnea, dry cough, "Velcro" basal crackles, clubbingHRCT UIP pattern: subpleural, basal reticulation, honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis. Exclude CTD (ANA, RF, anti-CCP, myositis panel) and exposures. A biopsy is usually not needed if the UIP pattern is typical.Nintedanib or pirfenidone (slow FVC decline). O₂, pulmonary rehab, early lung transplant referral. Avoid steroids and immunosuppression.
Hypersensitivity pneumonitisBirds (pigeon breeder), moldy hay (farmer's lung), hot tubs; symptoms 4–8 h after exposureHRCT: upper/mid-zone centrilobular nodules, ground-glass, mosaic air trapping. BAL lymphocytosis.Antigen avoidance; steroids if severe
Drug-inducedAmiodarone, bleomycin, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin, busulfan, checkpoint inhibitorsTiming; HRCTStop the drug ± steroids
AsbestosisShipyard, insulation, plumbing; latency >20 yLower-lobe fibrosis, calcified pleural plaquesSupportive. Highest cancer risk is bronchogenic carcinoma (synergy with smoking); also mesothelioma.
SilicosisMining, sandblasting, stone countertopsUpper-lobe nodules, eggshell hilar calcificationAnnual TB screening (macrophage dysfunction); IGRA
Connective tissue disease–ILDSystemic sclerosis, RA, myositis (anti-Jo-1)Often NSIP patternMycophenolate; nintedanib

Sarcoidosis. Typical patient: a young adult, often a Black woman in the US.

  • Features:
    • Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy
    • Noncaseating granulomas
    • Hypercalcemia or hypercalciuria (granuloma 1α-hydroxylase raises calcitriol)
    • Raised ACE (not diagnostic)
    • Uveitis, erythema nodosum, lupus pernio, facial nerve palsy
    • Cardiac involvement: heart block, VT, sudden death
  • Löfgren syndrome (erythema nodosum + bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy + ankle arthritis + fever) is diagnostic clinically. No biopsy is needed. Give NSAIDs; it usually remits.
  • Otherwise: tissue diagnosis, preferably by EBUS-guided lymph node biopsy. Exclude TB and fungal infection, which is very important in Indian patients.
  • Baseline evaluation: ECG, ophthalmology exam, calcium, creatinine, LFTs and PFTs.
  • Treatment: oral glucocorticoids only for symptomatic or progressive pulmonary disease or organ-threatening disease (cardiac, ocular, neurologic, hypercalcemia, renal). Asymptomatic stage I disease: observe. Steroid-sparing options: methotrexate, then anti-TNF.

sections.heading: 19. Lung nodules (Fleischner 2017) and lung cancer screening
sections.html:
The Fleischner guidelines apply to incidental nodules in adults ≥35 years. They do not apply to screening CTs (use Lung-RADS), known cancer or immunocompromised patients. Risk is low or high based on smoking, age, size, spiculation, upper lobe location, emphysema and family history.

Solid nodule (single)Low riskHigh risk
<6 mm (<100 mm³)No routine follow-upOptional CT at 12 months
6–8 mmCT at 6–12 months, then consider at 18–24 monthsCT at 6–12 months, then 18–24 months
>8 mmConsider CT at 3 months, PET/CT, or tissue sampling

Subsolid nodules:

  • Pure ground-glass: <6 mm needs no follow-up. ≥6 mm: CT at 6–12 months, then every 2 years to 5 years.
  • Part-solid ≥6 mm: CT at 3–6 months. If it persists with a solid part <6 mm, repeat annually for 5 years. A solid component ≥6 mm is highly suspicious: PET, biopsy or resection.

Benign patterns: popcorn calcification (hamartoma), central or laminated calcification, and stability for 2 years (solid nodule).

High-yield (USPSTF 2021, grade B): annual low-dose CT for adults 50–80 years with a ≥20 pack-year history who currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years. Stop once the person has not smoked for 15 years, or if a health problem limits life expectancy or the ability to have curative surgery. A chest X-ray and sputum cytology are not screening tests. The 2023 ACS (American Cancer Society) guideline dropped the "years since quitting" limit, but USPSTF is the standard tested on CK.

Lung cancer clues to know:

  • Squamous cell: central, cavitation, PTHrP hypercalcemia.
  • Small cell: central; SIADH, ectopic ACTH, Lambert-Eaton.
  • Adenocarcinoma: peripheral, non-smokers. Do molecular testing for EGFR, ALK, ROS1, KRAS G12C and others, plus PD-L1.
  • Pancoast tumour: Horner syndrome and C8–T2 pain.
  • SVC syndrome: establish the tissue diagnosis first unless there is airway compromise or cerebral edema. Then stent and/or radiate.

sections.heading: 20. Pleural effusion
sections.html:
When to tap: a new unexplained effusion (>1 cm on lateral decubitus film or ultrasound) needs diagnostic thoracentesis. The exception is obvious bilateral HF effusions; tap those only if atypical (unilateral, fever, pleuritic pain) or if there is no response to diuresis in ~3 days.

Light's criteria: the effusion is an exudate if any one of these holds:

  1. Pleural/serum protein >0.5
  2. Pleural/serum LDH >0.6
  3. Pleural LDH >2/3 of the upper limit of normal serum LDH

In a diuresed HF patient who "looks exudative", a serum-pleural albumin gradient >1.2 g/dL confirms a transudate.

TransudateExudateSpecial clues
HF (most common overall), cirrhosis (hepatic hydrothorax, right-sided), nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminemia, peritoneal dialysis, hypothyroidismPneumonia (parapneumonic), malignancy, TB, PE, pancreatitis, RA, SLE, post-CABG, chylothoraxGlucose <60: empyema, RA, TB, malignancy. Amylase↑: pancreatitis, esophageal rupture. Lymphocytic exudate with adenosine deaminase (ADA) >40: TB. TG >110: chylothorax. Hematocrit >50% of blood: hemothorax (chest tube).

Parapneumonic effusion:

  • Uncomplicated: pH ≥7.2 and glucose ≥60. Antibiotics alone.
  • Complicated (pH <7.2, glucose <60, LDH >1,000, positive Gram stain/culture) or empyema (frank pus): chest tube drainage + antibiotics. Add intrapleural tPA + DNase for loculations. VATS decortication if this fails.

Malignant effusion that recurs: indwelling pleural catheter or pleurodesis.

sections.heading: 21. Obstructive sleep apnea
sections.html:
• Clinical clues:
    • Snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime sleepiness, morning headaches
    • Obesity, large neck
    • Resistant HTN, AF, pulmonary HTN, polycythemia
  • Screening: STOP-BANG. USPSTF finds insufficient evidence (I) for screening asymptomatic adults.
  • Diagnosis:
    • In-lab polysomnography, or a home sleep apnea test in uncomplicated patients with high pretest probability (not if significant cardiopulmonary or neuromuscular disease)
    • AHI ≥15, or ≥5 with symptoms or comorbidity, confirms OSA
    • Severity by AHI: 5–14 mild, 15–29 moderate, ≥30 severe
  • Treatment:
    • CPAP first line
    • Weight loss; tirzepatide is FDA-approved for moderate–severe OSA with obesity
    • Positional therapy, oral appliance (mild–moderate)
    • Hypoglossal nerve stimulation (CPAP-intolerant, BMI criteria)
    • Avoid alcohol and sedatives
    • Counsel on drowsy driving
  • Obesity hypoventilation syndrome: BMI ≥30 + daytime PaCO₂ >45 + raised serum HCO₃ (no other cause). Treat with PAP, often BiPAP.
===================== CRITICAL CARE =====================

sections.heading: 22. ARDS and ventilator management
sections.html:
Berlin definition:

  • Onset within 1 week of an insult
  • Bilateral opacities not fully explained by effusion, collapse or nodules
  • Edema not fully explained by HF or fluid overload (echo if no risk factor)
  • PaO₂/FiO₂ (P/F) on PEEP ≥5: mild 201–300, moderate 101–200, severe ≤100

The 2023 global definition also accepts high-flow nasal oxygen and SpO₂/FiO₂ ≤315.

Causes: sepsis (most common), pneumonia, aspiration, trauma, pancreatitis, transfusion (TRALI) and drugs.

Evidence-based ARDS care:

  • Low tidal volume: 6 mL/kg predicted body weight (range 4–8). PBW for men = 50 + 2.3 × (height in inches − 60); women = 45.5 + 2.3 × (height in inches − 60).
  • Plateau pressure ≤30 cm H₂O; driving pressure (Pplat − PEEP) ≤15.
  • Higher PEEP for moderate–severe ARDS.
  • Permissive hypercapnia (pH ≥7.20–7.25).
  • Prone positioning ≥12–16 h/day if P/F <150 (mortality benefit).
  • Conservative fluids once shock resolves.
  • Short-term neuromuscular blockade in selected early severe ARDS.
  • Corticosteroids may be considered.
  • VV-ECMO for refractory cases.
Goal / problemAdjust
Improve oxygenation (PaO₂)↑ FiO₂ or ↑ PEEP (mean airway pressure)
Improve ventilation (PaCO₂)Change minute ventilation: RR × tidal volume. In ARDS, raise RR, not tidal volume.
High peak + high plateau (compliance problem)ARDS, pulmonary edema, pneumothorax, right mainstem intubation, atelectasis, abdominal distension
High peak + normal plateau (resistance problem)Bronchospasm, mucus plug, kinked tube, biting the tube: suction, bronchodilator, bite block
Sudden desaturation on vent: DOPEDisplacement, Obstruction, Pneumothorax, Equipment failure. Disconnect and bag with 100% O₂, check tube position and breath sounds. Unilateral absent breath sounds + hypotension → needle decompression.
Hypotension in an obstructive patient (COPD/asthma) on ventAuto-PEEP (breath stacking). Briefly disconnect from the ventilator to let the patient exhale; then ↓RR, ↓tidal volume, ↑inspiratory flow (shorter I time, longer expiratory time); treat bronchospasm.

Liberation from the ventilator:

  • Daily sedation interruption with a spontaneous breathing trial (SBT). Readiness: cause improving, FiO₂ ≤0.4–0.5, PEEP ≤5–8, hemodynamically stable, awake, adequate cough.
  • A rapid shallow breathing index (RR/VT in L) <105 predicts success.
  • Extubate to NIV or high-flow nasal O₂ in high-risk patients, such as hypercapnic COPD.

Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) prevention: head of bed at 30–45°, daily SBT and early mobility.

sections.heading: 23. Sepsis and shock (Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026)
sections.html:
Sepsis-3 definitions:

  • Sepsis: life-threatening organ dysfunction (acute SOFA rise ≥2) caused by a dysregulated host response to infection.
  • Septic shock: vasopressors needed to keep MAP ≥65 and lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation.

Screening: use NEWS2, MEWS or SIRS. Do not use qSOFA alone.

ElementRecommendation
AntibioticsSeptic shock or probable sepsis: immediately, ideally within 1 h. Possible sepsis without shock: rapid workup, antibiotics within 3 h if concern persists. Draw blood cultures before antibiotics if this causes no significant delay.
RegimenBroad spectrum, with MRSA coverage if high risk. Avoid routine empiric anaerobic and antifungal coverage unless indicated. Extended or continuous β-lactam infusion after a loading dose. De-escalate once cultures return. Achieve source control (drain abscess, remove infected line).
Fluids≥30 mL/kg IV crystalloid within the first 3 h for hypotension or lactate ≥4. Use adjusted or ideal body weight if BMI >30. Balanced crystalloids (lactated Ringer's) are preferred over 0.9% saline. Add albumin if large volumes are needed. Guide further fluids with dynamic measures (passive leg raise, stroke volume change) and capillary refill time. Avoid starches. Remove fluid actively after resuscitation.
LactateMeasure; repeat if >2 to guide resuscitation
VasopressorsNorepinephrine first line. It can start through a peripheral IV (proximal, short-term) without waiting for a central line. Initial MAP target ~65 (60–65 in age ≥65). Add vasopressin if norepinephrine needs are rising (≈0.25–0.5 µg/kg/min). Add epinephrine if cardiac dysfunction persists; dobutamine for low output. Avoid dopamine (arrhythmias). Arterial line when feasible.
CorticosteroidsIV hydrocortisone (e.g., 200 mg/day) for septic shock with ongoing vasopressor requirement
OtherTransfuse at Hb <7 g/dL. Insulin when glucose ≥180 (target 144–180). VTE and stress-ulcer prophylaxis (if risk). Bicarbonate only if pH ≤7.2 with AKI. No vitamin C.
[[figure:ch08-fig06]]
High-yield: Two more shock profiles to know.
  • Anaphylaxis: IM epinephrine 0.3–0.5 mg (1 mg/mL) in the lateral thigh, given first. Antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts.
  • Adrenal crisis: refractory hypotension in a patient on chronic steroids. Give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV immediately; do not wait for the cortisol result.
===================== NEPHROLOGY =====================

sections.heading: 24. Acute kidney injury (KDIGO)
sections.html:
KDIGO definition (any one of):

  • Creatinine rise ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 h
  • Creatinine ≥1.5 × baseline within 7 days
  • Urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 h

Initial workup:

  • Volume status
  • Medication review (NSAIDs, ACEi/ARB, diuretics, aminoglycosides, vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam, contrast, PPIs)
  • Bladder scan or Foley catheter
  • Urinalysis with microscopy
  • Urine Na/Cr, then FENa
  • Renal ultrasound to exclude obstruction
CategoryCausesUrine findingsManagement
PrerenalHypovolemia, HF (cardiorenal), cirrhosis (hepatorenal), NSAIDs/ACEi, renal artery stenosisBUN/Cr >20, FENa <1%, UNa <20, Uosm >500, bland sediment (hyaline casts). On diuretics: use FEUrea <35%.Volume repletion; stop the offending drug. Hepatorenal: albumin + terlipressin (or norepinephrine).
Intrinsic: acute tubular necrosis (ATN)Prolonged ischemia, sepsis, contrast, aminoglycosides, cisplatin, rhabdomyolysis (heme), tumour lysisMuddy brown granular casts, FENa >2%, Uosm <350Supportive; avoid nephrotoxins; dose-adjust drugs. Rhabdo: aggressive IV isotonic fluids (urine output ~200–300 mL/h).
Intrinsic: acute interstitial nephritis (AIN)Drugs (β-lactams, PPIs, NSAIDs, sulfonamides, rifampin), infection, sarcoid, checkpoint inhibitorsWBC casts, sterile pyuria; ± fever, rash, eosinophiliaStop the drug; steroids if no improvement
Intrinsic: glomerularRPGNDysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, proteinuriaSerologies + urgent biopsy (section 28)
PostrenalBPH, stones (bilateral or solitary kidney), cancer, anticholinergics, neurogenic bladderLarge post-void residual; hydronephrosis on ultrasoundFoley catheter (bladder outlet), or ureteral stent / nephrostomy. Watch for post-obstructive diuresis.

Urgent dialysis indications ("AEIOU"), when refractory to medical therapy:

  • Acidosis (pH <7.1)
  • Electrolytes (K)
  • Ingestion of dialyzable toxins: salicylates, lithium, toxic alcohols, valproate, metformin-associated lactic acidosis ("SLIME")
  • Fluid Overload
  • Uremia: pericarditis, encephalopathy, bleeding

Contrast-associated AKI: risk is highest with eGFR <30. Give isotonic IV fluids before and after. N-acetylcysteine and bicarbonate add nothing. Do not withhold contrast for STEMI or a dissection workup.

sections.heading: 25. Chronic kidney disease (KDIGO 2024)
sections.html:
Definition: abnormal kidney structure or function for >3 months. Classify by Cause, GFR (G1–G5) and Albuminuria (A1–A3), the "CGA" system. eGFR uses the race-free 2021 CKD-EPI equation (creatinine ± cystatin C).

GFR stageeGFR (mL/min/1.73 m²)AlbuminuriaUACR (mg/g)
G1≥90A1 (normal–mild)<30
G260–89
G3a45–59A2 (moderate)30–300
G3b30–44
G415–29A3 (severe)>300
G5<15 (or dialysis)
IssueManagement
Slowing progressionACEi or ARB at maximal tolerated dose if albuminuria with DM or HTN (especially A2–A3). A creatinine rise ≤30% is acceptable; continue the drug. SGLT2 inhibitor if eGFR ≥20 (with T2DM; or UACR ≥200; or HF); continue until dialysis. T2DM + albuminuria: add finerenone (nonsteroidal MRA) and a GLP-1 RA (semaglutide reduces kidney events).
BPSBP <120 if tolerated (KDIGO); ACC/AHA <130/80
LipidsStatin (± ezetimibe) for age ≥50, or younger with risk factors. Do not start statins in patients already on dialysis.
AnemiaCheck iron (ferritin, TSAT); give iron first. Start an ESA (epoetin, darbepoetin) if Hb <10, targeting Hb ≤11.5 (higher Hb raises stroke and thrombosis risk). HIF-PH inhibitors (daprodustat) are an option on dialysis.
CKD-MBD (mineral and bone disorder)Phosphate↑ → dietary restriction + binders (sevelamer, calcium acetate, lanthanum). PTH↑ (secondary hyperparathyroidism) → calcitriol/vitamin D analogues, cinacalcet. Renal osteodystrophy.
Metabolic acidosisOral sodium bicarbonate if HCO₃ <18
Drugs to avoid or adjustNSAIDs. Metformin: stop if eGFR <30; do not start at 30–45. Gadolinium in eGFR <30 (nephrogenic systemic fibrosis risk with older agents). Magnesium/phosphate enemas. Dose-adjust renally cleared drugs.
PlanningRefer to nephrology at eGFR <30, rapid decline, A3 or refractory HTN. Discuss dialysis modality and transplant when eGFR is <30. Place an AV fistula months ahead (preserve the non-dominant arm veins: no IVs or blood draws). Pre-emptive transplant listing at eGFR ≤20. Start dialysis based on symptoms and complications, not a number. Hepatitis B vaccine.

sections.heading: 26. Sodium disorders
sections.html:
Hyponatremia

  • Step 1: confirm hypotonicity. Normal serum osmolality means pseudohyponatremia (severe hypertriglyceridemia, paraproteinemia). High osmolality means hypertonic hyponatremia: hyperglycemia (add ~1.6–2.4 mEq/L Na per 100 mg/dL glucose above 100), mannitol, or IVIG with maltose.
  • Step 2: urine osmolality. A value <100 means ADH is suppressed.
  • Step 3: urine sodium and volume status.
[[figure:ch08-fig07]]
CauseTreatment
HypovolemicIsotonic saline. Beware rapid correction once ADH switches off (watch urine output).
SIADH (CNS disease, small cell lung cancer, pneumonia, drugs: SSRIs, carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine, cyclophosphamide, MDMA, postoperative pain/nausea)Fluid restriction (<800–1,000 mL/day) first. Then oral salt tablets ± loop diuretic, or oral urea. Tolvaptan (start in hospital; avoid in liver disease; ≤30 days). Normal saline can worsen SIADH if Uosm is high (desalination).
Hypervolemic (HF, cirrhosis)Fluid and sodium restriction, loop diuretics, treat the underlying disease
Thiazide-inducedStop the thiazide; it can recur on rechallenge
Primary polydipsia / beer potomaniaRestrict water, increase solute. High overcorrection risk.
Overcorrection (above the limit)Re-lower with D5W ± IV desmopressin (DDAVP)

Hypernatremia

Cause: usually a water deficit in someone without access to water (elderly or intubated patients), or diabetes insipidus. Urine osmolality separates central from nephrogenic DI.

  • Free water deficit = TBW × (Na/140 − 1).
  • Correct chronic hypernatremia ≤10–12 mEq/L per 24 h.
  • Give isotonic saline first if the patient is hemodynamically unstable, then hypotonic fluids (D5W).

sections.heading: 27. Potassium: hyperkalemia emergency
sections.html:
Rule out pseudohyperkalemia first. Causes: hemolysed sample, fist clenching, extreme leukocytosis or thrombocytosis. Repeat the sample if the ECG is normal and the result is unexpected.

ECG progression: peaked T waves → PR prolongation and P-wave flattening → QRS widening → sine wave → VF or asystole. The ECG does not reliably track the K level.

StepAgent and doseOnsetNote
1. Stabilise the myocardium (if ECG changes or K ≥6.5)Calcium gluconate 10%, 10–30 mL IV (calcium chloride via central line)1–3 min; lasts 30–60 minDoes not lower K. Repeat if the ECG is unchanged.
2. Shift K into cellsRegular insulin 10 units IV + dextrose 25 g (omit dextrose if glucose ≥250); nebulised albuterol 10–20 mg; sodium bicarbonate only if metabolic acidosis15–30 minMonitor glucose hourly for hypoglycemia
3. Remove K from the bodyLoop diuretic (if making urine); sodium zirconium cyclosilicate or patiromer; hemodialysis (definitive in ESRD/oliguric AKI)HoursSodium polystyrene sulfonate is less favoured (slow; risk of colonic necrosis)
4. Prevent recurrenceStop K supplements, ACEi/ARB/MRA, NSAIDs, trimethoprim, heparin; low-K dietDigoxin toxicity with hyperkalemia: digoxin immune Fab

Hypokalemia:

  • ECG: U waves, flat T waves.
  • Replace magnesium first or together. Low Mg causes refractory hypokalemia.
  • Oral KCl is preferred. IV KCl ≤10 mEq/h peripherally (≤20 mEq/h centrally with monitoring).
  • In DKA, hold insulin if K <3.5 (ADA 2024 consensus; older guidance used <3.3).

sections.heading: 28. Acid–base
sections.html:
1. pH: acidemia (<7.35) or alkalemia (>7.45).
  2. Primary process: metabolic (HCO₃) or respiratory (PaCO₂).
  3. Expected compensation. If the measured value differs, there is a second disorder.
  4. Anion gap = Na − (Cl + HCO₃). Normal is ~8–12. Correct for albumin: add 2.5 for each 1 g/dL below 4.
  5. If the anion gap is high, check the delta ratio: ΔAG/ΔHCO₃. A value <1 means a coexisting normal-gap acidosis; >2 means a coexisting metabolic alkalosis.
  6. Osmolar gap (measured − calculated Osm; calculated = 2Na + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8). A gap >10 suggests a toxic alcohol.
Primary disorderExpected compensation
Metabolic acidosisWinter's formula: PaCO₂ = 1.5 × HCO₃ + 8 ± 2
Metabolic alkalosisPaCO₂ ↑ ~0.7 per 1 mEq/L ↑ HCO₃
Respiratory acidosisHCO₃ ↑ 1 (acute) or ↑ 3.5–4 (chronic) per 10 mm Hg ↑ PaCO₂
Respiratory alkalosisHCO₃ ↓ 2 (acute) or ↓ 4–5 (chronic) per 10 mm Hg ↓ PaCO₂
DisorderCausesKey test / treatment
High-AG metabolic acidosis ("GOLDMARK")Glycols (ethylene/propylene), Oxoproline (chronic acetaminophen), L-lactate, D-lactate (short bowel), Methanol, Aspirin, Renal failure, Ketoacidosis (DKA, alcoholic, starvation)Ethylene glycol: oxalate crystals, AKI. Methanol: visual loss. Both: high osmolar gap → fomepizole ± hemodialysis. Salicylate: respiratory alkalosis + high-AG acidosis, tinnitus → urinary alkalinisation with bicarbonate; HD if severe.
Normal-AG (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosisDiarrhea, RTA, large-volume saline, acetazolamide, ureteral diversion, early CKDUrine anion gap (Na + K − Cl): negative = GI loss (NH₄⁺ excretion intact); positive = RTA
Type 1 (distal) RTASjögren, SLE, amphotericin, lithiumUrine pH >5.5, hypokalemia, calcium phosphate stones. Treat with citrate/bicarbonate.
Type 2 (proximal) RTAFanconi syndrome (myeloma, tenofovir, ifosfamide), acetazolamideUrine pH <5.5 once HCO₃ is depleted; hypokalemia; rickets/osteomalacia
Type 4 RTA (hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism)Diabetic nephropathy, ACEi/ARB, spironolactone, trimethoprim, heparin, NSAIDsHyperkalemia, urine pH <5.5. Fludrocortisone, loop diuretic, low-K diet.
Metabolic alkalosisUrine Cl <20 (saline-responsive): vomiting, NG suction, remote diuretics. Urine Cl >20: with HTN → hyperaldosteronism, Cushing, licorice. Without HTN → current diuretics, Bartter (loop-like), Gitelman (thiazide-like, low Mg, low urine Ca).Saline + KCl for chloride-responsive alkalosis
Respiratory acidosis / alkalosisAcidosis: COPD, opioids, neuromuscular disease, OHS. Alkalosis: anxiety, PE, early salicylate, pregnancy, cirrhosis, sepsis.Treat the cause; NIV or intubation for acidosis

sections.heading: 29. Glomerular disease
sections.html:
Workup:

  • UA with microscopy (dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, lipiduria)
  • Spot UPCR/UACR
  • BMP, albumin, lipids
  • C3/C4
  • ANA, anti-dsDNA
  • ANCA (MPO, PR3), anti-GBM
  • HBV, HCV, HIV serologies
  • SPEP/UPEP with serum free light chains (age >50)
  • Anti-PLA2R
  • ASO / anti-DNase B
  • Cryoglobulins
  • Kidney biopsy for most adults. Exceptions: diabetic nephropathy with a typical course, PLA2R-positive membranous with preserved GFR, and childhood minimal change disease.
Nephritic (hematuria, RBC casts, HTN, AKI, <3.5 g proteinuria)ComplementClues / treatment
Post-streptococcal GN↓C3Child; 1–3 weeks after pharyngitis or 3–6 weeks after impetigo; cola urine, edema. Supportive (diuretics, BP control). C3 normalises in 8 weeks.
IgA nephropathyNormalHematuria 1–3 days after URI (synpharyngitic). Most common GN worldwide. ACEi/ARB + SGLT2i; sparsentan or targeted-release budesonide if proteinuria persists.
Lupus nephritis↓C3 and C4Class III/IV: glucocorticoids + mycophenolate (or cyclophosphamide) ± belimumab/voclosporin; hydroxychloroquine for all
MPGN / cryoglobulinemic↓C3 (± C4)HCV (cryoglobulinemia: palpable purpura, arthralgia, low C4); treat HCV
ANCA vasculitis (GPA, MPA, EGPA)NormalPauci-immune RPGN, pulmonary hemorrhage, sinusitis (GPA). Glucocorticoids + rituximab (or cyclophosphamide); avacopan as a steroid-sparing option.
Anti-GBM (Goodpasture)NormalHemoptysis + RPGN; linear IgG on immunofluorescence; smokers. Plasma exchange + glucocorticoids + cyclophosphamide, started urgently (even before biopsy if serology is positive).
Nephrotic (>3.5 g/day, albumin <3, edema, hyperlipidemia, hypercoagulability)Clues / treatment
Minimal change diseaseChildren (most common cause); adults with NSAIDs or Hodgkin lymphoma. Effacement on EM only. Responds to steroids.
FSGSMost common primary cause in Black adults (APOL1 variants); HIV (collapsing), heroin, obesity, reflux. Steroids or calcineurin inhibitor for primary FSGS.
Membranous nephropathyMost common primary cause in white adults; anti-PLA2R. Secondary: solid tumours (age-appropriate cancer screening), HBV, SLE (class V), NSAIDs, gold. Renal vein thrombosis risk (flank pain, hematuria). Rituximab if high risk.
Diabetic nephropathyMost common cause of nephrotic-range proteinuria and ESRD in the US. Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules. Treatment as for CKD (ACEi/ARB, SGLT2i, finerenone, GLP-1 RA).
AmyloidosisMyeloma/AL or chronic inflammation (AA); large kidneys; Congo red apple-green birefringence

Supportive care for nephrotic syndrome:

  • ACEi/ARB
  • Loop diuretic and salt restriction
  • Statin
  • Anticoagulation in membranous disease with albumin <2.0–2.5 g/dL plus additional risk

sections.heading: 30. Nephrolithiasis
sections.html:
• Presentation: colicky flank pain radiating to the groin, hematuria.
  • Imaging:
    • Non-contrast low-dose CT abdomen/pelvis is the most accurate test.
    • Ultrasound first in pregnancy and children. It is also reasonable in the ED to look for hydronephrosis.
    • Also obtain a UA and creatinine.
  • Acute management:
    • Analgesia: NSAIDs (ketorolac) are first line if renal function allows; opioids as rescue.
    • Stone <5 mm: usually passes with fluids and analgesia.
    • 5–10 mm distal ureteral stone: medical expulsive therapy with tamsulosin.
    • >10 mm, or failure after 4–6 weeks: urology for ureteroscopy or shock-wave lithotripsy.
    • >2 cm or staghorn: percutaneous nephrolithotomy.
  • Emergency: an obstructing stone + infection (fever, pyuria, sepsis) needs urgent decompression by ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy, plus IV antibiotics. Definitive stone removal is delayed. Also urgent: AKI, a solitary kidney, bilateral obstruction, and intractable pain or vomiting.
StoneFeaturesPrevention
Calcium oxalate (~75–80%)Envelope or dumbbell crystals. Hypercalciuria, hypocitraturia, hyperoxaluria (Crohn disease / bowel resection: enteric oxalate absorption), low fluid intake.Fluids for urine >2.5 L/day. Normal dietary calcium (low-calcium diets increase stones). Low sodium, less animal protein. Thiazide for hypercalciuria; potassium citrate for hypocitraturia.
Calcium phosphateAlkaline urine; type 1 RTA, hyperparathyroidismTreat cause; thiazide
Uric acidRadiolucent on X-ray, visible on CT; acidic urine; gout, myeloproliferative disorders, tumour lysisAlkalinise urine with potassium citrate (can dissolve stones); allopurinol if hyperuricosuric
Struvite (Mg-NH₄-PO₄)Urease-producing organisms (Proteus, Klebsiella); staghorn; alkaline urine; coffin-lid crystalsComplete surgical removal (PCNL) + antibiotics
CystineAutosomal recessive; hexagonal crystals; childhood onset; positive nitroprusside testHigh fluids, alkalinise urine; tiopronin or penicillamine
Exam trap: A febrile patient with an obstructing ureteral stone does not get tamsulosin, a "trial of passage" or immediate lithotripsy. The answer is antibiotics + emergent decompression. An infected, obstructed kidney is a urologic emergency.

title: Step 2 CK · Internal Medicine II: GI/Hepatology, Endocrinology, Hematology-Oncology, Infectious Disease, Rheumatology
meta: Exam: Step 2 CK · GI/Hepatology, Endocrinology, Hematology-Oncology, Infectious Disease, Rheumatology · Approx study time: 5–6 days (notes 3 days, questions + review 2–3 days)

sections.heading: Overview
sections.html:
From NEET PG to USMLE

  • The question is almost always "what do you do next?" NEET PG rewards recall of the diagnosis; Step 2 CK hands you the diagnosis and asks for the sequence (stabilize → empiric therapy → confirm → definitive). Learn the order of steps, not just the list.
  • US screening is USPSTF-driven: colorectal cancer from 45, mammography biennially from 40, lung LDCT 50–80 with ≥20 pack-years, HCV once for all adults 18–79, HIV 15–65, diabetes screening 35–70 if overweight. Indian practice (opportunistic screening) does not translate.
  • Restrictive transfusion (Hb <7 g/dL; <8 with cardiovascular disease or orthopedic/cardiac surgery) is the US default — "transfuse to 10" is always wrong.
  • Units: glucose mg/dL (÷18 = mmol/L), calcium mg/dL (÷4 = mmol/L), creatinine mg/dL (×88 = µmol/L), BUN not urea (urea mg/dL ≈ BUN × 2.14). CD4 in cells/µL.
  • Drug names: acetaminophen (= paracetamol), albuterol (= salbutamol), meperidine (= pethidine), epinephrine (= adrenaline). Combination ART is written as e.g. bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide (BIC/FTC/TAF, "Biktarvy").
  • Antibiotic choices follow IDSA/CDC, not local Indian resistance patterns: gonorrhea = ceftriaxone 500 mg IM alone; chlamydia = doxycycline 7 days (azithromycin only in pregnancy); H. pylori = bismuth quadruple therapy first-line; C. difficile = fidaxomicin (or oral vancomycin) — metronidazole is no longer first-line.
  • Diabetes drugs are chosen by comorbidity, not just A1c (ADA Standards of Care): SGLT2 inhibitor for HF/CKD, GLP-1 RA for ASCVD/obesity — regardless of A1c. Sulfonylureas are rarely the answer.
  • Never delay life-saving therapy for a test: antibiotics before CT/LP in meningitis, glucocorticoids before temporal artery biopsy, hydrocortisone before cosyntropin results in adrenal crisis, dexamethasone before MRI in cord compression, plasma exchange before ADAMTS13 returns.
============================ GI / HEPATOLOGY ============================

sections.heading: 1. Gastrointestinal bleeding
sections.html:
Localize: upper GI bleed (UGIB) = proximal to the ligament of Treitz — hematemesis, coffee-ground emesis, melena, BUN:creatinine ratio >30 (blood protein absorbed). Brisk UGIB can present as hematochezia with hemodynamic instability. Lower GI bleed (LGIB) = hematochezia, usually diverticular (painless, older patient), angiodysplasia, hemorrhoids, ischemic colitis (painful), post-polypectomy, cancer.

StepUpper GI bleed (ACG 2021)Lower GI bleed (ACG 2023)
ResuscitationTwo large-bore IVs, crystalloid; RBC if Hb <7 g/dL (<8 with CVD); hold anticoagulants/antiplatelets per riskSame; exclude UGIB (NG aspirate / EGD) if unstable hematochezia + high BUN
Risk stratificationGlasgow-Blatchford score (GBS): BUN, Hb, SBP, HR, melena, syncope, liver disease, heart failure. GBS 0–1 → outpatient managementOakland score ≤8 → discharge with outpatient colonoscopy
Pre-endoscopy drugsIV PPI bolus (reasonable); IV erythromycin 30–120 min pre-EGD (gastric emptying). Varices: octreotide + ceftriaxone—
Diagnostic/therapeuticEGD within 24 h (within 12 h if variceal)Unstable/ongoing brisk bleed → CT angiography first → catheter embolization. Stable → colonoscopy after bowel prep (non-urgent, in hospital)
RebleedRepeat EGD → transcatheter arterial embolization → surgeryRepeat CTA/embolization → surgery (segmental colectomy if localized)
Endoscopic stigmata (Forrest)Rebleed riskManagement
Active spurting/oozing (Ia/Ib), non-bleeding visible vessel (IIa)High (≈ 40–90% without therapy)Endoscopic therapy (thermal, clips, epinephrine only in combination) + high-dose PPI (bolus + infusion or intermittent) for 72 h, then BID PPI to 2 weeks
Adherent clot (IIb)IntermediateConsider clot removal + therapy; high-dose PPI
Flat pigmented spot (IIc), clean base (III)Low (<10%)Oral PPI daily, resume diet, early discharge
[[figure:ch09-fig01]]
High-yield: In cirrhosis with any GI bleed, ceftriaxone prophylaxis reduces infection, rebleeding and mortality — it is part of the initial bundle, not an optional add-on. Over-transfusion raises portal pressure and rebleeding.
Exam trap: Hematochezia + hypotension + BUN 60 = brisk upper source until proven otherwise → EGD first. Hematochezia + hypotension + normal BUN with ongoing bleeding → CT angiography, not colonoscopy (cannot prep an unstable patient). Hold IV propranolol acutely (worsens hypotension); start NSBB after bleeding is controlled.

Zenker: barium swallow (avoid blind EGD — perforation) → endoscopic/surgical myotomy

Solids only, intermittent, "steakhouse"Schatzki ringEGD → dilation
Young atopic man, food impactions, rings/furrows ("trachealization")Eosinophilic esophagitis (≥15 eos/hpf)EGD with ≥6 biopsies → PPI, swallowed topical steroid (budesonide/fluticasone), elimination diet, dupilumab; dilation for strictures
Solids and liquids from onset, regurgitation of undigested food, "bird's beak"Achalasia (loss of inhibitory neurons; LES fails to relax)EGD (exclude pseudoachalasia from cardia cancer) → high-resolution manometry (diagnostic) → POEM, laparoscopic Heller myotomy + fundoplication, or pneumatic dilation; botulinum toxin if poor surgical candidate
Intermittent chest pain + dysphagia, "corkscrew"Distal esophageal spasmManometry → CCB, nitrates, PPI

Pill esophagitis (doxycycline, NSAIDs, bisphosphonates, KCl)Local injuryStop drug; take pills upright with water
Food bolus impaction unable to swallow secretionsComplete obstructionEmergent EGD (within 6 h if complete obstruction; within 24 h otherwise); glucagon may be tried but must not delay EGD; biopsy afterwards for EoE

GERD: typical symptoms without alarm features → empiric PPI 8 weeks. EGD if alarm features (dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, GI bleeding, anemia, vomiting) or failure of PPI. Barrett screening: chronic GERD + ≥3 risk factors (male, >50, White, obesity, smoking, family history). Barrett without dysplasia → surveillance EGD every 3–5 y; low-/high-grade dysplasia → endoscopic eradication (radiofrequency ablation, resection).

sections.heading: 3. Peptic ulcer disease and H. pylori
sections.html:
Causes: H. pylori and NSAIDs (≈ 90%). Think Zollinger-Ellison (fasting gastrin >10× ULN with gastric pH <2; secretin stimulation test) if ulcers are multiple, distal duodenal/jejunal, refractory, or with diarrhea; MEN1 screening. Gastric ulcers must be biopsied (exclude cancer) and re-scoped at 8–12 weeks if suspicious.

Regimen (ACG 2024)Components & durationWhen
Bismuth quadruple (preferred first-line)PPI BID + bismuth subsalicylate + tetracycline + metronidazole × 14 daysTreatment-naive; penicillin allergy; any prior macrolide exposure; also salvage
Rifabutin tripleOmeprazole + amoxicillin + rifabutin × 14 daysFirst-line alternative (no penicillin allergy); salvage
Vonoprazan dualVonoprazan (potassium-competitive acid blocker) + amoxicillin × 14 daysFirst-line alternative (no penicillin allergy)
Clarithromycin triplePPI + clarithromycin + amoxicillin × 14 daysOnly if clarithromycin susceptibility is documented (US resistance >15%)
Levofloxacin triplePPI + levofloxacin + amoxicillinSalvage only, if susceptible
High-yield: Test of cure is mandatory after treatment — urea breath test, stool antigen, or biopsy ≥4 weeks after antibiotics and ≥2 weeks off PPI (PPIs, bismuth and antibiotics cause false negatives). Serology cannot document eradication (stays positive). Test household members? No — but test anyone with PUD, MALT lymphoma, family history of gastric cancer, uninvestigated dyspepsia age <60, long-term NSAID/aspirin starters, unexplained IDA, ITP.

Dyspepsia: age ≥60 → EGD. Age <60 without alarm features → test-and-treat H. pylori → PPI trial → tricyclic (functional dyspepsia). Perforated ulcer: sudden severe pain, rigidity, free air under diaphragm (upright CXR / CT) → NPO, IV PPI, antibiotics, emergency surgery (omental/Graham patch).

sections.heading: 4. Inflammatory bowel disease
sections.html:
FeatureUlcerative colitisCrohn disease
DistributionRectum upward, continuous, mucosalMouth to anus, skip lesions, transmural; terminal ileum most common
CluesBloody diarrhea, tenesmus; PSC (p-ANCA); smoking protectiveFistulas, strictures, perianal disease, B12/bile acid malabsorption, oxalate stones, gallstones; smoking worsens
Mild–moderate5-ASA (mesalamine) oral + rectal (proctitis: rectal suppository alone); add budesonide MMX for flaresIleocecal: oral budesonide (5-ASA not effective in Crohn)
Moderate–severeBiologics/small molecules: anti-TNF (infliximab, adalimumab), vedolizumab (gut-selective α4β7), ustekinumab, IL-23 (risankizumab, mirikizumab, guselkumab), JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, upadacitinib), S1P modulators (ozanimod, etrasimod)Anti-TNF ± thiopurine (combination with infliximab is superior), ustekinumab, risankizumab, vedolizumab, upadacitinib; systemic steroids only to induce
Acute severeAdmit; exclude C. difficile and CMV (flex sig biopsy); IV methylprednisolone 60 mg/d; VTE prophylaxis (heparin even with bloody stool); no response by day 3–5 → infliximab or cyclosporine rescue; failure, toxic megacolon (>6 cm), perforation → colectomyAbscess → drain (CT/percutaneous) + antibiotics before immunosuppression; obstruction from fibrotic stricture → resection/strictureplasty
SurgeryTotal proctocolectomy is curative (IPAA)Not curative; recurrence at anastomosis
High-yield before any biologic or JAK inhibitor: screen for latent TB (IGRA preferred, esp. BCG-vaccinated), HBV (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs), HCV, HIV; update vaccines (inactivated — live vaccines contraindicated once immunosuppressed). Before thiopurines: TPMT/NUDT15 genotype or activity. Colonoscopy surveillance begins 8 years after onset of colitis (every 1–3 years); with PSC, begin at diagnosis and repeat annually.

sections.heading: 5. Liver enzyme workup
sections.html:
Define the pattern with the R ratio = (ALT ÷ ULN) ÷ (ALP ÷ ULN): R ≥5 hepatocellular, R ≤2 cholestatic, 2–5 mixed. True liver function tests are INR, albumin, bilirubin (and platelets as a portal-hypertension surrogate).

[[figure:ch09-fig02]]
ScenarioNext step
Acetaminophen ingestion, time known4-h (or later) level on Rumack-Matthew nomogram; above treatment line → N-acetylcysteine. Unknown time or ↑ALT with any detectable level → NAC now. Activated charcoal if <4 h
Acute liver failure (INR ≥1.5 + encephalopathy, no prior liver disease)ICU, NAC (even non-acetaminophen), transfer to transplant center; King's College criteria
Autoimmune hepatitis (young woman, ↑IgG, ASMA/ANA, anti-LKM1)Biopsy → prednisone/budesonide + azathioprine
Hemochromatosis (TSAT >45%, ferritin ↑)HFE genotype (C282Y homozygote) → phlebotomy to ferritin 50–100; screen first-degree relatives; biopsy/MRI if ferritin >1000 or ↑ALT
Wilson disease (<40 y, neuro/psych, hemolysis, Kayser-Fleischer rings, low ALP:bilirubin ratio in acute failure)Ceruloplasmin ↓, 24-h urine copper ↑, slit lamp → penicillamine or trientine; zinc maintenance; transplant for fulminant
MASLD (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, formerly NAFLD)FIB-4 → if ≥1.3, elastography (FibroScan) → hepatology if advanced fibrosis; weight loss 7–10%; GLP-1 RA; resmetirom (THR-β agonist, 2024) or semaglutide (2025) for MASH with F2–F3 fibrosis

sections.heading: 6. Cirrhosis and its complications
sections.html:
Severity: Child-Turcotte-Pugh (bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, encephalopathy) and MELD 3.0 (bilirubin, INR, creatinine, Na, albumin, sex) — MELD ≥15 → transplant referral. Every patient with cirrhosis: HCC surveillance (ultrasound ± AFP every 6 months), variceal screening (EGD, unless elastography <20 kPa with platelets >150,000), HAV/HBV vaccination, avoid NSAIDs and alcohol, acetaminophen ≤2 g/day is acceptable.

ComplicationDiagnosisManagement (AASLD)
Ascites (new or admission with ascites)Diagnostic paracentesis: cell count, albumin, total protein, culture in blood-culture bottles. SAAG ≥1.1 = portal hypertension; protein <2.5 = cirrhosis, ≥2.5 = cardiac/Budd-ChiariNa <2 g/day; spironolactone + furosemide (100:40 ratio); fluid restriction only if Na <125. Refractory → serial large-volume paracentesis (>5 L → albumin 6–8 g per liter removed), TIPS, transplant. Avoid ACEi/ARB, NSAIDs
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (fever, abdominal pain, encephalopathy, AKI — or no symptoms)Ascitic PMN ≥250/µL (treat before culture). Usually E. coli, Klebsiella, strep. Polymicrobial/very high protein/glucose low → secondary peritonitis → CTIV cefotaxime or ceftriaxone × 5–7 days + IV albumin 1.5 g/kg day 1 and 1 g/kg day 3 if Cr >1 mg/dL, BUN >30, or bilirubin >4 (prevents HRS). Hold NSBB if hypotensive. Lifelong prophylaxis afterwards (ciprofloxacin or TMP-SMX)
SBP prophylaxis—Prior SBP; GI bleed (ceftriaxone 7 days); ascitic protein <1.5 g/dL with renal dysfunction or liver failure
VaricesScreening EGDPrimary prophylaxis of medium/large varices: NSBB (carvedilol preferred; propranolol, nadolol) or band ligation. Acute bleed: Figure 1. Secondary: NSBB + EBL
Hepatic encephalopathy (asterixis, confusion, sleep inversion)Clinical; ammonia not needed for diagnosis. Search for precipitant: infection (tap ascites!), GI bleed, hypokalemia/alkalosis, dehydration/diuretics, sedatives, constipation, TIPS, hepatomaLactulose titrated to 2–3 soft stools/day; add rifaximin for recurrence (secondary prevention). Do not restrict protein (1.2–1.5 g/kg/day). Intubate if grade 3–4 for airway protection
Hepatorenal syndrome–AKICirrhosis + ascites, Cr rise ≥0.3 in 48 h or ≥50%, no response after 2 days of diuretic withdrawal + albumin 1 g/kg/day, no shock, no nephrotoxins, no parenchymal disease (proteinuria <500 mg, <50 RBC/hpf, normal US). Urine Na <10Terlipressin + albumin (FDA 2022; avoid if SpO2 <90% or volume overload); ICU: norepinephrine + albumin; if neither available: midodrine + octreotide + albumin. Definitive: liver transplant
Hepatopulmonary syndromePlatypnea-orthodeoxia; contrast (bubble) echo with delayed left-sided bubblesO2; transplant
Portopulmonary HTNEcho → right heart cathPulmonary vasodilators; transplant if controlled
Hepatic hydrothoraxRight-sided transudateDiuretics, thoracentesis, TIPS (no chest tube)
HCCMultiphase CT/MRI: arterial enhancement + washout (LI-RADS 5) is diagnostic — biopsy not requiredResection, ablation, transplant (Milan criteria), TACE, atezolizumab + bevacizumab
Exam trap: A cirrhotic admitted with confusion, fever or AKI needs a diagnostic paracentesis even with normal coagulation labs — coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia are not contraindications (only DIC/fibrinolysis is). Do not give FFP or platelets "to make it safe".

sections.heading: 7. Viral hepatitis — serology and treatment
sections.html:
HBsAgAnti-HBcAnti-HBsInterpretation
+IgM +−Acute HBV
−IgM +−Window period
+ (>6 months)IgG +−Chronic HBV → HBeAg, HBV DNA, ALT, HDV antibody, HCC risk
−IgG ++Resolved infection (reactivation risk with rituximab/chemo → prophylactic entecavir/tenofovir)
−−+Vaccinated
−IgG + (isolated)−Resolved (lost anti-HBs), occult HBV, or false positive → HBV DNA

Screening: CDC 2023 — every adult ≥18 once with the triple panel (HBsAg, anti-HBs, total anti-HBc); every pregnancy (HBsAg). HCV: USPSTF/CDC — every adult 18–79 once (anti-HCV with reflex RNA), every pregnancy; repeat if ongoing risk (PWID).

Chronic HBV — who to treat (AASLD)Drugs
Cirrhosis with any detectable DNA (decompensated: treat regardless); HBeAg+ with DNA >20,000 IU/mL and ALT ≥2× ULN; HBeAg− with DNA >2,000 IU/mL and ALT ≥2× ULN; significant fibrosis on elastography/biopsy; HCC family history, extrahepatic disease, before immunosuppression/chemo. (Newer guidance, e.g., WHO 2024 and AASLD 2025, broadens treatment to lower ALT/DNA thresholds — on the exam, cirrhosis or high DNA + high ALT = treat.)Tenofovir (TDF or TAF) or entecavir — high barrier to resistance. Pegylated interferon (finite course, contraindicated in decompensated cirrhosis, pregnancy). Usually indefinite therapy
Pregnancy: HBV DNA >200,000 IU/mLTDF from 28–32 weeks to delivery (+ infant HBIG and HBV vaccine within 12 h of birth). Breastfeeding allowed; cesarean not indicated for HBV
Chronic HCV (AASLD/IDSA simplified)Detail
ConfirmAnti-HCV + → HCV RNA (anti-HCV stays positive after cure/clearance)
Pre-treatmentFIB-4/elastography (cirrhosis?), HBsAg + anti-HBc (HBV reactivation risk with DAAs), HIV, drug interactions (PPI/amiodarone with sofosbuvir → bradycardia), pregnancy test; genotype not required for treatment-naive pangenotypic therapy
Regimens (pangenotypic)Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir 8 weeks or sofosbuvir/velpatasvir 12 weeks (treatment-naive, compensated). Decompensated → sofosbuvir/velpatasvir + ribavirin; avoid protease inhibitors (glecaprevir) in Child B/C. Acute HCV: treat at once (same regimens)
CureSVR12 = undetectable RNA 12 weeks after therapy; cirrhotics still need HCC surveillance every 6 months

Hepatitis A: supportive; post-exposure: vaccine (± IG if >40 y, immunocompromised, liver disease) within 2 weeks. Hepatitis E: pregnant women (fulminant, high mortality), raw pork/deer; chronic in transplant recipients (ribavirin). Hepatitis D: needs HBsAg; screen all HBsAg+ patients.

sections.heading: 8. Pancreatitis and biliary disease
sections.html:
Diagnosis (revised Atlanta) — 2 of 3: characteristic epigastric pain radiating to back; lipase (or amylase) >3× ULN; imaging findings. CT is not needed if the first two are met — reserve contrast CT for diagnostic doubt or failure to improve after 48–72 h (necrosis, collections). Causes: gallstones (ALT >150 suggests), alcohol, triglycerides >1000 mg/dL, hypercalcemia, post-ERCP, drugs (azathioprine, valproate, didanosine, GLP-1 RA), trauma, IgG4 autoimmune.

Management elementCurrent standard (ACG 2024 / AGA)
FluidsGoal-directed, moderate lactated Ringer (bolus 10 mL/kg if hypovolemic, then 1.5 mL/kg/h) — aggressive fluids increase fluid overload without benefit (WATERFALL trial). Monitor HR, urine output, BUN, hematocrit
NutritionEarly oral feeding (within 24–48 h, low-fat solid diet) as pain allows — no need to wait for normal lipase. If not tolerated → enteral (NG or NJ) preferred over TPN
AnalgesiaOpioids (hydromorphone) acceptable; NSAIDs if renal function normal
AntibioticsNot prophylactic, even with sterile necrosis. Infected necrosis (gas on CT, clinical deterioration after 7–10 days) → carbapenem; delay debridement ≥4 weeks (walled-off), step-up endoscopic/percutaneous approach
ERCPWithin 24 h only if concurrent cholangitis; not for gallstone pancreatitis without cholangitis or obstruction
CholecystectomyMild gallstone pancreatitis → same admission (reduces recurrence); necrotizing → delay until collections resolve
SeverityOrgan failure >48 h = severe; SIRS, BUN rising, hematocrit >44, BISAP; ICU for organ failure
HypertriglyceridemiaInsulin infusion (+ dextrose), plasmapheresis if severe; fibrate later
Biliary syndromeFeaturesNext step
Biliary colicPostprandial RUQ pain <6 h, normal labsUS → elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy
Acute cholecystitisPain >6 h, fever, Murphy sign, leukocytosis; US: wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy (HIDA if equivocal — non-filling)NPO, IV fluids, antibiotics (ceftriaxone + metronidazole or pip-tazo), cholecystectomy within 72 h; poor surgical candidate → percutaneous cholecystostomy
Choledocholithiasis↑ALP, bilirubin, dilated CBD; high risk (CBD stone on US, bilirubin >4 + dilated CBD) → ERCP; intermediate → MRCP/EUSERCP with stone extraction, then cholecystectomy
Acute cholangitisCharcot triad (fever, jaundice, RUQ pain); Reynolds pentad adds shock + confusionBlood cultures, IV antibiotics (pip-tazo), fluids → ERCP (urgent if septic, within 24–48 h otherwise)
Painless jaundice + palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier), weight lossPancreatic head cancerPancreas-protocol CT → EUS-FNA; CA 19-9 for monitoring, not diagnosis

Other CK favorites: Acute diverticulitis — CT for diagnosis; uncomplicated in immunocompetent → outpatient, antibiotics selectively (not mandatory); abscess >3–4 cm → percutaneous drainage; perforation/peritonitis → surgery (Hartmann); colonoscopy 6–8 weeks after complicated episode (or if not recently screened). Acute mesenteric ischemia — pain out of proportion, AF → CT angiography → heparin + revascularization. Ischemic colitis — watershed (splenic flexure), older patient, painful bloody diarrhea after hypotension → supportive, colonoscopy. Celiac — tTG-IgA + total IgA while on gluten → duodenal biopsy; gluten-free diet; screen for dermatitis herpetiformis, IDA, osteoporosis. Microscopic colitis — older woman, watery diarrhea, normal colonoscopy, biopsy diagnostic → budesonide; stop NSAIDs/PPIs/SSRIs. IBS — Rome IV; exclude celiac, check CBC/CRP or fecal calprotectin; no alarm features → diet (low FODMAP), fiber, antispasmodic, TCA. Acute infectious diarrhea — no stool studies unless fever, bloody stool, severe dehydration, immunocompromise, >7 days, or outbreak; avoid antibiotics in suspected STEC (HUS risk).

============================ ENDOCRINOLOGY ============================

sections.heading: 10. Diabetes mellitus (ADA Standards of Care)
sections.html:
ItemStandard
Diagnosis (any one, confirm on repeat unless unequivocal hyperglycemia + symptoms)A1c ≥6.5% · fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL · 2-h OGTT ≥200 · random ≥200 with classic symptoms. Prediabetes: A1c 5.7–6.4, FPG 100–125, OGTT 140–199
ScreeningUSPSTF: age 35–70 with overweight/obesity, every 3 y. ADA: everyone ≥35; earlier if BMI ≥25 (≥23 Asian American) + a risk factor (South Asian ancestry is a risk factor — relevant to many IMGs' patients)
A1c target<7% for most nonpregnant adults; <6.5% if achievable without hypoglycemia (young, short duration); <8% for limited life expectancy, frequent hypoglycemia, advanced complications. Older adults with complex health: <8.0%; avoid hypoglycemia. Pregnancy: <6% if no hypoglycemia
BP / lipidsBP <130/80. Statin: moderate intensity for all age 40–75; high intensity if ASCVD or 40–75 with ≥1 risk factor (LDL goal <70; <55 with ASCVD)
Annual checksUrine albumin-to-creatinine ratio + eGFR; dilated eye exam (T2DM at diagnosis; T1DM within 5 y); comprehensive foot exam (monofilament); lipids
Albuminuria (UACR ≥30)ACEi or ARB (titrate to max tolerated), SGLT2 inhibitor (eGFR ≥20), finerenone if persistent albuminuria, GLP-1 RA (semaglutide — FLOW trial)
AspirinSecondary prevention; primary only if high CV risk and low bleeding risk after discussion
Comorbidity (choose drug independent of A1c)Preferred add-on (with or without metformin)
Established ASCVD or high CV riskGLP-1 RA with proven benefit (semaglutide, liraglutide, dulaglutide) or SGLT2 inhibitor with proven benefit (empagliflozin, canagliflozin, dapagliflozin)
Heart failure (HFrEF or HFpEF)SGLT2 inhibitor (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin). Avoid pioglitazone (fluid retention) and saxagliptin (HF admissions)
CKD (eGFR 20–60 or albuminuria)SGLT2 inhibitor; GLP-1 RA if SGLT2 not tolerated or for additional glucose lowering
Obesity / weight-loss goalTirzepatide (dual GIP/GLP-1) or semaglutide (greatest weight loss)
Cost a major barrierMetformin, sulfonylurea, pioglitazone, human insulin
MASLD/MASHGLP-1 RA, pioglitazone, tirzepatide
Drug classKey adverse effects / contraindications
MetforminGI upset, B12 deficiency, lactic acidosis — contraindicated eGFR <30; do not start at eGFR 30–45; hold for iodinated contrast if eGFR <30 or AKI
SGLT2 inhibitors (-gliflozin)Genital mycotic infections, euglycemic DKA (hold 3 days before surgery; avoid in T1DM), volume depletion, Fournier gangrene (rare)
GLP-1 RA (-glutide), tirzepatideNausea, gastroparesis (aspiration risk at anesthesia), pancreatitis, gallstones; contraindicated with personal/family history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN2
DPP-4 inhibitors (-gliptin)Weight-neutral, low potency; pancreatitis; saxagliptin/alogliptin HF caution; do not combine with GLP-1 RA
SulfonylureasHypoglycemia (glyburide worst — avoid in elderly/CKD), weight gain
PioglitazoneEdema/HF, weight gain, fractures, bladder cancer signal
InsulinHypoglycemia, weight gain. Start basal 10 U/day or 0.1–0.2 U/kg; titrate to fasting 80–130
High-yield: Start insulin at diagnosis of T2DM if A1c >10% or glucose ≥300 mg/dL, or if catabolic (weight loss, ketosis) — consider T1DM/LADA (GAD-65 antibodies) in a lean adult. Otherwise, metformin + lifestyle, adding comorbidity-driven agents early (combination therapy is encouraged when A1c is ≥1.5% above target). Before injectable insulin, consider a GLP-1 RA.
Exam trap: Morning hyperglycemia on bedtime NPH: check 3 a.m. glucose. Low → Somogyi (rebound) → reduce evening insulin. Normal/high → dawn phenomenon (GH/cortisol surge) → increase or move NPH to bedtime. Hypoglycemia unawareness → relax targets, CGM.

[[figure:ch09-fig03]]
High-yield: Total-body K+ is depleted in DKA even when serum K+ is high (acidosis + insulin deficiency shift K+ out). Insulin drives K+ into cells → fatal hypokalemia if started with K+ <3.5. HHS: same steps, but fluids are the priority (insulin started after initial fluid resuscitation, typically 0.05–0.1 U/kg/h), and glucose should fall gradually; add dextrose at glucose <300 mg/dL.

sections.heading: 16. Anemia workup
sections.html:
Start with the MCV and the reticulocyte index (RI = retic % × [Hct/45] ÷ maturation factor; RI >2 = appropriate marrow response → loss or hemolysis). Look at the other cell lines: pancytopenia → marrow (biopsy), B12/folate, hypersplenism, HIV, drugs.

DiagnosisWells score. PE unlikely → PERC (all negative = no test) → D-dimer (age-adjusted: age × 10 µg/L if >50) → negative excludes. sections.heading: 30. Rheumatoid arthritis
sections.html:
Symmetric small-joint (MCP, PIP, wrist) polyarthritis, morning stiffness >1 h, ≥6 weeks; spares DIP. sections.html:
PhaseManagement
DiagnosisArthrocentesis: negatively birefringent needle-shaped monosodium urate crystals (WBC 2,000–50,000; send Gram stain/culture — infection can coexist). Serum urate may be normal during a flare. DECT/US double-contour sign supportive

title: Step 2 CK · Surgery, Trauma & Emergency Medicine
meta: Exam: Step 2 CK · Trauma, general surgery, perioperative medicine, surgical oncology, vascular, urology, orthopedics, anesthesia, emergency medicine & toxicology · Approx study time: 14–18 hours (notes) + 4 hours (questions)

sections.heading: Overview
sections.html:
From NEET PG to USMLE

  • Order matters more than facts. NEET PG asks "what is the investigation of choice?"; Step 2 CK asks "what is the next best step for this patient right now?" The answer flips on one variable: hemodynamic stability. Unstable patients go to the OR (or get a bedside procedure); stable patients get a CT.
  • ATLS 10th edition is the US standard: 1 L warmed crystalloid (adults) then early blood products in a 1:1:1 ratio; needle decompression for adults at the 4th–5th intercostal space, anterior to the mid-axillary line (2nd ICS mid-clavicular is now the pediatric site/alternative). Many Indian textbooks still teach 2 L crystalloid and the 2nd ICS only.
  • Clinical diagnoses do not wait for imaging. Tension pneumothorax, testicular torsion, ruptured AAA in shock, and compartment syndrome — choosing "X-ray/ultrasound/CT first" is the classic wrong answer.
  • US drug names: acetaminophen (= paracetamol), N-acetylcysteine (NAC, Acetadote IV), dantrolene, naloxone (Narcan), pralidoxime (2-PAM), hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit), 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (Kcentra), idarucizumab (Praxbind), andexanet alfa, alvimopan, neostigmine, sugammadex, epinephrine 1 mg/mL (1:1000) IM.
  • Units: US labs report acetaminophen in mcg/mL (150 mcg/mL at 4 h = treatment line), salicylate in mg/dL, glucose in mg/dL, temperature often in °F (104 °F = 40 °C).
  • USPSTF screening appears in surgery blocks: one-time AAA ultrasound in men 65–75 who have ever smoked; do not screen asymptomatic adults for carotid stenosis; mammography biennially 40–74 (2024 update); colorectal 45–75.
  • Perioperative medicine is examined heavily (cardiac risk via ACC/AHA, anticoagulation bridging, insulin, steroids, SGLT2 inhibitors/GLP-1 agonists) — topics that NEET PG barely touches.
===================== TRAUMA =====================

sections.heading: 1. ATLS: Primary and secondary survey
sections.html:
The primary survey identifies and treats immediately life-threatening problems in strict order — Airway with cervical-spine protection, Breathing, Circulation with hemorrhage control, Disability, Exposure/environment. A problem is fixed before moving on. In the multiply injured patient, exsanguinating external hemorrhage is now controlled first (direct pressure, tourniquet) — sometimes written "xABCDE". Re-evaluate ABC after every intervention and whenever the patient deteriorates.

[[figure:ch10-fig01]]
Adjunct / stepKey pointsDo NOT
Foley catheterMonitor urine output (adult 0.5 mL/kg/h; child 1 mL/kg/h)Insert if blood at meatus, perineal/scrotal hematoma, or high-riding prostate → retrograde urethrogram first
Gastric tubeDecompress stomach, reduce aspirationNasal route with midface/basilar skull fracture (raccoon eyes, Battle sign, CSF rhinorrhea, hemotympanum) → use orogastric
FAST / eFAST4 views: pericardial, RUQ (Morison pouch), LUQ (splenorenal), pelvis; eFAST adds lungs (pneumothorax)Rely on it for retroperitoneal, hollow-viscus or diaphragm injury (insensitive)

Hemorrhage class (ATLS)Blood lossHRBPMental status / urineTreatment
I< 15% (< 750 mL)NormalNormalSlightly anxious; normal UOPMinimal
II15–30%Mildly ↑ (100–120)Normal (pulse pressure ↓)Anxious; UOP 20–30 mL/hCrystalloid ± blood

High-yield: Hypotension in trauma = hemorrhage until proven otherwise. Permissive hypotension (SBP ~ 80–90 mmHg) is used in penetrating torso trauma until surgical control — but NOT with traumatic brain injury (keep SBP ≥ 100–110 mmHg). Tranexamic acid helps only if given within 3 hours of injury (CRASH-2).
Exam trap: Elderly patients on β-blockers, athletes, and pregnant women may not become tachycardic; children maintain BP until > 30–40% blood loss and then crash. A "normal" HR does not exclude class III hemorrhage.

sections.html:

Epidural hematomaMiddle meningeal artery; temporal bone fractureBiconvex (lens), does not cross suturesLucid interval → rapid decline, ipsilateral blown pupil (uncal herniation)Emergent craniotomy & evacuation (small, asymptomatic: observe in neuro ICU)
