Raised ICP / herniation: Cushing reflex (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respirations). Immediate: head of bed 30°, keep neck straight (loosen collar), sedation, hyperosmolar therapy (mannitol 1 g/kg or hypertonic saline), brief hyperventilation (PaCO2 30–35 mmHg) only as a bridge, then neurosurgical decompression. Avoid hypoxia, hypotension, hyperthermia, hyponatremia. Seizure prophylaxis (levetiracetam/phenytoin) for 7 days in severe TBI. Glucocorticoids are harmful in TBI (CRASH trial).

Who needs a head CT? GCS < 15 at 2 h, suspected open/depressed/basilar fracture, vomiting ≥ 2 episodes, age ≥ 65, amnesia > 30 min, dangerous mechanism (Canadian CT Head Rule) — and any anticoagulated patient with head trauma.

Cervical spine — NEXUS: no imaging needed if ALL present: no midline tenderness, no focal neuro deficit, normal alertness, no intoxication, no painful distracting injury. Otherwise CT cervical spine (X-ray is no longer first-line in adults). MRI for neurologic deficit with normal CT or ligamentous injury.

Cord syndromeMechanismDeficit
Central cordHyperextension in elderly with cervical spondylosisUpper > lower extremity weakness (hands worst), variable sensory loss; best prognosis of the incomplete syndromes
Anterior cordFlexion injury, anterior spinal artery occlusion (also after aortic surgery)Bilateral motor + pain/temperature loss below lesion; dorsal columns spared (vibration, proprioception); worst prognosis
Brown-SéquardPenetrating hemisectionIpsilateral motor + proprioception loss; contralateral pain/temperature loss 1–2 levels below
Cauda equinaMassive disc, tumor, epidural abscess/hematomaSaddle anesthesia, urinary retention, LMN signs → emergent MRI + decompression
High-yield: Neurogenic shock (injury above T6) = loss of sympathetic tone → hypotension with bradycardia and warm, dry skin. Treat with fluids, then vasopressors (norepinephrine; atropine for bradycardia); target MAP 85–90 mmHg for 7 days after acute cord injury. Rule out hemorrhage first. "Spinal shock" is different: transient flaccid areflexia below the lesion. High-dose methylprednisolone is not recommended.

sections.heading: 3. Chest trauma
sections.html:
[[figure:ch10-fig02]]
InjuryClueNext step
Simple pneumothoraxStable, ↓ breath soundsChest tube (small/asymptomatic may be observed; always tube before positive-pressure ventilation or air transport)
Open pneumothorax ("sucking chest wound")Defect > 2/3 tracheal diameter3-sided occlusive dressing → chest tube remote from wound → surgical closure
Flail chest≥ 3 adjacent ribs fractured in ≥ 2 places; paradoxical motionThe danger is the underlying pulmonary contusion: analgesia (epidural/regional block), O2, judicious fluids, ventilate if failing
Pulmonary contusionHypoxia worsening over 24–48 h, patchy infiltrate not respecting lobesSupportive, avoid fluid overload
Blunt aortic injuryDeceleration; widened mediastinum > 8 cm, loss of aortic knob, left hemothorax, deviated NG tube, 1st/2nd rib fractureCT angiography chest → BP/HR control (esmolol, SBP < 100, HR < 80) → TEVAR
Blunt cardiac injurySternal fracture, new arrhythmiaECG + troponin; abnormal → telemetry, echo
Tracheobronchial injuryPersistent large air leak after chest tube, pneumomediastinum, subcutaneous emphysemaBronchoscopy → repair
Diaphragm ruptureLeft > right; bowel/NG tube in chest on CXRSurgical repair (laparotomy acutely)
Esophageal perforationPenetrating or post-EGD/vomiting (Boerhaave); pneumomediastinum, Hamman crunchWater-soluble contrast esophagram (or CT) → surgery, NPO, broad antibiotics
Exam trap: Penetrating wound in the "cardiac box" (clavicles, nipples, costal margins) with hypotension → OR, not CT. A trauma patient who becomes hypotensive right after intubation and positive pressure ventilation → think tension pneumothorax (or reduced preload) — decompress.

sections.heading: 4. Abdominal and pelvic trauma
sections.html:
[[figure:ch10-fig03]]

Penetrating abdominal trauma: gunshot wound to the abdomen → laparotomy (selected stable tangential wounds may get CT). Stab wound: laparotomy if unstable, peritonitis, evisceration or impalement (leave the object in place until the OR); if stable without these → local wound exploration/CT with serial examinations. Flank/back stab → triple-contrast CT.

InjuryKey featuresManagement
SpleenMost commonly injured organ in blunt trauma; LUQ pain, left shoulder pain (Kehr sign), lower left rib fracturesStable → nonoperative (even high grade, with angioembolization for blush); unstable → splenectomy
LiverMost commonly injured organ in stab wounds (small bowel is most common in gunshot wounds); RUQStable → nonoperative; unstable → packing, Pringle maneuver (clamp hepatoduodenal ligament), damage-control surgery
Duodenal hematomaHandlebar/seat-belt injury in a child; bilious vomiting days later; "coiled spring" on contrast studyNG decompression + parenteral nutrition; resolves in 1–3 weeks
PancreasEpigastric blow (handlebar), rising amylase/lipase, CT may initially be normalDuct injury → distal pancreatectomy (body/tail) or drainage
Seat-belt signAbdominal wall bruising: hollow viscus/mesentery injury and Chance fracture (L1–L2 flexion–distraction)CT; low threshold for laparotomy
Abdominal compartment syndromeAfter massive resuscitation/damage control: tense abdomen, ↑ peak airway pressure, oliguria; bladder pressure > 20 mmHg with new organ dysfunctionDecompressive laparotomy (leave open)

Pelvic fracture: open-book fractures can bleed several liters (mostly venous plexus). Unstable patient: pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters + blood. If still unstable and FAST negative → angiographic embolization or preperitoneal packing (REBOA in some centers); if FAST positive → laparotomy first (with packing). Associated: urethral injury (posterior urethra, membranous part, in men), bladder rupture.

GU injuryClueTestTreatment
Posterior urethraPelvic fracture, blood at meatus, high-riding prostate, inability to voidRetrograde urethrogramSuprapubic catheter; delayed repair
Anterior urethraStraddle injury (bulbar urethra), perineal butterfly hematomaRetrograde urethrogramSuprapubic catheter or gentle single attempt by urology
Bladder — extraperitonealPelvic fractureCT cystogram (retrograde)Foley drainage 10–14 days
Bladder — intraperitonealFull bladder + blow to lower abdomen (dome rupture); ascites, ↑ creatinine (urine reabsorption)CT cystogramSurgical repair
KidneyHematuria with flank traumaCT with contrast (delayed phase)Nonoperative usually
Exam trap: In pregnant trauma patients, place the patient in left lateral tilt (manual uterine displacement) to relieve IVC compression; do whatever imaging the mother needs (CT is not withheld); give RhIG if Rh-negative; perform cardiotocographic monitoring ≥ 4–6 h if ≥ 20 weeks (abruption). Perimortem cesarean within 4–5 min of arrest if fundus at/above umbilicus.

sections.heading: 5. Burns
sections.html:
DepthAppearancePainHealing
Superficial (1st degree) — epidermisRed, dry, no blisters, blanches (sunburn)Painful3–6 days; not counted in TBSA for fluids
Superficial partial thickness — papillary dermisBlisters, moist, pink, blanchesVery painful~2–3 weeks, minimal scar
Deep partial thickness — reticular dermisMottled/white, less blanchingPressure sensation, less pain> 3 weeks; usually excision + graft
Full thickness (3rd degree)Leathery, white/charred, non-blanching, insensatePainlessExcision + grafting
4th degreeInto fascia, muscle, bonePainlessDebridement, reconstruction/amputation
[[figure:ch10-fig04]]

Fluid resuscitation — Parkland formula: 4 mL × weight (kg) × %TBSA (partial + full thickness) of lactated Ringer's over 24 h; half in the first 8 h from the time of burn (not from arrival), half over the next 16 h. Indicated for ≥ 20% TBSA in adults (≥ 10–15% in children; children also get maintenance dextrose-containing fluid). The formula is only a starting point — titrate to urine output 0.5 mL/kg/h in adults (~30–50 mL/h), 1 mL/kg/h in children < 30 kg, and 1–1.5 mL/kg/h (or visibly clear urine) in electrical burns/myoglobinuria. The American Burn Association now favors starting at 2 mL/kg/%TBSA in adults (3 mL in children) to avoid "fluid creep"; Step 2 CK still tests the Parkland arithmetic.

IssueRecognitionAction
Inhalation injuryEnclosed-space fire, facial burns, singed nasal hair, carbonaceous sputum, hoarseness, stridorEarly intubation before edema closes the airway; bronchoscopy confirms
Carbon monoxideHeadache, confusion; SpO2 falsely normal100% O2 via non-rebreather; co-oximetry COHb
Cyanide (burning plastics)Severe lactic acidosis (> 8–10 mmol/L), hypotension, comaHydroxocobalamin IV
Circumferential full-thickness burnLimb: ↓ pulses, compartment signs. Chest: ↑ peak airway pressures, poor ventilationEscharotomy (bedside)
Electrical burnSmall skin wounds, massive deep injury; arrhythmias, rhabdomyolysis, compartment syndrome, cataracts laterECG + monitoring, CK, aggressive fluids, fasciotomy prn
Chemical burnAlkali (deeper, liquefactive) > acid (coagulative)Remove clothing, copious water irrigation (do not neutralize)

Topicals: silver sulfadiazine (broad; transient leukopenia; avoid in sulfa allergy, face, pregnancy near term/neonates), mafenide acetate (penetrates eschar, good for cartilage — ears; carbonic anhydrase inhibition → metabolic acidosis; painful), silver nitrate (hyponatremia, staining), bacitracin for face. No prophylactic systemic antibiotics. Give tetanus. Early excision and grafting; high-protein feeding (enteral). Sepsis after day 5 often Pseudomonas. Succinylcholine is contraindicated > 24 h after a major burn (up-regulated extrajunctional receptors → hyperkalemia). Curling ulcer: stress ulcer prophylaxis.

High-yield: Burn-center referral criteria: partial-thickness > 10% TBSA; any full-thickness; burns of face, hands, feet, genitalia, perineum, major joints; electrical (incl. lightning), chemical, inhalation injury; significant comorbidity; children in hospitals without pediatric capability. Burns in children with stocking/glove distribution, sharp demarcation, or sparing of flexural creases → suspect abuse (immersion).
===================== ACUTE ABDOMEN =====================

sections.heading: 6. Acute abdomen
sections.html:
First decide: does this patient need the OR now? Peritonitis (rigidity, rebound, guarding), free air, hemodynamic instability, or strangulation/ischemia → resuscitate (IV fluids, antibiotics, NPO, analgesia — opioids do not mask diagnosis) and operate. Everyone else gets an imaging-directed workup. Always check β-hCG in women of reproductive age, lipase, LFTs, urinalysis, lactate when ischemia is possible, and an ECG in older patients with epigastric pain (inferior MI).

[[figure:ch10-fig05]]

Appendicitis

Periumbilical pain migrating to McBurney point, anorexia, nausea after pain onset, low-grade fever, leukocytosis. Signs: Rovsing (LLQ pressure → RLQ pain), psoas (retrocecal), obturator (pelvic). Imaging: CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast in non-pregnant adults; ultrasound first in children and pregnant women (MRI without gadolinium if US non-diagnostic in pregnancy). Clear classic presentation in a young man → surgery can proceed without imaging.

ScenarioManagement
UncomplicatedLaparoscopic appendectomy + preoperative antibiotic (e.g., cefoxitin or ceftriaxone + metronidazole). Antibiotics-only is an acceptable option in selected patients (CODA trial) but ~25–40% need appendectomy within years; appendicolith predicts failure.
Perforated with diffuse peritonitisEmergent appendectomy + 4 days of antibiotics after source control
Late presentation (> 5 days) with well-formed abscess, stableIV antibiotics + CT-guided percutaneous drainage; ± interval appendectomy (colonoscopy if age > 40 to exclude cecal cancer)
Phlegmon without abscess, stableIV antibiotics, nonoperative
PregnancyAppendix displaced upward; laparoscopic appendectomy safe in any trimester; perforation → fetal loss risk

Biliary disease

ConditionClinicalLabs/imagingManagement
Biliary colicPostprandial RUQ pain < 6 h, no feverNormal labs; US: stonesElective lap cholecystectomy
Acute cholecystitisRUQ pain > 6 h, fever, Murphy sign↑ WBC; RUQ US first (stones, wall > 3 mm, pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy); HIDA if US equivocal (non-filling gallbladder = positive)NPO, IV fluids, antibiotics → lap cholecystectomy within 72 h (same admission); too sick for surgery → percutaneous cholecystostomy
Acalculous cholecystitisICU, burns, TPN, sepsis, post-opUS/HIDAAntibiotics + percutaneous cholecystostomy
Emphysematous cholecystitisDiabetic, elderly; gas in wall (Clostridium)CT/USEmergent cholecystectomy
CholedocholithiasisJaundice, ↑ ALP/bilirubin, dilated CBD > 6 mmMRCP/EUS if intermediate riskERCP stone extraction → cholecystectomy
Ascending cholangitisCharcot triad (fever, jaundice, RUQ pain); + hypotension + confusion = Reynolds pentadBlood cultures, US (dilated duct)Fluids + IV antibiotics (piperacillin–tazobactam) → ERCP biliary decompression (urgent < 24 h if septic); PTC if ERCP fails
Gallstone pancreatitisEpigastric pain, ↑ lipase, ↑ ALT > 150USSupportive; cholecystectomy during the same admission once mild pancreatitis resolves; ERCP only if concurrent cholangitis/obstruction
Gallstone ileusElderly woman, SBOCT: pneumobilia + SBO + ectopic stone (Rigler triad)Enterolithotomy
Porcelain gallbladderCalcified wall on imaging—Cholecystectomy (cancer risk, lower than once thought)

Diverticulitis

LLQ pain, fever, leukocytosis in an older adult. CT with IV contrast confirms and stages. Avoid colonoscopy and barium enema in the acute phase (perforation risk).

TypeManagement
Uncomplicated, immunocompetent, tolerating POOutpatient; clear liquids; antibiotics (amoxicillin–clavulanate, or ciprofloxacin/TMP-SMX + metronidazole) — may be selectively omitted in mild cases (AGA 2021, ACP 2022)
Can't tolerate PO, elderly, immunosuppressed, severe painAdmit, IV antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone + metronidazole)
Abscess ≥ 3–4 cmIV antibiotics + CT-guided percutaneous drainage (smaller: antibiotics alone)
Free perforation with purulent/feculent peritonitisEmergent surgery: sigmoid resection with end colostomy (Hartmann procedure) or primary anastomosis ± diverting loop ileostomy in stable patients
Fistula (colovesical: pneumaturia, fecaluria; recurrent UTIs)Elective resection with fistula repair
After recoveryColonoscopy in 6–8 weeks after complicated disease or if not up to date (exclude cancer); elective colectomy individualized (not automatically after 2 episodes)

Bowel obstruction

TypeCause / clueImagingManagement
Small bowel obstructionAdhesions (prior surgery) most common, then hernias, tumors; crampy pain, vomiting, distension, obstipation, high-pitched bowel soundsUpright AXR (air–fluid levels, dilated loops > 3 cm); CT confirms transition point & ischemiaUncomplicated: NPO, NG decompression, IV fluids, electrolytes; water-soluble contrast challenge (diagnostic and therapeutic; contrast in colon by 24 h predicts resolution). Surgery if strangulation, closed loop, no improvement in 48–72 h, or no prior surgery ("virgin abdomen")
Strangulation signsFever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, ↑ lactate, constant (not colicky) pain, peritonitisCT: reduced wall enhancement, mesenteric edema, pneumatosisEmergent laparotomy
Large bowel obstructionColorectal cancer most common; volvulus; diverticular strictureCTCancer: resection ± stoma, or stent as bridge; competent ileocecal valve → closed loop, cecal perforation risk (cecum > 12 cm)
Sigmoid volvulusElderly, institutionalized, constipated, neuro/psych disease"Coffee bean"/bent inner tube from LLQNo peritonitis → flexible sigmoidoscopic detorsion + rectal tube → elective sigmoidectomy same admission (recurrence ~ 50%). Gangrene/peritonitis → emergent resection
Cecal volvulusYounger; mobile cecumComma-shaped/"embryo" dilated cecum in LUQSurgery (right hemicolectomy); endoscopic detorsion rarely works
Ogilvie syndrome (acute colonic pseudo-obstruction)Postop (ortho, cesarean), ICU, opioids, electrolyte derangementMassive colonic dilation without obstructionCorrect K/Mg, stop opioids/anticholinergics, NG + rectal tube; cecum > 12 cm or no response 24–48 h → IV neostigmine (cardiac monitoring; atropine at bedside) → colonoscopic decompression → surgery

Mesenteric ischemia and perforation

EntityCluesWorkupTreatment
Acute arterial embolism (≈ 50%)Atrial fibrillation, recent MI; sudden severe pain out of proportion to exam, gut emptying (vomiting/diarrhea), ↑ lactate (late)CT angiographyFluids, broad antibiotics, IV heparin → embolectomy/endovascular revascularization + resection of dead bowel; second-look laparotomy. Peritonitis → straight to OR
Arterial thrombosisAtherosclerosis; prior "intestinal angina" (postprandial pain, food fear, weight loss)CTARevascularization (stent/bypass)
Nonocclusive (NOMI)Shock, vasopressors, cardiac surgery, cocaine, dialysisCTA/angiographyTreat cause, stop vasoconstrictors; intra-arterial papaverine
Mesenteric venous thrombosisHypercoagulable state, OCPs, cirrhosis, pancreatitis; more insidiousCT portal venous phaseAnticoagulation
Ischemic colitisElderly, after hypotension or AAA repair (IMA ligation); watershed areas (splenic flexure, rectosigmoid); mild pain then bloody diarrheaCT; colonoscopy (cyanotic edematous mucosa)Supportive (bowel rest, fluids, antibiotics); gangrene → resection
Perforated peptic ulcerSudden severe epigastric pain → diffuse peritonitis, rigid abdomen; NSAIDs, H. pyloriUpright CXR: free air under diaphragm (CT if unclear)NPO, NG, IV PPI, broad antibiotics → emergent surgery (omental/Graham patch); test & treat H. pylori
Exam trap: Elderly patient with AF + severe abdominal pain + benign abdomen → do not choose "reassure/observe" or "colonoscopy"; choose CT angiography (or laparotomy if peritonitis). Lactate can be normal early.

sections.heading: 7. Hernias
sections.html:
TypeAnatomyKey points
Indirect inguinalThrough deep ring, lateral to inferior epigastric vessels; patent processus vaginalis; can reach scrotumMost common hernia in both sexes and in children (especially premature boys)
Direct inguinalThrough Hesselbach triangle (inferior epigastrics laterally, rectus medially, inguinal ligament inferiorly), medial to inferior epigastricsOlder men, weak transversalis fascia; rarely incarcerates
FemoralBelow inguinal ligament, medial to femoral vein, lateral to lacunar ligamentWomen; highest incarceration/strangulation risk → always repair (urgently if incarcerated)
Umbilical (child)Fascial defectMost close spontaneously by 4–5 years; repair if persists, > 1.5–2 cm, or incarcerates
Umbilical (adult)Ascites, obesity, pregnancyRepair (cirrhotics: control ascites first)
IncisionalPrior laparotomy; risk ↑ with wound infection, obesity, smokingMesh repair
Spigelian, obturatorLateral rectus border; obturator canal (thin elderly women, Howship–Romberg sign: medial thigh pain)Often present as SBO

Management: Asymptomatic/minimally symptomatic inguinal hernia in adult men → watchful waiting is acceptable; symptomatic → elective (open Lichtenstein mesh or laparoscopic) repair. Inguinal hernia in an infant → prompt elective repair (high incarceration risk). Incarcerated (irreducible, no ischemia) → attempt gentle reduction with sedation/Trendelenburg, then repair within days. Strangulated (tender, erythematous, fever, leukocytosis, SBO) → do not reduce; emergent surgery.

===================== PERIOP =====================

sections.heading: 8. Preoperative risk assessment
sections.html:
Cardiac (ACC/AHA perioperative guideline; 2024 update): (1) Emergency surgery → operate. (2) Active cardiac condition (ACS, decompensated HF, significant arrhythmia, severe symptomatic valve disease) → treat first, delay elective surgery. (3) Estimate risk (RCRI or NSQIP calculator). Low risk (< 1% MACE) → proceed. (4) Elevated risk → functional capacity ≥ 4 METs (climb a flight of stairs, walk up a hill, heavy housework) → proceed. (5) < 4 METs or unknown → pharmacologic stress testing only if the result will change management (e.g., would lead to revascularization or a different operation). BNP/NT-proBNP may refine risk. Resting echo only for unexplained dyspnea, HF with change in status, or suspected significant valve disease. Routine preop ECG is not needed for low-risk surgery.

RCRI (1 point each)Timing rules for elective surgery
High-risk surgery (intraperitoneal, intrathoracic, suprainguinal vascular)
Ischemic heart disease
Heart failure
Cerebrovascular disease
Insulin-treated diabetes
Creatinine > 2 mg/dL		After MI: wait ≥ 60 days
After PCI with BMS: ≥ 30 days; DES: ideally ≥ 6 months (≥ 12 months after ACS)
Do not stop dual antiplatelet therapy early; continue aspirin when bleeding risk allows
Ischemic stroke: wait ≥ 3 months (ideally 9)
Smoking: stop ≥ 4–8 weeks before

Medications: Continue β-blockers and statins (do not start a β-blocker on the day of surgery — POISE: ↑ stroke and death). ACE inhibitors/ARBs are commonly held 24 h before to reduce intraoperative hypotension (continuing is reasonable in stable HFrEF). Pulmonary risk: age, COPD, smoking, OSA (STOP-BANG), upper abdominal/thoracic surgery, albumin < 3.5 g/dL → lung expansion (incentive spirometry), smoking cessation; routine PFTs/CXR not needed. Liver: Child-Pugh C or MELD > 15 → avoid elective surgery. Nutrition: albumin < 3 g/dL is a strong predictor of complications; severe malnutrition → 7–14 days of nutrition preop (enteral preferred). Pregnancy test in all women of reproductive age.

Anticoagulation management

DrugBefore elective surgeryBridging?Emergency reversal
WarfarinStop 5 days before; check INR day before (< 1.5 to operate; low-dose oral vitamin K if still high); restart 12–24 h afterOnly high thrombotic risk: mechanical mitral valve, caged-ball/tilting-disc aortic valve, mechanical valve + stroke risk factors, stroke/TIA within 3 months, VTE within 3 months, severe thrombophilia, very high CHA2DS2-VASc (≥ 7) with prior stroke. Most AF patients: no bridge (BRIDGE trial: bridging ↑ bleeding without ↓ stroke)4-factor PCC + IV vitamin K 10 mg (FFP if PCC unavailable)
Apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxabanHold 1 day (low bleed risk) or 2 days (high bleed risk/neuraxial) before (PAUSE)NeverAndexanet alfa or 4F-PCC
DabigatranHold 1–2 days (CrCl ≥ 50) or 2–4 days (CrCl < 50)NeverIdarucizumab; dialyzable
Heparin (UFH) / LMWHUFH infusion off 4–6 h; LMWH last therapeutic dose 24 h before—Protamine (full for UFH, partial for LMWH)
Aspirin / P2Y12Continue aspirin with recent stents; clopidogrel/ticagrelor stop 5 days, prasugrel 7 days—Platelet transfusion
Exam trap: AF patient on warfarin (no recent stroke, no mechanical valve) for elective hernia repair: the answer is "stop warfarin 5 days before, no bridging." Mechanical mitral valve: "stop warfarin and bridge with LMWH/UFH." Low-bleeding-risk procedures (dental extraction, cataract surgery, skin biopsy, many endoscopies) — continue warfarin.

Diabetes and glucocorticoids

AgentPerioperative instruction
Target glucose100–180 mg/dL perioperatively (ADA); first case of the morning
MetforminHold on the day of surgery
SGLT2 inhibitorsStop 3 days before (ertugliflozin 4 days) — risk of euglycemic DKA
Sulfonylureas, DPP-4 inhibitorsHold on day of surgery (hypoglycemia with sulfonylureas)
GLP-1 receptor agonistsAspiration risk from delayed gastric emptying: ASA (2023) advised holding the weekly agent 1 week before; 2024 multisociety guidance allows continuing in most low-risk patients with a 24-h clear-liquid diet — follow local protocol; GI symptoms on the day → delay or treat as full stomach
Basal insulin (glargine)Give ~75–80% of usual dose the evening before/morning of surgery; hold prandial insulin while NPO; correction insulin
Type 1 diabetesNever stop basal insulin (DKA); IV insulin infusion for major surgery
Insulin pumpContinue basal rate for short procedures

Steroids: HPA-axis suppression should be assumed with prednisone ≥ 20 mg/day (or equivalent) for ≥ 3 weeks, or any Cushingoid patient → give stress-dose hydrocortisone (major surgery: 100 mg IV at induction, then 50 mg q8h, taper over 1–2 days). Prednisone < 5 mg/day any duration or any dose < 3 weeks → not suppressed; continue the usual dose. Intermediate (5–20 mg for > 3 weeks) → test (morning cortisol/ACTH stimulation) or give empiric stress dosing. Refractory intraoperative hypotension in a chronic steroid user → IV hydrocortisone.

Other pre-op essentials: NPO (ASA): clear liquids up to 2 h, breast milk 4 h, infant formula/non-human milk/light meal 6 h, fatty/fried meal 8 h. Thyroid: hypothyroid mild → proceed; myxedema → treat first. Hyperthyroid → make euthyroid first (or β-blocker + thionamide ± iodine) to prevent thyroid storm. Pheochromocytoma → α-blockade (phenoxybenzamine) 1–2 weeks before β-blockade. Sickle cell → transfuse to Hb 10 g/dL before major surgery. Jehovah's Witness (competent adult) → respect refusal of blood; discuss acceptable alternatives (cell saver, albumin, EPO).

High bleeding risk (neurosurgery) → mechanical first.
===================== SURGICAL ONCOLOGY =====================

sections.heading: 10. Surgical oncology essentials
sections.html:
Breast mass

[[figure:ch10-fig07]]
ScenarioAnswer
Firm, mobile, rubbery mass in a woman < 30Fibroadenoma likely → US; observe if typical; core biopsy/excision if enlarging or > 2–3 cm. Rapidly enlarging "leaf-like" mass → phyllodes → wide excision
Unilateral bloody nipple dischargeIntraductal papilloma most common; diagnostic mammogram + US (retroareolar) → duct excision. Bilateral milky discharge → prolactin, TSH, pregnancy test, drugs
Eczematous nipple not responding to topical steroidsPaget disease → punch/wedge biopsy + mammogram (underlying DCIS/cancer)
Erythema, peau d'orange, warmth, no fever, not lactatingInflammatory breast cancer (dermal lymphatic invasion) → mammogram/US + punch skin biopsy → neoadjuvant chemo → modified radical mastectomy → radiation (no SLNB, no immediate reconstruction)
Lactating woman, painful red breast + feverMastitis (S. aureus) → dicloxacillin/cephalexin, continue breastfeeding; fluctuant mass → US + aspiration/drainage of abscess
DCISLumpectomy + radiation (or mastectomy); no routine axillary staging with BCT
LCIS / atypical hyperplasiaRisk marker → surgical excision of atypia on core, chemoprevention (tamoxifen/raloxifene/AI), enhanced screening
Invasive cancer, clinically node-negativeBreast-conserving surgery + whole-breast RT ≈ mastectomy survival; sentinel lymph node biopsy. Palpable nodes → US-guided node biopsy
Contraindications to breast conservationPrior chest radiation, RT in pregnancy (can do surgery in pregnancy and delay RT until after delivery), multicentric disease, diffuse malignant calcifications, persistently positive margins, tumor large relative to breast, active scleroderma/lupus
Adjuvant systemicHR+: tamoxifen (premenopausal) or aromatase inhibitor (postmenopausal) 5–10 y; HER2+: trastuzumab (monitor LVEF by echo); triple-negative: chemotherapy; consider BRCA testing

Thyroid nodule

Step 1: TSH. Low TSH → radioiodine uptake scan: "hot" nodule → treat hyperthyroidism (rarely malignant, no FNA); "cold" → US ± FNA. Normal/high TSH → thyroid ultrasound → FNA by sonographic pattern and size: high/intermediate suspicion ≥ 1 cm, low suspicion ≥ 1.5 cm, very low suspicion ≥ 2 cm (or observe); pure cysts no FNA. Results by Bethesda category: benign → follow US; indeterminate (AUS/follicular neoplasm) → repeat FNA, molecular testing, or diagnostic lobectomy (follicular carcinoma requires capsular/vascular invasion — cannot be diagnosed on FNA); malignant → thyroidectomy.

CancerKey featuresTreatment
Papillary (~ 85%)Radiation exposure; psammoma bodies, Orphan Annie nuclei; lymphatic spread; excellent prognosisLobectomy (1–4 cm low-risk) or total thyroidectomy; RAI for high-risk; TSH suppression with levothyroxine
FollicularHematogenous (bone, lung); iodine deficiencyLobectomy → completion thyroidectomy if invasive; RAI
MedullaryParafollicular C cells, calcitonin, CEA, amyloid; MEN 2A/2B (RET)Screen for pheochromocytoma (plasma metanephrines) first and hyperparathyroidism → total thyroidectomy + central neck dissection; RAI ineffective; prophylactic thyroidectomy in RET carriers
AnaplasticElderly, rapidly enlarging hard mass, compressive symptomsPoor prognosis; airway; BRAF-targeted therapy if mutated

After thyroidectomy: expanding neck hematoma with stridor → open the incision at the bedside (then OR); hypocalcemia (perioral tingling, Chvostek/Trousseau, prolonged QT) from parathyroid injury → IV calcium gluconate if symptomatic; unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury → hoarseness; bilateral → stridor/airway emergency; superior laryngeal (external branch) → loss of high-pitched voice.

Colorectal cancer

TopicKey points
Screening (USPSTF)Ages 45–75 average risk: colonoscopy q10y, FIT yearly, stool DNA-FIT q1–3y, CT colonography or flex sig q5y; positive stool test → colonoscopy. One first-degree relative < 60 → colonoscopy at 40 (or 10 y before the youngest diagnosis), every 5 y
PresentationRight-sided: iron-deficiency anemia, occult bleeding, fatigue. Left-sided: change in bowel habits, "pencil" stools, obstruction, hematochezia. Iron-deficiency anemia in a man or postmenopausal woman → colonoscopy (± EGD). S. gallolyticus (bovis) endocarditis or C. septicum → colonoscopy
StagingColonoscopy with biopsy (complete colon), CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, baseline CEA (for surveillance, not diagnosis). Rectal: pelvic MRI (or endorectal US) for T/N staging
TreatmentColon: segmental colectomy with ≥ 12 lymph nodes; stage III (node+) → adjuvant FOLFOX/CAPOX. Rectal stage II–III → total neoadjuvant therapy (chemoradiation + chemo) → total mesorectal excision (low anterior resection vs abdominoperineal resection); dMMR tumors may respond completely to immunotherapy. Isolated resectable liver/lung metastases → resection (potentially curative)
SurveillanceCEA q3–6 months, CT yearly, colonoscopy at 1 year
===================== VASCULAR =====================

sections.heading: 11. Vascular surgery
sections.html:
AAA topicKey points
Screening (USPSTF)One-time abdominal US: men 65–75 who have ever smoked (≥ 100 cigarettes) — grade B; men 65–75 never smoked — selective (C); women never smoked — recommend against (D); women who ever smoked — insufficient evidence (I)
Surveillance (SVS)3.0–3.9 cm: US every 3 years; 4.0–4.9 cm: yearly; 5.0–5.4 cm: every 6 months. Stop smoking (most important modifiable factor), control BP, statin
Elective repair indicationsDiameter ≥ 5.5 cm in men (≥ 5.0 cm in women), growth > 0.5 cm in 6 months or > 1 cm/year, symptomatic (tender, back/abdominal pain) at any size, saccular morphology
EVAR vs openEVAR: lower early mortality, requires suitable anatomy and lifelong imaging surveillance (endoleak — type II from lumbar/IMA most common). Open: durable, younger fit patients
RuptureTriad: abdominal/back/flank pain + hypotension + pulsatile mass. Unstable → straight to OR (or EVAR suite) without CT; permissive hypotension. Stable with uncertain diagnosis → CTA
Post-op complicationsIschemic colitis (IMA ligation) — bloody diarrhea POD 2–3 → flexible sigmoidoscopy; renal failure; spinal cord ischemia (anterior cord); aortoenteric fistula months–years later (herald GI bleed in a patient with an aortic graft → CT angiography/EGD → surgery)
Carotid stenosisManagement
ScreeningUSPSTF recommends against screening asymptomatic adults (D). Carotid bruit alone is a poor predictor
Symptomatic (TIA, amaurosis fugax, non-disabling stroke in ipsilateral territory) 70–99%Carotid endarterectomy (CEA) ideally within 2 weeks + antiplatelet + high-intensity statin. Carotid stenting if high surgical risk (radiation neck, prior CEA, high lesion, severe cardiopulmonary disease)
Symptomatic 50–69%CEA reasonable (greater benefit in men, age > 75, recent hemispheric event) if perioperative stroke/death risk < 6%
Symptomatic < 50%Medical therapy
Asymptomatic ≥ 70% (60–99% in trials)Optimal medical therapy is the foundation; CEA may be considered if life expectancy > 5 years and perioperative risk < 3%
100% occlusionNo revascularization (nothing to prevent; risk without benefit)

Acute limb ischemia

The 6 Ps: pain, pallor, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paresthesia, paralysis. Embolic (AF, recent MI, sudden, normal contralateral pulses) vs thrombotic (PAD history, claudication, collaterals, diminished contralateral pulses). First step: IV unfractionated heparin bolus + infusion (unless contraindicated), then assess viability.

Rutherford categorySensory / motor / DopplerManagement
I — viableIntact / intact / arterial signal audibleUrgent imaging (CTA/angiography) → revascularization
IIa — marginally threatenedMinimal (toes) / intact / arterial often inaudible, venous audiblePrompt revascularization (catheter-directed thrombolysis or surgery)
IIb — immediately threatenedBeyond toes, rest pain / mild–moderate weaknessEmergent revascularization (surgical embolectomy/thrombectomy) — no time for prolonged thrombolysis
III — irreversibleProfound anesthesia / paralysis, rigor / no arterial or venous signalPrimary amputation
High-yield: After revascularization of limb ischemia lasting > 4–6 h, watch for reperfusion injury: compartment syndrome (fasciotomy), hyperkalemia, acidosis, myoglobinuric AKI. Then search for an embolic source (ECG/telemetry, echocardiogram) and anticoagulate long-term if AF. Chronic PAD: ABI ≤ 0.90 diagnostic; > 1.40 = non-compressible (diabetes, CKD) → toe–brachial index. Claudication → supervised exercise, smoking cessation, high-intensity statin, antiplatelet ± low-dose rivaroxaban, cilostazol (contraindicated in heart failure); revascularize for lifestyle-limiting symptoms despite therapy or chronic limb-threatening ischemia (rest pain, ulcers, gangrene).
===================== UROLOGY =====================

sections.heading: 12. Urologic emergencies
sections.html:
ConditionCluesManagement
Testicular torsionAdolescent, sudden severe unilateral pain, nausea/vomiting, high-riding horizontal testis ("bell-clapper"), absent cremasteric reflex, no relief with elevationClassic presentation → immediate surgical exploration (detorsion + bilateral orchiopexy); do not delay for imaging. Equivocal → color Doppler US. Salvage ~ 90% if < 6 h. Manual detorsion ("open the book," medial-to-lateral) only as a temporizing step if surgery is delayed
Torsion of appendix testisPrepubertal boy, gradual pain at upper pole, blue-dot sign, cremasteric reflex presentAnalgesics, rest (self-limited)
EpididymitisGradual pain, fever, dysuria, tender epididymis, Prehn sign positive (relief with elevation), cremasteric reflex present< 35 y/sexually active: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM + doxycycline 100 mg BID × 10 days; insertive anal intercourse: ceftriaxone + levofloxacin; > 35/enteric organisms: levofloxacin
Fournier gangreneDiabetic, perineal pain, crepitus, necrosisEmergent debridement + broad antibiotics
Ischemic priapism> 4 h, painful, rigid; sickle cell, trazodone, intracavernosal drugsCorporal aspiration + intracavernosal phenylephrine; sickle cell also hydration/O2/exchange transfusion as adjunct
ParaphimosisRetracted foreskin trapped behind glansManual reduction (compression, ice) → dorsal slit if fails
Obstructed infected kidney stoneFever + flank pain + hydronephrosisEmergent decompression (ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy) + antibiotics — not lithotripsy
Uncomplicated ureteral stoneColicky flank → groin pain, hematuriaNon-contrast CT (US in pregnancy/children); < 5 mm passes; 5–10 mm distal → tamsulosin (medical expulsive therapy) + NSAIDs; > 10 mm or failure → ureteroscopy/ESWL
Testicular massPainless, firmScrotal US → tumor markers (AFP, β-hCG, LDH) → radical inguinal orchiectomy (never trans-scrotal biopsy)
===================== ORTHO =====================

sections.heading: 13. Orthopedics
sections.html:
InjuryClue / complicationManagement
Open fractureBone communicates with woundIV antibiotics ASAP (cefazolin; add gram-negative coverage e.g. ceftriaxone for Gustilo III; consider penicillin/metronidazole for farm/soil contamination), tetanus, sterile dressing, splint → operative irrigation & debridement within 24 h + fixation
Scaphoid fractureFOOSH, anatomic snuffbox tenderness; X-ray often negative initially; AVN of proximal pole, nonunionNegative X-ray → thumb spica splint + repeat X-ray in 7–14 days (or MRI now). Displaced/proximal → ORIF
Hip fracture (elderly)Shortened, externally rotated legSurgery within 24–48 h. Displaced femoral neck → arthroplasty (hemi/total); non-displaced femoral neck → internal fixation; intertrochanteric → intramedullary nail/sliding hip screw. VTE prophylaxis. Occult (X-ray negative, can't bear weight) → MRI
Posterior hip dislocationDashboard injury; shortened, internally rotated, adducted; sciatic nerveEmergent closed reduction (< 6 h; AVN risk)
Anterior shoulder dislocationArm externally rotated, abducted; axillary nerve (deltoid sensation)Neurovascular exam, X-ray, closed reduction, post-reduction X-ray
Posterior shoulder dislocationSeizure, electrocution; arm internally rotated; "light bulb" signReduction; easily missed — axillary/scapular Y view
Humeral shaft fractureRadial nerve — wrist dropFunctional brace (most)
Supracondylar humerus (child)FOOSH; brachial artery, median/AIN nerve; Volkmann ischemic contractureDisplaced → closed reduction + percutaneous pinning; pulseless pink hand → urgent reduction
Clavicle fractureMiddle thirdSling; surgery if open, skin tenting, neurovascular injury, marked displacement
Monteggia / GaleazziProximal ulna + radial head dislocation / distal radius + DRUJ dislocationORIF (adults)
Boxer fracture5th metacarpal neck after punching; fight bite → amoxicillin–clavulanate, wash outUlnar gutter splint
Fat embolism syndrome24–72 h after long-bone/pelvic fracture: hypoxemia, confusion, petechiae (axilla, conjunctiva)Supportive; early fracture fixation prevents
Compartment syndrome: tibial fracture, crush, reperfusion, tight cast, burns. Earliest/most sensitive sign is pain out of proportion and pain with passive stretch; pulselessness is late. Remove/bivalve cast and dressings, keep limb at heart level (not elevated). Diagnosis is clinical; if uncertain measure pressure: compartment pressure > 30 mmHg or ΔP (diastolic BP − compartment pressure) ≤ 30 mmHg → emergent fasciotomy. Do not wait for pressures in a classic case.
Pediatric orthoAge / clueNext step
Developmental dysplasia of hipNewborn; Barlow/Ortolani; risk: breech, female, firstborn, family historyUS if < 4–6 months (X-ray after); Pavlik harness; closed/open reduction if older
Legg-Calvé-Perthes4–10 y boy, painless/mild limp, ↓ internal rotation & abduction; idiopathic AVNX-ray (may be normal early → MRI); observation/bracing; osteotomy if older
Slipped capital femoral epiphysisObese adolescent, hip/knee pain, obligatory external rotation on hip flexion; hypothyroidism, GH, renal osteodystrophyAP + frog-leg lateral X-ray → non-weight-bearing (crutches/wheelchair) + surgical pinning in situ (do not attempt reduction)
Septic arthritis vs transient synovitisKocher criteria: non-weight-bearing, fever > 38.5 °C, ESR > 40, WBC > 12,000 (+ CRP > 2 mg/dL)Several positive → US-guided arthrocentesis → surgical drainage + antibiotics. Transient synovitis (post-viral, afebrile, well) → NSAIDs
Nursemaid's elbowToddler pulled by arm; holds arm pronatedReduction by hyperpronation or supination–flexion (no X-ray needed if classic)
Osgood-SchlatterActive adolescent, tibial tubercle painRest, NSAIDs, ice
Salter-Harris (physeal)Type II most common; III–V affect growth (V crush, often missed)I–II closed reduction; III–IV ORIF
Non-accidental traumaSpiral fracture in non-ambulatory infant, posterior rib, metaphyseal corner ("bucket-handle"), multiple agesSkeletal survey, report to child protective services, ophthalmology (retinal hemorrhages), head CT/MRI
ScoliosisAdolescent girl; Adam forward-bendCobb angle: < 25° observe; 25–40° bracing if growing; > 45–50° surgery
ClubfootNewbornPonseti serial casting
Bone tumorsOsteosarcoma (metaphysis, sunburst, Codman triangle); Ewing (diaphysis, onion-skin, t(11;22), fever)Biopsy at a sarcoma center; neoadjuvant chemo + limb-sparing surgery
===================== ANESTHESIA =====================

sections.heading: 14. Anesthesia basics
sections.html:
TopicKey points
Malignant hyperthermiaTriggers: volatile anesthetics (sevoflurane, desflurane, isoflurane) and succinylcholine; RYR1 mutation (autosomal dominant) → uncontrolled SR Ca2+ release. Earliest sign: rising end-tidal CO2 despite ↑ ventilation; masseter rigidity, tachycardia, hyperkalemia, mixed acidosis, rhabdomyolysis; hyperthermia is late. Treat: stop triggers, dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV (repeat up to 10 mg/kg), hyperventilate with 100% O2, active cooling, treat hyperkalemia (insulin/glucose, calcium; avoid calcium-channel blockers with dantrolene), urine output > 2 mL/kg/h, ICU monitoring 24 h. Family: caffeine–halothane contracture test/genetic testing; future anesthesia with non-triggering agents (propofol TIVA, nitrous oxide, non-depolarizers, local)
Succinylcholine cautionsHyperkalemia (burns > 24 h, crush, denervation/stroke/spinal cord injury, prolonged immobilization, myopathies), MH, pseudocholinesterase deficiency → prolonged apnea (ventilate until recovery). Alternative: rocuronium (reversal: sugammadex)
Local anesthetic systemic toxicityPerioral numbness, tinnitus, seizures → arrhythmia/arrest (bupivacaine) → 20% lipid emulsion; max lidocaine 4.5 mg/kg (7 mg/kg with epinephrine)
ASA physical statusI healthy, II mild systemic disease, III severe systemic disease, IV constant threat to life, V moribund, VI brain-dead donor; "E" = emergency
Spinal/epiduralHypotension (sympathectomy → fluids/phenylephrine), post-dural puncture headache (positional → caffeine, epidural blood patch); epidural hematoma if anticoagulated → urgent MRI/decompression
Postoperative nausea/vomitingRisk: female, nonsmoker, history of PONV/motion sickness, opioids → ondansetron, dexamethasone, scopolamine patch prophylaxis
Emergence delirium / hypoxia in PACUCheck airway obstruction, residual neuromuscular block (train-of-four), opioid effect, hypothermia
===================== TOXICOLOGY =====================

sections.heading: 15. Emergency toxicology
sections.html:
General approach: ABCs → fingerstick glucose in any altered patient → ECG (QRS, QTc) → acetaminophen and salicylate levels in every intentional ingestion (co-ingestion is silent) → BMP (anion gap), serum osmolality (osmolar gap), β-hCG, CK. Decontamination: activated charcoal 1 g/kg within ~1–2 h of ingestion if the airway is protected (not for metals, lithium, iron, alcohols, hydrocarbons, caustics); whole-bowel irrigation for iron, lithium, sustained-release drugs, body packers. Do not induce emesis. Psychiatric evaluation once medically stable.

ToxidromeVitals / pupils / skinExamples
Sympathomimetic↑ HR, ↑ BP, ↑ T, mydriasis, diaphoresisCocaine, amphetamines → benzodiazepines (avoid β-blockers acutely)
Anticholinergic↑ HR, ↑ T, mydriasis, dry flushed skin, urinary retention, ↓ bowel sounds, deliriumDiphenhydramine, TCAs, jimsonweed → physostigmine (not if TCA/QRS wide)
Cholinergic↓ HR, miosis, wet (salivation, lacrimation, bronchorrhea, diarrhea, urination), fasciculationsOrganophosphates, carbamates, nerve agents
Opioid↓ RR (most important), ↓ HR, miosis, ↓ bowel sounds, comaHeroin, fentanyl, methadone (QT), tramadol (seizures)
Sedative–hypnoticNormal/↓ vitals, normal pupils, CNS depression, RR relatively preservedBenzodiazepines, barbiturates, alcohol
Serotonin syndromeHyperthermia, clonus/hyperreflexia (legs), diarrhea, rapid onset (< 24 h)SSRIs + MAOI/linezolid/tramadol/triptans → benzodiazepines, cyproheptadine
Neuroleptic malignant syndromeHyperthermia, lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia, ↑ CK, slow onset (days)Antipsychotics, dopamine-agonist withdrawal → stop drug, cooling, dantrolene/bromocriptine

Acetaminophen

Toxic metabolite NAPQI (CYP2E1) is detoxified by glutathione; NAC replenishes glutathione. Toxic dose ≥ 150 mg/kg (or ≥ 7.5–10 g). Stages: (1) 0–24 h: nausea or asymptomatic; (2) 24–72 h: RUQ pain, ↑ AST/ALT; (3) 72–96 h: fulminant hepatic failure (AST > 10,000, INR ↑, encephalopathy, lactic acidosis, AKI); (4) recovery or death. The Rumack–Matthew nomogram applies only to a single acute ingestion with known time, 4–24 h after ingestion. The US treatment line starts at 150 mcg/mL at 4 h (halving every 4 h, ~4.7 mcg/mL at 24 h). A level drawn before 4 h is uninterpretable (absorption incomplete).

[[figure:ch10-fig08]]

Other high-yield poisonings

PoisonCluesTreatment
SalicylatesTinnitus, vomiting, tachypnea, hyperthermia; respiratory alkalosis + anion-gap metabolic acidosis; noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, AMS (CNS hypoglycemia despite normal serum glucose)Charcoal (repeat doses; bezoars), IV sodium bicarbonate → urine pH 7.5–8.0 (ion trapping), replete K+ (hypokalemia prevents urine alkalinization), dextrose if AMS. Hemodialysis: AMS/seizures/coma, pulmonary edema (new O2 need), AKI, pH ≤ 7.20, level > 100 mg/dL (> 90 with impaired kidneys), failure of standard therapy. Avoid intubation if possible; if intubated, match the high pre-intubation minute ventilation
Tricyclic antidepressantsAnticholinergic signs, seizures, coma, hypotension; ECG: QRS > 100 ms, R wave in aVR > 3 mm, right-axis deviation of terminal 40 msIV sodium bicarbonate boluses (Na load + alkalinization relieve Na-channel blockade) → target pH 7.50–7.55 and QRS narrowing; benzodiazepines for seizures; norepinephrine for refractory hypotension; lipid emulsion for arrest. Avoid physostigmine, flumazenil, class IA/IC antiarrhythmics
OrganophosphatesFarmer/pesticide; DUMBELS (diarrhea, urination, miosis, bronchorrhea/bradycardia/bronchospasm, emesis, lacrimation, salivation) + nicotinic fasciculations, weakness, respiratory failureStaff PPE; remove clothing and wash skin; atropine (2–4 mg IV doubling every 5 min) titrated to drying of bronchial secretions (not pupil size or HR); pralidoxime early (before "aging" of the enzyme) for nicotinic effects; benzodiazepines for seizures. Avoid succinylcholine (prolonged paralysis)
Carbon monoxideHeadache, nausea, dizziness in several household members, winter, generator/furnace; cherry-red skin rare; pulse oximetry falsely normalCo-oximetry COHb level; 100% O2 via non-rebreather (half-life ~ 300 → ~ 75 min). Hyperbaric O2 (half-life ~ 20 min) for COHb > 25% (> 15–20% in pregnancy), loss of consciousness/syncope, seizures, coma, focal neurologic deficits, myocardial ischemia, severe acidosis, or fetal distress. Delayed neuropsychiatric sequelae weeks later
OpioidsRR < 12, miosis, AMSBag-valve-mask ventilation first if apneic; naloxone 0.04–0.4 mg IV titrated (2–4 mg intranasal, larger doses in fentanyl era) to adequate breathing — not full arousal (precipitated withdrawal). Short half-life (30–90 min) → observe; methadone/long-acting → infusion. Leave with naloxone kit, offer buprenorphine
BenzodiazepinesSedation with relatively preserved vitalsSupportive; flumazenil generally avoided (seizures in chronic users/co-ingested TCA)
CyanideFire victims, nitroprusside; lactate very high, bright red venous blood, almond odorHydroxocobalamin (→ cyanocobalamin); alternative sodium nitrite + thiosulfate
MethemoglobinemiaDapsone, benzocaine, nitrites; chocolate blood, SpO2 ~ 85% unresponsive to O2Methylene blue (not in G6PD deficiency → exchange transfusion/ascorbic acid)
Methanol / ethylene glycolHigh anion gap + high osmolar gap; vision loss (methanol), calcium oxalate crystals + AKI (EG)Fomepizole; hemodialysis for severe acidosis, vision changes, AKI
β-blockerBradycardia, hypotension, hypoglycemia, (propranolol: seizures, wide QRS)Atropine, IV fluids, glucagon, high-dose insulin + dextrose, vasopressors, pacing
Calcium-channel blockerBradycardia, hypotension, hyperglycemiaIV calcium, high-dose insulin euglycemia, vasopressors
DigoxinN/V, yellow vision, any arrhythmia (bidirectional VT, atrial tachycardia with block), hyperkalemia (acute)Digoxin immune Fab; avoid calcium (classic teaching)
IronGI bleeding, then latent phase, then shock/acidosis; radiopaque pillsWhole-bowel irrigation, deferoxamine (vin rosé urine)
LithiumTremor, ataxia, confusion; precipitated by thiazides, ACE-i, NSAIDs, dehydrationIV saline; hemodialysis if severe neuro signs, renal failure, very high level
IsoniazidRefractory seizures, AG acidosisPyridoxine (B6)
SulfonylureaRecurrent hypoglycemiaDextrose + octreotide; admit (long duration)
CocaineChest pain, HTN, hyperthermia, agitationBenzodiazepines first, nitroglycerin, CCB; avoid pure β-blockers acutely
Exam trap: The "multiple family members with headache in winter" stem with normal SpO2 → CO, not a viral illness. Organophosphate patient still wheezing with copious secretions after atropine → give more atropine (no maximum dose), even if tachycardic.
===================== ENVIRONMENTAL =====================

sections.heading: 16. Environmental emergencies
sections.html:
ConditionDefinition / cluesManagement
Heat exhaustionCore T < 40 °C, normal mental status, fatigue, nausea, headacheRemove from heat, oral/IV fluids, rest
Heat strokeCore T ≥ 40 °C (104 °F) + CNS dysfunction (confusion, seizures, coma). Exertional (young athlete, military; may still sweat) vs classic (elderly, heat wave, anticholinergics/diuretics; dry skin)Rapid cooling: cold-water/ice-water immersion for exertional ("cool first, transport second"); evaporative cooling (mist + fans) ± ice packs for classic. Stop at ~ 38.5–39 °C to avoid overshoot. Antipyretics (acetaminophen/NSAIDs) and dantrolene are ineffective. Complications: rhabdomyolysis, AKI, DIC, liver failure, hypoglycemia
Hypothermia — mild (32–35 °C)Shivering, tachycardia, confusionPassive external rewarming (dry, blankets, warm environment)
Moderate (28–32 °C)Shivering stops, bradycardia, AF, Osborn (J) waves, lethargyActive external rewarming (forced warm air, heating pads to trunk) + warmed IV fluids (40–42 °C) + warm humidified O2; handle gently (VF risk)
Severe (< 28 °C)Coma, fixed pupils, VF/asystole possibleActive internal (core) rewarming: ECMO/cardiopulmonary bypass (best, especially if arrest), warm thoracic/peritoneal lavage. CPR continues — "not dead until warm and dead" (rewarm to ≥ 32–35 °C before declaring death). Defibrillation may be attempted; epinephrine dosing spaced/withheld below ~ 30 °C per many protocols. K+ > 12 mmol/L suggests non-survivable
FrostbiteNumb, white, waxy; blisters after rewarmingRapid rewarming in 37–39 °C water (only if no refreezing risk), analgesia, tetanus; severe → tPA or iloprost within 24 h; delay amputation (weeks) until demarcation
DrowningHypoxia is the injuryVentilation/oxygenation first (rescue breaths), CPR, PEEP; C-spine only if diving/trauma; observe 4–6 h if asymptomatic
Lightning / high-voltageAsystole, fern-like (Lichtenberg) marks, tympanic rupture, cataracts"Reverse triage" — resuscitate apparently dead first; ECG, CK
Altitude illnessAMS (headache), HAPE (dyspnea), HACE (ataxia, confusion)Descent (definitive); acetazolamide (prevent/AMS), dexamethasone (HACE), nifedipine (HAPE), O2/hyperbaric bag
Snake bite (pit viper)Swelling, ecchymosis, coagulopathyImmobilize at heart level, no tourniquet/incision/suction; CBC, coags; progressive swelling or coagulopathy → Crotalidae antivenom (CroFab/Anavip)
Black widow / brown recluseMuscle cramping, rigid abdomen / painless necrotic ulcerAnalgesia, benzodiazepines, antivenom rarely / wound care
===================== ANAPHYLAXIS =====================

sections.heading: 17. Anaphylaxis and angioedema
sections.html:
Diagnose clinically: acute onset (minutes–hours) of skin/mucosal involvement plus respiratory compromise or hypotension/end-organ dysfunction — or hypotension/bronchospasm/laryngeal involvement after exposure to a known allergen (skin signs may be absent in ~ 10–20%).

StepDetail
1. IM epinephrine — first and most important0.01 mg/kg of 1 mg/mL (1:1000), max 0.5 mg adult (0.3 mg child), anterolateral thigh; repeat every 5–15 min. No absolute contraindication (including CAD, elderly, pregnancy)
2. Position, O2, IV fluidsSupine with legs elevated (sitting if respiratory distress); 1–2 L crystalloid bolus for hypotension
3. Refractory shockIV epinephrine infusion; add other vasopressors. On β-blockers → IV glucagon (bypasses β-receptor via adenylyl cyclase)
4. Adjuncts (never instead of epinephrine)H1 antihistamine (diphenhydramine/cetirizine) for itch/urticaria, H2 blocker, inhaled albuterol for persistent bronchospasm; glucocorticoids have no proven benefit for preventing biphasic reactions
5. DispositionObserve (biphasic reactions in up to ~ 5%, typically within 12 h); discharge with 2 epinephrine auto-injectors, action plan, allergist referral; serum tryptase (draw within 1–3 h) supports diagnosis
AirwayStridor/voice change/oropharyngeal swelling → early intubation by most experienced operator (awake fiberoptic), prepare for cricothyrotomy
Angioedema typeMediatorClueTreatment
Allergic (mast cell)HistamineUrticaria, pruritusEpinephrine, antihistamines
ACE-inhibitor inducedBradykininLips/tongue, no urticaria; any time on drug (more common in Black patients)Airway first; stop ACE inhibitor permanently; epinephrine/antihistamines often ineffective; icatibant/FFP sometimes used
Hereditary (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency)BradykininFamily history, abdominal attacks, trigger = trauma/dental work; low C4C1-INH concentrate, icatibant, ecallantide; prophylaxis before procedures
===================== AIRWAY =====================

sections.heading: 18. Emergency airway
sections.html:
TopicKey points
Indications to intubateFailure to protect airway (GCS ≤ 8, absent gag), failure to oxygenate/ventilate (hypoxemia despite O2, rising PaCO2 with fatigue), anticipated deterioration (inhalation burn, expanding neck hematoma, angioedema, combative trauma needing CT)
Trials of non-invasive supportBiPAP: COPD exacerbation, cardiogenic pulmonary edema; contraindicated if vomiting, AMS unable to protect airway, facial trauma. High-flow nasal cannula for hypoxemic failure
Rapid sequence intubationPreoxygenate (100% O2 3 min, apneic oxygenation) → induction (etomidate: hemodynamically neutral; ketamine: hypotension/asthma) → paralysis (succinylcholine or rocuronium) → video/direct laryngoscopy. Trauma: manual in-line stabilization, remove front of collar
Confirm tube placementContinuous waveform end-tidal CO2 (best immediate confirmation) + bilateral breath sounds; then CXR (tip 2–5 cm above carina) for depth. Right mainstem intubation → withdraw tube
Failed intubationVentilate with BVM (2-person, oral/nasal airway) → supraglottic airway (LMA) → "can't intubate, can't oxygenate" → surgical cricothyrotomy (adults); needle cricothyrotomy with jet ventilation if < 12 years (cricoid is the narrowest/most fragile part of the child airway)
Severe maxillofacial traumaCricothyrotomy if oral intubation impossible; avoid nasal intubation with midface/basilar fractures
Deterioration after intubation ("DOPE")Displacement, Obstruction (mucus plug — suction), Pneumothorax (decompress), Equipment failure → disconnect from ventilator and bag with 100% O2
Epiglottitis / deep neck infectionDrooling, tripod, stridor → do not lie flat or examine throat; secure airway in OR with ENT/anesthesia present (trach set ready)
Foreign body (choking)Conscious adult/child > 1 y: abdominal thrusts; infant: 5 back blows + 5 chest thrusts; unconscious → CPR; partial obstruction coughing → let them cough, rigid bronchoscopy
High-yield: Tracheostomy is never the emergency answer — it is slow and done for prolonged ventilation (typically > 1–2 weeks). The emergency surgical airway is the cricothyrotomy.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.html:
From NEET PG to USMLE

  • Guidelines change the answer. US items follow AAP (pediatrics), ACOG/SMFM (obstetrics), ASCCP/USPSTF (cervical screening), CDC (STIs, immunizations, contraception through the US MEC/SPR). Several of these differ from DGHS/FOGSI/WHO protocols you learned. Examples: no routine episiotomy, PPH defined as ≥1000 mL for any route of delivery, GBS culture at 36–37 wk, cervical screening on fixed intervals.
  • "Next best step" is about order. Before you pick a management option, ask: is the patient stable? Has pregnancy been ruled out (β-hCG comes first in any reproductive-age woman)? Is a confirmatory test needed before an irreversible step (for example, CVS or amniocentesis after an abnormal cfDNA, never termination on a screening test)?
  • Drug names are US generics. Learn the US forms: methylergonovine (Methergine), carboprost (Hemabate, 15-methyl PGF2α), dinoprostone (Cervidil/Prepidil), betamethasone (the standard antenatal steroid), alprostadil (PGE1), nirsevimab (Beyfortus), etonogestrel implant (Nexplanon), LNG-IUD (Mirena/Liletta/Kyleena), ulipristal (ella). Paracetamol is called acetaminophen.
  • Units. Bilirubin and glucose are in mg/dL. Temperature is in °C on the exam (38.0 °C = 100.4 °F). Weight is in kg, but parents may give it in lb (1 kg = 2.2 lb).
  • Law and ethics. Every US physician is a mandated reporter of suspected child abuse. Reasonable suspicion is enough to report, and you do not need parental permission. Minors can consent to STI care, contraception, and (in most states) prenatal care without a parent. Abortion law varies by state after Dobbs (2022). Exam items avoid state-specific traps but expect you to honor confidentiality.
  • Vaccines. The US uses DTaP (pediatric) and Tdap (adolescents, adults, and every pregnancy), IPV only (no OPV), and rotavirus vaccine. Infants get RSV protection through either maternal RSVpreF vaccine at 32–36 wk or an infant monoclonal antibody (nirsevimab or clesrovimab). BCG is not used in the US.

sections.heading: Pediatrics 1 · Neonatology
sections.html:
Delivery-room assessment: APGAR and neonatal resuscitation (NRP)

Sign012
Appearance (color)Blue or pale all overAcrocyanosis (body pink)Completely pink
PulseAbsent<100/min≥100/min
Grimace (reflex irritability)NoneGrimaceCry, cough, sneeze
Activity (tone)LimpSome flexionActive motion
RespirationAbsentSlow, irregular, weak cryGood, strong cry

Score the infant at 1 and 5 minutes. If the 5-minute score is <7, keep scoring every 5 minutes up to 20 minutes. A score of 7–10 is reassuring. The APGAR score is never used to decide whether to resuscitate, and it does not predict long-term neurologic outcome by itself.

NRP step (AHA/AAP algorithm; 2025 update)Trigger → action
Initial steps (first 30 s)Warm, dry, stimulate, position the airway, suction only if secretions are obstructing. Delay cord clamping (≥60 s per the 2025 AHA/AAP update; at least 30 s) in vigorous term and preterm infants.
Positive-pressure ventilation (PPV)Start PPV within the "golden minute" if the infant is apneic or gasping, or if HR is <100. Use 21% O2 at ≥35 wk and 21–30% at <35 wk. Effective ventilation is the most important step in neonatal resuscitation.
Ventilation corrective steps (MR SOPA)Mask adjust, Reposition, Suction, Open mouth, Pressure increase, Alternative airway (ETT or laryngeal mask)
Chest compressionsStart compressions if HR stays <60 after 30 s of effective PPV (ideally through an ETT). Give 3 compressions to 1 breath (90 compressions + 30 breaths per minute) and increase O2 to 100%.
EpinephrineGive epinephrine if HR stays <60 after 60 s of compressions. The IV (umbilical venous catheter) or IO route is preferred. Give a volume bolus if there was blood loss.
Meconium-stained fluidRoutine intubation and tracheal suctioning of a non-vigorous infant is no longer recommended. Do the initial steps and give PPV as needed.
Target pre-ductal SpO2 (right hand)1 min 60–65%, 3 min 70–75%, 5 min 80–85%, 10 min 85–95%
Exam trap: A newborn has a scaphoid abdomen, respiratory distress, and bowel sounds in the chest, which means congenital diaphragmatic hernia (usually left-sided, Bochdalek). Do not bag-mask ventilate, because air would distend the intrathoracic bowel. Intubate immediately and place an orogastric tube for decompression.

Neonatal respiratory distress

ConditionSettingCXRManagement / pearls
Respiratory distress syndrome (surfactant deficiency)Preterm (risk rises as GA falls), maternal diabetes (insulin delays surfactant), male sex, C-section without laborDiffuse reticulogranular "ground glass," air bronchograms, low lung volumesCPAP; intratracheal surfactant if needed. Prevention: antenatal betamethasone. Fetal lung maturity is shown by L/S ratio ≥2 or the presence of phosphatidylglycerol. Complications: BPD (O2 need at 36 wk PMA), ROP, IVH, PDA.
Transient tachypnea of the newbornTerm or late preterm, C-section without labor, rapid delivery, maternal asthma/diabetesFluid in the fissures, perihilar streaking, hyperinflationSupportive (O2 as needed). Resolves in 24–72 h because retained fetal lung fluid is cleared slowly.
Meconium aspirationTerm or post-term, fetal distressPatchy infiltrates, hyperinflation, pneumothoraxSupportive care, surfactant, ventilation. Risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN): pre-/post-ductal SpO2 difference; treat with O2, inhaled NO, ECMO.
Neonatal pneumonia / sepsisGBS colonization, ROM ≥18 h, maternal feverVariable; can mimic RDSBlood culture, then ampicillin + gentamicin

Early-onset sepsis (EOS) and GBS prophylaxis

ItemKey facts
OrganismsEarly onset (<72 h; GBS-EOS is defined as <7 d): GBS, E. coli (the leading cause in very-low-birth-weight infants), Listeria. Late onset: GBS, coagulase-negative staph (central lines), gram-negatives, S. aureus.
Empiric therapyAmpicillin + gentamicin. If meningitis is suspected, add a third- or fourth-generation cephalosporin: cefotaxime if available, otherwise ceftazidime or cefepime. Avoid ceftriaxone in neonates, because it displaces bilirubin from albumin and precipitates with IV calcium.
Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis indicationsPositive rectovaginal culture at 36 0/7–37 6/7 wk; GBS bacteriuria at any time in this pregnancy; a previous infant with invasive GBS disease. If status is unknown, give prophylaxis for any of: <37 wk, ROM ≥18 h, intrapartum T ≥38.0 °C, or positive intrapartum NAAT.
RegimenIV penicillin G (ampicillin is acceptable) given ≥4 h before delivery is "adequate." For low-risk penicillin allergy, use cefazolin. For high-risk allergy (anaphylaxis, angioedema), use clindamycin if the isolate is susceptible, otherwise vancomycin.
No prophylaxis neededPlanned cesarean before labor with intact membranes, even if the patient is GBS-positive. A negative culture within 5 weeks.

Necrotizing enterocolitis and other neonatal problems

ProblemCluesNext step
Necrotizing enterocolitisPreterm (esp. <32 wk / VLBW), formula feeding (breast milk is protective), age 1–3 weeks. Feeding intolerance, distension, bloody stool, temperature instability, apnea, thrombocytopenia, metabolic acidosis.Abdominal X-ray: pneumatosis intestinalis (pathognomonic), portal venous gas. Management: NPO, orogastric decompression, IV fluids/TPN, cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ampicillin + gentamicin + metronidazole), serial X-rays. Pneumoperitoneum or clinical deterioration → surgery (laparotomy or peritoneal drain).
Neonatal hypoglycemiaIDM, SGA, LGA, preterm, stress. Jitteriness, poor feeding, seizures.Screen glucose in at-risk infants. Asymptomatic: feed and/or buccal dextrose gel. Symptomatic or persistently low: IV D10W 2 mL/kg bolus, then infusion.
Infant of a diabetic motherMacrosomia, hypoglycemia (fetal hyperinsulinism), polycythemia → hyperbilirubinemia, hypocalcemia, RDS, hypertrophic (septal) cardiomyopathy, small left colon, caudal regression (most specific anomaly), TGAGlucose checks, calcium, hematocrit, bilirubin
Polycythemia (venous Hct >65%)IDM, delayed cord clamping, twin–twin transfusion recipient, SGASymptomatic: partial exchange transfusion with normal saline
Neonatal opioid withdrawalOnset 1–3 d (heroin, short-acting opioids) or up to 5–7 d (methadone, buprenorphine). Irritability, high-pitched cry, poor feeding, diarrhea, sneezing, yawning."Eat, Sleep, Console" nonpharmacologic care, rooming-in, breastfeeding if the mother is stable on treatment. Morphine or methadone if needed. Prenatally, buprenorphine or methadone is standard (no detox).
Intraventricular hemorrhage<32 wk, first 72 h (germinal matrix)Screening cranial US for <30–32 wk infants
Retinopathy of prematurity≤30 wk or ≤1500 g, O2 exposureOphthalmology screening starting at 31 wk PMA or 4 wk of chronologic age; laser or anti-VEGF

Neonatal jaundice (hyperbilirubinemia)

Most neonatal jaundice is unconjugated and benign: physiologic jaundice appears after 24 h, peaks on day 3–5 in term infants, and resolves by about 2 weeks. It happens because the newborn has more RBC mass, shorter RBC lifespan, immature UGT1A1, and increased enterohepatic circulation. The goal of management is to prevent acute bilirubin encephalopathy and kernicterus (choreoathetoid cerebral palsy, upward gaze palsy, sensorineural hearing loss, dental enamel dysplasia).

FeatureSuggests pathology
TimingVisible jaundice in the first 24 h (hemolysis until proven otherwise); persistence beyond 2 weeks (term) or 3 weeks (preterm)
Rate of rise≥0.3 mg/dL/h in the first 24 h, or ≥0.2 mg/dL/h thereafter (suggests hemolysis)
LevelAt or above the AAP hour-specific phototherapy threshold
Conjugated (direct) bilirubin>1.0 mg/dL is always abnormal. This is cholestasis: biliary atresia, neonatal hepatitis, infection, galactosemia, hypothyroidism, α1-antitrypsin deficiency, Alagille. Pale stools and dark urine favor biliary atresia, which needs US + HIDA, cholangiogram/biopsy, and a Kasai portoenterostomy ideally before 30–60 days.
Unconjugated causeClueManagement
Isoimmune hemolysis (ABO: mother O, infant A/B; Rh; minor antigens such as Kell)Jaundice <24 h, positive DAT (Coombs), ↑ retic, spherocytes (ABO)Phototherapy at lower thresholds. IVIG if TSB keeps rising despite intensive phototherapy or is within 2–3 mg/dL of the exchange level. Exchange transfusion if needed.
G6PD deficiencyMale; Mediterranean, African, Middle Eastern, or South/Southeast Asian ancestry; DAT negative; Heinz bodies and bite cellsPhototherapy, avoid oxidants. G6PD deficiency is a neurotoxicity risk factor.
Hereditary spherocytosisFamily history, splenomegaly, ↑ MCHC, DAT negativePhototherapy, folate, later splenectomy
Breastfeeding (suboptimal intake) jaundiceFirst week, poor latch, >8–10% weight loss, few stools/wetsImprove breastfeeding (8–12 feeds/day), lactation support, supplement if dehydrated. Do not stop breastfeeding.
Breast-milk jaundiceStarts after the first week, peaks at 2 wk, can last 2–3 months. Thriving, well infant (β-glucuronidase and other milk factors).Confirm conjugated bilirubin is normal and the newborn screen (thyroid, galactosemia) is normal. Continue breastfeeding. Phototherapy only if TSB reaches threshold.
Crigler–Najjar type I / II; GilbertAbsent UGT1A1 (type I → kernicterus) vs. reduced (type II responds to phenobarbital); Gilbert is mild and shows up with fasting or illnessType I: phototherapy, liver transplant
OtherCephalohematoma or bruising, polycythemia, sepsis, hypothyroidism, IDM, upper GI obstructionTreat the cause

The Bhutani nomogram and the AAP 2022 update. The Bhutani nomogram plots hour-specific total serum bilirubin (TSB) for healthy infants ≥35 wk into risk zones: high risk (>95th percentile), high-intermediate (75th–95th), low-intermediate (40th–75th), and low risk (<40th). The zone predicts later significant hyperbilirubinemia and has traditionally set the timing of post-discharge follow-up. The AAP 2022 guideline keeps hour-specific plotting but makes the treatment decision with gestational-age-specific phototherapy and exchange thresholds. Thresholds are lower if neurotoxicity risk factors are present: GA <38 wk, albumin <3.0 g/dL, isoimmune hemolysis/positive DAT, G6PD deficiency or other hemolysis, sepsis, or significant clinical instability in the past 24 h. Follow-up is set by how close the TSB/TcB is to the phototherapy threshold. Stop phototherapy when TSB falls ≥2 mg/dL below the threshold at which it was started. Escalation of care (intensive phototherapy, IV hydration, labs, IVIG for isoimmune disease, preparing for exchange) starts when TSB is within 2 mg/dL of the exchange threshold. Signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy (hypertonia, arching, retrocollis, opisthotonus, high-pitched cry) mean immediate exchange transfusion.

[[figure:ch11-fig01]]
High-yield: Phototherapy converts unconjugated bilirubin to water-soluble lumirubin, which is excreted without conjugation. In a cholestatic infant (raised direct bilirubin), phototherapy can cause "bronze baby" syndrome, so it is not the treatment for cholestasis.
Exam trap: In breast-milk jaundice, the answer is almost never "stop breastfeeding permanently." Exam questions about breastfeeding problems usually test whether you will support continued breastfeeding. Water or dextrose-water supplements are contraindicated, because they worsen intake and hyponatremia without lowering bilirubin.

Congenital (TORCH) infections, compact

AgentClassic neonatal findingsUS-exam pearl
ToxoplasmaChorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, diffuse intracranial calcificationsCat feces, undercooked meat. Pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + leucovorin. Spiramycin in pregnancy.
CMV (most common congenital infection)Periventricular calcifications, microcephaly, SNHL (the most common nonhereditary cause of SNHL), petechiae/"blueberry muffin"Diagnose by urine or saliva PCR within 21 days of life. Valganciclovir for symptomatic disease.
RubellaPDA, cataracts, SNHL, blueberry muffin rashCheck rubella immunity at the first prenatal visit. MMR is given postpartum, never in pregnancy.
HSVSkin/eye/mouth, CNS, or disseminated disease at 1–3 weeksIV acyclovir. Offer cesarean if active genital lesions or prodrome at labor. Suppressive valacyclovir from 36 wk.
SyphilisSnuffles, desquamating palms/soles rash, hepatosplenomegaly, periostitis; later Hutchinson teeth, saddle nose, saber shinsCongenital syphilis is rising sharply in the US. Screen at the first visit; ACOG (2024) now advises repeating at 28 wk and at delivery for all patients (CDC: at minimum if high risk or in a high-prevalence area). Treat with penicillin only (desensitize if allergic).
VaricellaLimb hypoplasia, cicatricial skin scarsIf maternal rash appears 5 days before to 2 days after delivery, give the neonate VariZIG
ZikaSevere microcephalyTravel history

sections.heading: Pediatrics 2 · Development and Growth
sections.html:
Milestones are tested in two ways: "how old is this child?" and "is this a red flag?" Use corrected age for preterm infants until 24 months (chronologic age minus weeks born early). The AAP recommends standardized developmental screening at 9, 18, and 30 months (e.g., ASQ) and autism-specific screening (M-CHAT-R/F) at 18 and 24 months, plus surveillance at every visit.

[[figure:ch11-fig02]]
Red flag (refer for evaluation)Think
No social smile by 3 mo; no babbling by 9 mo; no pointing/gesturing by 12 mo; no single words by 16 mo; no 2-word spontaneous phrases by 24 mo; any loss of language or social skills at any ageHearing loss (always get a formal audiology evaluation), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), global delay. Regression in a girl at 1–4 y with hand-wringing → Rett syndrome (MECP2).
Persistent primitive reflexes (Moro beyond 6 mo, ATNR beyond 6 mo), hand preference <12 mo, toe-walking, scissoring, hypertoniaCerebral palsy (neuroimaging with MRI)
Not walking by 18 mo; Gowers sign; calf pseudohypertrophy in a boyDuchenne muscular dystrophy (↑ CK first, then genetic testing for DMD)
Hypotonia with tongue fasciculations, areflexiaSpinal muscular atrophy (SMN1; on the newborn screen; nusinersen, risdiplam, onasemnogene gene therapy)

ASD workup and management: A positive M-CHAT-R/F (including the follow-up interview) or parental concern should lead to a referral for comprehensive diagnostic evaluation, a formal audiology evaluation, and immediate referral to early intervention (birth to 3 y, Part C of IDEA). Do not wait for the diagnosis to start services. Genetic testing for ASD: chromosomal microarray first-tier, plus Fragile X testing (or exome sequencing per newer ACMG guidance). The core treatment is behavioral (applied behavior analysis). Risperidone and aripiprazole are FDA-approved only for irritability/aggression in ASD and do not treat the core symptoms.

Primitive reflexDisappears by
Moro, rooting, palmar grasp, ATNR (fencing)4–6 mo (palmar grasp ~6 mo; Moro 4–6 mo)
Plantar grasp; Babinski (upgoing toe)9–12 mo; up to 12–24 mo
Parachute (protective)Appears at 8–9 mo and persists for life

Growth

ParameterRule of thumb
WeightTerm infants lose ≤7–10% in the first days and regain birth weight by 10–14 d. Weight doubles by ~5 mo, triples by 12 mo, quadruples by ~2 y.
Length / height+50% by 12 mo, doubles by 4 y. After age 2, about 5–6 cm/y until puberty. Mid-parental target height (boys) = (father + mother + 13 cm)/2; girls = (father + mother − 13 cm)/2.
Head circumference+2 cm/mo for months 0–3, +1 cm/mo for 3–6, +0.5 cm/mo for 6–12. Macrocephaly → hydrocephalus, familial; microcephaly → congenital infection, genetic, craniosynostosis.
ChartsWHO charts for 0–2 y; CDC charts for 2–19 y. BMI is used from age 2. Obesity is BMI ≥95th percentile; severe obesity is ≥120% of the 95th percentile.
Short stature patternHeight velocityBone ageClues
Familial (genetic)Normal (parallel to curve)= chronologic ageShort parents; reaches target height
Constitutional delay of growth and pubertyNormal, with deceleration in early childhoodDelayedFamily history of "late bloomers"; normal adult height; no treatment (short testosterone course optional for boys)
PathologicDecreased (crosses percentiles)Delayed (endocrine) or variableHypothyroidism, GH deficiency, Cushing, Turner syndrome (karyotype any unexplained short girl), celiac disease, IBD, CKD, chronic illness. Weight falling before height suggests nutritional/GI cause; height falling before weight suggests endocrine cause.
High-yield: In failure to thrive (weight <2nd percentile on WHO charts, or crossing ≥2 major percentile lines), the most common cause in the US is inadequate caloric intake (psychosocial/feeding problems), not organic disease. The best first step is a detailed feeding and psychosocial history with calorie count and observed feeding. Order targeted tests only. Persistent FTT despite adequate intake → malabsorption (CF, celiac).

Puberty: Thelarche is usually the first sign in girls (about age 10); testicular enlargement ≥4 mL is first in boys (about age 11.5). Precocious puberty is <8 y in girls or <9 y in boys. The first test is bone age plus LH (basal/stimulated). Central (↑LH) → brain MRI → GnRH agonist. Peripheral (↓LH) → CAH, McCune–Albright, gonadal/adrenal tumor, exogenous estrogen. Delayed puberty is no breast development by 13 y or no testicular enlargement by 14 y. Most cases are constitutional delay. Check LH/FSH: high = gonadal failure (Turner, Klinefelter); low = CDGP vs. Kallmann (anosmia), hypothalamic (anorexia, athletes).

Pediatric obesity (AAP 2023 CPG): Treat early and intensively, with no "watchful waiting." Use intensive health behavior and lifestyle treatment for ≥26 contact hours. Offer pharmacotherapy from ≥12 y (GLP-1 RAs such as semaglutide or liraglutide, orlistat, phentermine-topiramate) and refer for metabolic/bariatric surgery at ≥13 y with severe obesity. Screen for comorbidities at ≥10 y: lipids, HbA1c/fasting glucose, ALT (for MASLD).

Schedule note (2025–2026): The federal (CDC/ACIP) childhood schedule was revised in 2025–2026 for several products (e.g., the universal HepB birth dose and COVID-19 wording), and it now differs from the AAP schedule, which many US pediatricians follow. Exam items are built on the long-standing core schedule above. Always check the current-year version in practice.
True contraindications / precautionsNOT contraindications (vaccinate)
Anaphylaxis to a prior dose or component (gelatin, neomycin for MMR/varicella; yeast for HepB)Egg allergy of any severity (influenza and MMR are given in the usual way; no special observation is needed beyond standard practice)
Live vaccines (MMR, varicella, LAIV, rotavirus): pregnancy, severe immunodeficiency (SCID, chemotherapy, high-dose steroids ≥2 mg/kg/d or ≥20 mg/d for ≥14 d), HIV with CD4 <15% (or <200 if ≥5 y)Mild acute illness ± low-grade fever, current antibiotics, convalescence

Well-child screeningWhen / how
Newborn metabolic screen (dried blood spot)At 24–48 h (repeat if collected <24 h). PKU, congenital hypothyroidism, galactosemia, CAH, hemoglobinopathies, CF (IRT), SCID (TRECs), SMA, MCAD, etc.
Hearing"1-3-6": screen by 1 mo (OAE/ABR), diagnose by 3 mo, intervene by 6 mo. Infants who fail → diagnostic ABR. Screen for congenital CMV in failed screens where available.

BilirubinBefore discharge (TcB/TSB), plotted by hour
