sections.heading: Pediatrics 4 · Congenital Heart Disease
sections.html:
CHD presents in a predictable pattern: cyanosis in the first hours or days (right-to-left lesions, often ductal-dependent pulmonary flow); shock at 1–2 weeks when the ductus closes (left-sided obstructive, ductal-dependent systemic flow); heart failure at 4–8 weeks as pulmonary vascular resistance falls (large left-to-right shunts: VSD, AVSD, PDA). Use the hyperoxia test: if PaO2 rises >150 mmHg on 100% O2, the cause is lung disease; if it does not, think cyanotic heart disease. Any neonate in shock or with severe cyanosis and a suspected ductal-dependent lesion gets IV prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) immediately, before the echo if necessary. Watch for apnea (have intubation ready), fever, and hypotension.

LesionKey findingsAssociations / management
Tetralogy of Fallot (most common cyanotic CHD after infancy)VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction, RVH. Harsh systolic ejection murmur at LUSB (louder murmur = less severe obstruction). Boot-shaped heart, ↓ pulmonary markings. "Tet spells" with crying or feeding.22q11 deletion, Down. Tet spell: knee-chest position first (↑ SVR), then O2, IV morphine, IV fluid, phenylephrine, IV propranolol/esmolol. Complete repair at 3–6 mo.
Transposition of the great arteries (most common cyanotic lesion in the newborn)Profound cyanosis in the first hours, not improved by O2. Single loud S2, often no murmur. "Egg on a string."Infant of a diabetic mother. PGE1, then balloon atrial septostomy if mixing is inadequate, then arterial switch in the first 1–2 weeks.
Truncus arteriosusSingle trunk, VSD, early CHF + mild cyanosis22q11 deletion
Tricuspid atresiaCyanosis, left axis deviation, small RVPGE1; staged Glenn → Fontan
Total anomalous pulmonary venous return"Snowman" (supracardiac). Obstructed form: severe cyanosis and pulmonary edema, a surgical emergency (PGE1 does not help).Emergent repair
Ebstein anomalyAtrialized RV, tricuspid regurgitation, massive cardiomegaly, WPWMaternal lithium (small absolute risk)
Hypoplastic left heartShock and gray color when the ductus closes (days 1–14), weak pulsesPGE1; Norwood → Glenn → Fontan, or transplant
VSD (most common CHD overall)Holosystolic murmur at LLSB (small VSD = loud). Large VSD → CHF at 4–8 wk.Most small muscular VSDs close spontaneously. Large VSD: diuretics, then surgery before Eisenmenger develops.
ASD (secundum)Fixed, wide split S2, systolic ejection murmur at LUSB (flow across the pulmonic valve). Often found incidentally in childhood or adulthood. Paradoxical emboli.Primum ASD and AVSD → Down syndrome. Device closure if large.
PDAContinuous "machine-like" murmur, bounding pulses, wide pulse pressurePrematurity, congenital rubella. Close with indomethacin, ibuprofen, or acetaminophen (preterm), or with a device/ligation. Keep it open with PGE1.
Coarctation of the aortaNeonate: shock when the ductus closes, lower-body hypoperfusion. Older child: arm HTN, brachio-femoral delay, BP arms > legs, rib notching, "3" sign.Turner syndrome, bicuspid aortic valve. PGE1 in neonates; then repair or balloon/stent.
Pulmonic stenosis / supravalvular ASEjection click (PS); murmur at the RUSB radiating to the carotidsPS → Noonan. Supravalvular AS → Williams (also hypercalcemia).
High-yield: Untreated large left-to-right shunts can lead to Eisenmenger syndrome: shunt reversal with late cyanosis, clubbing, and polycythemia. Once established, surgery is contraindicated. Innocent murmurs (Still's: vibratory, LLSB, soft, louder when supine; venous hum: continuous, disappears when supine or with neck compression) need no workup. Diastolic murmurs, grade ≥3, holosystolic murmurs, and murmurs with symptoms are pathologic and need an echo.

SignsBarking cough, hoarse voice, inspiratory stridorDrooling, dysphagia, muffled ("hot potato") voice, tripod posture, little coughToxic, purulent tracheal secretions, no response to epinephrineRhinorrhea → wheeze, crackles, tachypnea, retractions; apnea in young infants
ImagingSteeple sign (not required)Thumb sign (do not delay airway care to get it)Ragged tracheal wallNot routinely needed
TreatmentDexamethasone single dose (0.15–0.6 mg/kg PO) for all severities. Add nebulized racemic epinephrine for stridor at rest or moderate–severe distress, then observe 2–4 h for rebound.Secure the airway in the OR (anesthesia + ENT); keep the child calm with a parent, no throat exam, no IV/lab until airway secured. Then ceftriaxone + vancomycin. Rifampin prophylaxis for contacts (Hib).Intubation, bronchoscopy, IV vancomycin + ceftriaxoneSupportive: nasal suctioning, hydration, O2 if SpO2 <90%. No routine albuterol, steroids, epinephrine, antibiotics, CXR, or viral testing. Admit for apnea, hypoxemia, dehydration, or severe distress.

Other airway emergencies: foreign body aspiration (sudden choking, unilateral wheeze, hyperinflation on expiratory or decubitus film) → rigid bronchoscopy. Retropharyngeal abscess (<5 y; neck stiffness/extension pain, widened prevertebral soft tissue) → CT, IV ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin, drainage. Peritonsillar abscess (adolescent, trismus, uvula deviation) → needle aspiration/I&D plus antibiotics. Pertussis (paroxysms, whoop, post-tussive emesis; infants get apnea and lymphocytosis) → azithromycin at all ages, including <1 mo (monitor for pyloric stenosis), plus prophylaxis for close contacts.

Acute otitis media (AAP 2013) and pharyngitis

ScenarioManagement
DiagnosisRequires moderate–severe TM bulging, new otorrhea, or mild bulging with acute otalgia/intense erythema. Effusion without inflammation is OME, which does not get antibiotics.
Antibiotics indicatedAge <6 mo; severe AOM at any age (moderate–severe otalgia, otalgia ≥48 h, or T ≥39 °C); bilateral AOM at 6–23 mo; otorrhea
Observation option (48–72 h, with reliable follow-up)Non-severe unilateral AOM at 6–23 mo; non-severe AOM (uni- or bilateral) at ≥24 mo
First-line drugHigh-dose amoxicillin 80–90 mg/kg/d in 2 doses (10 d if <2 y or severe; 7 d at 2–5 y and 5–7 d at ≥6 y if mild/moderate)
Amoxicillin–clavulanate insteadAmoxicillin in the past 30 d, concurrent purulent conjunctivitis (nontypeable H. influenzae), recurrent AOM unresponsive to amoxicillin, or treatment failure at 48–72 h
Penicillin allergyNon-severe: cefdinir, cefuroxime, cefpodoxime. Severe: macrolide/clindamycin (less effective). Second failure or unable to take oral: IM ceftriaxone ×3 d.
Tympanostomy tubesRecurrent AOM (≥3 in 6 mo or ≥4 in 12 mo with 1 in the last 6 mo) with effusion; bilateral OME ≥3 mo with hearing loss
Group A strep pharyngitisTest (rapid antigen; back-up culture if negative in children/adolescents) when viral features are absent. Usually no testing <3 y. Treat with penicillin V or amoxicillin ×10 d (IM benzathine penicillin once if adherence is a concern). Treatment prevents rheumatic fever, not PSGN.

Kawasaki disease, MIS-C, and the exanthems

Kawasaki disease (medium-vessel vasculitis; usually <5 y, peak in Asian children): fever ≥5 days + ≥4 of 5 "CRASH" criteria: Conjunctivitis (bilateral, nonexudative, limbic sparing), Rash (polymorphous, often perineal), Adenopathy (cervical, ≥1.5 cm, usually unilateral), Strawberry tongue / cracked red lips, Hands/feet (erythema, edema; periungual desquamation in weeks 2–3). Incomplete Kawasaki (fever ≥5 d + 2–3 criteria) → check CRP/ESR and supplemental labs (albumin ≤3, anemia, ↑ALT, platelets ≥450k after day 7, WBC ≥15k, urine WBC ≥10/hpf) and an echo. Treatment: IVIG 2 g/kg + aspirin (moderate- or high-dose until afebrile, then low-dose 3–5 mg/kg/d for 6–8 wk), ideally within 10 days of fever onset. Echocardiogram at diagnosis, 1–2 wk, and 4–6 wk to look for coronary artery aneurysms. Refractory disease → second IVIG, steroids, or infliximab. Delay live vaccines 11 mo after IVIG. Aspirin plus influenza or varicella carries a risk of Reye syndrome, so give inactivated influenza vaccine.

MIS-C (2–6 wk after SARS-CoV-2): fever, GI symptoms, shock, myocardial dysfunction, very high inflammatory markers. Treat with IVIG + steroids and aspirin.

ExanthemAgentDistinguishing clue
Measles (rubeola)ParamyxovirusCough, coryza, conjunctivitis, then Koplik spots, then cephalocaudal maculopapular rash. Vitamin A for hospitalized children. Airborne isolation. MMR within 72 h or IG within 6 d as post-exposure prophylaxis. US outbreaks are rising.
RubellaTogavirusMild, postauricular/suboccipital nodes, rash spreads fast (3 d)
Roseola (exanthem subitum)HHV-6/73–5 d of high fever (febrile seizures) → rash appears when the fever breaks
Erythema infectiosumParvovirus B19"Slapped cheek," lacy reticular rash; not contagious once rash appears. Aplastic crisis in sickle cell; hydrops fetalis in pregnancy (follow MCA Doppler).
VaricellaVZVLesions in different stages ("dewdrop on a rose petal"). Acyclovir for ≥13 y, chronic disease, or immunocompromised. Avoid aspirin.
Hand-foot-mouthCoxsackie A16, EV-A71Oral ulcers + palm/sole vesicles; later onychomadesis
Scarlet feverGAS (erythrogenic toxin)Sandpaper rash, Pastia lines, circumoral pallor, strawberry tongue

UTI (2–24 months, febrile): Get a catheterized or suprapubic specimen for culture (bag specimens are only for screening UA). Diagnosis = pyuria/bacteriuria + ≥50,000 CFU/mL of one uropathogen. Treat with oral antibiotics (cephalexin, cefixime, amoxicillin-clavulanate per local resistance) for 7–14 d. Use IV if ill-appearing, vomiting, or <2 mo. Renal-bladder US after the first febrile UTI. Get a VCUG only if the US shows hydronephrosis/scarring/high-grade VUR features, or after a second febrile UTI. Meningitis: neonates (GBS, E. coli, Listeria) → ampicillin + cefotaxime/gentamicin. >1 mo (pneumococcus, meningococcus) → vancomycin + ceftriaxone, plus dexamethasone before or with the first dose if Hib is suspected. Septic arthritis vs transient synovitis (Kocher criteria: non-weight-bearing, T >38.5, ESR >40, WBC >12,000; CRP >2) → urgent arthrocentesis/US when concerning.

sections.heading: Pediatrics 6 · Child Abuse and Mandatory Reporting
sections.html:
Red flagSpecifics
HistoryStory changes, is inconsistent with the injury or development ("rolled off the couch" in a 2-month-old), delayed care, or the injury is blamed on a sibling
Sentinel injuries in non-mobile infantsAny bruise in an infant who is not cruising ("those who don't cruise rarely bruise"), intraoral injury (torn frenulum), or subconjunctival hemorrhage. TEN-4-FACESp: bruising of Torso, Ears, Neck; Frenulum, Angle of jaw, Cheeks, Eyelids, Subconjunctiva, or any bruise in an infant ≤4 months; or patterned bruising.
Fractures with high specificityClassic metaphyseal lesions ("corner/bucket-handle"), posterior rib fractures (squeezing), scapula, sternum, spinous process; multiple fractures of different ages; femur fracture in a non-ambulatory child. (Spiral tibia fracture in a walking toddler = "toddler's fracture," usually accidental.)
Abusive head traumaSubdural hematomas (often of different ages), multilayered retinal hemorrhages, irritability/lethargy/vomiting/seizures/apnea without a good history. Get a CT head (MRI later) and a dilated ophthalmology exam.
BurnsImmersion "stocking-glove" burns with sharp demarcation and sparing of flexural creases, cigarette burns
Sexual abuseGonorrhea, syphilis, or HIV outside the perinatal period; chlamydia/trichomonas in a prepubertal child (beyond the perinatal window); sexualized behavior; anogenital injury. (Note: most exams are normal.)
Medical child abuse (factitious disorder imposed on another)Recurrent unexplained illness that happens only in the caregiver's presence. Separate the child and observe; report.
Workup of suspected physical abuseDetail
Skeletal surveyAll children <2 y with suspected abuse (repeat in 2 weeks for healing fractures). Siblings <2 y in the household also get one.
NeuroimagingAny neurologic signs; consider for all infants <6–12 mo with concerning injuries even if the exam is normal (occult head injury is common)
LabsBruising → CBC/platelets, PT/INR, PTT, ± vWF/factor levels. Abdominal trauma screen (AST/ALT, lipase, UA for blood). Fractures → Ca, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, PTH, 25-OH vitamin D. Consider OI (blue sclerae, dentinogenesis imperfecta, family history).
ReportReport to Child Protective Services (and/or law enforcement) on reasonable suspicion. Proof is not required, and neither is parental consent or informing the parents first. Good-faith reporters are immune from liability; failure to report is a crime.
SafetyHospitalize if the child cannot be safely discharged. Most states allow a physician to place a temporary protective hold without parental consent.
Exam trap: Mimics include congenital dermal melanocytosis (Mongolian spots: present from birth, do not change color, gray-blue on the sacrum), coagulopathy (hemophilia, vWD, vitamin K deficiency), osteogenesis imperfecta, rickets, Menkes (copper; subdurals + kinky hair), and cultural practices (coining, cupping). The exam rewards a complete medical workup and a report. Do not choose an option that confronts or accuses the parents, or one that waits for proof.

sections.heading: Pediatrics 7 · Genetic Syndromes
sections.html:
SyndromeGeneticsKey featuresWhat the exam asks
DownTrisomy 21 (95% meiotic nondisjunction, ↑ with maternal age; 4% Robertsonian translocation, so karyotype the parents)Hypotonia, flat facies, upslanting palpebral fissures, single palmar crease, sandal gap, Brushfield spotsEcho at birth (AVSD), duodenal atresia, Hirschsprung, TSH (newborn, 6 mo, 12 mo, then yearly), CBC (transient myeloproliferative disorder, AML-M7 <5 y, ALL), hearing/vision, OSA, celiac if symptoms, atlantoaxial instability (no routine X-ray if asymptomatic; ask about neuro symptoms), early-onset Alzheimer
EdwardsTrisomy 18Clenched fists with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, micrognathia, prominent occiput, VSDDeath usually in the first year. Quad screen: all markers low.
PatauTrisomy 13Holoprosencephaly, cleft lip/palate, polydactyly, cutis aplasia, microphthalmiaLow PAPP-A + hCG in the first trimester
Turner45,X (or mosaic)Neonatal lymphedema of the hands/feet, webbed neck, shield chest, short stature, primary amenorrhea, streak ovariesKaryotype. Echo/MRI (bicuspid AV, coarctation, aortic dissection), renal US (horseshoe kidney), hearing, TSH, celiac. GH therapy; estrogen at ~11–12 y. If Y material is present → gonadectomy (gonadoblastoma).
Klinefelter47,XXYTall, small firm testes, gynecomastia, learning problems, infertility (azoospermia)↓ testosterone, ↑↑ FSH/LH. Testosterone therapy. ↑ breast cancer risk.
Fragile XX-linked FMR1 CGG expansion (>200), anticipation through the motherLong face, large ears, macroorchidism (post-puberty), ID, autism, mitral prolapsePremutation carriers (55–200 repeats): primary ovarian insufficiency in women and FXTAS (tremor/ataxia) in older men. Test FMR1 in any woman with POI <40.
22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge/velocardiofacial)Microdeletion (FISH/microarray), ADCATCH-22: Cardiac (conotruncal: TOF, truncus, interrupted arch), Abnormal facies, Thymic hypoplasia (T-cell deficiency), Cleft palate, Hypocalcemia (hypoparathyroidism)Neonatal tetany/seizure + conotruncal defect. Irradiated blood products. Avoid live vaccines if severe T-cell deficiency. Later psychiatric illness (schizophrenia).
Williams7q11.23 deletion (elastin)Elfin facies, overfriendly "cocktail party" personality, IDSupravalvular AS, hypercalcemia, renal artery stenosis
NoonanPTPN11 (RAS pathway), AD, normal karyotypeWebbed neck, short stature like Turner but affects both sexesPulmonic stenosis, HCM, bleeding diathesis, cryptorchidism
Prader–Willi / Angelman15q11–13 imprinting: paternal deletion or maternal UPD (PWS); maternal deletion of UBE3A or paternal UPD (AS)PWS: neonatal hypotonia/poor feeding → later hyperphagia, obesity, hypogonadism, small hands. AS: happy demeanor, seizures, ataxia, absent speech.DNA methylation analysis is the first test. PWS: GH therapy, food security.
Beckwith–Wiedemann11p15 imprintingMacrosomia, macroglossia, omphalocele, hemihypertrophy, neonatal hypoglycemiaWilms tumor + hepatoblastoma surveillance: abdominal US every 3 mo to ~7 y, AFP to ~4 y
MarfanFBN1, ADTall, arachnodactyly, upward lens subluxation, pectusAortic root dilation → echo; β-blocker/ARB; avoid contact sports. (Homocystinuria: downward lens dislocation, thrombosis, ID.)
Cystic fibrosisCFTR (ΔF508), ARMeconium ileus, FTT with steatorrhea, recurrent pneumonia (S. aureus early, Pseudomonas later), nasal polyps, CBAVDNewborn screen (IRT ± DNA) → sweat chloride ≥60 mmol/L confirms. CFTR modulators (elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor), pancreatic enzymes, ADEK vitamins, airway clearance.
Fetal alcohol syndromeTeratogenSmooth philtrum, thin vermilion border, short palpebral fissures, microcephaly, ID, ADHDThe most common preventable cause of ID. No safe amount of alcohol in pregnancy.

sections.heading: Pediatrics 8 · Inborn Errors of Metabolism
sections.html:
Suspect an inborn error in a neonate who is well at birth and then develops poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, seizures, or coma after starting feeds (sepsis mimic). It may come with an unusual odor or a family history of neonatal death. The first labs are glucose, blood gas with anion gap, ammonia, lactate, ketones (urine), LFTs, plasma amino acids, urine organic acids, and acylcarnitine profile.

Lab patternCategoryExamples
↑↑ Ammonia, no metabolic acidosis (often respiratory alkalosis), normal glucoseUrea cycle defectOTC deficiency (X-linked; the most common; ↑ orotic acid, ↓ citrulline). CPS I deficiency (orotic acid normal/low). Citrullinemia (↑ citrulline). Argininosuccinic aciduria (trichorrhexis nodosa).
↑ Anion gap acidosis + ketosis ± hyperammonemia, neutropenia/thrombocytopeniaOrganic acidemiaPropionic acidemia, methylmalonic acidemia (B12-responsive forms), isovaleric acidemia ("sweaty feet" odor)
Ketoacidosis, encephalopathy, maple syrup odorBranched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency (MSUD)Restrict leucine/isoleucine/valine; thiamine trial; dialysis in crisis
Hypoketotic hypoglycemia with fasting/illness, ↑ LFTs, ± hyperammonemiaFatty-acid oxidation defectMCAD deficiency (sudden death after fasting). Avoid fasting, IV dextrose in illness. (Also consider hyperinsulinism if ketones are low.)
Fasting hypoglycemia + lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, hyperlipidemia, big liverGlycogen storage disease type I (von Gierke, glucose-6-phosphatase)Frequent feeds, cornstarch. Pompe (II): cardiomegaly + hypotonia, enzyme replacement. McArdle (V): exercise cramps, myoglobinuria.
Jaundice, hepatomegaly, vomiting, cataracts, E. coli sepsis after milk feeds; urine reducing substancesClassic galactosemia (GALT)Stop breast milk/lactose; switch to soy formula. Classic galactosemia is a contraindication to breastfeeding.
Hypoglycemia, vomiting after fruit/juice/sucrose at weaningHereditary fructose intolerance (aldolase B)Remove fructose, sucrose, sorbitol
Musty odor, fair skin/hair, eczema, ID (if untreated)PKU (phenylalanine hydroxylase or BH4)Low-Phe diet for life; sapropterin if responsive. Maternal PKU: Phe <6 mg/dL before conception and through pregnancy prevents microcephaly, ID, and CHD in the fetus.
Neurodegeneration, cherry-red maculaLysosomal storageTay–Sachs (no hepatosplenomegaly, hyperacusis), Niemann–Pick (with HSM), Gaucher (no cherry-red spot; bone crises, Erlenmeyer flask, pancytopenia; enzyme replacement), Hurler (corneal clouding) vs Hunter (X-linked, no clouding, aggression), Fabry (painful neuropathy, angiokeratomas, renal/cardiac; X-linked)
Acute decompensation, next steps (any IEM): Stop protein (and galactose/fructose). Give IV dextrose (D10) at 1.5× maintenance to stop catabolism (± insulin). Correct acidosis. For hyperammonemia, give IV sodium phenylacetate/sodium benzoate + arginine. Hemodialysis if ammonia is very high (several hundred μmol/L), rising, or causing encephalopathy. Do not wait for confirmatory results to start treatment.

sections.heading: Pediatrics 9 · Pediatric GI Surgery and Emergencies
sections.html:
ConditionAge / clueKey testNext step
Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis2–8 wk (classically 3–6), firstborn male, nonbilious projectile vomiting after feeds, hungry baby, palpable "olive," visible peristalsis. Early macrolide exposure is a risk factor.Ultrasound (muscle thickness ≥3–4 mm, channel length ≥15–17 mm). Labs: hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis (paradoxical aciduria late).Correct fluids and electrolytes first (NS bolus, then D5 ½NS + KCl once voiding; target HCO3− <30 and normal Cl/K). Then laparoscopic pyloromyotomy. It is never an emergency operation.
Duodenal atresiaBilious vomiting in the first day (if distal to the ampulla), Down syndrome, polyhydramniosX-ray: "double bubble," no distal gasNG decompression, fluids, duodenoduodenostomy. Echo (Down).
Malrotation with midgut volvulusBilious emesis in the first month (can occur at any age). Abdomen may be non-distended early. Later peritonitis, bloody stool, shock.Upper GI contrast series (the gold standard when stable): duodenojejunal junction right of midline, "corkscrew" duodenum. US: whirlpool sign, SMV left of SMA.Bilious vomiting in a neonate is a surgical emergency. NPO, NG decompression, IV fluids, emergent UGI. If unstable or peritoneal → straight to Ladd procedure.
Jejunoileal atresiaBilious vomiting, distension; vascular accident in utero (maternal cocaine/vasoconstrictors)Triple bubble / multiple air-fluid levelsResection
Meconium ileusNo meconium, distension, CFContrast enema: microcolon; "soap-bubble" RLQHyperosmolar (Gastrografin) enema (diagnostic + therapeutic); sweat test
Hirschsprung diseaseNo meconium in 48 h, chronic constipation, distension, explosive "squirt" stool on rectal exam, empty rectal vault; Down syndromeContrast enema (transition zone, screening). Rectal suction biopsy is diagnostic: absent ganglion cells, ↑ acetylcholinesterase/calretinin-negative.Pull-through surgery. Watch for Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis (fever, explosive diarrhea, sepsis) → rectal irrigation, antibiotics.
Intussusception6–36 mo; intermittent colicky pain with legs drawn up, lethargy between episodes, vomiting, "currant jelly" stool (late), RUQ sausage mass. Lead point: hypertrophied Peyer patches (post-viral, adenovirus) or Meckel/polyp/lymphoma (>3–5 y), HSP.Ultrasound: target/doughnut signAir (pneumatic) or hydrostatic contrast enema: diagnostic and therapeutic (recurrence ~10%). Surgery if peritonitis, perforation (free air), shock, or failed enema.
Meckel diverticulumRule of 2s; painless bright red/maroon rectal bleeding in a toddler (ectopic gastric mucosa)Technetium-99m pertechnetate scanResection
Biliary atresia2–8 wk, jaundice + acholic stools, dark urine, ↑ direct bilirubin, ↑ GGTUS (triangular cord sign, absent gallbladder), HIDA (no excretion); intraoperative cholangiogram is definitiveKasai before ~60 d. Most still need a liver transplant eventually.
Gastroschisis vs omphaloceleGastroschisis: right of umbilicus, no sac, isolated, ↑ AFP. Omphalocele: midline, sac-covered, associated anomalies (trisomies 13/18, BWS, cardiac).Prenatal US; ↑ MSAFPCover bowel (sterile, warm bag), NG tube, IV fluids; repair. Karyotype + echo for omphalocele.
Appendicitis (child)Periumbilical pain → RLQ; young children perforate earlyUltrasound first (avoid CT radiation); MRI if equivocalAppendectomy (nonoperative antibiotics in select cases)
IgA vasculitis (HSP)Palpable purpura on buttocks/legs, arthralgia, abdominal pain (intussusception risk, often ileo-ileal), hematuriaUA, BP, creatinineSupportive; steroids for severe GI disease; monitor UA/BP for 6 months
Exam trap: In pyloric stenosis, the answer to "next step" after a positive US with K+ 2.9 and HCO3− 34 is IV fluid and electrolyte repletion, not immediate surgery, because anesthesia with metabolic alkalosis can cause postoperative apnea. In contrast, bilious emesis needs an emergent UGI series or surgery. The bile color separates a scheduled problem from an emergency.

sections.heading: Pediatrics 10 · Pediatric Oncology
sections.html:
TumorCluesWorkup / pearls
ALL (most common childhood cancer; peak 2–5 y)Pallor, fatigue, bone pain/limp, fever, petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy. Mediastinal mass in T-ALL.CBC with smear (blasts may be absent: "aleukemic"), then bone marrow + flow cytometry. Good prognosis: age 1–10, WBC <50k, hyperdiploidy, t(12;21) ETV6-RUNX1. Poor: infant, KMT2A, t(9;22). CNS-directed intrathecal therapy. Tumor lysis syndrome (↑K, ↑PO4, ↑uric acid, ↓Ca, AKI) → hydration, allopurinol/rasburicase (contraindicated in G6PD deficiency).
AMLDown syndrome (AMKL <4 y), gum infiltration, chloroma, DIC (APL)Auer rods; APL t(15;17) → ATRA + arsenic
Brain tumors (most common solid tumor; leading cause of pediatric cancer death)Morning headache, vomiting, ataxia, papilledema, head tilt. Posterior fossa in children: pilocytic astrocytoma (cystic + mural nodule, best prognosis; NF1), medulloblastoma (vermis, drop metastases), ependymoma (4th ventricle, hydrocephalus). Craniopharyngioma: bitemporal hemianopia, growth failure, DI, calcified suprasellar mass.MRI brain with contrast
Neuroblastoma (most common extracranial solid tumor in children; <2 y)Abdominal mass that crosses the midline, calcifications, periorbital ecchymoses ("raccoon eyes"), opsoclonus–myoclonus, Horner syndrome, HTN, watery diarrhea (VIP), "blueberry muffin" skin metastases in infants↑ urine HVA/VMA, MIBG scan, biopsy; MYCN amplification = poor prognosis. Stage MS (infants) can regress spontaneously.
Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma; 3–4 y)Well child with a smooth flank mass that does not cross the midline; hematuria, HTN. WAGR (WT1), Denys–Drash, Beckwith–Wiedemann, hemihypertrophy, aniridia.US, then CT/MRI abdomen + CT chest. Avoid repeated palpation (rupture). Nephrectomy + chemotherapy; excellent prognosis.
Hepatoblastoma<3 y, ↑↑ AFP; BWS, FAP, prematurityResection + chemo
RetinoblastomaLeukocoria (absent red reflex), strabismus. RB1: bilateral = germline (AD-like, two-hit)Urgent dilated ophthalmologic exam, MRI orbits (avoid CT radiation in germline cases). Later osteosarcoma risk.
OsteosarcomaAdolescent growth spurt, metaphysis of distal femur/proximal tibia, night pain. Codman triangle, "sunburst." Risks: prior RB, Li–Fraumeni, Paget disease, radiation.X-ray → MRI + biopsy; CT chest (lung metastases). Neoadjuvant chemo + limb-sparing surgery.
Ewing sarcomaDiaphysis of long bones, pelvis; fever, ↑ ESR (mimics osteomyelitis); "onion-skin" periosteal reactiont(11;22) EWSR1-FLI1, small round blue cells (CD99). Radiosensitive.
Hodgkin lymphomaAdolescent, painless cervical/supraclavicular nodes, mediastinal mass, B symptomsExcisional biopsy (Reed–Sternberg). CXR before sedation (anterior mediastinal mass → airway collapse).
RhabdomyosarcomaMost common soft-tissue sarcoma; orbit, GU ("grape-like" sarcoma botryoides in a vagina)Desmin/myogenin+
Langerhans cell histiocytosisLytic skull lesions, diabetes insipidus, seborrheic rash, otitisCD1a/S100; Birbeck granules

sections.heading: Pediatrics 11 · Adolescent Medicine and Consent
sections.html:
Interview the adolescent alone for part of every visit, after explaining the limits of confidentiality to both parent and teen. Use HEADSSS: Home, Education/employment, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide/depression, Safety. Confidentiality must be broken when there is a risk of serious harm: suicidal or homicidal intent, or abuse.

Minors can consent without a parent for (true in all or most states)Requires parent/guardian (or court) generally
Emergency care (implied consent). STI diagnosis and treatment (all states), including HPV vaccine in some states. Contraception (most states; Title X clinics confidential). Prenatal care (most states). Substance use treatment and outpatient mental health (many states). HIV testing (most).Most elective non-emergency medical/surgical care, including routine immunizations in most states. Abortion: state-specific (parental notification/consent or judicial bypass; banned in some states after Dobbs). Sterilization of a minor generally is not permitted.
Emancipated minors (married, active military, financially independent, court-declared) consent for themselves. In many states a minor parent consents for their own child's care.Parents cannot refuse life-saving treatment for a child (e.g., a Jehovah's Witness parent refusing blood in an emergency). Treat in the emergency and get a court order if time allows.
Adolescent topicKey point
ContraceptionLARC (implant, IUD) is first-line for adolescents (AAP/ACOG). A pelvic exam is not required to start contraception. Counsel on condoms for STI protection.
DepressionScreen yearly ≥12 y. Treat with CBT ± SSRI (fluoxetine ≥8 y and escitalopram ≥12 y are FDA-approved). Boxed warning for suicidality: close follow-up in the first weeks.
Eating disordersAdmit for HR <50 (day) / <45 (night), BP <90/45, orthostasis, T <35.6 °C, electrolyte abnormalities (↓K, ↓PO4), <75% median BMI, arrhythmia, refusal to eat. Watch for refeeding syndrome (hypophosphatemia).
Sports pre-participationSyncope/chest pain with exertion, family history of sudden death <50 y, or a murmur that increases with Valsalva/standing → HCM: echo, no competitive sports until evaluated
Gynecomastia (pubertal)Common (~50% of boys), tender, bilateral or unilateral, resolves in 6 mo–2 y. Reassure. Evaluate if prepubertal, very large, or accompanied by small testes (Klinefelter) or a testicular mass.
ScoliosisAdam forward bend test; refer if Cobb angle >20° in a growing child. Bracing 25–40°, surgery >45–50°. Painful scoliosis or a left thoracic curve → MRI (tumor, syrinx).
Slipped capital femoral epiphysisObese adolescent, hip or knee pain, limp, loss of internal rotation. Get AP + frog-leg X-ray, keep non-weight-bearing, and arrange surgical pinning (check the other hip; check TSH in atypical cases).
===================== OBSTETRICS =====================

sections.heading: Obstetrics 1 · Prenatal Care and Screening Timeline
sections.html:
Dating: Use the first-trimester crown–rump length (the most accurate method). Redate by US if it differs from the LMP by >5 days before 9 0/7 wk or >7 days at 9 0/7–13 6/7 wk. Visits are every 4 wk until 28 wk, every 2 wk from 28–36 wk, then weekly. Term definitions: early term 37 0/7–38 6/7; full term 39 0/7–40 6/7; late term 41 0/7–41 6/7; post-term ≥42 0/7.

First prenatal visit (all patients)Selective / risk-based
CBC; blood type, Rh(D), and antibody screen; rubella IgG; varicella immunity (history/serology); HBsAg; HIV (opt-out); syphilis; hepatitis C antibody (every pregnancy); urine culture for asymptomatic bacteriuria (treat even if asymptomatic: pyelonephritis/preterm birth risk); urine protein; cervical cytology/HPV if due; chlamydia (+ gonorrhea) if <25 y or at risk; offer aneuploidy screening and carrier screening (CF, SMA, hemoglobinopathy via CBC ± electrophoresis) to allEarly GDM screening if overweight/obese (BMI ≥25, ≥23 in Asian Americans) + another risk factor, or prior GDM (A1c ≥6.5% = overt diabetes); TSH if symptoms, history, or T1DM; TB testing if risk; lead if risk; Fragile X carrier screening if family history of ID or POI; Tay–Sachs (Ashkenazi); repeat HIV/syphilis/chlamydia/gonorrhea in the third trimester if high risk
Folic acid 0.4 mg/d from ≥1 mo before conception (4 mg/d after a prior NTD-affected pregnancy). Counsel on avoiding alcohol, tobacco, cannabis, listeriosis foods (unpasteurized cheese, deli meat), high-mercury fish, and cat litter. Gestational weight gain: underweight 28–40 lb; normal 25–35 lb; overweight 15–25 lb; obese 11–20 lb.Low-dose aspirin 81 mg/d from 12–28 wk (ideally <16 wk) until delivery if ≥1 high-risk factor (prior preeclampsia, multifetal gestation, chronic HTN, pregestational DM, CKD, autoimmune disease such as SLE/APS) or ≥2 moderate risk factors (nulliparity, BMI >30, family history of preeclampsia, age ≥35, IVF, low income, Black race as a marker of structural racism, prior adverse pregnancy outcome, >10-y interval)
[[figure:ch11-fig04]]

Aneuploidy and anomaly screening

TestTimingTrisomy 21 patternNotes
Cell-free DNA (placental DNA in maternal blood)≥10 wkHigh-risk resultMost sensitive screen (~99% DR for T21, FPR <0.1%), but PPV depends on prevalence, so it is still a screen. False positives: confined placental mosaicism, vanishing twin, maternal mosaicism/CNV, maternal malignancy. "No-call" results correlate with aneuploidy and obesity → offer diagnostic testing.
First-trimester combined11 0/7–13 6/7 wk↑ NT, ↓ PAPP-A, ↑ β-hCGNT ≥3.0 mm (or ≥99th percentile) → offer diagnostic testing (microarray) + fetal echo, even with normal cfDNA
Quadruple screen15–22 wk↓ AFP, ↑ hCG, ↓ estriol, ↑ inhibin A ("HI" = hCG + inhibin high)T18: ↓ AFP, ↓ hCG, ↓ estriol, normal inhibin
MSAFP (for open NTD and ventral wall defects)15–22 wk (best 16–18)—↑ MSAFP (≥2.0–2.5 MoM): wrong dates (most common), open NTD, gastroschisis/omphalocele, multiple gestation, fetal demise, placental abnormality. Next step: ultrasound (dating + anatomy). ↓ MSAFP: aneuploidy, overestimated GA.
CVS (diagnostic)10–13 wkKaryotype/microarrayEarlier results. Limb reduction if <10 wk. Placental mosaicism (~1%).
Amniocentesis (diagnostic)≥15 wkKaryotype/microarray; AF-AFP + acetylcholinesterase for NTDLoss risk ~0.1–0.3%. Rh-negative → RhIG after either procedure.
Exam trap: A positive cfDNA or abnormal serum screen is never the basis for termination or for telling the patient "your baby has Down syndrome." The next step is genetic counseling + diagnostic testing (CVS now or amniocentesis at ≥15 wk). If US shows a structural anomaly, the diagnostic test of choice is chromosomal microarray.

sections.heading: Obstetrics 2 · Diabetes in Pregnancy
sections.html:
StepDetails (ACOG)
Universal screening at 24–28 wkTwo-step (most US practices): 50-g 1-h glucose challenge (non-fasting) → if ≥130, 135, or 140 mg/dL (institution-specific cutoff) → 100-g 3-h OGTT. GDM = ≥2 abnormal values (Carpenter–Coustan: fasting 95, 1 h 180, 2 h 155, 3 h 140). One-step (IADPSG): 75-g 2-h OGTT; GDM if ≥1 value: fasting ≥92, 1 h ≥180, 2 h ≥153.
Early screenFirst visit if high risk (above). Overt diabetes if A1c ≥6.5%, fasting ≥126, or random ≥200 with symptoms.
Treatment targetsFasting <95, 1-h postprandial <140, or 2-h postprandial <120 mg/dL
A1GDM (diet-controlled)Medical nutrition therapy + exercise; deliver 39 0/7–40 6/7 wk
A2GDM (needs medication)Insulin is first-line (does not cross the placenta). Metformin is a reasonable alternative if the patient declines or cannot use insulin (crosses the placenta; long-term offspring data are limited; ↑ risk of later childhood weight). Glyburide is no longer preferred (neonatal hypoglycemia, macrosomia). Antenatal testing (NST ± AFI) from 32 wk. Deliver 39 0/7–39 6/7 wk (earlier if poorly controlled).
MacrosomiaOffer cesarean if EFW ≥4500 g with diabetes (≥5000 g without). Shoulder dystocia: McRoberts + suprapubic pressure first.
PostpartumStop treatment. 75-g 2-h OGTT at 4–12 wk postpartum, then screen every 1–3 y for life (50% lifetime T2DM risk).
Pregestational DMPreconception A1c <6.5% (anomaly risk tracks A1c). Folic acid, aspirin from 12 wk, baseline retinal exam, creatinine/urine protein, TSH (T1DM), ECG if vascular disease. Fetal echo (CHD is the most common anomaly; caudal regression is the most specific; NTDs). Stop ACE inhibitors/statins. Insulin requirements rise sharply in the second and third trimesters. A sudden fall in requirement can signal placental insufficiency.

sections.heading: Obstetrics 3 · Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy
sections.html:
DisorderDefinitionDelivery timing
Chronic HTNBP ≥140/90 before pregnancy or before 20 wk (or persisting >12 wk postpartum)38 0/7–39 6/7 wk if no meds; 37 0/7–39 6/7 if on meds. Treat to <140/90 (CHAP trial; ACOG 2022).
Gestational HTNNew BP ≥140/90 on 2 readings ≥4 h apart after 20 wk, no proteinuria or end-organ signs37 0/7 wk
Preeclampsia without severe featuresGestational HTN + proteinuria (≥300 mg/24 h, protein/creatinine ≥0.3, or dipstick 2+ if others unavailable). Or HTN + new end-organ dysfunction even without proteinuria.37 0/7 wk. Before then: twice-weekly BP/labs, antenatal testing.
Preeclampsia with severe featuresAny of: SBP ≥160 or DBP ≥110 on 2 occasions ≥4 h apart (can confirm within minutes to allow timely treatment); platelets <100,000; AST/ALT ≥2× ULN or severe persistent RUQ/epigastric pain; creatinine >1.1 mg/dL or doubling; pulmonary edema; new headache unresponsive to medication; visual disturbances. (Proteinuria amount and FGR are not severe features.)≥34 0/7 wk: deliver after maternal stabilization. <34 wk and stable: expectant management in a tertiary center with betamethasone. Deliver at any GA if uncontrollable BP, eclampsia, pulmonary edema, DIC/HELLP, abruption, nonreassuring fetal status, or fetal demise.
HELLP syndromeHemolysis (LDH ≥600 IU/L, schistocytes, ↑ bilirubin), Elevated LFTs (AST/ALT ≥2× ULN), Low platelets (<100,000). HTN may be mild or absent. RUQ pain, nausea/malaise.Deliver after maternal stabilization at ≥34 wk, and generally at <34 wk too (a delay of 24–48 h for steroids only if mother and fetus are stable). Complications: hepatic hematoma/rupture, DIC, abruption, AKI.
EclampsiaNew-onset tonic-clonic seizure in a preeclamptic patient (can occur postpartum or without prior HTN)ABCs, left lateral position, magnesium sulfate, BP control, then delivery once stable (eclampsia alone does not require cesarean)
Postpartum preeclampsiaUp to 6 wk postpartum; headache is the most common symptomMg + antihypertensives. BP check 72 h after discharge (severe) or 7–10 d.
DrugUseKey cautions
IV labetalol (20 → 40 → 80 mg q10 min)Acute severe HTN (≥160/110 persisting ≥15 min). Treat within 30–60 min. Target ~140–150/90–100.Avoid in asthma, heart block, decompensated HF, bradycardia. Neonatal bradycardia/hypoglycemia.
IV hydralazine (5–10 mg q20 min)Acute severe HTNReflex tachycardia, maternal hypotension → fetal distress
Oral immediate-release nifedipine (10–20 mg)Acute severe HTN when no IV access; also maintenance (ER)Headache, tachycardia
Labetalol PO, nifedipine ERFirst-line for chronic HTN in pregnancy (methyldopa is now second-line)Contraindicated: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, direct renin inhibitors (fetal renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, skull hypoplasia). Avoid atenolol (FGR).
Magnesium sulfateSeizure prophylaxis in preeclampsia with severe features/HELLP (intrapartum and 24 h postpartum); treatment of eclampsia. Load 4–6 g IV over 15–20 min, then 1–2 g/h. If no IV: 10 g IM (5 g each buttock). Also used for fetal neuroprotection <32 wk.Renal excretion: reduce dose if oliguria or ↑ creatinine. Toxicity sequence: loss of patellar reflexes (~7–10 mEq/L) → respiratory depression (~10–13) → cardiac arrest (>25). Monitor reflexes, RR, urine output. Toxicity: stop the infusion + IV calcium gluconate 1 g. Contraindicated in myasthenia gravis. Not an antihypertensive.
High-yield: Differentiate HELLP from acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP: third trimester, nausea/vomiting, hypoglycemia, ↑ ammonia, ↑ bilirubin, coagulopathy with ↓ fibrinogen, AKI; fetal LCHAD deficiency, so test the newborn; deliver) and from TTP/aHUS (severe thrombocytopenia with neuro/renal findings, normal or only mildly ↑ LFTs, ADAMTS13 <10%; plasma exchange; does not resolve with delivery). Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy: pruritus of palms/soles without rash, ↑ bile acids (≥10 μmol/L); ursodiol; deliver between 36 and 39 wk depending on bile acid level (36 wk if ≥100 μmol/L, because of stillbirth risk).

sections.heading: Obstetrics 4 · Antepartum Hemorrhage (Second/Third Trimester)
sections.html:
ConditionPresentationRisk factorsManagement
Placenta previaPainless bright-red bleeding (often post-coital or "sentinel" bleed), soft non-tender uterus, malpresentation; fetus usually finePrior cesarean/uterine surgery, multiparity, AMA, smoking, multiple gestation, IVFNo digital cervical exam until previa is excluded by ultrasound (transabdominal, then transvaginal, which is safe). A low-lying placenta or previa at 18–22 wk → repeat US at ~32 wk (most resolve). Stable: pelvic rest, steroids if <34 wk, anti-D if Rh−. Planned cesarean at 36 0/7–37 6/7 wk. Emergent cesarean for heavy bleeding or fetal compromise. Prior cesarean + anterior previa → evaluate for accreta.
Placental abruptionPainful bleeding (can be concealed), tender hypertonic uterus with frequent small contractions, fetal distress/demise, DIC (↓ fibrinogen), Couvelaire uterusHypertension/preeclampsia (most common), cocaine, smoking, trauma (MVC), PPROM/chorioamnionitis, rapid decompression (polyhydramnios), prior abruption, thrombophiliaClinical diagnosis (US is insensitive). Two large-bore IVs, CBC, fibrinogen, coags, type & cross, continuous monitoring. Maternal instability or nonreassuring FHR with a live fetus → emergent cesarean. Fetal demise + stable mother → vaginal delivery. Mild, stable, preterm → expectant with steroids. After maternal trauma, monitor ≥4–6 h; Kleihauer–Betke + RhIG if Rh−.
Vasa previaPainless bleeding at rupture of membranes, then fetal bradycardia or sinusoidal pattern (fetal exsanguination); the mother is stableVelamentous cord insertion, succenturiate/bilobed placenta, low-lying placenta, IVF, multiplesEmergent cesarean. If diagnosed prenatally (color Doppler TVUS) → planned cesarean at 34 0/7–37 0/7 wk before labor/ROM. Neonatal transfusion.
Uterine ruptureSudden abdominal pain, prolonged fetal bradycardia (most common sign), loss of fetal station, cessation of contractions, palpable fetal parts, maternal shockTOLAC (prior classical/T incision is highest risk), prior myomectomy into the cavity, oxytocin/prostaglandins in a scarred uterus, traumaEmergent laparotomy and delivery; repair or hysterectomy. Misoprostol is contraindicated for ripening in TOLAC. TOLAC candidates: 1–2 prior low transverse incisions.
Placenta accreta spectrum (accreta / increta / percreta)Often asymptomatic antenatally; massive hemorrhage at attempted placental removalPrevia + prior cesarean (risk rises with each cesarean), Asherman, prior uterine surgeryUS/MRI diagnosis. Planned cesarean hysterectomy at 34 0/7–35 6/7 wk at a center of excellence, with the placenta left in situ
Exam trap: In any third-trimester bleed, the first actions are maternal stabilization + fetal monitoring + ultrasound for placental location. A speculum exam is permitted. A digital exam is forbidden until previa is excluded. "Painless bleeding + fetal distress after ROM" is vasa previa (fetal blood), not previa. The Apt test distinguishes fetal from maternal hemoglobin.

sections.heading: Obstetrics 5 · Preterm Labor and PPROM
sections.html:
InterventionIndication / timingDetails
Diagnosis of preterm labor20 0/7–36 6/7 wk: regular contractions + cervical change (or dilation ≥2 cm)TVUS cervical length (<20 mm high risk; ≥30 mm low risk). Fetal fibronectin (22–34 wk; strong negative predictive value). Rule out infection (UA/culture, GBS, GC/CT).
Antenatal corticosteroids24 0/7–33 6/7 wk if delivery is likely within 7 d (consider from 22 0/7 wk if resuscitation is planned). Late preterm 34 0/7–36 6/7: single course if no prior steroids and delivery risk within 7 d (use caution in pregestational diabetes because of neonatal hypoglycemia).Betamethasone 12 mg IM ×2, 24 h apart (or dexamethasone 6 mg IM q12h ×4). One rescue course if <34 wk and ≥7–14 d since the first. ↓ RDS, IVH, NEC, neonatal death.
Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection<32 0/7 wk when delivery is anticipated↓ cerebral palsy
Tocolysis24–34 wk, short term (≤48 h) only, to allow steroids and transferNifedipine (hypotension, headache). Indomethacin <32 wk only (premature ductus closure, oligohydramnios). Terbutaline (tachycardia, hyperglycemia; boxed warning against >48–72 h). Maintenance tocolysis is ineffective. Contraindications: IUFD, lethal anomaly, nonreassuring FHR, severe preeclampsia/eclampsia, hemorrhage with instability, intraamniotic infection, maternal contraindication to the drug.
GBS prophylaxisPreterm labor with unknown or positive GBSIV penicillin until GBS-negative or labor stops
Prevention: history of spontaneous preterm birthSerial TVUS cervical length 16–24 wkCerclage if cervical length <25 mm before 24 wk. 17-α-hydroxyprogesterone caproate (Makena) was withdrawn from the US market in 2023. Some clinicians offer vaginal progesterone.
Prevention: no prior PTB, short cervixCervical length ≤20 mm at ≤24 wkVaginal progesterone
Cervical insufficiencyPainless second-trimester dilation/lossHistory-indicated cerclage at 12–14 wk (≥1 prior painless 2nd-trimester loss). Physical-exam-indicated cerclage for painless dilation in the 2nd trimester.
PPROM (ROM before labor and before 37 wk)Management
DiagnosisSterile speculum exam: pooling, nitrazine (alkaline, pH >6.5), ferning. US for oligohydramnios. Placental α-microglobulin-1 (AmniSure) if equivocal. Avoid digital exams (they shorten latency and raise infection risk).
≥34 0/7 wkDeliver (induction). GBS prophylaxis as indicated.
24 0/7–33 6/7 wkExpectant management in hospital: latency antibiotics (IV ampicillin + erythromycin ×48 h, then oral amoxicillin + erythromycin ×5 d; azithromycin is an accepted substitute), betamethasone, magnesium if <32 wk and delivery imminent, GBS culture/prophylaxis. No tocolysis. Deliver at 34 0/7 wk, or earlier for infection, abruption, labor, or nonreassuring status.
<23–24 wk (periviable)Counsel on outcomes (pulmonary hypoplasia); expectant vs induction; antibiotics may be offered from 20 wk
Intraamniotic infection (chorioamnionitis)Maternal fever (≥39.0 °C once, or 38.0–38.9 °C persistent) + fetal tachycardia, maternal WBC >15k, or purulent fluid. Uterine tenderness and foul fluid are late. Treat with ampicillin + gentamicin (add clindamycin or metronidazole after cesarean). Deliver: chorioamnionitis is an indication for delivery, not for cesarean by itself. Neonatal sepsis evaluation.

sections.heading: Obstetrics 6 · Labor, Delivery, and Fetal Heart Rate Monitoring
sections.html:
StageDefinitionNormal / abnormal (ACOG–SMFM 2014 "safe prevention of primary cesarean")
Stage 1 latentOnset of regular contractions → ~6 cmProlonged latent phase (>20 h nulliparous, >14 h multiparous) is not an indication for cesarean. Use therapeutic rest or oxytocin/amniotomy.
Stage 1 active≥6 cm → complete dilationActive-phase arrest: ≥6 cm with ruptured membranes and no cervical change for ≥4 h with adequate contractions (≥200 Montevideo units by IUPC) or ≥6 h with inadequate contractions despite oxytocin → cesarean. Inadequate contractions without arrest → oxytocin first.
Stage 2Complete dilation → delivery of the infantArrest: nulliparous ≥3 h of pushing, multiparous ≥2 h (longer may be appropriate with epidural or with progress). Options: operative vaginal delivery (if criteria met) or cesarean.
Stage 3Delivery of the infant → placentaNormal ≤30 min. Signs of separation: gush of blood, cord lengthening, fundus rises and becomes globular. Active management (oxytocin after delivery, controlled cord traction, uterine massage) ↓ PPH. Retained >30 min → manual removal.
Stage 4First 1–2 h postpartumHighest PPH risk; monitor vitals and fundal tone

Cardinal movements: engagement, descent, flexion, internal rotation, extension, external rotation (restitution), expulsion. Bishop score (dilation, effacement, station, consistency, position) ≥8 = favorable, so oxytocin ± amniotomy will likely succeed. Unfavorable → cervical ripening (misoprostol, dinoprostone, Foley balloon). ACOG supports elective induction at 39 wk in low-risk nulliparas (ARRIVE trial: ↓ cesarean) and recommends induction by 41 0/7–42 0/7 wk. Operative vaginal delivery requires full dilation, ruptured membranes, engaged head (station ≥0), known fetal position, adequate analgesia, empty bladder, and an indication. Shoulder dystocia: call for help, McRoberts maneuver + suprapubic pressure first, then deliver the posterior arm or do rotational maneuvers. Never apply fundal pressure. Brachial plexus (Erb C5–C6 "waiter's tip") injury. Breech: offer external cephalic version at ≥37 0/7 wk (RhIG if Rh−). Cord prolapse: elevate the presenting part manually, use knee-chest/Trendelenburg position, and do an emergent cesarean. Epidural hypotension: IV fluids + phenylephrine/ephedrine. Post-dural puncture headache: epidural blood patch if conservative measures fail.

[[figure:ch11-fig05]]
FHR elementDefinitionCauses / meaning
BaselineMean FHR over 10 min: 110–160 bpmTachycardia >160: maternal fever/intraamniotic infection (most common), hyperthyroidism, β-agonists, fetal anemia/hypoxia, arrhythmia. Bradycardia <110: hypoxia, cord prolapse, uterine rupture, congenital heart block (maternal anti-Ro/SSA), maternal β-blockers, hypothermia.
VariabilityAbsent (undetectable), minimal (≤5), moderate (6–25), marked (>25)Moderate variability reliably excludes ongoing metabolic acidemia. Minimal: fetal sleep (≤40 min), opioids, magnesium, acidemia.
Accelerations≥15 bpm for ≥15 s (≥32 wk); ≥10 × 10 s before 32 wkReassuring. Reactive NST = ≥2 accelerations in 20 min. Scalp stimulation → an acceleration implies pH >7.20.
Prolonged deceleration≥15 bpm below baseline for ≥2 min but <10 minCord prolapse, rupture, tachysystole, epidural hypotension, rapid descent. Check the cervix.
SinusoidalSmooth sine wave, 3–5 cycles/min, ≥20 minSevere fetal anemia (alloimmunization, fetomaternal hemorrhage, vasa previa, parvovirus) → Category III
Tachysystole>5 contractions/10 min averaged over 30 minReduce/stop oxytocin. Terbutaline if FHR changes.
Intrauterine resuscitation, in order (for Category II/III): (1) Stop oxytocin/remove ripening agent; (2) maternal repositioning (left or right lateral); (3) IV fluid bolus; correct epidural hypotension (phenylephrine/ephedrine); (4) treat tachysystole (terbutaline); (5) amnioinfusion for recurrent variable decelerations; (6) cervical exam (prolapse, rapid descent). Supplemental O2 is no longer routinely recommended unless the mother is hypoxemic (ACOG 2022). If Category III persists → expedited delivery (operative vaginal if fully dilated and criteria met, otherwise cesarean).

sections.heading: Obstetrics 7 · Postpartum Hemorrhage
sections.html:
Definition (ACOG): cumulative blood loss ≥1000 mL, or blood loss with signs/symptoms of hypovolemia, within 24 h of birth, regardless of route. Primary PPH occurs ≤24 h; secondary PPH occurs 24 h–12 wk (retained products, subinvolution, endometritis, vWD). Uterine atony causes ~70–80%. Risk factors for atony: overdistension (macrosomia, twins, polyhydramnios), prolonged or precipitous labor, oxytocin exposure, chorioamnionitis, magnesium, halogenated anesthetics, fibroids, grand multiparity, prior PPH.

[[figure:ch11-fig06]]
UterotonicDose / routeAvoid inSide effects
Oxytocin (first-line)10 U IM or 10–40 U in 500–1000 mL IV infusion— (avoid an undiluted rapid IV bolus)Hypotension (bolus), water intoxication/hyponatremia (ADH-like) at high doses
Methylergonovine (ergot)0.2 mg IM q2–4 hHypertension, preeclampsia, CAD, Raynaud, HIV protease inhibitors/CYP3A4 inhibitorsSevere HTN, vasospasm, stroke
Carboprost (15-methyl PGF2α)0.25 mg IM (or intramyometrial) q15–90 min, ≤8 dosesAsthma (bronchospasm); caution in hepatic, renal, cardiac diseaseDiarrhea, fever, nausea, bronchospasm
Misoprostol (PGE1)600–1000 μg PO/SL/rectal once— (safe in HTN and asthma)Fever, shivering, diarrhea
Tranexamic acid (antifibrinolytic, not a uterotonic)1 g IV over 10 min within 3 h of birth; repeat once after 30 min if bleeding continuesActive thromboembolism↓ death from bleeding (WOMAN trial); no benefit if started after 3 h
Exam trap: Uterine inversion (fundus not palpable abdominally, a mass at the introitus, shock out of proportion to blood loss, often after excess cord traction on a fundal placenta). Next step: stop uterotonics, call for help, and manually replace the uterus immediately with the placenta still attached. Use uterine relaxants (terbutaline, nitroglycerin, or general anesthesia) if a constriction ring prevents replacement. Give oxytocin only after reposition. Amniotic fluid embolism: sudden hypoxia + hypotension/arrest + DIC during labor or immediately after delivery. Management is supportive (CPR, perimortem cesarean if ≥20 wk and no ROSC within 4 min, massive transfusion).

sections.heading: Obstetrics 8 · Rh(D) Alloimmunization
sections.html:
Situation (Rh-negative, antibody screen negative = unsensitized)Action
RoutineRhIG 300 μg IM at 28 wk (after repeat antibody screen), and again within 72 h of delivery if the newborn is Rh(D)-positive (or unknown). Fetal RhD genotyping by cfDNA can identify Rh-negative fetuses and avoid unnecessary RhIG where available.
Sensitizing eventsSpontaneous/induced abortion, ectopic, molar pregnancy, amniocentesis/CVS, antepartum bleeding, abdominal trauma, ECV, fetal death → RhIG. (ACOG 2024 permits forgoing RhIG for spontaneous or induced abortion <12 0/7 wk. When given in the first trimester, 50 μg is sufficient.)
Dose quantification300 μg covers ~30 mL fetal whole blood (15 mL fetal RBCs). After delivery or major bleeding/trauma, a rosette screen → Kleihauer–Betke (or flow cytometry) determines whether additional vials are needed.
Already sensitized (anti-D positive)RhIG is useless. Determine paternal genotype (or fetal cfDNA RhD). Serial maternal titers every 2–4 wk. At or above the critical titer (usually 1:16; 1:8 for anti-Kell, and titers are unreliable for Kell) → serial middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity Doppler every 1–2 wk from ~16–18 wk. MCA-PSV >1.5 MoM → cordocentesis (PUBS) ± intrauterine transfusion. A previously affected pregnancy → go straight to MCA Doppler. Deliver at 37–38 wk (earlier if needed).
Clinical cluesFetal anemia → hydrops (ascites, pleural/pericardial effusion, skin edema), sinusoidal FHR. Neonate: early jaundice, positive DAT. ABO incompatibility (mother O) can affect the first pregnancy, is milder, and is not prevented by RhIG. Anti-Lewis antibodies (IgM) are harmless ("Lewis lives, Kell kills").

sections.heading: Obstetrics 9 · Early Pregnancy: Ectopic Pregnancy and Pregnancy Loss
sections.html:
Every woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain or bleeding gets a β-hCG. If positive, do a transvaginal ultrasound. An intrauterine gestational sac with a yolk sac confirms IUP (heterotopic risk is high only with IVF). Ectopic risk factors: prior ectopic (strongest), tubal surgery/sterilization, PID/chlamydia, IVF, smoking, IUD in place at conception (IUDs lower absolute risk, but a pregnancy that occurs with one is more likely ectopic), age >35.

ScenarioNext step
Hemodynamically unstable, peritoneal signs, or free fluid in Morison pouchResuscitate → surgery (laparoscopy if feasible, laparotomy if unstable). Salpingectomy is preferred if the other tube is normal; salpingostomy preserves the tube but needs hCG follow-up (persistent trophoblast).
Stable, TVUS shows an adnexal mass and no IUPMedical (methotrexate) vs surgical, according to criteria
Stable, pregnancy of unknown location (no IUP, no adnexal mass)Repeat hCG in 48 h (± TVUS). A viable IUP usually rises ≥35–50% in 48 h. If hCG is above the discriminatory zone (up to ~3,500 mIU/mL) and no IUP is seen, the pregnancy is nonviable/ectopic until proven otherwise. A plateauing hCG → uterine aspiration (villi = failed IUP; no villi with persistent hCG = ectopic).
Methotrexate (single-dose 50 mg/m² IM)Details
CandidatesHemodynamically stable, unruptured, reliable for follow-up, no contraindication. Best when hCG is <5,000 mIU/mL, there is no embryonic cardiac activity, and the mass is <3.5–4 cm.
Absolute contraindicationsIntrauterine pregnancy, breastfeeding, immunodeficiency, moderate–severe anemia/leukopenia/thrombocytopenia, hepatic or renal disease, active pulmonary disease, peptic ulcer, MTX sensitivity, ruptured ectopic/instability
Baseline labsCBC, creatinine, LFTs, blood type/Rh
Follow-uphCG on days 4 and 7. A ≥15% fall from day 4 to day 7 = response, then weekly until undetectable. A fall of <15% → second dose or surgery. Pain around days 3–7 is common ("separation pain"), but suspect rupture if severe.
CounselingAvoid folic acid/prenatal vitamins, NSAIDs, alcohol, sun exposure, and intercourse until resolved. Delay conception ≥3 months.
Early pregnancy loss typeOsFindingsManagement
ThreatenedClosedBleeding, viable IUPExpectant (most continue)
InevitableOpenNo tissue passed yetExpectant, misoprostol, or aspiration
IncompleteOpenSome products passed, some retainedAspiration (or misoprostol/expectant if stable)
CompleteClosedAll tissue passed; empty uterus; falling hCGConfirm hCG declines to zero (to exclude ectopic)
Missed (early pregnancy loss)ClosedCRL ≥7 mm without cardiac activity, or mean sac diameter ≥25 mm without an embryoExpectant, mifepristone 200 mg + misoprostol 800 μg vaginal 24 h later (more effective than misoprostol alone), or uterine aspiration
SepticUsually openFever, purulent discharge, uterine tendernessBroad-spectrum IV antibiotics + prompt uterine evacuation

Recurrent pregnancy loss (≥2 losses): antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2GPI ×2, 12 wk apart; APS → prophylactic heparin + low-dose aspirin), parental karyotypes (balanced translocation), uterine cavity evaluation (septum → hysteroscopic resection), TSH, A1c. Gestational trophoblastic disease: complete mole (46,XX paternal, "snowstorm," very high hCG, hyperemesis, early preeclampsia <20 wk, hyperthyroidism, theca-lutein cysts) → suction curettage, then weekly hCG to undetectable and contraception during follow-up. Persistent or rising hCG → GTN → methotrexate. Choriocarcinoma metastasizes to the lungs.

sections.heading: Obstetrics 10 · Teratogens and Medications in Pregnancy and Lactation
sections.html:
The FDA's 2015 Pregnancy and Lactation Labeling Rule replaced the A/B/C/D/X letter categories with narrative risk summaries. Exam questions now ask "which drug is safest?" or "which drug should be switched?" The window of maximal organogenesis is ~3–8 weeks after conception (5–10 wk from LMP). Exposure in the first 2 weeks after conception is "all or none." Ionizing radiation <50 mGy (5 rad) has not been associated with anomalies, so most diagnostic imaging (including CT for PE or trauma) should not be withheld.

TeratogenEffect
ACE inhibitors / ARBs / direct renin inhibitorsFetal renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, skull ossification defects, IUGR (2nd/3rd trimester especially). Switch to labetalol or nifedipine before conception or once pregnancy is known.
ValproateNTDs (spina bifida, ~1–2%), cardiac, cleft, reduced IQ and autism. Avoid in people who could become pregnant.
Carbamazepine / phenytoinNTDs, craniofacial defects, fingernail hypoplasia (fetal hydantoin syndrome: hypoplastic distal phalanges, cleft, microcephaly)
Isotretinoin, acitretin, high-dose vitamin ACraniofacial, CNS, cardiac, thymic defects. Isotretinoin has the iPLEDGE REMS (2 contraceptive methods, monthly pregnancy tests).
WarfarinNasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses (6–12 wk), CNS hemorrhage later. Switch to LMWH. (Some mechanical-valve patients stay on warfarin if dose ≤5 mg/d after counseling.)
Methimazole (first trimester)Aplasia cutis, choanal/esophageal atresia. Use PTU in the first trimester (hepatotoxic), then switch to methimazole for the 2nd/3rd trimester.
LithiumEbstein anomaly (absolute risk low). May be continued with counseling, fetal echo, and level monitoring (clearance rises in pregnancy and falls abruptly postpartum).
Methotrexate, mycophenolate, leflunomide, thalidomideAbortion/multiple anomalies; mycophenolate: ear/cleft/limb; thalidomide: phocomelia. Leflunomide needs a cholestyramine washout.
Misoprostol (failed abortion)Möbius sequence, limb defects
TetracyclinesTooth discoloration, enamel hypoplasia, bone growth inhibition (after ~15 wk)
AminoglycosidesOtotoxicity (CN VIII)
FluoroquinolonesCartilage damage (animal data). Generally avoid.
TMP-SMXFolate antagonism (1st trimester, NTD); kernicterus near term
NSAIDs≥20 wk: fetal renal dysfunction/oligohydramnios (FDA 2020). ≥30 wk: premature ductus closure. Low-dose aspirin is safe.
DES (historic)Clear cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina, T-shaped uterus, cervical insufficiency in daughters
Androgens, danazolVirilization of female fetus
Alcohol, cocaine, tobaccoFAS; abruption/IUGR/vasoconstriction (cocaine); IUGR, previa, abruption, PTB, SIDS (tobacco)
Maternal conditionsDiabetes (caudal regression, CHD, NTD), PKU (microcephaly, CHD), obesity (NTD), hyperthermia (NTD)
Condition in pregnancyPreferredAvoid / note
HypertensionLabetalol, nifedipine (methyldopa second-line)ACEi/ARB, atenolol
DiabetesInsulin (metformin is an alternative)Most other oral agents; SGLT2i, GLP-1 RA (stop GLP-1 RAs ≥2 months before conception)
Hyperthyroidism (Graves)PTU in the 1st trimester → methimazole after; β-blocker for symptomsRadioactive iodine (contraindicated). Thyroidectomy only if needed, best in the 2nd trimester. Gestational transient thyrotoxicosis (hCG-mediated, hyperemesis) needs no antithyroid drug.

AsthmaContinue ICS (budesonide best studied), SABA, LABAUndertreatment is the bigger risk
Depression / anxietySSRIs (sertraline commonly chosen); continue effective therapyParoxetine (cardiac defects; avoid initiating). Late-pregnancy SSRIs → neonatal adaptation syndrome, small PPHN risk.
Nausea / hyperemesisPyridoxine ± doxylamine first-line → antihistamines, metoclopramide, ondansetron → IV fluids (thiamine before dextrose) → steroids (after 10 wk)Hyperemesis: weight loss >5%, ketonuria, hypokalemia
Asymptomatic bacteriuria / cystitisCephalexin, amoxicillin(-clavulanate), fosfomycin, nitrofurantoin (avoid 1st trimester if alternatives exist, and avoid at term because of neonatal hemolysis in G6PD)Fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines, TMP-SMX (1st trimester/near term). Test of cure after treatment. Pyelonephritis → admit, IV ceftriaxone.
Pain / feverAcetaminophen (ACOG continues to recommend it when indicated; 2025 federal statements on an autism association did not change ACOG guidance)NSAIDs ≥20 wk
HIVContinue/start ART (dolutegravir-based regimens preferred); intrapartum IV zidovudine if VL >1000 copies/mL; scheduled cesarean at 38 wk if VL >1000Infant ARV prophylaxis (zidovudine; multidrug if high risk)
Hepatitis BTenofovir from 28–32 wk if HBV DNA >200,000 IU/mL; infant HepB vaccine + HBIG within 12 hBreastfeeding OK; cesarean not indicated for HBV
Opioid use disorderBuprenorphine or methadoneMedically supervised withdrawal is not recommended (relapse, overdose)
Lactation: compatible (continue breastfeeding)Lactation: avoid / contraindicated
Most antibiotics (penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides), acetaminophen, ibuprofen, sertraline and most SSRIs, levothyroxine, insulin, metformin, labetalol, nifedipine, enalapril/captopril (ACEi are acceptable postpartum), heparin/LMWH, warfarin, prednisone, most antiepileptics (monitor infant), inhaled drugs, progestin-only contraception, IUDsCodeine and tramadol (ultrarapid CYP2D6 metabolizers → infant opioid toxicity/death; FDA warning). Chemotherapy, radioactive iodine, amiodarone, ergots, bromocriptine/cabergoline (suppress lactation), lithium (relative; monitor infant levels), methotrexate. Combined estrogen methods in the first weeks (may reduce supply; also VTE risk).
True contraindications to breastfeeding: classic galactosemia in the infant; maternal HTLV-1/2; untreated brucellosis; Ebola; maternal illicit drug use such as PCP or cocaine; active untreated TB (avoid direct contact until ≥2 wk of treatment, but expressed milk is OK); HSV lesions on the breast (temporarily, that side). HIV in the US: formula is still recommended, but current DHHS/AAP guidance supports shared decision-making for people on ART with a sustained undetectable viral load who want to breastfeed. Hepatitis B and C (unless nipples bleed), maternal fever, mastitis, and CMV in term infants are not contraindications.

Postpartum and other high-yield obstetric problems

ProblemCluesManagement
Postpartum bluesUp to 85%; days 2–3, resolves by 2 wk; mood lability, no functional impairmentReassurance, support, follow-up
Postpartum depressionMajor depression with peripartum onset (during pregnancy or within 4 wk of delivery by DSM; clinically up to 12 months); screen with EPDS/PHQ-9Psychotherapy ± SSRI (sertraline is compatible with breastfeeding). Zuranolone (oral, 14 days; FDA 2023) or brexanolone (IV). Ask about suicidality and thoughts of harming the infant.
Postpartum psychosisWithin 2 weeks; delusions, hallucinations, disorganization; often bipolar disorderPsychiatric emergency → hospitalize (risk of infanticide/suicide); antipsychotic + mood stabilizer; ECT if refractory
Postpartum endometritisFever, uterine tenderness, foul lochia, usually 2–3 d after delivery. Cesarean is the biggest risk factor.IV clindamycin + gentamicin until afebrile 24–48 h (add ampicillin if GBS or no response). Persistent fever despite antibiotics → imaging for abscess or septic pelvic thrombophlebitis (→ heparin).
Lactational mastitisTender, erythematous wedge, fever, flu-like symptomsContinue breastfeeding/emptying, NSAIDs, ice. Antibiotics if not improving in 12–24 h or systemic: dicloxacillin or cephalexin (TMP-SMX/clindamycin if MRSA risk). Fluctuance → US-guided aspiration/drainage of abscess.
Postpartum thyroiditisHyperthyroid 1–4 mo (painless, low RAIU), then hypothyroid 4–8 mo; anti-TPO+β-blocker for the hyperthyroid phase (no antithyroid drugs); levothyroxine if symptomatic hypothyroid
Peripartum cardiomyopathyHF with LVEF <45% in the last month of pregnancy to 5 months postpartumStandard HF therapy (no ACEi antepartum: use hydralazine/nitrates); anticoagulation if EF very low; counsel about recurrence
Multiple gestationChorionicity on first-trimester US (lambda sign = dichorionic; T sign = monochorionic)Delivery timing: di-di 38 0/7–38 6/7; mono-di 34 0/7–37 6/7; mono-mono 32 0/7–34 0/7 (cesarean). Monochorionic: twin–twin transfusion surveillance every 2 wk from 16 wk (laser ablation).
Fetal growth restrictionEFW or abdominal circumference <10th percentileUmbilical artery Doppler. Delivery: normal Doppler 38–39 wk; ↓ diastolic flow 37 wk; absent EDV 33–34 wk; reversed EDV 30–32 wk. Steroids/Mg as indicated.
Oligohydramnios (DVP <2 cm or AFI ≤5)ROM, placental insufficiency, renal agenesis/obstruction, ACEi/NSAIDs, post-termIsolated at term → deliver 36 0/7–37 6/7 wk
Polyhydramnios (DVP ≥8 cm or AFI ≥24)Diabetes, GI atresia (esophageal/duodenal), anencephaly, TTTS recipient, fetal anemiaDetailed US, glucose testing; risk of malpresentation, cord prolapse, abruption, PPH
Trauma / cardiac arrest in pregnancyAfter 20 wk, the gravid uterus compresses the IVCLeft lateral uterine displacement during CPR. Perimortem cesarean if no ROSC by 4 min (deliver by 5 min). Trauma: ≥4–6 h fetal monitoring, KB test, RhIG.
===================== GYNECOLOGY =====================

sections.heading: Gynecology 1 · Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (PALM-COEIN)
sections.html:
Structural (PALM)Non-structural (COEIN)
Polyp (intermenstrual bleeding; saline-infusion sonohysterography/hysteroscopy → hysteroscopic polypectomy)
Adenomyosis (dysmenorrhea, heavy menses, uniformly enlarged, boggy, tender uterus; MRI; LNG-IUD or hysterectomy)
Leiomyoma (heavy menses, irregular, firm, enlarged uterus, bulk symptoms; red degeneration in pregnancy)
Malignancy/hyperplasia (endometrial, cervical)		Coagulopathy (von Willebrand disease: heavy menses since menarche, PPH, epistaxis → screen in adolescents)
Ovulatory dysfunction (PCOS, thyroid, prolactin, extremes of reproductive age, stress, obesity): irregular, unpredictable bleeding
Endometrial (local endometrial dysfunction)
Iatrogenic (anticoagulants, hormonal contraception, IUD, tamoxifen, SSRIs)
Not otherwise classified (AV malformation, isthmocele, chronic endometritis)
Workup stepDetails
1. Pregnancy testAlways first (ectopic, miscarriage)
2. LabsCBC (± ferritin), TSH, prolactin if anovulatory, coagulation screen/vWF panel if heavy since menarche or bleeding history, GC/CT if at risk
3. ImagingTransvaginal ultrasound (structural causes); sonohysterography/hysteroscopy for intracavitary lesions
4. Endometrial biopsy (office)Age ≥45 with AUB; age <45 with unopposed estrogen exposure (obesity, PCOS, chronic anovulation), failed medical management, persistent AUB, or Lynch syndrome; any postmenopausal bleeding (or TVUS first)
Postmenopausal bleedingEndometrial cancer until proven otherwise (~10%). First step: TVUS (endometrial thickness ≤4 mm has >99% NPV) or EMB. Thickness >4 mm, persistent bleeding, or non-visualized endometrium → EMB. Non-diagnostic EMB with persistent bleeding → hysteroscopy with D&C.
TreatmentOptions
Acute heavy bleedingUnstable → resuscitate, IV conjugated equine estrogen 25 mg q4–6 h, intrauterine balloon tamponade, D&C (also diagnostic). Stable → high-dose combined OCP taper, high-dose oral progestin (medroxyprogesterone), or tranexamic acid (antifibrinolytic). Rule out pregnancy first.
Chronic heavy menstrual bleedingLNG-IUD 52 mg (most effective medical therapy), COCs, cyclic/continuous progestins, TXA or NSAIDs during menses (no contraception), GnRH antagonist combinations (elagolix or relugolix + E2/NETA for fibroids). Endometrial ablation only if childbearing is complete. Hysterectomy is definitive.
FibroidsAbove + myomectomy (fertility desired; hysteroscopic for submucosal), uterine artery embolization, GnRH agonist preoperatively (shrink, correct anemia), hysterectomy. Rapid growth after menopause → consider leiomyosarcoma.
EndometriosisCyclic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, deep dyspareunia, dyschezia, infertility, fixed retroverted uterus, uterosacral nodularity, "chocolate cyst" (endometrioma). Empiric NSAIDs + COCs or progestins first-line (no surgical diagnosis needed). Then GnRH agonist (with add-back) or antagonist (elagolix). Laparoscopy for diagnosis/excision if refractory or for infertility.

sections.heading: Gynecology 2 · Amenorrhea
sections.html:
Primary amenorrhea: no menses by age 15 (or 3 years after thelarche). Secondary: absence for 3 months in a previously regular woman, or 6 months if previously irregular. Pregnancy is the most common cause of secondary amenorrhea and is excluded first. The most common causes of primary amenorrhea are gonadal dysgenesis (Turner), Müllerian agenesis, and constitutional delay/hypothalamic causes.

[[figure:ch11-fig07]]
DiagnosisDistinguishing featuresTreatment
Müllerian agenesis (MRKH)46,XX, normal breasts and pubic/axillary hair, blind vaginal pouch, normal ovaries; renal/skeletal anomalies (renal US)Vaginal dilators (first-line) or vaginoplasty; IVF with gestational carrier
Complete androgen insensitivity46,XY, breasts present, scant/absent pubic and axillary hair, blind vagina, inguinal testes, male-range testosteroneGonadectomy after puberty (malignancy risk), estrogen; disclosure counseling
Functional hypothalamic amenorrheaAthletes, low energy availability, eating disorder, stress. ↓ GnRH → ↓ LH/FSH, ↓ estradiol, low BMD (female athlete triad)Increase caloric intake/reduce exercise; CBT. Transdermal estradiol + cyclic progestin if persistent (COCs do not restore bone as well)
HyperprolactinemiaGalactorrhea, headache, bitemporal hemianopia (macroadenoma). Drugs: antipsychotics (risperidone), metoclopramide, verapamil; hypothyroidism; CKD.Stop the offending drug; cabergoline (first-line) or bromocriptine; surgery if refractory
Primary ovarian insufficiency<40 y, ↑ FSH (>25–40 IU/L on 2 tests ≥4 wk apart), ↓ estradiol, hot flashes. Causes: idiopathic, chemo/radiation, autoimmune (check adrenal antibodies, TSH), Turner mosaic, Fragile X premutation.Hormone therapy (estrogen + progestin) until the average age of menopause to protect bone and cardiovascular health. Higher doses than menopausal HRT; COCs are an alternative. Fertility: donor oocytes. DEXA.
Asherman syndromeIntrauterine adhesions after D&C (especially postpartum/post-abortal) or infection. Normal hormones; no withdrawal bleed with estrogen + progestin.Hysteroscopic adhesiolysis
Sheehan syndromeAfter severe PPH: failure to lactate, amenorrhea, hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiencyReplace hormones (glucocorticoid first)
Imperforate hymen / transverse septumCyclic pelvic pain, bulging bluish membrane, hematocolposSurgical incision

sections.heading: Gynecology 3 · PCOS and Hyperandrogenism
sections.html:
Rotterdam criteria (2 of 3) after excluding mimics: (1) oligo/anovulation, (2) clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, (3) polycystic ovarian morphology on US (≥20 follicles per ovary or volume ≥10 mL; AMH can substitute in adults per the 2023 international guideline). Exclude pregnancy, thyroid disease, hyperprolactinemia, nonclassic CAH (morning 17-hydroxyprogesterone), Cushing, and androgen-secreting tumors (rapid virilization, testosterone >150–200 ng/dL → ovarian tumor; DHEAS >700 μg/dL → adrenal tumor).

PCOS goalFirst-lineAdd / alternatives
Menstrual regulation + endometrial protection (unopposed estrogen → hyperplasia/cancer)Combined hormonal contraceptionCyclic progestin or LNG-IUD if CHC is contraindicated
Hirsutism / acneCOCs (≥6 months to see effect)Spironolactone added after 6 months (requires effective contraception, since it is a feminizing teratogen), topical eflornithine, laser
Ovulation induction (fertility)Letrozole (higher live-birth rate than clomiphene)Clomiphene, gonadotropins, laparoscopic ovarian drilling, IVF. Weight loss 5–10% helps ovulation. Metformin alone is a weak ovulation inducer.
MetabolicLifestyle, weight lossScreen with 2-h 75-g OGTT (or A1c), lipids, BP, OSA, depression, MASLD. Metformin for IGT/DM; GLP-1 RA for obesity (stop before conception).

sections.heading: Gynecology 4 · Contraception (US MEC 2024 / US SPR)
sections.html:
MethodTypical-use 1st-year failureKey points
Etonogestrel implant (Nexplanon)0.1%Most effective reversible method; 3 y (data to 5 y). Irregular bleeding is the main reason for removal.
LNG-IUD (52 mg: Mirena/Liletta up to 8 y)0.1–0.4%↓ bleeding and dysmenorrhea (treats HMB, adenomyosis), endometrial protection. Also emergency contraception within 5 days (US SPR 2024).
Copper IUD (ParaGard; 10 y, effective to 12)0.8%Non-hormonal; most effective emergency contraception (within 5 days). ↑ menstrual bleeding/cramps. Avoid in Wilson disease or copper allergy.
DMPA injection (every 13–15 wk)4%Reversible ↓ BMD (boxed warning; not a reason to withhold), weight gain, delayed return to fertility (up to 10–18 months). Good for sickle cell disease and seizure disorders. Amenorrhea common.
COC pill / patch / ring7%↓ ovarian and endometrial cancer, ↓ dysmenorrhea, acne. ↑ VTE (patch > pill), HTN, hepatic adenoma, stroke in migraine with aura. Interactions: rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, oxcarbazepine, topiramate >200 mg, St John's wort. Estrogen lowers lamotrigine levels. Patch is less effective at weight ≥90 kg.
Progestin-only pill7%Norethindrone (take within 3 h of the same time); drospirenone (24-h window); norgestrel (Opill) is OTC since 2023. OK when estrogen is contraindicated or while breastfeeding.
Condom (male)13%Only method that protects against STIs
Withdrawal / fertility awareness20% / 2–23%—
Tubal sterilization / vasectomy0.5% / 0.15%Opportunistic salpingectomy ↓ ovarian cancer risk. Vasectomy: confirm azoospermia by semen analysis ~8–16 wk later. Regret is highest if done <30 y.
Category 4 for combined (estrogen-containing) methods (unacceptable health risk)Notes
Migraine with aura (any age)Migraine without aura = category 2. Use progestin-only methods, IUDs, or the implant.
Smoker aged ≥35 y and ≥15 cigarettes/day (<15/day = category 3)Any smoking <35 y = category 2
<21 days postpartum (category 3 at 21–42 d with VTE risk factors or breastfeeding)Progestin-only methods and IUDs can start immediately postpartum
History of DVT/PE (not on anticoagulation) or acute VTE; known thrombogenic mutation (factor V Leiden, prothrombin, protein C/S, antithrombin deficiency); major surgery with prolonged immobilizationCopper IUD = 1–2
BP ≥160/100 or HTN with vascular disease (140–159/90–99 or controlled HTN = category 3)—
Ischemic heart disease, stroke, complicated valvular disease, peripartum cardiomyopathy, multiple CVD risk factors—
Diabetes with nephropathy/retinopathy/neuropathy/vascular disease or >20 y duration (category 3/4)—
Current breast cancer (all hormonal methods category 4, including LNG-IUD)Copper IUD is the method of choice
SLE with positive (or unknown) antiphospholipid antibodiesCopper IUD preferred
Severe (decompensated) cirrhosis, hepatocellular adenoma, malignant hepatoma—
Emergency contraceptionWindowNotes
Copper IUD≤5 days (120 h)Most effective (>99%), unaffected by BMI, and gives ongoing contraception
LNG 52 mg IUD≤5 daysNon-inferior to copper IUD (US SPR 2024)
Ulipristal acetate 30 mg (prescription)≤5 daysMore effective than LNG pills, especially on days 4–5 and at higher BMI. Wait 5 days before starting hormonal contraception (back-up method for 7 days after).
Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg (OTC, no age limit)Best ≤72 hLess effective with BMI ≥30. Can start contraception immediately.
High-yield: A pelvic exam and Pap smear are not required before starting any hormonal contraception. Only a BP check is needed before CHC. If the provider is reasonably certain the patient is not pregnant (CDC criteria, e.g., ≤7 days after menses start, abstinent since last menses, correctly using contraception), any method can be started the same day ("quick start") with back-up as needed. Emergency contraception does not disrupt an established pregnancy.

sections.heading: Gynecology 5 · Infertility
sections.html:
Definition: no conception after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse if <35 y; 6 months if ≥35 y; evaluate immediately if >40 y or if there is a known cause (amenorrhea, known tubal disease, endometriosis, chemotherapy, male factor). Evaluate both partners at the same time. Male factor contributes in ~40–50%.

FactorTestTreatment
MaleSemen analysis (first, cheap, non-invasive): volume, count ≥16 million/mL (WHO 2021), motility, morphologyAbnormal → repeat, then urology (hormones, karyotype/Y-microdeletion, CFTR if azoospermic with CBAVD). Varicocele repair, IUI, IVF/ICSI. Exogenous testosterone causes azoospermia, so stop it.
Ovulatory (~25%)History (regular cycles = ovulatory), mid-luteal (day 21) progesterone >3 ng/mL, LH kits; TSH, prolactin. Ovarian reserve: AMH, day-3 FSH/estradiol, antral follicle count.PCOS → letrozole. Hypothalamic → pulsatile GnRH/gonadotropins. Hyperprolactinemia → cabergoline. Diminished reserve → IVF/donor oocytes.
Tubal / peritonealHysterosalpingography (or sonohysterosalpingography); laparoscopy (gold standard; endometriosis)IVF (remove or occlude hydrosalpinx before IVF, since it lowers implantation). Endometriosis → excision or IVF.
UterineUS, sonohysterography, hysteroscopyResect septum, submucosal fibroid, polyp, adhesions
UnexplainedAll normalOvarian stimulation + IUI → IVF

Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (after hCG trigger in IVF, PCOS high risk): ascites, hemoconcentration, oliguria, hyponatremia, VTE, ovarian enlargement. Treat supportively (fluids, albumin, paracentesis, prophylactic LMWH). Prevent with a GnRH-agonist trigger and freeze-all.

sections.heading: Gynecology 6 · Menopause and Hormone Therapy
sections.html:
Menopause is 12 months of amenorrhea after the final menstrual period (average age 51 in the US). It is a clinical diagnosis at ≥45 y with typical symptoms, and FSH testing is not needed. Before 40 = POI; 40–45 = early menopause.
