Symptoms: vasomotor (hot flashes, night sweats), sleep and mood disturbance, genitourinary syndrome of menopause (vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, recurrent UTI), bone loss (DEXA at ≥65, or earlier if at risk).

IssueRecommendation (NAMS/The Menopause Society 2022, ACOG)
Indications for systemic HTModerate–severe vasomotor symptoms (most effective therapy); prevention of osteoporosis in high-risk women who cannot take alternatives; POI/early menopause (until ~51)
Benefit > riskAge <60 y or within 10 y of menopause, with no contraindications ("timing hypothesis"). Individualize dose and duration; no arbitrary stop age.
RegimenIntact uterus → estrogen + progestogen (or CEE/bazedoxifene) to prevent endometrial hyperplasia/cancer. Hysterectomy → estrogen alone. Transdermal estradiol has lower VTE and stroke risk than oral (preferred with obesity, hypertriglyceridemia, migraine, or VTE risk factors).
ContraindicationsUnexplained vaginal bleeding, known/suspected breast or estrogen-dependent cancer, endometrial cancer, prior VTE/stroke/MI/CAD, active liver disease, known thrombophilia, pregnancy
WHI risksE+P: ↑ breast cancer (after ~3–5 y), VTE, stroke, CHD in older starters; ↓ fractures, colon cancer. E alone: no increase (slight decrease) in breast cancer, ↑ stroke/VTE. USPSTF: do not use HT for primary prevention of chronic conditions (grade D). In Nov 2025 the FDA announced removal of most class boxed warnings from menopausal HT labels; individualized prescribing principles are unchanged.
Non-hormonal for vasomotor symptomsSSRIs/SNRIs (paroxetine 7.5 mg is FDA-approved; venlafaxine, escitalopram), gabapentin, oxybutynin, clonidine, CBT. Fezolinetant (NK3 receptor antagonist, 2023; check LFTs because of a liver-injury boxed warning) and elinzanetant (NK1/NK3 antagonist, FDA-approved 2025). With tamoxifen, avoid paroxetine/fluoxetine (CYP2D6 inhibition); prefer venlafaxine.
Genitourinary syndromeMoisturizers/lubricants → low-dose vaginal estrogen (minimal systemic absorption; no progestogen needed), vaginal DHEA (prasterone), ospemifene

sections.heading: Gynecology 7 · Cervical Cancer Screening and Management
sections.html:
More than 95% of cervical cancer is caused by persistent high-risk HPV (types 16 and 18 cause ~70%). Squamous cell carcinoma arises at the transformation zone. Risk factors: early sexual debut, multiple partners, smoking, immunosuppression/HIV, no screening (the most important risk factor in the US). HPV vaccination is routine at 11–12 y (from 9) and catch-up through 26 y. Adults 27–45 y get it by shared decision. Vaccinated people are screened the same way.

[[figure:ch11-fig08]]
Colposcopy / histology resultManagement
CIN1 (LSIL histology)Observe: repeat HPV-based testing in 1 y (regresses in most)
CIN2Treatment (excision) preferred. Observation acceptable in young patients concerned about future pregnancy (cervical insufficiency/PTB risk after excision).
CIN3 / AISExcision (LEEP or cold-knife cone; AIS: cold-knife cone, hysterectomy after childbearing). After treatment: HPV-based testing at 6 mo, then annually until 3 negatives, then q3y for ≥25 y.
Invasive cancerFIGO 2018 staging (imaging/pathology). IA1 → cone or simple hysterectomy. IB–IIA (small) → radical hysterectomy + nodes (or radiation). Locally advanced (IB3–IVA) → cisplatin-based chemoradiation. Hydronephrosis/uremia is a common cause of death in advanced disease.

sections.heading: Gynecology 8 · Adnexal Masses and Ovarian Cancer
sections.html:
Age / scenarioLikelyNext step
Premenarchal girlGerm cell tumor (teratoma, dysgerminoma), functional cyst less likelyUS + tumor markers (AFP, hCG, LDH, inhibin). Surgery for solid/complex masses (ovary-sparing).
Reproductive age, simple cystFollicular/corpus luteum cyst<5 cm: no follow-up needed. 5–10 cm: repeat US in 6–12 wk (after a menstrual cycle). Persistent, >10 cm, or complex → surgery (laparoscopic cystectomy).
Reproductive age, hemorrhagic cyst / "ground-glass" cystHemorrhagic corpus luteum vs endometrioma (chocolate cyst)Follow-up US; endometrioma → surgery if symptomatic/large
Mature cystic teratoma (dermoid)Most common ovarian neoplasm in young women. Fat, calcification (teeth), Rokitansky nodule. ↑ torsion risk.Laparoscopic cystectomy. Struma ovarii → hyperthyroidism. Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis association.
Ovarian torsionSudden severe unilateral pain, nausea/vomiting, adnexal mass (often >5 cm), pregnancy/IVF, dermoidPelvic US with Doppler (preserved flow does not rule out torsion). Emergent laparoscopy with detorsion, conserving the ovary even if it looks dusky. Remove the cyst if feasible. Do not delay for imaging if suspicion is high.
Postmenopausal massHigher malignancy riskTVUS + CA-125. Simple cyst <10 cm with normal CA-125 → serial US (O-RADS 2). Complex/solid components, ascites, ↑ CA-125, or metastases → refer to gynecologic oncology for surgical staging. Do not aspirate a suspicious mass (spillage).
Ovarian tumorMarker / feature
High-grade serous carcinoma (most common malignancy; origin in the fallopian tube fimbria)CA-125, psammoma bodies, BRCA1/2, Lynch. Omental caking, ascites, bloating, early satiety in a woman >50.
MucinousCEA/CA19-9; pseudomyxoma peritonei (rule out appendiceal primary)
Endometrioid / clear cellEndometriosis association; endometrioid can coexist with endometrial cancer
Dysgerminoma↑ LDH (± hCG); radiosensitive; the female counterpart of seminoma
Yolk sac (endodermal sinus) tumor↑ AFP, Schiller–Duval bodies, aggressive in young girls
Choriocarcinoma (non-gestational)↑ hCG
Granulosa cell tumor↑ inhibin, estrogen excess → precocious puberty, AUB/endometrial hyperplasia; Call–Exner bodies
Sertoli–LeydigAndrogens → virilization
Fibroma / thecomaMeigs syndrome (ovarian fibroma + ascites + right pleural effusion, resolves after resection)
Krukenberg tumorBilateral metastases from gastric (signet-ring) cancer
Screening: There is no screening for ovarian cancer in average-risk women (USPSTF grade D: CA-125/TVUS cause harm without mortality benefit). BRCA carriers: risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy at 35–40 y (BRCA1) or 40–45 y (BRCA2) after childbearing. COCs ↓ ovarian cancer risk ~50% with long use. Treatment of epithelial cancer: cytoreductive surgery + platinum/taxane. PARP inhibitor maintenance for BRCA/HRD tumors.

sections.heading: Gynecology 9 · Endometrial Hyperplasia and Cancer
sections.html:
ItemDetails
EpidemiologyThe most common gynecologic cancer in the US. Incidence and mortality are rising, with higher mortality in Black women (more type II).
Risk factors (unopposed estrogen)Obesity (biggest), chronic anovulation/PCOS, nulliparity, early menarche/late menopause, unopposed estrogen therapy, tamoxifen, diabetes, Lynch syndrome (endometrial cancer is often the sentinel cancer), estrogen-secreting granulosa tumor. Protective: COCs, progestins/LNG-IUD, multiparity, smoking (not advised).
Type I vs IIType I endometrioid (estrogen-driven, low grade, PTEN, good prognosis) vs Type II serous/clear cell (older, thin, atrophic background, TP53, aggressive). FIGO 2023 staging adds molecular class (POLE-mutant best; p53-abnormal worst; MMR-deficient; NSMP).
Presentation / diagnosisPostmenopausal bleeding (90%). TVUS (>4 mm abnormal) → endometrial biopsy (office pipelle). Hysteroscopy/D&C if non-diagnostic. Atypical glandular cells on Pap in women ≥35 → endometrial sampling.
Hyperplasia without atypiaProgestin therapy (LNG-IUD preferred, or oral), repeat biopsy at 3–6 months; address the estrogen source (weight loss)
Atypical hyperplasia (EIN)~40% coexisting cancer → total hysterectomy. If fertility is desired: high-dose progestin (LNG-IUD/megestrol) with biopsy every 3 mo, then hysterectomy after childbearing.
Cancer treatmentSurgical staging: total hysterectomy + bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy + sentinel lymph node mapping. Adjuvant radiation/chemo by stage and molecular class. Immunotherapy (dostarlimab, pembrolizumab) for dMMR. Universal MMR/MSI testing of all endometrial cancers (screens for Lynch).

sections.heading: Gynecology 10 · STIs, Vaginitis, and PID (CDC 2021 STI Guidelines)
sections.html:
InfectionDiagnosisTreatment
ChlamydiaNAAT (vaginal swab preferred, may be self-collected)Doxycycline 100 mg BID ×7 d. Pregnancy: azithromycin 1 g once (test of cure at 4 wk). Retest all at 3 months. Expedited partner therapy is allowed in most states.
GonorrheaNAAT; culture for susceptibility if treatment failsCeftriaxone 500 mg IM once (1 g if ≥150 kg). Add doxycycline if chlamydia is not excluded. Pharyngeal: test of cure at 7–14 d. Severe cephalosporin allergy: gentamicin 240 mg IM + azithromycin 2 g.
SyphilisTreponemal/non-treponemal screening (reverse algorithm common); darkfield for chancrePrimary, secondary, early latent: benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM once. Late latent/unknown: weekly ×3. Neurosyphilis/ocular/otic: aqueous penicillin G IV 10–14 d. Pregnancy: penicillin only; desensitize if allergic. Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction (fever, myalgia in 24 h) can trigger preterm labor.
TrichomoniasisNAAT (wet mount insensitive): motile flagellates, strawberry cervix, frothy yellow-green discharge, pH >4.5Women: metronidazole 500 mg BID ×7 d. Men: 2 g once. Treat partners; retest at 3 mo.
Bacterial vaginosisAmsel (≥3 of 4): thin gray discharge, pH >4.5, positive whiff test, clue cells; or Nugent scoreMetronidazole 500 mg BID ×7 d (or gel/clindamycin cream). Partner treatment not needed. Treat symptomatic pregnant patients. Abstaining from alcohol is no longer required (CDC 2021).
Vulvovaginal candidiasisThick white "cottage-cheese" discharge, pruritus, normal pH (≤4.5), pseudohyphae on KOHFluconazole 150 mg PO once, or topical azole (topical only in pregnancy). Recurrent (≥3/y): check glucose, HIV; weekly fluconazole ×6 mo. Oteseconazole for recurrent infection if not of reproductive potential.
Genital herpesPainful grouped vesicles/ulcers; PCR of lesionValacyclovir/acyclovir. Suppression from 36 wk in pregnancy if history; cesarean if lesions or prodrome at labor.
Chancroid / LGV / donovanosisH. ducreyi painful ulcer + suppurative nodes; LGV (L1–L3) painless ulcer → painful buboes, proctocolitis; Klebsiella granulomatis painless beefy ulcerAzithromycin or ceftriaxone (chancroid); doxycycline 21 d (LGV); azithromycin (donovanosis)
HIV preventionScreen everyone 15–65 at least once (USPSTF), plus all pregnanciesPrEP: TDF/FTC daily, TAF/FTC (not for receptive vaginal sex), injectable cabotegravir q2mo, or lenacapavir twice yearly (FDA 2025). Doxy-PEP (200 mg within 72 h of sex) for MSM and transgender women with a bacterial STI in the past year (CDC 2024).
PIDDetails
Diagnosis (clinical)Treat empirically if a sexually active woman has pelvic/lower abdominal pain and ≥1 of: cervical motion tenderness, uterine tenderness, or adnexal tenderness. Supportive: T >38.3 °C, mucopurulent discharge, WBC on saline microscopy, ↑ ESR/CRP, positive GC/CT. Always check β-hCG.
Outpatient regimenCeftriaxone 500 mg IM once + doxycycline 100 mg PO BID ×14 d + metronidazole 500 mg PO BID ×14 d. Re-evaluate in 72 h.
Hospitalize ifSurgical emergency not excluded (appendicitis), tubo-ovarian abscess, pregnancy, severe illness/nausea/vomiting/high fever, inability to tolerate or follow oral regimen, no response to oral therapy in 72 h
Inpatient regimenCeftriaxone 1 g IV q24h + doxycycline 100 mg q12h + metronidazole 500 mg q12h; or cefoxitin/cefotetan + doxycycline; or clindamycin + gentamicin. TOA: IV antibiotics; drainage (IR) if large (>7–8 cm) or no response; rupture → surgery.
NotesIUD can stay in place (remove only if no improvement in 48–72 h). Treat partners from the previous 60 days. Sequelae: infertility, ectopic, chronic pelvic pain. Fitz-Hugh–Curtis = perihepatitis (RUQ pain, "violin-string" adhesions).

sections.heading: Gynecology 11 · Breast
sections.html:
ScenarioNext step
Palpable mass, age <30Ultrasound first (dense breast tissue, radiation concern). Add mammogram if US is suspicious or the patient is at high risk.
Palpable mass, age ≥30Diagnostic mammogram + targeted ultrasound
Simple cyst on USReassure. Aspirate if symptomatic. Bloody aspirate or residual mass → cytology/biopsy.
Solid mass / BI-RADS 4–5Core needle biopsy (image-guided). Triple assessment (exam + imaging + pathology) must be concordant. Discordance → excisional biopsy.
FibroadenomaYoung woman, mobile, rubbery, well-circumscribed; biopsy-proven → observe (excise if growing or symptomatic). Rapidly enlarging, large "leaf-like" mass → phyllodes tumor (wide local excision).
Nipple dischargeBilateral, milky, multiductal → hCG, prolactin, TSH, medication review. Unilateral, spontaneous, single-duct, bloody/serous → diagnostic mammogram + US (± MRI/ductography). Most common cause is intraductal papilloma (excise), but cancer must be excluded.
Erythema / edema / peau d'orange without response to antibioticsInflammatory breast cancer (T4d) → imaging + punch biopsy of skin + core biopsy. Do not keep switching antibiotics.
Eczematous, scaly nipple not responding to steroidsPaget disease of the nipple → mammogram + full-thickness nipple biopsy (underlying DCIS/invasive cancer)
Breast pain alone (cyclic)Reassurance, supportive bra, NSAIDs. Imaging only if focal/non-cyclic.
Screening / preventionRecommendation
Average riskUSPSTF 2024: biennial mammography ages 40–74 (grade B). Insufficient evidence ≥75 and for supplemental imaging in dense breasts. ACR/ACS favor annual screening from 40–45.
High risk (lifetime risk ≥20%, BRCA, chest radiation 10–30 y)Annual MRI (from 25 in BRCA) + annual mammography from 30. Radiation: start 8 y after treatment (not before 25).
Familial riskUse a familial risk assessment tool (e.g., Ontario, Pedigree) → genetic counseling → BRCA testing (USPSTF B). Do not test without counseling.
Chemoprevention (≥35 y, high risk, low bleeding/VTE risk)Tamoxifen (pre- or postmenopausal; ↑ VTE, endometrial cancer), raloxifene (postmenopausal; no endometrial risk), aromatase inhibitors (postmenopausal)
Treatment principlesHR+ → tamoxifen (premenopausal) or aromatase inhibitor (postmenopausal; bone loss → DEXA). HER2+ → trastuzumab (cardiotoxicity → baseline and serial echo). Triple-negative → BRCA1-associated, chemo ± pembrolizumab. Sentinel node biopsy for clinically node-negative disease. Breast-conserving surgery + radiation = mastectomy survival.
Exam trap: Male breast mass: in a pubertal boy → reassure (physiologic). In an older man → mammogram/US + biopsy (male breast cancer, BRCA2, Klinefelter). Gynecomastia in an adult → drugs (spironolactone, ketoconazole, androgens/anabolic steroids, marijuana), cirrhosis, hypogonadism, hCG-secreting testicular tumor (testicular exam + US).

title: Step 2 CK · Psychiatry, Neurology, Ethics, Biostatistics & Patient Safety
meta: Exam: Step 2 CK · Psychiatry, Neurology, Behavioral science/Ethics & law, Biostatistics/Epidemiology, Patient safety & quality improvement · Approx study time: 4–5 days

sections.heading: Overview
sections.html:
From NEET PG to USMLE

  • Ethics & communication is worth a lot on CK (roughly 10–15% of items when ethics, communication, biostats and safety are combined). In NEET PG these topics hardly exist. On CK the right answer is almost always the one that is patient-centered, honest, non-judgmental, and keeps the patient safe. You go to a court or an ethics committee only when there is real ambiguity and time to do so.
  • Autonomy beats paternalism. In India families often decide for adult patients. In the US, an adult with decision-making capacity decides for themselves, even if the family disagrees and even if the choice will kill them. Family members get information only with the patient's permission (HIPAA).
  • Use US drug names: acetaminophen (paracetamol), epinephrine (adrenaline), albuterol (salbutamol), meperidine (pethidine). Benzodiazepine of choice for status epilepticus in the US is IV lorazepam, or IM midazolam if there is no IV.
  • Substance use is managed as a chronic disease with medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD). The answer is almost never "detox and discharge." Since 2023 any clinician with a DEA registration can prescribe buprenorphine (the X-waiver is gone). Methadone for OUD is dispensed only through federally certified opioid treatment programs.
  • Stroke systems: tenecteplase is FDA-approved for acute ischemic stroke (2025) and many US centers now use it in place of alteplase. Thrombectomy for large-vessel occlusion is offered up to 24 h when imaging is favorable. Know the BP thresholds exactly.
  • Biostatistics on CK is applied: you read a drug advertisement or abstract and decide whether it applies to your patient, compute NNT from absolute risks, and spot misleading relative-risk headlines.
  • Patient safety vocabulary is US-specific: root cause analysis, Swiss cheese model, PDSA, I-PASS/SBAR handoffs, forcing functions, "just culture," sentinel events. The system is usually at fault, not the individual.
===================== PSYCHIATRY =====================

sections.heading: Psychiatry I — Depressive disorders
sections.html:
Major depressive disorder (MDD): at least 5 of 9 symptoms for at least 2 weeks. One of the 5 must be depressed mood or anhedonia. The 9 are SIG E CAPS plus mood: Sleep, Interest, Guilt, Energy, Concentration, Appetite, Psychomotor change, Suicidality. First rule out hypothyroidism, substances and medications (interferon, glucocorticoids, isotretinoin is debated), and bipolar disorder: always ask about past mania before you start an antidepressant. Screen with PHQ-2, then PHQ-9. USPSTF recommends depression screening for all adults, including pregnant and postpartum people, and for adolescents aged 12–18.

DisorderKey criteriaFirst-line management
MDD≥5 symptoms, ≥2 wk, functional impairmentSSRI and/or psychotherapy (CBT/IPT). Treat a first episode for 6–12 months after remission. Maintenance is indefinite after ≥3 episodes.
Persistent depressive disorderDepressed mood most days for ≥2 yr (≥1 yr in children)SSRI + psychotherapy
MDD with psychotic featuresMood-congruent delusions (guilt, nihilism)Antidepressant + antipsychotic, or ECT
Peripartum onsetOnset in pregnancy or within 4 wk postpartum (clinically up to 1 yr)Sertraline (safe in breastfeeding), psychotherapy. Zuranolone (oral, 14 days) or brexanolone (IV infusion) for postpartum depression.
Seasonal patternFall/winter recurrencesBright-light therapy, SSRI, bupropion XL (for prevention)
Premenstrual dysphoric disorderLuteal phase, resolves with mensesSSRI (continuous or luteal-only), drospirenone-containing OCP
Adjustment disorderWithin 3 mo of a stressor, resolves within 6 mo of its endPsychotherapy
Normal grief vs prolonged grief disorderProlonged grief: intense yearning ≥12 mo after the death (≥6 mo in children)Grief-focused psychotherapy
AntidepressantChoose it when…Avoid / key adverse effects
SSRIs: sertraline, escitalopram, fluoxetineDefault first line for depression and anxiety. Fluoxetine is FDA-approved for adolescents and for bulimia. Sertraline is preferred in pregnancy, breastfeeding and cardiac disease.Sexual dysfunction, GI upset, SIADH/hyponatremia in the elderly, bleeding risk with NSAIDs or anticoagulants. Citalopram prolongs QT (max 20 mg/day if >60 yr). Paroxetine: anticholinergic, discontinuation syndrome, avoid in pregnancy.
BupropionSmoker who wants to quit, worried about sexual dysfunction or weight gain, fatigueContraindicated with seizure disorder, bulimia/anorexia, or abrupt alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal. Can worsen anxiety.
MirtazapineInsomnia, poor appetite or weight loss (elderly, cancer)Sedation, weight gain. Agranulocytosis is rare.
SNRIs: venlafaxine, duloxetineComorbid neuropathic pain, fibromyalgia (duloxetine), GADDose-dependent hypertension (venlafaxine), harsh discontinuation syndrome
TCAs (nortriptyline, amitriptyline)Refractory cases, chronic pain, migraine prophylaxis3 C's in overdose: Convulsions, Coma, Cardiotoxicity (wide QRS → IV sodium bicarbonate). Anticholinergic, orthostasis.
MAOIs (phenelzine)Atypical depression refractory to other agentsTyramine hypertensive crisis. Serotonin syndrome with SSRIs, meperidine, linezolid, dextromethorphan. Wash-out of 2 wk (5 wk after fluoxetine).
TrazodoneLow-dose hypnoticPriapism, orthostasis
Vortioxetine, vilazodoneAlternatives with less sexual dysfunctionNausea
[[figure:ch12-fig01]]

Treatment-resistant depression (TRD) means no response to at least 2 adequate antidepressant trials. Options:

  • Augment with an atypical antipsychotic. Aripiprazole, brexpiprazole and quetiapine XR are FDA-approved as adjuncts.
  • Augment with lithium (it also reduces suicide) or T3.
  • Esketamine nasal spray. It was originally approved with an oral antidepressant, and as monotherapy since 2025. Under a REMS it must be given in a certified setting with at least 2 h of observation because of dissociation, sedation and raised BP.
  • ECT, the most effective treatment of all. First-line for psychotic depression, catatonia, acute suicidality, refusal to eat or drink, and severe depression in pregnancy. Adverse effects are transient retrograde amnesia and headache. There are no absolute contraindications, but recent MI or stroke and raised ICP are high-risk.
  • rTMS: outpatient, no anesthesia, no cognitive side effects.
High-yield: Antidepressants carry a black-box warning for suicidality in patients younger than 25. Monitor them closely in the first weeks. Energy can return before mood improves, which creates a window of risk. Do not withhold treatment for this reason.
Exam trap: If a "depressed" patient becomes euphoric, sleepless and talkative after starting an SSRI, the diagnosis is bipolar disorder unmasked, not a side effect. Stop the antidepressant and start a mood stabilizer or antipsychotic.

sections.heading: Psychiatry II — Bipolar disorder
sections.html:
Bipolar I requires at least one manic episode: ≥1 week, or any duration if hospitalized, with ≥3 DIG FAST symptoms (Distractibility, Impulsivity, Grandiosity, Flight of ideas, Activity increase, Sleep deficit, Talkativeness) and marked impairment or psychosis. Bipolar II is hypomania (≥4 days, no marked impairment, no psychosis) plus major depression. Cyclothymia is ≥2 years of subthreshold mood swings.

PhasePreferred treatmentNotes
Acute maniaLithium, valproate, or a second-generation antipsychotic (SGA: olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, aripiprazole, haloperidol). For severe mania, combine lithium or valproate with an SGA.Stop any antidepressant. For an agitated patient, use IM olanzapine or haloperidol ± lorazepam. ECT if refractory or in pregnancy.
Bipolar depressionQuetiapine, lurasidone, lumateperone, cariprazine, olanzapine-fluoxetine combination. Lamotrigine (mainly for maintenance).Never give antidepressant monotherapy. It can trigger mania or rapid cycling.
MaintenanceLithium (gold standard, reduces suicide), valproate, lamotrigine (prevents depressive poles), quetiapine, aripiprazoleContinue whichever agent worked in the acute phase
PregnancyLithium (cardiac risk lower than once believed, but get fetal echo) or an antipsychotic. Avoid valproate (neural tube defects, lower IQ) and carbamazepine.Lithium clearance rises in pregnancy and falls abruptly after delivery. Check levels often.

Lithium monitoring: check BUN/Cr, TSH, calcium, ECG (if >40 or cardiac disease) and β-hCG at baseline. Target level 0.6–1.2 mEq/L (0.8–1.0 for acute treatment; 0.6–0.8 often enough for maintenance). Long-term effects: hypothyroidism, nephrogenic DI, hyperparathyroidism/hypercalcemia, CKD, tremor, weight gain, acne. Valproate: check LFTs, CBC (thrombocytopenia) and lipase (pancreatitis). Hepatotoxicity, weight gain, PCOS. Lamotrigine: titrate slowly because of SJS/TEN risk. Halve the dose if the patient is on valproate.

Lithium toxicityDetails
PrecipitantsDehydration, vomiting/diarrhea, low-salt diet, thiazides, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, AKI. Loop diuretics have a smaller effect.
Clinical pictureAcute: GI symptoms first. Chronic: neurological. Coarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria, confusion, myoclonus, hyperreflexia, seizures, coma. ECG: T-wave flattening, bradycardia, QT prolongation. Late effect: SILENT (irreversible cerebellar damage).
ManagementStop lithium. Give aggressive isotonic saline (if not volume-overloaded). Repeat levels every 2–4 h. Activated charcoal does not bind lithium. Use whole-bowel irrigation for large sustained-release ingestions.
Hemodialysis (EXTRIP)Recommended if level >4.0 mEq/L with impaired kidney function, or with decreased consciousness, seizures or life-threatening dysrhythmia at any level. Suggested if level >5.0, there is significant confusion, or the expected time to fall below 1.0 is >36 h.

sections.heading: Psychiatry III — Psychotic disorders
sections.html:
DisorderDuration / feature
Brief psychotic disorder1 day to <1 month, full return to baseline; often stress-triggered
Schizophreniform1 to <6 months
Schizophrenia≥6 months of disturbance, including ≥1 month of active symptoms. At least 2 of: delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized/catatonic behavior, negative symptoms. At least one must be one of the first three.
SchizoaffectivePsychosis for ≥2 weeks without mood symptoms, plus mood episodes present for most of the illness
Delusional disorder≥1 month of non-bizarre delusions, otherwise functioning well

Workup for first-episode psychosis: CBC, CMP, TSH, urine drug screen, HIV, RPR, B12 ± MRI. Consider anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis (young woman, ovarian teratoma) and steroid or stimulant use.

Treatment: SGAs are first-line, chosen by side-effect profile. Long-acting injectables (paliperidone palmitate, aripiprazole, haloperidol decanoate) help with nonadherence. Xanomeline–trospium (approved 2024) is a muscarinic agonist with no D2 blockade, so there is no EPS or prolactin rise, but it causes cholinergic GI effects.

Adverse effectTypical culpritManagement
Acute dystonia (hours–days)High-potency FGA (haloperidol)IM/IV benztropine or diphenhydramine
Akathisia (days–weeks)FGAs, aripiprazolePropranolol, lower the dose, benzodiazepine
Parkinsonism (weeks)FGAs, risperidoneBenztropine, lower the dose or switch
Tardive dyskinesia (months–years)Long-term D2 blockadeSwitch to clozapine or quetiapine. VMAT2 inhibitors valbenazine, deutetrabenazine. Avoid anticholinergics, which worsen TD.
Metabolic syndromeClozapine, olanzapine > quetiapine, risperidoneBaseline and follow-up weight, waist, glucose/HbA1c, lipids. Metformin.
HyperprolactinemiaRisperidone, paliperidone, FGAsSwitch to aripiprazole or add it
QT prolongationZiprasidone, IV haloperidol, thioridazineECG, correct K/Mg

Clozapine is used for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (failure of ≥2 adequate antipsychotic trials, including one SGA) and for persistent suicidality in schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder. It is the only antipsychotic proven to reduce suicide.

  • Severe neutropenia/agranulocytosis (highest risk in the first 6 months). Baseline ANC must be ≥1500/µL (≥1000 in benign ethnic neutropenia, BEN). Then check ANC weekly for 6 months, every 2 weeks for months 6–12, then monthly. The FDA eliminated the clozapine REMS registry in 2025, but ANC monitoring is still recommended in the labeling.
  • ANC response, general population:
    • 1000–1499 (mild): continue clozapine; check ANC three times weekly.
    • 500–999 (moderate): interrupt clozapine; check ANC daily until ≥1000, then resume.
    • <500 (severe): stop; rechallenge only if benefit clearly outweighs risk.
  • Myocarditis (first 4–8 weeks): fever, tachycardia, chest pain. Check troponin and CRP and stop clozapine.
  • Seizures (dose-related).
  • Severe constipation and ileus, which can be fatal: give prophylactic laxatives.
  • Sialorrhea, orthostasis, weight gain and diabetes.

sections.heading: Psychiatry IV — NMS vs serotonin syndrome vs anticholinergic toxicity vs malignant hyperthermia
sections.html:
[[figure:ch12-fig02]]
Look-alikeClueTreatment
Anticholinergic toxicityDry, flushed skin; mydriasis; urinary retention; decreased bowel sounds; no rigiditySupportive care, benzodiazepines; physostigmine in selected cases
Malignant hyperthermiaIntraoperative, after succinylcholine or volatile anesthetic; rising end-tidal CO2, masseter rigidity; RYR1 mutationStop the trigger, dantrolene
Sympathomimetic toxicity (cocaine, amphetamine)Diaphoresis, mydriasis, hypertension, chest painBenzodiazepines. Avoid pure β-blockers in the acute setting.

sections.heading: Psychiatry V — Anxiety, trauma, and obsessive-compulsive disorders
sections.html:
DisorderKey featuresFirst-line treatment
Generalized anxiety disorderExcessive worry most days for ≥6 mo, ≥3 somatic symptomsCBT and/or SSRI/SNRI (escitalopram, sertraline, duloxetine, venlafaxine). Buspirone as an adjunct or alternative (takes 2–4 wk). Benzodiazepines only as a short-term bridge.
Panic disorderRecurrent unexpected attacks plus ≥1 mo of worry or avoidance. Exclude MI, hyperthyroidism, pheochromocytoma, stimulants.CBT + SSRI. Short-term benzodiazepine while the SSRI takes effect.
Social anxiety disorderFear of scrutiny ≥6 moCBT + SSRI/SNRI. Performance-only type: propranolol PRN.
Specific phobiaCircumscribed fearExposure therapy (systematic desensitization). Drugs have little role.
Acute stress disorder3 days–1 month after traumaTrauma-focused CBT. No routine psychological debriefing (may harm). Avoid benzodiazepines.
PTSD>1 month: intrusion, avoidance, negative mood or cognition, hyperarousalTrauma-focused psychotherapy first (cognitive processing therapy, prolonged exposure, EMDR). SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) or venlafaxine. Prazosin for nightmares (mixed evidence). Avoid benzodiazepines.
OCDEgo-dystonic obsessions and compulsions taking >1 h/day; insight variesExposure and response prevention (ERP) + SSRI at high dose for 8–12 wk. Then clomipramine, or augment with an antipsychotic (risperidone, aripiprazole). Deep TMS. Consider PANDAS in children with abrupt onset.
Body dysmorphic disorderPreoccupation with a perceived flawCBT + SSRI. Discourage cosmetic surgery.
Hoarding, trichotillomania—CBT / habit-reversal training; N-acetylcysteine for trichotillomania

sections.heading: Psychiatry VI — Childhood: ADHD and related disorders
sections.html:
• ADHD criteria: ≥6 symptoms of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity (≥5 if age ≥17), present before age 12, in ≥2 settings, for ≥6 months. Use teacher and parent rating scales (Vanderbilt).
  • Treatment by age (AAP 2019):
    • Age 4–5: parent training in behavior management (PTBM) first. Add methylphenidate if symptoms remain moderate–severe.
    • Age 6–11: FDA-approved medication (stimulants are first-line) plus behavioral treatment.
    • Adolescents: medication ± behavioral therapy.
  • Stimulants (methylphenidate, amphetamines) cause appetite suppression, insomnia, growth slowing, tics and raised BP/HR. Ask about cardiac history and family history of sudden death.
  • Nonstimulants: atomoxetine (suicidality warning, hepatotoxicity), viloxazine, guanfacine/clonidine (useful with tics; rebound hypertension if stopped abruptly).
  • Related disorders:
    • Oppositional defiant disorder: parent management training.
    • Conduct disorder: violates the rights of others. It may become antisocial personality disorder after age 18.
    • Tourette: tics for >1 yr with onset before 18. Treat with CBIT behavioral therapy, then α2 agonists, then aripiprazole.
    • Autism: give early intensive behavioral therapy (ABA). Risperidone or aripiprazole for irritability.

sections.heading: Psychiatry VII — Eating disorders & refeeding
sections.html:
FeatureAnorexia nervosaBulimia nervosaBinge-eating disorder
WeightSignificantly low (adult BMI <18.5; severity by BMI; extreme <15)Normal or overweightOften obese
BehaviorRestriction ± binge/purge; distorted body imageBinge + compensation ≥1/wk for 3 moBinges with distress, no compensation
SignsBradycardia, hypotension, lanugo, amenorrhea, osteoporosis, hypothermiaRussell sign, parotid enlargement, dental erosion, hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosisMetabolic syndrome
TreatmentNutritional rehabilitation. Family-based therapy for adolescents; CBT-E. Olanzapine may help weight gain.CBT + fluoxetine (FDA-approved). Avoid bupropion.CBT; lisdexamfetamine (FDA-approved); weight-management interventions

Hospitalization criteria (any one is enough):

  • HR <40 in adults (<50 daytime in adolescents)
  • BP <90/60, or orthostatic changes (HR rise >20, or SBP fall >20)
  • Temperature <35.6 °C (96 °F)
  • Electrolyte derangements (K, PO4, Mg)
  • Arrhythmia or prolonged QTc
  • <75% of median BMI (adolescents) or BMI <15 (adults)
  • Acute food refusal, suicidality, or failed outpatient treatment

Refeeding syndrome usually appears in the first 2–5 days of nutrition. Insulin surges and drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells. Hypophosphatemia is the hallmark, and the falling ATP and 2,3-BPG cause weakness, rhabdomyolysis, respiratory failure, heart failure, arrhythmia, seizures and delirium. Fluid retention and edema also occur.

Prevention:

  • Check baseline and then daily PO4, K, Mg and glucose.
  • Give thiamine before feeding.
  • Increase calories steadily. Current US practice often starts at ~1400–2000 kcal/day in monitored inpatients rather than very low calories.
  • Replace electrolytes proactively.
  • Use telemetry if the patient is high risk.

sections.heading: Psychiatry VIII — Personality, somatic & other disorders
sections.html:
ClusterDisordersManagement point
A (odd)Paranoid, schizoid, schizotypalBe clear, honest and non-intrusive. Schizotypal is in the schizophrenia spectrum.
B (dramatic)Antisocial (≥18 yr, conduct disorder before 15), borderline, histrionic, narcissisticBorderline: dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) is first-line. Drugs are for target symptoms only. Splitting: the care team must be consistent and set firm boundaries.
C (anxious)Avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive PD (ego-syntonic perfectionism, unlike OCD)Psychotherapy
  • Somatic symptom disorder: schedule regular brief visits with a single PCP, limit testing, and address function rather than "cure."
  • Illness anxiety disorder: manage the same way, plus CBT.
  • Conversion disorder (functional neurological disorder): explain the diagnosis non-judgmentally and refer for physical therapy and CBT.
  • Factitious disorder (internal gain; "Munchausen"; by proxy means child abuse, so report it) vs malingering (external gain).
  • Delirium vs dementia: delirium is acute and fluctuating with impaired attention. Find and treat the cause (infection, drugs, metabolic). Use non-drug measures first: reorientation, sleep hygiene, glasses and hearing aids, early mobilization, avoiding restraints. Use low-dose haloperidol or quetiapine only for dangerous agitation. Avoid benzodiazepines except in alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal.
  • Insomnia: CBT-I is first-line, before hypnotics. Avoid sedative-hypnotics in the elderly (Beers criteria).

sections.heading: Psychiatry IX — Substance use disorders & medications for addiction
sections.html:
Screening: USPSTF recommends screening all adults for unhealthy alcohol use (AUDIT-C, single question) with brief counseling. It also recommends screening adults for unhealthy drug use by asking questions, when accurate diagnosis and treatment can be offered. Use SBIRT: screening, brief intervention, referral to treatment. Motivational interviewing uses open questions, affirmations, reflections and summaries, and matches the patient's stage of change (precontemplation → contemplation → preparation → action → maintenance).

Medication (OUD)MechanismHow / whenKey points
Buprenorphine (± naloxone; SL, monthly SC depot)Partial μ agonist, high affinityStart when the patient is in mild–moderate withdrawal (COWS ≥8–12), typically 12–24 h after short-acting opioids. With fentanyl, precipitated withdrawal is common, so use "low-dose (micro-) induction" or high-dose induction protocols.Ceiling effect on respiratory depression, so it is safer in overdose. Office-based; X-waiver eliminated 2023. Preferred in pregnancy along with methadone (less neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome with buprenorphine).
MethadoneFull μ agonist, long half-lifeOnly through a certified opioid treatment program (OTP) for OUD. A hospital may give it to inpatients being treated for another condition, and the ED may dispense for up to 72 h while arranging referral.QTc prolongation (get an ECG). Many drug interactions. Overdose risk during induction.
Naltrexone (oral; XR-IM monthly)μ antagonistPatient must be opioid-free 7–10 days, otherwise precipitated withdrawalAlso treats AUD. Loss of tolerance raises overdose risk after stopping. Avoid in acute hepatitis or liver failure.
NaloxoneAntagonistIntranasal 4 mg, available OTC since 2023Co-prescribe to everyone at risk of opioid overdose
Clonidine / lofexidineα2 agonistsSymptom relief during withdrawalSupportive only. Withdrawal management alone, without MOUD, has high relapse and overdose rates.
Alcohol use disorder medicationUseAvoid in
Naltrexone (first-line)Reduces craving and heavy drinkingOpioid use or need for opioid analgesia; acute hepatitis, decompensated liver disease
Acamprosate (first-line)Maintains abstinence; safe in liver diseaseCrCl ≤30 (reduce dose if 30–50)
DisulfiramAversive (aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibitor); only for highly motivated, supervised patientsCardiac disease, psychosis, pregnancy, liver disease
Off-label optionsGabapentin, topiramate. Baclofen is used in alcohol-associated liver disease.—

Tobacco: USPSTF recommends asking every adult about tobacco use, advising cessation, and offering behavioral support plus pharmacotherapy. Varenicline is the most effective single agent. Combination NRT (patch + short-acting) is equivalent. Bupropion is another option. Use behavioral counseling, not drugs, in adolescents and pregnant people (insufficient evidence for drugs in pregnancy).

SubstanceIntoxicationWithdrawalManagement pearls
OpioidsMiosis, respiratory depression, comaMydriasis, yawning, lacrimation, rhinorrhea, piloerection, diarrhea. Not life-threatening.Naloxone for intoxication; buprenorphine or methadone for withdrawal
AlcoholDisinhibition, ataxia, nystagmusCan be fatal (seizures, DTs)Benzodiazepines; thiamine first
BenzodiazepinesSedation; respiratory depression only with other depressantsLike alcohol, with seizuresSlow taper. Flumazenil can precipitate seizures in chronic users.
CocaineMydriasis, hypertension, chest pain (vasospasm), agitationCrash: hypersomnia, hyperphagia, depressionBenzodiazepines, nitrates, CCB; avoid unopposed β-blockade acutely
Amphetamine/methamphetamineLike cocaine; psychosis, dental decayDepression, fatigueBenzodiazepines, antipsychotic for psychosis
PCPViolence, vertical/rotatory nystagmus, hyperthermia—Benzodiazepines, low stimulation
CannabisConjunctival injection, appetite, slowed timeIrritability, insomniaCannabinoid hyperemesis: hot showers, capsaicin cream, haloperidol/droperidol, abstinence
Xylazine (mixed into fentanyl)Sedation not fully reversed by naloxone; chronic necrotic wounds—Still give naloxone for the opioid component; supportive ventilation; wound care

Alcohol withdrawal

[[figure:ch12-fig03]]
  • CIWA-Ar scores 10 items (nausea, tremor, sweats, anxiety, agitation, tactile, auditory and visual disturbances, headache, orientation). The maximum is 67. Symptom-triggered dosing uses less drug than fixed schedules. It cannot be used in patients who cannot communicate, such as intubated patients, who are managed with a sedation scale (RASS).
  • Lorazepam or oxazepam are preferred in cirrhosis, the elderly, and severe hypoalbuminemia because they are glucuronidated and have no active metabolites.
  • A history of DTs or withdrawal seizures predicts severe withdrawal, so give prophylactic treatment.
  • Phenobarbital is used as monotherapy or as an adjunct in many US centers.
  • Antipsychotics and β-blockers are adjuncts only. They do not prevent seizures.
  • Wernicke encephalopathy: confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia, though the full triad is often absent. Give high-dose IV thiamine (e.g., 500 mg IV TID). Glucose given first may precipitate or worsen it. Untreated, it progresses to Korsakoff syndrome (anterograde amnesia, confabulation).

sections.heading: Psychiatry X — Suicide risk assessment & involuntary holds
sections.html:
• Ask directly about ideation, intent, plan, means (especially firearms), preparatory acts and prior attempts. Asking does not increase risk. Use the Columbia (C-SSRS) or ASQ (youth).
  • Risk factors:
    • Strongest: prior attempt.
    • Demographic: male sex, older age (highest rates in older white men), and also adolescents.
    • Clinical: psychiatric illness (depression, bipolar, schizophrenia, substance use, borderline PD), chronic pain or illness, recent psychiatric discharge.
    • Social: firearm access (over half of US suicides use firearms), social isolation, divorce or widowhood, unemployment, LGBTQ+ youth facing rejection.
  • Disposition by risk level:
    • High risk (intent + plan + means, or recent serious attempt): psychiatric hospitalization. If the patient refuses → involuntary hold.
    • Moderate risk: consider admission or an intensive outpatient program, with a safety plan, means restriction and close follow-up.
    • Low risk: outpatient care with a safety plan, lethal-means counseling, crisis line (988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline), and follow-up within days.
  • "No-suicide contracts" are not effective and are never the right answer.
  • Involuntary commitment criteria (state laws vary): a mental illness and (1) danger to self, (2) danger to others, or (3) grave disability (unable to provide food, clothing or shelter). Emergency holds typically last 48–72 h (e.g., California 5150 = 72 h) and then need a court hearing to extend. Patients keep the right to refuse non-emergency treatment unless a separate court order exists.
  • Leaving against medical advice (AMA) is allowed if the patient has capacity. Assess capacity, explain the risks, offer alternatives and follow-up, and document. Prescriptions and follow-up are still provided.
Exam trap: A patient who is intoxicated and suicidal in the ED cannot be assessed or discharged until sober. Hold the patient and re-evaluate. Never let a high-risk patient leave to "think about it."
===================== NEUROLOGY =====================

sections.heading: Neurology I — Acute ischemic stroke
sections.html:
Door-to-needle goal: under 60 min (ideally under 45). There are three time-critical tasks:

  1. Check fingerstick glucose, because hypoglycemia mimics stroke.
  2. Get a noncontrast head CT to exclude hemorrhage. Add CTA head and neck for suspected large-vessel occlusion (LVO), with or without CT perfusion.
  3. Fix the time last known well (LKW). For a wake-up stroke, LKW is when the patient went to bed.

Do not delay thrombolysis for coagulation results unless anticoagulant use or a coagulopathy is suspected. Only glucose must be checked before it. Calculate the NIHSS.

[[figure:ch12-fig04]]
Major contraindications to IV thrombolysisNotes
Hemorrhage on CT; extensive hypodensity (established infarct)—
Ischemic stroke or severe head trauma within 3 months; prior ICH; intracranial neoplasm (intra-axial), AVM—
GI bleeding within 21 days; intracranial or spinal surgery within 3 months—
Platelets <100,000, INR >1.7, aPTT elevatedCheck only if suspected; do not wait otherwise
DOAC within 48 h (unless specific assays normal); therapeutic LMWH within 24 hThrombectomy is still possible
BP persistently >185/110 despite treatmentTreat BP first, then lyse
Infective endocarditis; aortic dissectionDissection → no lytic
Mild non-disabling deficits (NIHSS 0–5)Thrombolysis not recommended; use DAPT. Disabling deficits (aphasia, hemianopia) are treated regardless of score.

Post-thrombolysis neuro decline, headache or vomiting: suspect symptomatic ICH. Stop the infusion and get an emergent CT. Give cryoprecipitate (fibrinogen) and tranexamic acid. Orolingual angioedema is more common with ACE inhibitors; treat with antihistamine and steroids, then icatibant or epinephrine if needed.

Hemorrhagic stroke (quick contrast)

  • ICH: target SBP about 140; avoid lowering it below 130 or dropping it abruptly.
  • Reverse anticoagulation:
    • Warfarin: 4-factor PCC + IV vitamin K.
    • Dabigatran: idarucizumab.
    • Factor Xa inhibitors: 4F-PCC or andexanet alfa (where available).
  • Neurosurgery: cerebellar hemorrhage >3 cm or brainstem compression/hydrocephalus → evacuation.
  • Aneurysmal SAH:
    • Secure the aneurysm early (coiling or clipping).
    • Nimodipine 60 mg every 4 h for 21 days to reduce delayed cerebral ischemia from vasospasm (days 4–14).
    • Keep SBP <160 before the aneurysm is secured.
    • Watch for hyponatremia (SIADH or cerebral salt wasting) and hydrocephalus, which needs an EVD.

TIA & secondary prevention

  • TIA is transient neurologic dysfunction without infarction on imaging (tissue-based definition). Use ABCD2 to estimate risk; ≥4 is high risk.
  • Same-day workup: MRI with DWI, vascular imaging (CTA, MRA or carotid duplex), ECG plus prolonged rhythm monitoring (30-day monitor or implantable loop recorder for cryptogenic stroke), echocardiogram, lipids, HbA1c.
EtiologySecondary prevention
Minor stroke (NIHSS ≤3) or high-risk TIA, non-cardioembolicAspirin + clopidogrel for 21 days (start within 24 h), then single antiplatelet (POINT/CHANCE). Ticagrelor + aspirin for 30 days is an alternative (THALES), especially for CYP2C19 loss-of-function carriers.
Other non-cardioembolicAspirin, clopidogrel, or aspirin–ER dipyridamole (long term)
Atrial fibrillationDOAC (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran) preferred over warfarin. Timing after stroke: early start (within ~48 h for minor/moderate strokes, later for large ones) is supported by ELAN/OPTIMAS. Warfarin for mechanical valves or moderate–severe mitral stenosis. Do not add aspirin unless there is another indication.
Symptomatic carotid stenosis 70–99%Carotid endarterectomy within 2 weeks. 50–69%: CEA depending on patient factors (men, age >75, surgical risk <6%). <50% or occluded: medical therapy only. Stenting is an alternative (higher stroke risk in the elderly; better for radiation neck or high surgical risk).
Intracranial atherosclerosis 70–99%Aggressive medical therapy: DAPT for 90 days, high-intensity statin, SBP <140. No stenting (SAMMPRIS).
PFO with cryptogenic stroke, age 18–60, high-risk PFO featuresPFO closure + antiplatelet
AllHigh-intensity statin (LDL target <70 mg/dL); BP <130/80; diabetes control; smoking cessation; Mediterranean diet; exercise
High-yield: Dissection (neck pain, Horner syndrome, young patient after neck trauma or chiropractic manipulation) is treated with antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy, which are equivalent (CADISS). It is diagnosed on CTA or MRA.

sections.heading: Neurology II — Seizures & status epilepticus
sections.html:
• First unprovoked seizure: check glucose, electrolytes, Ca, Mg, toxicology, pregnancy test; get brain imaging (MRI preferred, CT in the ED) and an EEG. Usually do not start an antiseizure medication (ASM) after a single unprovoked seizure with a normal workup. Start one if the EEG is epileptiform, imaging shows a lesion, the seizure was nocturnal, or the patient has had ≥2 unprovoked seizures more than 24 h apart.
  • Driving: state laws typically require a seizure-free interval (often 3–6 months). The physician informs the patient. A few states (e.g., California, Pennsylvania) mandate physician reporting.
Seizure typeFirst-line ASMNotes
FocalLamotrigine, levetiracetam (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine)Carbamazepine: HLA-B*15:02 testing in Asians (SJS), hyponatremia, CYP inducer
Generalized tonic-clonicValproate (not in people who may become pregnant), lamotrigine, levetiracetamLevetiracetam: irritability or depression
AbsenceEthosuximide (valproate if GTC also occurs)3-Hz spike-and-wave
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsyValproate; levetiracetam or lamotrigine if pregnancy is possibleLifelong treatment
PregnancyLamotrigine or levetiracetam + folic acid (higher dose often used)Lamotrigine levels fall in pregnancy, so monitor them
EclampsiaMagnesium sulfateNot standard ASMs
[[figure:ch12-fig05]]
Exam trap: Psychogenic nonepileptic seizures (PNES) are suggested by eyes closed during the event, side-to-side head movements, pelvic thrusting, and asynchronous movements. The gold standard is video EEG. Normal prolactin does not exclude a true seizure.

sections.heading: Neurology III — Headache
sections.html:
Red flags (SNOOP4):

  • Systemic symptoms or illness: fever, weight loss, cancer, HIV, immunosuppression
  • Neurologic deficits or altered consciousness, papilledema
  • Onset sudden (thunderclap)
  • Older age (new headache >50, think GCA)
  • Positional, Precipitated by Valsalva or exertion, Progressive pattern change, Pregnancy or postpartum (CVST, RCVS, preeclampsia)

Any red flag → imaging.

HeadacheCluesAcute treatmentPrevention
MigraineUnilateral, pulsating, 4–72 h, nausea, photophobia/phonophobia ± auraNSAIDs/acetaminophen, triptans (avoid in CAD, uncontrolled HTN, hemiplegic migraine). Gepants (ubrogepant, rimegepant) and lasmiditan are safe with vascular disease. ED: IV metoclopramide or prochlorperazine + diphenhydramine, IV fluids, ketorolac; dexamethasone reduces recurrence. Avoid opioids.For ≥4 headache days/month or disability: propranolol/metoprolol, topiramate (teratogenic), amitriptyline, venlafaxine, candesartan. CGRP mAbs (erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab, eptinezumab), atogepant, rimegepant. OnabotulinumtoxinA for chronic migraine.
Tension-typeBilateral, band-like, no nauseaNSAIDs, acetaminophenAmitriptyline
ClusterMen, orbital/temporal, 15–180 min, ipsilateral lacrimation, rhinorrhea, Horner, restlessness, circadian timing100% O2 at 12–15 L/min via nonrebreather; SC or intranasal sumatriptanVerapamil (ECG monitoring). Transitional: prednisone, greater occipital nerve block. Lithium.
Medication overuseAnalgesics ≥15 days/mo or triptans ≥10 days/moWithdraw the overused drugStart preventive therapy
Idiopathic intracranial hypertensionObese young woman, papilledema, pulsatile tinnitus, CN VI palsy. Can be caused by tetracyclines, vitamin A/isotretinoin.MRI/MRV first (exclude CVST), then LP: opening pressure >25 cm H2OAcetazolamide, weight loss. Vision loss → optic nerve sheath fenestration or CSF shunt.
Giant cell arteritis>50 yr, temporal headache, jaw claudication, PMR, visual symptoms; ↑ESR/CRPStart high-dose prednisone immediately. With vision loss, give IV methylprednisolone. Biopsy or temporal artery ultrasound within ~2 weeks; steroids do not invalidate it.Tocilizumab as a steroid-sparing agent

Thunderclap headache: think SAH, RCVS, CVST, pituitary apoplexy, dissection.

  • Get a noncontrast CT first. Within 6 h of onset, a negative CT read by an expert nearly rules out SAH.
  • If more than 6 h have passed, or suspicion is high and the CT is negative, do a lumbar puncture looking for xanthochromia and RBCs that do not clear across tubes. CTA is an alternative.

Meningitis: blood cultures, then immediate empiric antibiotics plus dexamethasone. Do not delay them for CT or LP. Get a CT before the LP only if the patient is immunocompromised, has CNS disease, a seizure, papilledema, altered consciousness or a focal deficit.

sections.heading: Neurology IV — Demyelinating, movement & neurodegenerative disease
sections.html:
Multiple sclerosis

  • Diagnosis: MRI showing dissemination in space and time (McDonald criteria; the 2024 revision adds the optic nerve as a site and supports the central vein sign). CSF oligoclonal bands can substitute for dissemination in time.
  • Acute relapse (≥24 h of new deficit without fever or infection): high-dose IV methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 3–5 days (or oral equivalent). Plasma exchange if steroids fail. First rule out pseudo-relapse (UTI, heat) with a UA.
  • Disease-modifying therapy should start early. The trend is toward high-efficacy agents from the start.
    • Anti-CD20: ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, ublituximab. Ocrelizumab is the only agent approved for primary progressive MS.
    • Natalizumab: PML risk; test JCV antibody.
    • S1P modulators (fingolimod, siponimod, ozanimod): first-dose bradycardia, macular edema, VZV (check immunity first).
    • Others: dimethyl fumarate (flushing, lymphopenia), teriflunomide (teratogenic), cladribine, interferon-β, glatiramer (safe in pregnancy), alemtuzumab (autoimmunity).
  • Symptomatic treatment: spasticity → baclofen, tizanidine. Fatigue → amantadine, modafinil. Gait → dalfampridine (contraindicated with seizures). Bladder → antimuscarinics or catheterization.
  • Differentiate from NMOSD (AQP4-IgG: severe optic neuritis + longitudinally extensive myelitis; avoid some MS drugs) and MOGAD.

Parkinson disease

DrugUseAdverse effects
Carbidopa-levodopaMost effective; first-line when symptoms impair function, and at any age once disablingNausea, orthostasis, dyskinesias, wearing-off, hallucinations
Dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine)Younger patients with mild diseaseImpulse control disorders (gambling, hypersexuality), sleep attacks, edema, hallucinations
MAO-B inhibitors (rasagiline, selegiline, safinamide)Mild early disease; adjunct for wearing-offSerotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs
COMT inhibitors (entacapone, opicapone)Adjunct for wearing-offOrange urine, diarrhea
AmantadineLevodopa-induced dyskinesiasLivedo reticularis, confusion, renal dosing
Anticholinergics (trihexyphenidyl)Tremor in young patients onlyConfusion; avoid in the elderly
Deep brain stimulationLevodopa-responsive patients with motor fluctuations and no dementia—
  • PD psychosis: first rule out delirium and reduce anticholinergics, amantadine and dopamine agonists. Then use pimavanserin (5-HT2A inverse agonist, FDA-approved), quetiapine or clozapine. Never use haloperidol, risperidone or metoclopramide.
  • Nausea: use domperidone (not FDA-approved) or ondansetron, not metoclopramide or prochlorperazine.
  • Orthostatic hypotension: midodrine, droxidopa, fludrocortisone.

Essential tremor: action tremor that improves with alcohol and is often familial. Treat with propranolol or primidone; focused ultrasound or DBS if refractory.

Dementia workup & treatment

Workup:

  • History from an informant, plus cognitive testing (MoCA, MMSE).
  • Labs for reversible causes: B12, TSH, CBC, CMP (Ca, glucose, renal, hepatic). RPR and HIV if there are risk factors.
  • Screen for depression ("pseudodementia").
  • Review medications (anticholinergics, benzodiazepines).
  • Structural imaging: MRI preferred, or noncontrast CT.
  • Selected cases: amyloid PET, CSF Aβ42/tau, plasma p-tau217, ApoE genotyping before anti-amyloid therapy.

USPSTF finds insufficient evidence to screen asymptomatic older adults for cognitive impairment.

TypeCluesTreatment / caution
AlzheimerInsidious memory loss; hippocampal atrophyCholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine: bradycardia, GI) for all stages. Memantine for moderate–severe disease. Lecanemab or donanemab for MCI or mild AD with confirmed amyloid: ARIA risk (MRI monitoring; higher in ApoE4 homozygotes), avoid with anticoagulation.
VascularStepwise decline, focal signsVascular risk factor control
Lewy bodyFluctuations, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, REM sleep behavior disorderSevere antipsychotic sensitivity. Rivastigmine/donepezil; low-dose quetiapine or pimavanserin if essential.
FrontotemporalEarly personality change, disinhibition, younger onsetSSRIs for behavior; cholinesterase inhibitors don't help
Normal pressure hydrocephalusMagnetic gait, incontinence, dementia; ventriculomegalyHigh-volume LP (tap test) → if gait improves, VP shunt
Creutzfeldt-JakobRapid decline, myoclonus, periodic sharp waves on EEG, DWI cortical ribboning, CSF RT-QuICSupportive care; infection-control precautions for instruments

Behavioral symptoms of dementia: use non-drug measures first. Antipsychotics carry a black-box warning for increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia. Brexpiprazole is FDA-approved for agitation in AD.

sections.heading: Neurology V — Neuromuscular emergencies & spinal cord
sections.html:
ConditionCluesNext best steps
Guillain-Barré syndromeAscending symmetric weakness, areflexia, after Campylobacter or viral illness; autonomic instability. CSF: high protein with normal cells. NCS: demyelination. Miller Fisher variant: ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia (anti-GQ1b).Admit with serial FVC/NIF. Intubate if FVC <20 mL/kg, NIF weaker than −30 cm H2O, or MEP <40 ("20/30/40 rule"), or if there is bulbar dysfunction. IVIG or plasma exchange (equivalent; do not combine). Steroids do not help. Give DVT prophylaxis. Chronic form (CIDP, >8 weeks) does respond to steroids.
Myasthenic crisisFatigable ptosis, diplopia, bulbar and respiratory weakness. Triggers: infection, surgery, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, Mg, β-blockers, steroid initiation, pregnancy.Serial FVC/NIF; intubate as above. Plasma exchange (faster) or IVIG. Hold pyridostigmine while intubated (secretions). Start or raise steroids together with PLEX/IVIG, because steroids alone may transiently worsen weakness. Remove the trigger. Chronic care: CT chest for thymoma and thymectomy (AChR+ generalized MG, age <65). Other options: complement inhibitors (eculizumab, ravulizumab, zilucoplan), FcRn blockers (efgartigimod, rozanolixizumab).
Lambert-EatonProximal weakness improves with repeated effort; autonomic symptoms; small-cell lung cancerCT chest; amifampridine; treat the cancer
BotulismDescending paralysis, dilated pupils, honey (infants), home canning, injection drug useAntitoxin (heptavalent; BabyBIG for infants); notify the health department
Malignant spinal cord compressionKnown cancer (lung, breast, prostate, myeloma, renal) + back pain worse lying down ± weakness, sensory level, bladder dysfunctionIV dexamethasone immediately (if neuro deficits), then emergent MRI of the entire spine. Then radiation and/or surgical decompression. Dexamethasone does not need to wait for the MRI.
Cauda equina syndromeSaddle anesthesia, urinary retention (high post-void residual), bilateral sciatica, decreased rectal toneEmergent MRI → surgical decompression within 48 h
Epidural abscessFever, back pain, IV drug use or diabetes; S. aureusMRI with gadolinium, blood cultures, vancomycin + ceftriaxone/cefepime, surgical drainage
ALSCombined UMN + LMN signs, no sensory lossRiluzole, edaravone; tofersen for SOD1. Early noninvasive ventilation (NIV), PEG, advance care planning.
NeuropathyKey points
Diabetic polyneuropathyStocking-glove distribution. Annual monofilament foot exam. Pain: pregabalin, duloxetine, gabapentin, TCAs (topical capsaicin). Avoid opioids.
Mononeuropathy multiplexVasculitis (PAN, ANCA), diabetes, HIV, hepatitis C/cryoglobulinemia. Nerve biopsy.
B12 deficiencySubacute combined degeneration (dorsal columns + corticospinal tracts). Nitrous oxide abuse. Methylmalonic acid ↑.
Carpal tunnelSplint, steroid injection, release; associations: hypothyroidism, pregnancy, amyloid, acromegaly
Bell palsyForehead involved (LMN). Oral steroids within 72 h ± valacyclovir in severe cases. Eye protection.
Peroneal (fibular) nerveFoot drop after leg crossing or fibular head trauma. Eversion is weak, inversion preserved (which separates it from L5 radiculopathy).

sections.heading: Neurology VI — Brain death (death by neurologic criteria)
sections.html:
2023 AAN/AAP/CNS/SCCM consensus. Prerequisites:

  • A known irreversible catastrophic brain injury.
  • Confounders excluded: core temperature ≥36 °C, SBP ≥100 or MAP ≥60, no sedative or paralytic effect, no severe metabolic or endocrine derangement.
  • An adequate observation period (≥24 h after cardiac arrest/anoxic injury).

Exam findings required:

  • Coma, unresponsive to noxious stimuli. Spinal reflexes may persist.
  • Absent brainstem reflexes: pupillary, corneal, oculocephalic, oculovestibular (cold calorics), gag, cough.
  • A positive apnea test: no respiratory effort with PaCO2 ≥60 mmHg and ≥20 above baseline.

Ancillary tests (blood-flow studies such as radionuclide perfusion scintigraphy or 4-vessel cerebral angiography; EEG is no longer an accepted ancillary test in the 2023 guideline) are used only when the exam or apnea test cannot be completed. Brain death is legal death. Family consent is not required to declare it or to stop ventilation, though brief accommodation is reasonable and some states (e.g., New Jersey, New York) have religious accommodation provisions. Notify the organ procurement organization for every imminent death. The OPO, not the treating team, approaches the family about donation.

StateDistinguishing point
Brain deathNo brainstem function, apneic, legally dead
Persistent vegetative stateSleep-wake cycles, eyes open, brainstem intact, no awareness
Minimally conscious stateInconsistent but reproducible awareness
Locked-in syndromeVentral pontine lesion; conscious; vertical eye movements and blinking preserved
===================== ETHICS AND LAW =====================

sections.heading: Ethics & Law I — Capacity, consent, surrogates
sections.html:
Decision-making capacity is a clinical judgment that any treating physician can make. It is decision-specific: a patient may have capacity for a simple decision but not for a complex, high-risk one. Competence is a legal determination made by a judge. A patient has capacity if they can do all four of the following:

  1. Communicate a choice.
  2. Understand the relevant information.
  3. Appreciate how it applies to their own situation.
  4. Reason about options consistently with their values.

A psychiatric diagnosis, dementia, or disagreeing with the doctor does not by itself mean lack of capacity. Psychiatry consultation helps in difficult cases but is not required.

ConceptCK rule
Informed consentDiagnosis, nature of procedure, risks, benefits, alternatives (including no treatment), and the chance to ask questions. Free of coercion. The physician doing the procedure obtains it; it cannot be delegated to a nurse as "consent," only as witnessing a signature.
Exceptions to consentEmergency with implied consent, patient waiver, therapeutic privilege (extremely rare; never because "the family asked"), lack of capacity (use a surrogate)
Refusal by a capacitated adultMust be respected: Jehovah's Witness refusing blood, refusal of dialysis, ventilator or feeding tube, leaving AMA. Withdrawing and withholding care are ethically equivalent.
Advance directivesA living will (written wishes) and a durable power of attorney for health care (DPOA-HC: names an agent). POLST/MOLST are actionable medical orders for the seriously ill. An oral advance directive given to a physician and documented is valid.
Surrogate standard(1) Patient's known expressed wishes → (2) substituted judgment (what the patient would want) → (3) best interests (only if wishes unknown). The surrogate's own preferences are not the standard.
DNRMeans no CPR or intubation only. All other care continues (antibiotics, surgery, ICU). Reconsider it before surgery ("required reconsideration"); do not automatically suspend it.
FutilityThe physician is not obligated to provide physiologically futile treatment. Follow institutional policy: ethics consult, second opinion, offer transfer.
Medical aid in dyingLegal in about 10 states + DC: a capacitated adult, terminal illness (<6 months), self-administered. Euthanasia (the physician administers) is illegal everywhere in the US. Palliative sedation and the double effect principle (opioids for dyspnea or pain) are ethical.
[[figure:ch12-fig06]]

sections.heading: Ethics & Law II — Minors
sections.html:
• Parents consent for minors, except in an emergency, where you treat immediately.
  • Parents refusing life-saving treatment (e.g., transfusion for a Jehovah's Witness child):
    • Emergency: treat the child, no court order needed.
    • Non-emergency: get a court order, often through child protective services.
  • Minors may consent on their own (most states) for:
    • contraception and STI testing and treatment, including HIV in most states
    • prenatal care
    • substance use treatment
    • outpatient mental health (varies by state)
  • Abortion: parental notification or consent laws vary by state and include a judicial bypass. Since 2022, abortion legality itself varies by state.
  • Emancipated minors (married, military, financially independent, court-declared) consent as adults. Being a parent lets a minor consent for their child's care. In most states it does not emancipate the minor for their own care, except pregnancy-related care.
  • Confidentiality: adolescents should be interviewed alone for part of the visit (HEADSSS). Confidentiality is broken only for serious risk of harm: suicidality, homicidality, or abuse.

sections.heading: Ethics & Law III — Confidentiality & mandatory reporting
sections.html:
SituationAction
Patient makes a credible threat against an identifiable person (Tarasoff)Duty to protect: warn the intended victim and/or notify police, and consider hospitalization. Rules vary by state, but warning plus police is the exam answer.
Reportable infections (e.g., TB, syphilis, gonorrhea, chlamydia, HIV, measles)Report to the health department. Partner notification is done by the health department; the physician encourages the patient to disclose. HIV: may notify an at-risk partner if the patient refuses (state law).
Child abuseMandatory report on reasonable suspicion to CPS. Proof is not needed. Admit the child if unsafe.
Elder or dependent-adult abuseMandatory report to Adult Protective Services in most states. Signs: neglect, injuries, financial exploitation.
Intimate partner violence (adult)Not generally mandatory to report (except certain injuries such as gunshot or knife wounds, in some states). Interview the patient alone, document, assess immediate safety (strangulation, weapons, escalation), give a safety plan and resources (National DV Hotline), and respect the patient's choice to stay. USPSTF: screen women of reproductive age.
Gunshot and stab woundsReportable in most states
Impaired driving (seizures, dementia)Counsel the patient. Report where the state requires or permits.
Family asks for informationNeed the patient's permission. Exceptions: the patient is incapacitated and family is involved in care, or an emergency.
Social media or a hallway conversation about a patientA HIPAA violation; avoid it

sections.heading: Ethics & Law IV — Communication & professionalism
sections.html:
ScenarioBest answer pattern
Limited English proficiencyUse a professional medical interpreter (in person, phone or video). Never use children, and avoid family or untrained staff, even if the patient prefers them. Speak to the patient, not the interpreter.
Medical errorDisclose promptly and honestly, even with no harm. Express regret or apologize, explain what happened and how it will be prevented, and report through the safety system. Communication-and-resolution programs reduce litigation. Many states have "apology laws."
Breaking bad newsSPIKES: Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge (warning shot, no jargon), Emotions (empathize, allow silence), Strategy/Summary
Family asks you not to tell the patient a diagnosisExplore the family's concerns, then ask the patient how much they want to know. The patient has the right to know; respect a patient's own choice not to know.
Impaired or incompetent colleagueIf patients are in immediate danger (intoxicated surgeon about to operate), stop them now and notify the supervisor, chief or chair. Otherwise, speak to the colleague and report to the appropriate supervisor or the physician health program. Report to the state board when patient safety is threatened or other channels fail. Ignoring it is never acceptable.
GiftsFrom patients: small, sentimental gifts are OK. Decline cash, large gifts, or anything given with expectations. From industry: nothing of substantial value. Modest educational items and meals at legitimate educational events are acceptable per AMA guidance. Disclose conflicts of interest.
Romantic relationship with a patientNever with a current patient: end the professional relationship first. For psychiatrists, never with a current or former patient.
Treating self, family, friendsAvoid, except in emergencies or for minor problems
Angry patientAcknowledge emotions, listen, apologize for the experience, address the concern
Patient requests an inappropriate test or drug (antibiotics, opioids, MRI)Explore the reason and concern, educate, offer alternatives. You are not obligated to provide non-indicated care.
Student or residentIntroduce yourself honestly as a student. Never practice procedures on patients without consent, including under anesthesia (pelvic exams need explicit consent).
Conscientious objectionThe physician may decline personally but must refer in a timely way and must provide emergency care
Patient non-adherenceAsk non-judgmentally about barriers (cost, side effects, beliefs, health literacy). Use teach-back.
High-yield answer-choice heuristics: Choose "talk to the patient first," "ask an open-ended question," "explore the reason," and "involve the patient." Avoid answers that refer away immediately, lie, coerce, threaten, or let family override a capacitated adult. Choose ethics consult or court only after direct communication fails, or for genuine non-emergency conflicts.
===================== BIOSTATISTICS =====================

sections.heading: Biostatistics & Evidence-Based Medicine
sections.html:
[[figure:ch12-fig07]]
ConceptCK interpretation
p-valueProbability of a result at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true. It is not the probability that the drug works. p < α (0.05) → reject the null.
95% confidence intervalFor a ratio (RR, OR, HR), a CI that includes 1 means not significant. For a difference (means, ARR), a CI that includes 0 means not significant. A narrow CI means a precise estimate (larger sample size).
Type I error (α)False positive: concluding there is an effect when there is none. Multiple comparisons inflate it (Bonferroni correction).
Type II error (β); power = 1 − βFalse negative. Power rises with sample size, effect size, and a higher α. "No difference" in a small trial may just mean it was underpowered.
Intention-to-treatAnalyze participants as randomized. Preserves randomization and is preferred for superiority trials. Per-protocol analysis exaggerates benefit; it is conservative mainly in non-inferiority trials.
Non-inferiority trialNew drug is "not worse than" the comparator by a prespecified margin. Non-inferior if the CI's upper bound for harm stays within the margin. It cannot claim superiority unless that was tested.
Surrogate vs clinical endpointsLDL or HbA1c reduction does not equal fewer MIs or deaths. Prefer patient-oriented outcomes.
Composite endpointsCheck which component drove the result. It is often the softest one (e.g., hospitalization rather than death).
Hazard ratioInstantaneous relative risk over time in survival analysis (Kaplan-Meier, Cox)
Correlation r−1 to +1; r² = proportion of variance explained. Correlation ≠ causation.
Testst-test: 2 means. ANOVA: ≥3 means. Chi-square: categorical proportions. Fisher exact: small counts. Pearson: correlation of continuous variables.
BiasDescriptionFix
Selection (incl. Berkson, healthy worker)Non-random sampling; hospital controls; workers healthier than the general populationRandomization, population-based sampling
RecallCases remember exposures better (case-control)Use records
ConfoundingA third variable linked to both exposure and outcomeRandomization, matching, stratification, multivariable adjustment
Lead-timeEarlier detection appears to lengthen survival, but the death date is unchangedCompare mortality rates, not survival time from diagnosis
Length-timeScreening preferentially finds slow-growing, indolent diseaseRCT with mortality as the outcome
OverdiagnosisFinding disease that would never cause harm (e.g., some prostate or thyroid cancers)—
Observer / measurementKnowing the assignment affects assessmentBlinding
Attrition / loss to follow-upDifferential dropoutITT, sensitivity analyses
HawthorneSubjects change behavior because they are being studied—
Publication biasPositive trials are published more often (funnel plot asymmetry)Trial registration

Reading a drug advertisement or abstract on CK. Work through these questions:

  1. Who was studied? Check inclusion and exclusion criteria. If your patient would have been excluded (age, CKD, pregnancy), the results may not apply. This is a matter of external validity/generalizability.
  2. What was the comparator? Placebo, or the standard of care at an equivalent dose?
  3. What endpoint? Hard outcome, surrogate or composite? Primary or secondary? A secondary or subgroup result is only hypothesis-generating.
  4. Relative or absolute? Headlines quote RRR. Compute ARR and NNT yourself. An RRR of 50% can mean 2% → 1% (NNT 100).
  5. Is it statistically significant (CI excludes 1 or 0)? Is it clinically meaningful?
  6. Harms: compute NNH. Note adverse events and discontinuation rates.
  7. Who funded it, and was the analysis ITT? Was it blinded?
Study designMeasureStrength / weakness
RCTRR, ARR, NNT, HRBest for causality; costly, limited generalizability
Prospective cohortRR, incidenceTemporal sequence; poor for rare diseases
Case-controlORGood for rare diseases; recall bias. OR ≈ RR when disease is rare.
Cross-sectionalPrevalenceSnapshot; no causality
EcologicalPopulation-levelEcological fallacy
Meta-analysisPooled estimate (forest plot)Only as good as its studies; heterogeneity (I²)

Prevention levels:

  • Primary: prevent disease (vaccines).
  • Secondary: detect early (screening).
  • Tertiary: reduce disability from established disease (rehabilitation).
  • Quaternary: avoid overmedicalization.
===================== PATIENT SAFETY =====================

sections.heading: Patient Safety & Quality Improvement
sections.html:
TermMeaning
Adverse eventHarm caused by medical care (preventable or not)
Near missAn error caught before reaching the patient. Still report it, because it is a free lesson.
Sentinel eventUnexpected death or serious harm (Joint Commission) → root cause analysis required
Never eventsWrong-site, wrong-patient or wrong-procedure surgery; retained foreign object; transfusion of incompatible blood; stage 3–4 pressure injury acquired in hospital
Active vs latent errorsActive: at the "sharp end" (the person giving the drug). Latent: hidden system flaws (look-alike vials, understaffing).
Root cause analysis (RCA)Retrospective, blame-free, interdisciplinary analysis of what happened, why, and how to prevent recurrence. Tools: fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram, "5 whys," flowcharts. Focuses on systems, not individuals.
FMEA (failure mode and effects analysis)Prospective: identify how a new process could fail before it is implemented
Swiss cheese model (Reason)Each defense layer has holes. Harm occurs when the holes align. Fix: add layers and shrink the holes.
Just cultureHuman error → console. At-risk behavior → coach. Reckless behavior → discipline.
Hierarchy of interventions (strongest first)Forcing functions and physical constraints (e.g., incompatible connectors, hard stops in EHR, removing concentrated KCl from wards) → automation and standardization (order sets, barcoding, checklists) → education, policies, warnings (weakest)
Universal ProtocolPre-procedure verification, site marking by the operating surgeon, and a time-out before incision
HandoffsI-PASS (Illness severity, Patient summary, Action list, Situation awareness/contingency, Synthesis by receiver) reduced preventable adverse events. SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) for escalation. Use read-back and closed-loop communication.
Medication safetyMedication reconciliation at every transition; avoid abbreviations ("U", trailing zeros "1.0 mg", "QD"); tall-man lettering; barcode administration; pharmacist review
MeasuresStructure (resources), process (was the step done: % of patients given aspirin), outcome (mortality, infection rate), balancing (unintended consequences elsewhere)
Data toolsRun chart (data over time), control chart (common-cause vs special-cause variation), Pareto chart (80/20: the few causes that account for most problems)
BurnoutEmotional exhaustion, depersonalization, low accomplishment. It is a systems problem. Encourage use of physician wellness resources.
[[figure:ch12-fig08]]
Exam trap: After an error, "fire or retrain the nurse" is almost never the best answer. The best answers are a system-level fix (forcing function, standardization, checklist), disclosure to the patient, and a report through the institution's safety reporting system.

title: Mock Exam B · Step 2 CK (2 blocks × 40 questions, 60 minutes per block)
meta: Exam: Step 2 CK · Mixed: internal medicine, surgery, pediatrics, OB/GYN, psychiatry, ethics/patient safety, biostatistics · Time: 2 × 60 min + 45 min review

sections.heading: Instructions
sections.html:
How to take this mock

  • Do each block in one timed sitting of 60 minutes (about 90 seconds per question). Use a timer and do not pause it.
  • No notes, no textbooks, no searching. Do not open any "Show answer" box until the whole block is finished.
  • Write your answers (1–40, then 41–80) on paper, then mark them against the answer key at the end.
  • Read the last line of each stem first ("next best step", "most likely diagnosis", "most appropriate pharmacotherapy"), then read the vignette looking for the details that decide it.
  • The questions use US guidelines (USPSTF, ACC/AHA, ADA, ACOG, AAP, CDC, IDSA, ASCCP, GINA/NAEPP). Where Indian teaching differs, the explanation says so.
  • How to read your score: ≥75% correct (≥60/80) = strong; 65–74% (52–59/80) = on track; <65% (<52/80) = needs more questions. Go back to the weak topics and do more timed blocks.
  • After scoring, read every explanation, including for the questions you got right. For each one you missed, write down in one line why the right answer beats the option you chose.
